Sukhoi T-4: The Soviet Mach 3 bomber that never reached its potential

The Soviet Union was developing its own high-speed contender in the Sukhoi T-4, nicknamed the Sotka. Conceived as a strategic strike and reconnaissance aircraft, it was built around the ambition of reaching Mach 3 and taking on high-value targets, including naval task forces.

Extensive use of titanium and stainless steel helped withstand the extreme temperatures associated with sustained supersonic flight. It also incorporated fly-by-wire flight controls, an impressive feature for the early 1970s.

Photo: Flyajetfighterdotcom

The prototype first flew on 22 August 1972, with Vladimir Ilyushin, a prominent Soviet test pilot and son of aircraft designer Sergei Ilyushin, at the controls. However, it completed just ten test flights, reaching approximately Mach 1.3 rather than its intended Mach 3.

Technical complexity, development costs and changing military priorities contributed to its cancellation. The Soviet Union instead favoured Tupolev’s Tu-22M Backfire, a more practical alternative for its strategic strike requirements.

Northrop YF-23: The stealth fighter that lost to the F-22 Raptor

Developed for the US Air Force’s Advanced Tactical Fighter competition, Northrop’s YF-23 offered a distinctive approach to next-generation air superiority. Its rival was Lockheed’s YF-22.

The YF-23 featured diamond-shaped wings and a carefully sculpted airframe to reduce radar visibility. It also demonstrated supercruise, maintaining supersonic speeds without afterburners.

Photo: National Museum of the United States Air Force

Two prototypes were built: PAV-1, Black Widow II, and PAV-2, Gray Ghost. During testing, the first prototype reached Mach 1.5 in supercruise.

In 1991, the US Air Force chose the YF-22, which became the F-22 Raptor . Northrop’s aircraft never entered production, although its distinctive approach to stealth, range and aerodynamic efficiency still attracts considerable interest.

The lasting legacy of cancelled military aircraft

The Arrow, TSR-2, T-4 and YF-23 came from very different countries and generations, but each challenged contemporary aerospace engineering.

Their stories show that technical excellence alone is not enough to secure a place in military service. After all, political considerations, budgetary constraints and evolving defence requirements can be just as decisive as performance.

Each programme certainly offers a fascinating glimpse into the alternative paths military aviation history might have taken.

Заголовок: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
Полный текст:
Radiation and collisions reshape the planetary building materials.

Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice.

The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars.

The missing ice

Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets.

Заголовок: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
Полный текст:
Healthy soils, native plants, and fewer chemicals are helping vineyards adapt.

More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.

Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.

As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.

Заголовок: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
Полный текст:
The red planet Mars will shine a little over 1 degree from Jupiter on the night of Nov. 15-16.

Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029.

Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky .

It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth .

The spectacular display occurs just once every 2-2.5 years , when Mars catches up to Jupiter as it plies its more distant orbit, making the pair appear side by side from our Earthly vantage point — an event known to astronomers as an appulse.

Jupiter, Mars and Regulus will appear close together on the night of Nov. 15-16. (Image credit: Created by Anthony Wood in Canva.)

Both Mars and Jupiter are "superior planets" whose orbits exist beyond that of Earth. As a result their disks always appear full to us through the eyepiece of a telescope, unlike the inner planets Mercury and Venus , which exhibit moon-like phases as they circle the sun .

A 6-inch telescope can reveal the wildly differing natures of the solar system worlds. Slew your scope to Jupiter to spot the gargantuan cloud bands (and zones) that ring the gas giant , formed from masses of ammonia and water that travel in different directions through Jupiter's hydrogen and helium atmosphere, driven by powerful jet streams.

How to measure distances in the night sky using your outstretched hand. (Image credit: Created in Canva Pro)

Mars, meanwhile, appears as a reddish, ochre disk complete with dark surface features, where basaltic rock has been scoured clean of the iron-rich dust that covers much of its surface, according to NASA .

Заголовок: The next challenge for hydrogen aviation: Refuelling before the next flight
Полный текст:
Hydrogen-powered flight is advancing from proving concept feasibility to tackling airport ground operations. European initiatives H2FLY and HyPRIME are currently testing liquid hydrogen refuelling infrastructure and boil-off management to align with standard commercial airline turnarounds.

Hydrogen-powered aviation is moving beyond proving that aircraft can fly on the fuel, with developers now concentrating on how to refuel them quickly, safely and repeatedly at commercial airports.

Two European programmes are working on different parts of that challenge. Germany’s H2FLY is developing hydrogen-electric propulsion and mobile refuelling systems, while the UK’s HyPRIME project is preparing to test equipment capable of delivering liquid hydrogen at rates relevant to commercial aircraft operations.

In exclusive interviews with Aerospace Global News , representatives of both programmes described the progress made in handling liquid hydrogen, the problems that remain and the changes airports will need before hydrogen-powered aircraft can operate regular services.

For H2FLY, which completed what it describes as the world’s first piloted flight of an electric aircraft powered by liquid hydrogen in 2023, the experience has also changed where the company is concentrating its engineering efforts.

Photo: ZeroAvia

Ralph Muller, H2FLY’s chief executive, said the equipment and procedures needed to handle the fuel on the ground are no longer the fundamental obstacle.

“Through our flight test programme, we have built up the capabilities to handle and refuel liquid hydrogen safely. Taking this to routine airport operations is mainly a matter of time and resources,” Muller told AGN.

“The harder engineering challenge lies in the aircraft-based systems: they have to be lightweight, reliable and cost-efficient enough for commercial operation.”

Refuelling within an airline turnaround

For hydrogen-powered aircraft to operate scheduled services, refuelling must fit into the time an aircraft normally spends on the ground between flights.

Muller said that, depending on the aircraft and its mission, the refuelling process would need to take between 15 and 60 minutes.

“For airline-style operations, refuelling has to fit within a normal commercial turnaround without extending it,” he said. “The required refuelling rate therefore depends on the aircraft size and tank capacity.”

Photo: H2FLY

Unlike conventional aviation fuel, liquid hydrogen must be kept at approximately minus 253°C. Its extremely low temperature means that tanks, transfer equipment and refuelling connections require specialised designs.

One way to increase refuelling rates is to cool the aircraft’s hydrogen tank before transferring the fuel.

Muller said this could become part of the normal ground-handling process.

“Pre-cooling the aircraft’s liquid hydrogen tank to cryogenic temperatures before refuelling allows higher flow rates, and this step can be integrated into the turnaround procedure,” he explained.

He also identified common standards for connections and handling procedures as important to making refuelling simpler.

H2FLY plans to demonstrate the third generation of its mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling unit through the European Union-funded GOLIAT project, working with partners from across the aviation industry.

The programme forms part of the company’s efforts to develop equipment that can eventually support routine aircraft operations rather than individual flight demonstrations.

HyPRIME prepares to test airport equipment

In the UK, HyPRIME is approaching the challenge from the airport side.

The project is designed to demonstrate that liquid hydrogen can be transported to airports, handled safely and dispensed at flow rates relevant to commercial aviation.

Photo: ZeroAvia

Chris Tye, senior technical project coordinator for HyPRIME, said the aviation industry has already spent considerable time examining the requirements for hydrogen infrastructure.

“The industry is under no illusions about the challenges associated with introducing hydrogen at airports, and the collective knowledge about how to do it has been growing steadily through activities across the world including feasibility studies, techno-economic studies and regulatory work,” he told AGN.

The next task is to test the equipment under conditions that resemble actual airport operations.

“What HyPRIME, and other projects within the DFT zero emission competition, brings is the opportunity to advance the industry into physical testing of commercially relevant assets, in commercially relevant environments,” Tye said.

The programme is developing a mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling system using high-flow-rate cryogenic equipment.

It aims to demonstrate refuelling within operationally relevant turnaround times, although the final performance targets are still being developed alongside airport operating procedures.

Tye said HyPRIME is addressing two central requirements: whether hydrogen refuelling can work in an airport environment and whether the equipment can eventually be operated economically.

Photo: ZeroAvia

“The project will demonstrate that liquid hydrogen can be safely transported to airports and dispensed at commercially relevant flow rates for aviation, while also showing how, through systems integration, this can support decarbonisation of the wider airport ecosystem through use of boil-off gas in ground equipment, simultaneously reducing waste and improving economics.”

The project is working with Bristol and Birmingham airports on operational concepts that will help define the refuelling performance it needs to demonstrate.

What happens to hydrogen that evaporates?

One of the difficulties of handling liquid hydrogen is that some of the fuel can evaporate as heat enters the storage or transfer system.

This is known as boil-off. Unless managed, the resulting gas can represent lost fuel and must be handled safely.

Photo: ZeroAvia

Tye identified boil-off management and refuelling speed as two of the most important technical issues still facing airport hydrogen systems.

“Boil-off gas is unavoidable in LH2 systems; left unmanaged it is a safety hazard, an economic loss of fuel, and an indirect emissions source,” he warned.

HyPRIME intends to capture the gas and put it to use elsewhere at the airport.

Its mobile liquid hydrogen refuelling system is designed to recover boil-off for use in ULEMCo’s hydrogen tow truck and GeoPura’s hydrogen power units.

The approach is intended to reduce venting and improve the overall efficiency of the hydrogen supply system.

HyPRIME will also examine the safety requirements associated with liquid hydrogen storage and refuelling. Its work includes dedicated cryogenic tank design and staged hazard identification, hazard and operability studies, and quantitative risk assessment.

Tye said the project would draw on ZeroAvia’s existing liquid hydrogen operational experience and its participation in UK Civil Aviation Authority sandbox trials at Exeter.

Photo: ZeroAvia

H2FLY, meanwhile, believes careful planning can substantially reduce the amount of hydrogen lost during routine airport operations.

“Boil-off is predictable and can be managed. In scheduled operations, today’s ground operations make it possible to largely avoid it,” Muller said.

He explained that airlines already have detailed information about their schedules and expected fuel consumption. That information could help airports decide when hydrogen needs to be produced, liquefied and made available for refuelling.

“Hydrogen can be produced locally, and gaseous hydrogen can be liquefied on site in line with flight schedules. Supply follows demand rather than sitting in storage,” he added.

Such arrangements would require hydrogen production and supply to be coordinated with aircraft operations, particularly at airports where demand may initially be limited.

How airports would have to change

Neither H2FLY nor HyPRIME expects every airport to require large permanent hydrogen facilities from the outset.

Muller said the infrastructure could develop alongside the aircraft entering service.

“In the early phase, flexible, mobile solutions allow airports and operators to start operations without large fixed installations,” he said.

“As fleets grow, these will be replaced step by step by permanent infrastructure, with dedicated liquid hydrogen storage and a reliable supply.”

Hydrogen could be produced at airports using electrolysers and then liquefied, or delivered from external suppliers by truck or pipeline.

Airports would also need new ground-handling procedures, personnel training and safety zones adapted to hydrogen.

Photo: H2FLY

For HyPRIME, the choice of infrastructure would depend heavily on the location.

Tye said hydrogen could arrive by tanker, be delivered as a gas and liquefied at the airport, or be produced and liquefied on site.

“The optimum approach will depend on the airport’s requirements, real estate and region’s availability of power and options for hydrogen production,” he said.

At larger scales, he expects dedicated storage and liquefaction facilities, together with mobile refuellers or cryogenic pipelines, to become necessary.

HyPRIME is also examining what these different arrangements would cost. One of its planned outputs is a techno-economic model covering capital expenditure and operating costs for a representative mid-sized airport.

The project intends to use actual testing data to identify which parts of the infrastructure have the greatest effect on commercial viability.

“Airports and investors will need confidence not only that the technology works, but also that the associated CAPEX and OPEX are commercially viable,” Tye said.

Smaller hydrogen aircraft expected first

H2FLY’s experience has also influenced its expectations for the types of aircraft likely to adopt hydrogen propulsion first.

Muller said the industry initially concentrated heavily on the possibility of developing large hydrogen-powered aircraft. He does not regard that early ambition as misplaced, but believes the transition will take longer and proceed in smaller steps.

“What proved too optimistic was the idea that aviation could make that leap in one step,” he said. “The lessons learned since then have led to a strategic shift: we see hydrogen aviation developing step by step, starting with smaller aircraft, where the technology, certification and infrastructure are less complex, and scaling up from there.”

Photo: H2FLY

H2FLY expects smaller hydrogen-electric aircraft to begin entering service in the early 2030s, with larger aircraft following around 2045.

These are the company’s expectations rather than confirmed commercial service dates. The company is continuing to develop the propulsion systems that would support that progression. Its HY4 aircraft has completed several flight demonstrations, including the liquid hydrogen-powered flights in 2023.

Since then, Muller said H2FLY has tripled the power density of its systems. “Our HY4 aircraft, demonstrated in flight several times, showed early on what is possible, and since then we have tripled the power density of our systems,” he said.

The company develops most of its key components in-house, allowing it to work on the weight and performance of the complete propulsion system rather than treating individual components separately.

Muller said improvements in electrification and digital technologies, including developments in drones and air taxis, have also benefited hydrogen-electric propulsion.

Nevertheless, reducing weight, improving reliability and bringing down costs remain central to its work.

What comes after the airport trials?

HyPRIME’s immediate objective is to produce evidence from operating the refuelling equipment, rather than simply demonstrating that the individual technologies work.

The project has identified four areas against which it intends to measure progress: refuelling performance, hydrogen losses, operational efficiency and costs.

Photo: H2FLY

It plans to examine repeatable refuelling cycles, including filling, transporting and dispensing liquid hydrogen, as well as recovering boil-off gas under different environmental conditions. The results will feed into its economic modelling.

Further demonstrations at different airports, continued work with airlines and airport operators, and the development of regulatory and certification frameworks would follow a successful trial.

Tye said HyPRIME is intended to provide information that can guide future infrastructure investment in the UK and elsewhere.

For H2FLY, the next steps include demonstrating its latest mobile refuelling equipment through GOLIAT while continuing to improve the aircraft systems needed for commercial hydrogen-electric flight.

Both programmes are working towards the same practical requirement: aircraft must be able to arrive, refuel and depart without hydrogen handling becoming an obstacle to scheduled operations.

The technology has already flown. The next challenge is making it part of an ordinary day at an airport.

November 13: Spot Mirach’s Ghost
Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.
This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.
Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.
Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.
Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.
Sunset: 4:44 P.M.
Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.
Moonset: 8:56 P.M.
Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)
*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. 
Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.
In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

SpaceX не смогла осуществить захват ускорителя Super Heavy по его возвращении на специальную платформу Mechazilla.

Менее чем через 10 минут после старта нижняя ступень приводнилась в Мексиканском заливе. Причины отказа от первоначального сценария пока неизвестны.

Заголовок: Next Vega C Launch Edges Closer to Christmas Day as Satellites Arrive Late
Полный текст:
Credit: ESA / S. Corvaja / Andrew Parsonson (edit)

Italian rocket manufacturer Avio has revealed that delays in the delivery of customer satellites have pushed the third Vega C launch of 2026 back toward Christmas, several weeks later than previously planned.

Speaking during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on 11 November, Avio CEO Giulio Ranzo explained that the mission, which will carry six satellites, had been delayed as the company awaited the arrival of the final spacecraft.

“The satellites from the customers are a little bit late, so we are waiting for the last few of them to arrive,” said Ranzo. “It’s an interesting mission, six different satellites. They’re coming in a little bit late, so we are coming very close to Christmas Day.”

During the company’s half-year earnings call on 10 September, Ranzo said that the mission was scheduled for “the very beginning of December”. Based on his latest comments, the launch appears to have slipped by approximately two to three weeks.

The flight is expected to carry six satellites for Italy’s IRIDE Earth observation constellation. According to photographs published by the French space agency CNES, a shipment of the Thales Alenia Space-built satellites arrived in French Guiana by air on 9 November 2026. The spacecraft were then transported from Félix Éboué Airport to the Guiana Space Centre, arriving at the facility’s S3B payload preparation building the following day.

The latest setback is not the first time this year that Avio has blamed changes to its Vega C launch schedule on delays in the delivery of customer payloads.

During the same 10 September earnings call, Ranzo explained that the company could have conducted more than three Vega C launches in 2026, adding that “one satellite was somewhat late.”

So far in 2026, Avio has completed two Vega C launches. The most recent, conducted on 15 September , successfully deployed the European Space Agency’s FLEX satellite and the European Commission’s Sentinel-3C Earth observation satellite into orbit.

The company is working to increase Vega C’s annual launch cadence, with Ranzo indicating during the November earnings call that Avio was aiming to progress to four and eventually five launches per year, provided customers could meet their spacecraft delivery schedules.

During a May earnings call, Ranzo suggested that Avio could conduct as many as five Vega C launches in 2027, just one short of its medium-term target of six flights per year. However, speaking during the company’s November earnings call, Ranzo appeared to temper those expectations, outlining a more gradual increase to four and then five launches annually, suggesting that the company could now be targeting four flights in 2027. He qualified that outlook with a caveat, adding, “if the customers maintain their deadlines”.

Заголовок: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
Полный текст:
Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short.

Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.

SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short.
Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.
The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.
As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers.
SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.
“That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”.
Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms.
Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”.
Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage.
Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster.
The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km.
The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights.
Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency.
As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return.
SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars.
Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028.
Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel.
SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws.
In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time, although its engine failed during the ascent.

Заголовок: When Einstein's Gravitational Waves Meet Newton's Tides
Полный текст:
A researcher at Freie Universität Berlin has developed a theoretical framework for searching high-precision measurements for possible relativistic traces in lunar tides.

In 1687, Sir Isaac Newton released his magnum opus, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy), in which he described his theories of motion and gravity. His theory of the latter accurately described the motion of the Earth's tides, something that scientists had been wrestling with for centuries. For over three hundred years, Newton's work remained scientific canon and the last word on gravity, until Albert Einstein introduced his Theory of General Relativity.
According to a recent study from the Freie Universität Berlin (FUB), some hints of General Relativity (GR) may be buried within Newton's tidal theories. While the pull of the Sun and Moon and their influence on the tides can be predicted very accurately using Newtonian gravity, GR offers a fuller description that includes gravitational waves (GWs). The new study merges these two theories into a single model that could offer a new way to test our understanding of gravity.
The study was authored by Muhittin Cenk Eser, a mathematician in the Department of Mathematics and Computer Science at FUB. His work extends the classical model of lunar tides to include the cross polarization of gravitational waves, one of the key ways GWs can deform spacetime as they pass through. As he explained in a FUB press release:
Isaac Newton explains the tides extremely well. Albert Einstein shows us that gravity is also dynamic and that changes in spacetime can propagate as waves. Our work brings both perspectives together and asks what traces of this might be found in high-precision measurements.
GWs were originally predicted by Einstein's Theory of General Relativity and refer to ripples in spacetime caused by the merger of massive objects. To date, thousands of GW events have been detected, the majority of which were caused by the merger of black holes or neutron stars. However, GWs can also result from smaller gravitational interactions, such as those produced by the interactions of the Earth, Moon, and Sun.
One issue addressed by Eser's study is the difficulty of distinguishing possible additional signals from measurement errors, the choice of reference frame, and uncertainties in calculating the positions of the Sun and Moon. By identifying which influences must be accounted for, Eser shows how a signal could be isolated and the possible physical effects identified. The study therefore presents a quantitative basis for future studies of tidal patterns that deviate from what Newtonian Gravity predicts. Said Eser:
We are not claiming to have discovered a new gravitational effect. What we show is how one could look for it in a targeted way. The EarthâMoon system is particularly interesting for this because we can already describe and measure its tidal effects very precisely.
Further Reading: Freie Universität Berlin

Заголовок: Astrophysicists Cross Another Dark Matter Candidate Off Their List: Stupendously Large Black Holes
Полный текст:
Astrophysicists are leaving no stone unturned in their search for what dark matter is. Different particles have been proposed, like WIMPs and axions. Hypothetical rimordial black holes have also been proposed. But there's another less well-known candidate, SLABs or Stupendously Large Black holes, a sub-type of primordial black holes. Alas, SLABs can't account for dark matter either, according to new research.

If cosmologists ever identify what dark matter actually is, it may be because of a process of elimination.
There are many potential candidates for dark matter, including WIMPs and axions, which are both hypothetical particles. But one of the most intriguing candidates are primordial black holes (PBHs) that formed in the early Universe. They're hypothetical too, but are massive objects, so their presence should be detectable in a way that particles aren't.
All dark matter candidates have their supporters and their dectractors, and PBHs are no different. But PBHs have fairly well-defined search strategies that should detect them if they exist. If they exist, then cosmologists should find evidence of them in the cosmic microwave background (CMB).
The CMB is relic radiation from the Big Bang itself, the oldest detectable light that exists. It was released when the Universe was only about 380,000 years old. For the most part, the CMB appears smooth and uniform, or isotropic. But increasingly powerful detectors let cosmologists examine the CMB for minor fluctuations. Those could show the presence of PBHs, or at least a subset of them called stupendously large black holes, or SLABs. SLABs, if they exist, are truly stupendously massive, with masses up to 10 billion billion solar masses. Yes, that's two billions one after another.
This is a temperature map of the CMB created with data from the ESA's Planck spacecraft. The CMB can only be measured from space, and Planck's job was to measure anisotropies in the CMB. The different colours show temperature differences, and those differences correspond to where the first galaxies formed. Image Credit: NOIRLab, CC BY 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=130789180
New research published in Physical Review Letters says that SLABs can't be dark matter. It's titled "Closing the Mass Window for Stupendously Large Black Holes," and the lead author is Christopher Gerlach. Gerlach is a theoretical physicist at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, and its PRISMA++ Cluster of Excellence.
âA possible solution to the puzzle of dark matter was that it might have collected shortly after the Big Bang in giant black holes with masses ranging from 100 million to 10 billion billion times that of the sun," said lead author Gerlatz.
This work is largely based on the ESA's Planck satellite. The Planck satellite ended its mission in 2013, but researchers are still generating new insights from its data. Part of that is because of more raw computing power. But it's also because they can cross-correlate it with new data from sources that didn't exist back in 2013. Physicists also have better ways to filter out interference, like that from the Milky Way.
âThat we are still generating new insights into the universeâs evolution and structure 13 years after it was shut down only emphasizes how important the Planck satellite was and is to physicists," explained Gerlach.
âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â - Nicholas Leister, Johannes Gutenberg University.
SLABs, if they're real, formed from overdensities of matter after the Big Bang. They didn't need to form massive stars, burn their fuel, and explode as supernovae. They skipped that step, and are too massive for that, anyway. Since they're theorized to have formed so early, before massive objects like galaxy clusters, they should be the only things that left such an imprint on the CMB.
âIf these SLABs had existed in large numbers and contained significant amounts of dark matter, they would have left a characteristic imprint on the CMB through their unique perturbations, or, in a word, making it grainy," said study co-author Nicholas Leister, also a JGU physicist.
This image is an artist's interpretation of what primordial black holes could look like. SLABs, Stupendously Large Black holes, a hypothetical sub-type of primordial black holes, would be far more massive than these. Image Credit: NASA
Previous work has all but eliminated the possibility that regular primordial black holes could account for all dark matter. But what about SLABs? Have they survived the process of dark matter elimination, unlike their less massive cousins?
To find out, the researchers first modelled SLABs and how they would affect the CMB. Then they compared the modelled effects to the actual CMB. The result was clear: the CMB doesn't have the characteristic graininess that SLABs should have imprinted on it.
"In this work, we have shown that the production of stupendously large PBHs would generate large DM isocurvature perturbations, tightly constrained by CMB and BAO data," the authors explain.
"We show that primordial black holes (PBHs) in the Stupendously Large Black Hole mass range (Mâ³1011Mâ) produce isocurvature perturbations exceeding current Planck Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) limits, thereby excluding them as a significant dark matter component," the authors conclude.
This artist's impression depicts a rapidly spinning supermassive black hole surrounded by an accretion disc. SMBH are massive and they're real. But they're still dwarfed by the hypothetical SLABs. Credit: ESO, ESA/Hubble, M. Kornmesser
The results also counter some other thinking regarding PBHs and dark matter. When the JWST discovered its notorious early massive galaxies, galaxies so massive that they challenged models of galaxy formation, it set the astrophysical community in motion searching for explanations. Astrophysicists cast their net wide, and one explanation they caught concerned PBHs. One 2022 study, titled "Accelerating Early Massive Galaxy Formation with Primordial Black Holes," suggested that PBHs make up a fraction of dark matter and were behind the JWST's early, massive galaxies.
But that's unlikely to be true, according to these results.
"They also challenge scenarios attributing the early massive galaxy candidates observed by James Webb Space Telescope to PBH-induced fluctuations," the researchers write.
SLABs were also potential explanations for another unexplained phenomenon. A gravitational wave background hum pervades the Universe, sensed by Pulsar Timing Arrays, and some researchers asked if SLABs could be responsible. "These questions are also unlikely to be answered by SLABs, since our findings show that they didnât exist in large numbers," said Nicholas Leister. âThe early universe still has many puzzles waiting to be solved.â
So the search for dark matter candidates continues. It's possible that no one type of object or particle makes up dark matter. Dark matter may be a collective effect generated by different particles, objects, or phenomena.
But it looks like SLABs are no longer in contention.

Заголовок: SpaceX Launches Starship But Passes Up Booster Catch for Safety's Sake
Полный текст:
SpaceX sent its Starship on a flight that was meant to feature a first-ever retrieval of both rocket stages, but a launch-pad catch of the first-stage booster had to be canceled due to safety concerns.
Instead, the Super Heavy booster was diverted during its descent to make an offshore splashdown. Observers at SpaceX's Starbase on the South Texas coast could hear the sonic boom and see the fiery plunge that took place minutes after launch at 4:47 p.m. CT (2247 GMT) today. "Wow, you could feel the rumble of that splashdown there," launch commentator Jessie Anderson said.
This 15th flight test still has a chance to make history: The mission plan calls for the Starship second stage to spend as much as 22 hours in orbit â ending with a return to the pad for a midair capture by the launch tower's giant mechanical arms. SpaceX has caught Starship's booster during three previous test flights, but this would be a first for a second stage.
Hours after launch, SpaceX launch commentator Kate Tice said the booster's control system triggered an abort of the launch-tower catch because the boostback engine burn ended early, apparently due to a low fuel mass alarm. SpaceX's team was still troubleshooting the root cause of the alarm, she said.
Anderson said the offshore splashdown averted the risk of damage or injuries at the launch site. "Safety is always our No. 1 priority," she said. If any further safety concerns arise, SpaceX's mission team has the option of ending the flight early and sending the second stage â known as Ship 42 â down to a controlled ocean splashdown.
After reaching orbit, Ship 42 deployed 26 satellites for SpaceX's Starlink broadband internet network. Three of the satellites were equipped with a suite of cameras to inspect Ship's heatshield after deployment.
Starship ranks as the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, standing 407 feet (124 meters) tall and providing 17 million pounds of thrust at liftoff. The rocket is designed to deploy dozens of Starlink V3 satellites at a time â and eventually send thousands of explorers and settlers to Mars.
NASA is counting on SpaceX to provide a Starship-based system for landing astronauts on the moon by as early as 2028. As a preparatory step, NASA is planning to test Starship as well as Blue Origin's Blue Moon landing system in low Earth orbit next year. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman referred to that test mission, known as Artemis III, in a post to X that took note of the video sent down from orbit via the Starlink network.
"Congratulations to the SpaceX team on another spectacular launch," Isaacman wrote. "Very much appreciate how you bring the world along in high resolution. We are looking forward to some of that on-orbit Starlink capability on Artemis III."
This report has been updated with further details about the aborted booster catch.

The setback ended the first half of the company’s ambitious plan to recover both stages of Starship during a single mission. However, the upper stage successfully reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink satellites and continued a flight that could culminate in the first-ever catch of a spacecraft returning from orbit on 14 November. The 124-metre-tall Starship lifted off from SpaceX’s Starbase facility in South Texas at 4:47 p.m. local time on 13 November (22:47 GMT), powered by 33 Raptor engines on its Super Heavy booster. The manoeuvre, known as hot-staging, allows the spacecraft to begin accelerating towards orbit before the two stages have completely separated.

Заголовок: Blue Origin puts its space station plans on hold to concentrate on moon missions instead
Полный текст:
Jeff Bezos' space venture indicates that it won't seek further NASA funding for an outpost once touted as a 'mixed-use business park' in orbit.

Artwork shows an early conception for the Orbital Reef space station, a project led by Blue Origin. (Blue Origin Media)

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef , alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program , which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

“Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the company said in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

Orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the company suspended its suborbital New Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week , NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force .

Заголовок: LOFAR Takes the Deepest Image of the Low-Frequency Radio Sky to Date
Полный текст:
Using the Low Frequency Array (LOFAR), an international team led by Leiden University has produced the sharpest and most sensitive radio image of the sky ever made at low radio frequencies.

An international team led by researchers from Leiden University has produced the deepest and most detailed view of low-frequency radio galaxies in the Universe. Using the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), the team observed ELAIS-N1 (European Large-Area ISO Survey-North 1), a region of the northern sky that contains very little galactic dust, gas, or stars. This makes the field highly favorable for deep multi-wavelength studies that probe the distant Universe.
For years, astronomers at the LOFAR observatory have been observing ELAIS-N1 to map low-frequency radio sources. The latest image has twenty times the resolution of the previous LOFAR image, which was made possible through advances in modern interferometry - a technique where light from multiple telescopes is combined to produce a single clearer image. The full image features 63,000 radio sources, including quasars and star-forming galaxies.
This new view of the low-frequency radio sky comes from 200 hours of observation and amounts to 400 terabytes of data in an 8-billion-pixel image. A few years ago, processing this amount of data from radio telescopes at such high resolution was impossible. But thanks to the Spider data-processing platform developed by researchers from the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy (ASTRON) and their collaborators, and other improvements in calibration and data-reduction methods, processing times have been reduced by a factor of ten.
The core of the LOFAR radio telescope array near Exloo, Netherlands. Credit: LOFAR/ASTRON
"The entire dataset could be processed on Spider, the high-performance data processing platform hosted at SURF in the Netherlands, in just a few months," said Jurjen de Jong, a postdoctoral researcher at Leiden Observatory and ASTRON (who led the research). LOFAR's high sensitivity also revealed numerous filaments surrounding the radio galaxies, especially near galaxy clusters, as well as their morphology and spectral characteristics. Resolving these structures required combining high-resolution and low-frequency observations made possible by LOFAR.
Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN), also known as quasars, are particularly dominant in the image - the bright centers of galaxies powered by supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and their accretion disks. AGNs are also known to produce relativistic jets of superheated gas and dust that emanate from the black holes' polar regions and emit considerable radiation themselves. These structures are something LOFAR is especially well suited to observe, given its sensitivity to extended low-frequency radio emissions.
In previous, lower-resolution surveys, these distant galaxies and their relativistic jets would appear as little more than featureless blobs, making it difficult to distinguish individual galaxies from clusters. The high-resolution LOFAR data, in contrast, allow scientists to discern individual radio sources and massive jets, which can be traced in detail. This new view of the cosmos provides scientists with new opportunities to study how these jets interact with their environment and evolve over cosmic time.
The other major population in the image is the small, young galaxies that are still experiencing high rates of star formation. Because radio waves can pass through gas and dust that obscure the visible and infrared light of star formation, radio observatories provide a clear view of the processes taking place within these galaxies. This allows astronomers to study how galaxies that existed in the early Universe evolved into the older, larger spiral and elliptical galaxies we see in the local Universe.
The giant LOFAR radio telescope took this picture of the black holes at the heart of the active galaxy Cygnus A. Credit: J. McKean and M. Wise/ASTRON
According to the research team, this work demonstrates the potential of the upgraded LOFAR2.0 telescope, which ASTRON is currently working on with its European partners. The upgrades will enable wider, higher-resolution images, allowing LOFAR to remain competitive with next-generation radio telescopes like the Square Kilometer Array (SKA), which will combine the MeerKAT array in South Africa and the Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara (Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory) in Australia.
The data will be especially useful when combined with images of the same patch of sky taken by other telescopes at other wavelengths. This includes optical, infrared, and X-ray observations, from which astronomers can determine properties like the distance and mass of each radio source.

Заголовок: Senate appropriators resuscitate Commerce space tracking program
Полный текст:
WASHINGTON — Senate appropriators have moved to rescue the Commerce Department’s space safety program for monitoring non-military satellites, giving a $50 million shot in the arm to the office in charge.
The Trump administration had requested only $11 million for the Office of Space Commerce, with just $1 million slated to essentially shelve past work on the Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS) program.
READ MORE: Whither TraCSS? DoD, industry face hard choices in showdown over Commerce spacewatch effort
But the Commerce, Justice and Science spending bill released on Thursday by Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, echoes language issued by House appropriators in May about the importance of TraCCS. The House bill also slated $50 million in FY27 funds for the Office of Space Commerce.
The fate of the TraCCS effort has been the subject of intense debate over the past couple of years, with commercial space monitoring firms growing increasingly frustrated with the slowness of the program’s development. The Commerce Department effort was launched nearly a decade ago due to Defense Department concerns about the increasing drain on its space monitoring resources as commercial space traffic continues to skyrocket.
The continuation of TraCCS development, at least for the moment, would lift concerns at the Defense Department, the Space Force and US Space Command that for the foreseeable future the military would be saddled with the job of warning nonmilitary space operators about pending on-orbit collisions.
The next step in the process is for the Senate and House appropriators to come together in conference committee to hash out their differences, and finalize an agreed upon bill. Whether that happens before the end of the legislative session at this point is anyone’s guess.

Заголовок: Maritime Launch Services Q3 2026: bigger rockets, fewer shares
Полный текст:
Maritime Launch Services is preparing to accommodate larger medium-class rockets as well, it said Friday with its third-quarter results. It also plans to ask shareholders early next year to consolidate a stock that has traded below a dollar all year.

Maritime Launch Services (MLS) is preparing to accommodate larger medium-class rockets as well, it said Friday with its third-quarter results. It also plans to ask shareholders early next year to consolidate a stock that has traded below a dollar all year.
Revenue for the three months to Sept. 30 was $5.6 million, level with the second quarter, when MLS earned its first operating profit, and net income rose 9 per cent to $3.5 million from $3.2 million. Lower professional fees, and the end of a one-time charge for paying off an Export Development Canada loan early in April, more than made up for higher wages as the company hired. About 99 per cent of the revenue comes from the Department of National Defence (DND) launch pad lease, which counts in equal monthly slices.
More launch interest
Maritime Launch now plans four launch pads at Spaceport Nova Scotia, near Canso, N.S. One is operational and has handled the suborbital flights so far, while the other three are being developed with customers in 2026 and 2027. The company says it can add pads beyond those four, either to let more launch companies operate from the site or to take different kinds of rockets, including medium-class ones. In its outlook, the company said it is talking to more launch companies than this phase has pads for, with payloads from 150 kilograms to more than 15,000 kg.
The company calls room for medium-class rockets, those able to lift a tonne or more, “a primary goal,” and says the Province of Nova Scotia has already approved it for construction. Isar Aerospace‘s Spectrum, due to fly from the site in 2028, carries up to 1,000 kg to low Earth orbit, about 7 per cent of the largest payloads in those talks.
In its quarterly report, Maritime Launch argues that medium rockets suit constellation operators, who need to replace failed satellites in batches, and that limits on future bookings for established heavy-lift rockets could push more customers toward newer spaceports. Ottawa wants Canadian medium-lift rockets too, and Budget 2026 made them a formal goal, with DND managing dedicated launch and test facilities.
Power and fibre being added
Local trades have started on the foundation of a utility hub, which will gather power and services at one central point before they are run out to the pads. Nova Scotia Power won a contract in October to bring up to 3 megawatts from Canso, along with a Bell fibre line, with work due to start within 60 days. The security building at the site entrance is out to tender this month, and clearing is planned for December.
The road to Isar’s pad was finished Nov. 1, in time for a contractual deadline, and the two companies are now laying out Isar’s section of a shared integration facility, where rockets and satellites are readied for launch. The launch control centre is still at the preliminary design stage.
On Nov. 4, Maritime Launch closed on 115 acres just south of the Crown land it leases, paying cash, after buying 71 acres at Portage Cove in May. The province also agreed in writing on Oct. 14 to lengthen the notice either side must give to cancel the Crown lease from 60 days to a year, though the change has yet to be written into the lease.
The company, which has 13 full-time employees, this week made Sarah McLean, a founding member of its leadership team, chief operating officer as it builds toward orbital launches.
Isar’s first payment is still waiting
Maritime Launch and Isar pushed the Sept. 1 date for their statement of work, the detailed plan for building Isar’s pad, to mid-September and finished it in time. Full orbital readiness is still targeted for the first quarter of 2028.
Maritime Launch has still not counted any of Isar’s money as revenue. Isar’s first quarterly payment, $5.3 million ($US 3.75 million), arrived in August and sits on the balance sheet as deferred revenue, because no lease had started by Sept. 30 and the accounting for the deal was not yet settled when the statements were approved. So DND’s share of revenue is about where it was last quarter, and the company notes that DND has put up no guarantee for its payments, though the department has so far paid ahead of schedule.
Maritime Launch ended September with $29.4 million in cash, up 30 per cent from $22.6 million in June, but deferred revenue, payment for pad access the company has yet to provide, came to $23.7 million, equal to about 80 per cent of that cash. “We feel we are well funded with over $29 million in cash on the balance sheet and contractual payments from our launch partners,” president and chief executive Stephen Matier said in the release.
DND pays $20 million a contract year and had paid $30 million by Sept. 30. Isar makes four quarterly payments in its first year, 13 per cent of the contract’s total value, then nothing for 30 months — from July 2027 to October 2029 — before its fees resume. Maritime Launch also expects to start claiming about $31.2 million in approved Nova Scotia capital investment tax credits in 2027.
What a share consolidation means
Maritime Launch expects to call a special meeting in the first quarter of 2027 to approve a share consolidation, with the board left to pick the ratio. The company says fewer, higher-priced shares would be easier to sell to investors and to trade, and would give it more ways to raise money.
It has plenty of shares to consolidate. Maritime Launch had 767.9 million outstanding on Nov. 10, the legacy of years spent raising money at pennies a share. The number of shares rose 78 per cent in 2025 alone, with 77 per cent of that increase arriving in November, when old convertible debt was turned into about 209 million shares after MDA Space invested $10 million.
A consolidation shrinks that number without changing what anyone owns. If the board chose one new share for every 10 old ones, for example, a shareholder holding 10,000 shares at 46 cents would end up with 1,000 shares at $4.60, and the company would have about 77 million shares instead of 768 million. Options and warrants are normally adjusted the same way.
Maritime Launch moved to the TSX on Nov. 3, and share price is one of the tests for joining the S&P/TSX Composite, Canada’s main stock index. A company needs a volume-weighted average price of at least $1 over the previous three months, as well as meeting size and trading requirements. As SpaceQ reported when the listing was approved, it also needs six full calendar months on the exchange, so mid-2027 is the earliest Maritime Launch could qualify. Its shares closed at 46 cents Thursday, up 64 per cent since the end of 2025 but 33 per cent below their 69-cent April peak.
What to watch
INNOSPACE, the South Korean company that signed a letter of intent in March to bring its HANBIT rocket to the site, set December as its deadline to turn that into a formal agreement. The special meeting and the consolidation ratio come in the first quarter, and Isar’s payments stay out of revenue until the company settles how to account for the deal.
Further out, Isar’s first Spectrum launch from Nova Scotia is targeted for 2028, and Reaction Dynamics is aiming for its first orbital flight from the site around the third quarter of that year.

Заголовок: 60 years ago the Leonid meteor shower produced 144,000 meteors per hour. Could it happen again?
Полный текст:
60 years ago, the Leonid meteor shower unleashed one of the most spectacular meteor storms in recorded history. As the 2026 peak approaches, here's what skywatchers can expect.

This year marks a rather auspicious anniversary for meteor watchers. Sixty years ago , one of the most stupendous Leonid meteor displays lit up the predawn skies over the central and western U.S. So, what will the 2026 Leonids bring us? And what might they bring in the years to come?

The Leonid meteor shower is one of the most celebrated of the year's annual displays of "shooting stars." The mere mention of the Leonids usually elicits mental images of a sky filled with shooting stars pouring down through the sky like rain. Such meteor storms have indeed occurred with the Leonids, such as in 1833 and 1966 when meteor rates of tens of thousands per hour were observed. In more recent years, most notably 1999 , 2001 and 2002 , lesser Leonid displays of up to "only" a few thousand meteors per hour took place.

Unfortunately, that's not likely to be the case this year. In fact, comparatively speaking, this is going to be a lean year for the Leonids chiefly because of the expected lack of any significant activity. Although the Leonids are one of the most famous of all the annual meteor displays, this year they're not likely to be very productive. It's probable they are going to be rather weak and there probably will be long stretches when not a single Leonid will be seen. I'll explain why in a moment. First, let's find out about this shower's lineage.

What causes the Leonids?

The Leonids are so named because the shower's radiant point, from where the meteors seem to fan out, is located within the constellation of Leo the Lion, from the backward question mark pattern of stars known as " The Sickle." The meteors are caused by the Tempel-Tuttle comet , which sweeps through the inner solar system every 33⅓ years. Each time the comet passes closest to the sun it leaves a "river of rubble" in its wake: a dense trail of dusty debris. A meteor storm becomes possible if the Earth were to score a direct hit on a fresh dust trail ejected by the comet over the past several centuries.

The "lion's share" (no pun intended) of comet dust can be found just ahead and trailing behind Tempel-Tuttle. That comet last swept through the inner solar system in 1998. That's why spectacular meteor showers were seen in 1999, 2001 and 2002, with declining numbers thereafter.

The most famous depiction of the 1833 Leonids, actually produced in 1888 for the Adventist book Bible Readings for the Home Circle . The engraving is by Adolf Vollmy based upon an original painting by the Swiss artist Karl Jauslin, that is in turn based on a first-person account of the 1833 storm by a minister, Joseph Harvey Waggoner on his way from Florida to New Orleans. (Image credit: Adolf Vollmy - Bible Readings for the Home Circle. Public Domain)

When is the best time to look for Leonids?

According to the International Meteor Organization's 2026 meteor shower calendar , the Leonids are expected to reach their regular maximum at 23:45 UTC (6:45 p.m. EST) on Nov. 17, with around 15 meteors per hour possible under ideal viewing conditions.

Other forecasts place the peak at slightly different times. Margaret Campbell-Brown and Peter Brown , meteor experts for the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada , predict that the peak of this year's Leonids will occur at 00:00 hours UTC on Nov. 18. Russian meteor expert Mikhail Maslov feels that the peak will come about a third of a day earlier, at 16:00 UTC on Nov. 17.

Several weaker encounters with older debris trails are also predicted between Nov. 17 and 19, although no major meteor storm is expected.

A meteor streaks across the sky above Payson, Arizona during the Leonid meteor shower. (Image credit: mdesigner125 via Getty Images)

Hardly any crumbs this year

Back in September 2014, comet Tempel-Tuttle was as far from the sun as it can get: 1.84 billion miles (2.96 billion km). The comet has since spent the last dozen years slowly approaching the inner solar system, but it's still 1.11 billion miles (1.79 billion km) from the sun , which is still well beyond the orbit of Saturn.

In contrast, at the point in the comet's orbit where we will be passing by on Tuesday morning, there is nothing save for a scattered few particles; bits and pieces likely loosened from the comet's nucleus a millennium or two ago.

So, this year's Leonids are expected to show only low activity; "maybe" at best 10 to 15 Leonids per hour might be seen, but more likely hourly counts will be less than that. The moon will not pose a problem; it's at first quarter phase, but it will set before 11 p.m. local time Monday evening, leaving the rest of the night dark.

What to look for

Watching a meteor shower consists of lying back, looking up at the sky... and waiting. Keep in mind that any local light pollution or obstructions like tall trees or buildings will further reduce your chances of making a meteor sighting. Leo does not start coming fully into view until the after-midnight hours, so that would be the best time to concentrate on looking for Leonids. As dawn is about to break at around 5 a.m., the Sickle will have climbed more than two-thirds of the way up from the southeast horizon to the point directly overhead (called the zenith).

Because the Leonids are moving along in their orbit around the sun in a direction opposite to that of Earth, they slam into our atmosphere nearly head-on, resulting in the fastest meteor velocities possible: 45 miles (72 km) per second. Such speeds tend to produce bright meteors, which leave long-lasting streaks or persistent trains in their wake. A mighty Leonid fireball can be quite spectacular, but such outstandingly bright meteors are likely to be very few and very far between this year (if any are seen at all).

1966: Stormy times

It was a different story 60 years ago, in 1966, when anticipation ran high for a potentially heavy display of Leonid meteors. The previous year, comet Tempel-Tuttle swept around the sun and was accompanied later that year by an unexpected surge of Leonid activity, with brilliant meteors darting across the sky at one or two per minute as seen from Hawaii and Australia. The most sanguine prediction for 1966 came from Dr. Kenneth L. Franklin (1923-2007), chief scientist at New York's Hayden Planetarium . Dr. Franklin had carefully examined the orbit of comet Tempel-Tuttle and concluded that " . . . the position of the comet is roughly what it was in 1833. So, a dramatic shower like the one that occurred in that year may yet be in the offing for 1966."

Based on Dr. Franklin's prediction, a "meteor party" was planned for the peak night of the Leonids in Central Park. New Yorkers of all ages were invited to gather on the Great Lawn at midnight to watch for the shooting stars. Ten thousand people turned out, but unfortunately skies were hopelessly cloudy.

But across the central and western US, where skies were mostly clear, Leonids were falling at a rate described by many as "too numerous to count." One observer stationed north of Mission, Texas said that meteors falling in all directions gave the impression of a "gigantic umbrella," appearing to "waterfall" out of the head of Leo. Perhaps the best views were from California and Arizona. At the Table Mountain Observatory, near Wrightwood, California, one resident astronomer commented that he and a colleague " . . . watched a rain of meteors, turn into a hail of meteors and finally a storm of meteors, too numerous to count by 3:50 a.m. Pacific Time. Instinctively we sought to shield our upturned faces from imagined celestial debris." From 6,850-foot Kitt Peak in southern Arizona, thirteen amateur astronomers saw Leonids falling at the staggering rate of 40 per second (144,000 per hour)!

From Sun, Moon and Stars by Agnes Giberne. (London, 1884). This artwork shows the Leonid meteor storm over Greenwich, London in 1866. (Image credit: Photo by Oxford Science Archive/Print Collector/Getty Images)

Looking ahead. . .

In 2005, French meteor expert Jeremie Vaubaillon published a technical paper with two colleagues in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics that forecast Leonid activity for years up to 2100. Sadly, in the year 2029, Jupiter is expected to throw Comet Tempel-Tuttle off its current path through space, making it all but impossible — at least through the beginning of the 22nd century — to see a repeat of the Great Leonid Storm of 1966.
But Vaubaillon expects the next big Leonid outburst in the year 2034, when rates could reach up to 2,000 per hour.

That's just 8 years from now. Mark your calendars.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium . He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine , Sky and Telescope , The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

Заголовок: Сегодня — исторический день.
Полный текст:
Сегодня — исторический день.

В Техасе всё готово к первому в истории полёту полностью многоразового корабля с попыткой вернуть как ускоритель, так и верхнюю ступень — IFT-15.

SpaceX сажает первую ступень F9 уже больше 12 лет и 3 раза успешно сажала ускоритель «Старшипа» на башню с захватом манипуляторами. На этот раз будет самое важное событие программы — двойная посадка: как ускорителя, так и самого «Старшипа».

Будут использоваться машины третьего поколения «комбо» B22/S42. Ускоритель B22 сядет через 6 минут после запуска, а корабль S42 должен совершить 14 витков вокруг Земли.

В отличие от предыдущих полетов, которые длились около часа и проходили по суборбитальной траектории, S42 должен провести в космосе почти сутки. После этого он выполнит маневр схода с орбиты и начнет возвращение точно в точку запуска, на вторую стартовую площадку техасского космодрома «Бока-Чика».

Полёт должен занять больше 22 часов, это нужно:
1) чтобы наклонение орбиты совпало с местом запуска из-за смещения вызванном вращением земли
2) чтобы убрать ранее севший ускоритель, освободить место для посадки корабля;
3) чтобы проанализировать все параметры перед посадкой;
4) чтобы дать запускающей команде отдохнуть после первого пуска, чтобы они могли контролировать посадку выспавшимися и отдохнувшими и принимать правильные решения — это тоже важно.

На S42 используется новая геометрия теплозащитных плиток. Изменения должны уменьшить риск проникновения горячей плазмы в зазоры между плитками — одна из проблем, обнаруженных во время предыдущих полётов. В наиболее нагруженных местах также усилено механическое крепление плиток.

«Старшип» должен вывести 26 спутников Starlink V3. Три из них оснащены камерами, которые после отделения смогут сфотографировать теплозащитный экран «Старшипа». Это поможет оценить состояние корабля перед окончательным решением о его возвращении.

Попытка посадки на башню добавляет дополнительные риски. Космодром имеет большую ценность, он и стоит дороже, и восстанавливается дольше, чем корабль. Поэтому при любом подозрении на нештатный исход в жертву принесут прежде всего корабль, а не стартовую площадку. Для безопасности корабль по умолчанию будет целиться в океан, куда он и полетит по баллистической траектории, если ничего не предпринимать. Только если все системы покажут 100%-полную готовность к посадке как корабля, так и башни, то произойдет посадка с захватом на тот же pad 2, куда ранее сел ускоритель.

Трансляция пуска будет идти сегодня ночью во всех запрещённых соцсетях, искать по ключевым словам «starship» и «IFT-15».
