Заголовок: Submarine maintenance delays saw ‘significant’ improvements in FY26, sub czar says
Полный текст:
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the direct reporting portfolio manager for submarines, said that the Navy faced roughly 780 days of maintenance delay for subs in FY26.

WASHINGTON — Submarine maintenance delays improved in fiscal 2026, with a more than 600-day drop in maintenance delays from previous years, according to the Pentagon’s first-ever submarine czar.
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DPRM) for Submarines, said that while the service faced roughly 1,400 days of maintenance delay for submarines in both FY24 and FY25, that number was down to 780 in FY26.
“I want to highlight the significant reduction in days of maintenance delay,” Gaucher said Thursday at the Naval Submarine League Annual Symposium. “That’s more than 40 percent improvement.”
“And I attribute a significant part of this to investments made in Virginia-class spare parts over the past few years. … I expect maintenance delays will drop further in fiscal year ‘27 to around 500 days,” he continued.
Specifically, Gaucher pointed to the Virginia-class submarines John Warner and Illinois, which will be delivered for depot maintenance in a “few weeks.” While both are late for delivery in comparison to their original schedules, they are “several months early to their re-baseline schedules, and that’s something we were not even able to come close to doing several years ago,” according to Gaucher.
The service needed to update the delivery schedules, or “re-baseline,” on several occasions, Gaucher said. “So getting early to the re-baseline is a huge mark of progress. And as of today, every fast attack submarine in Portsmouth Naval Shipyard and Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard is on plan, with several — I dare say — tracking early to plan.”
The Navy has routinely suffered from submarine maintenance delays, and an August Government Accountability Office report determined public shipyards, which perform maintenance on nuclear-powered vessels like submarines, completed only 11 percent of submarine depot maintenance periods on schedule between FY16-25.

Заголовок: Canadian Space Agency reports spending hit record $1.16 billion
Полный текст:
The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) spent $1.16 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year, the most it has ever spent and nearly twice the year before. Almost half of it went to the European Space Agency (ESA), notably to to support defence research and development.
The 2025-26 Departmental Results Report, posted Nov. 6, is the Canadian Space Agency’s annual report that outlines what it spent in its fiscal year, which, like those of all government departments, ends on March 31. Its annual plan called for $834 million in spending, and the agency ended up spending $326 million more.
The defence payment that made the difference
The CSA paid $562.9 million under its cooperation agreement with ESA, against the original $31.4 million it had planned. Most of the difference is $528.5 million the government announced in November 2025 as an early measure under the Defence Industrial Strategy. The report says the money reached the CSA as a transfer from the Department of National Defence (DND) to support defence research and development.
That money was part of Canada’s $664.6-million commitment at ESA’s ministerial council in Bremen, Germany, in late November 2025, which the report calls Canada’s “largest-ever commitment” to the agency. Canada takes part in ESA as a cooperating state, and ESA awards contracts to companies in each participating country roughly in proportion to what that country pays in. The CSA expects about 80 per cent of the money to come back to Canadian industry that way.
Canada’s industrial return coefficient, the value of ESA contracts won by Canadian organizations divided by what Canada has paid in, stood at 0.74 at the end of March, measured cumulatively since 2015-16. A coefficient of 1.0 would mean Canadian organizations had won back the full value of Canada’s contributions.
The CSA target is 0.93 by March 2030, just after the current agreement ends on Jan. 1, 2030. Access to ESA contracts depends on which ESA programs Canada subscribes to, and those subscriptions are set every three years. The CSA puts the low figure down to “the significant and sudden increase in funding” under the Defence Industrial Strategy and expects it to climb steadily toward 1.0 as Canadian organizations win ESA contracts.
Sixty-five Canadian organizations took part in ESA-funded projects during the year. Canadian companies also gained access to four ESA programs Canada had not funded before, which Ottawa authorized in March: Moonlight, a lunar communications and navigation service; FutureNAV, for next-generation satellite navigation; ACCESS, a commercialization program; and ERS-EO, Earth observation for security and resilience.
Canadarm3 work continued as NASA paused Gateway
The CSA kept building Canadarm3, the robotic arm Canada agreed to supply for the Lunar Gateway, NASA’s planned station in orbit around the Moon. In July 2025 it advanced the arm’s detailed design and completed the critical review of the Gateway External Robotic Interfaces, the fittings the arm would use on the station. NASA announced March 24 that it intended to pause Gateway and shift to the lunar surface. The CSA “intends to repurpose Canadarm3 investments to support the next phase of lunar exploration,” the report says.
Assets under construction on the CSA’s balance sheet rose by $259 million during the year, to $865.8 million at March 31, and the agency’s financial statements point to Canadarm3 as the main asset being built.
As of March 31, before the WildFireSat contract was terminated, the agency also had $770 million in contractual obligations for building assets over the four fiscal years to 2029-30, mostly for Canadarm3 and WildFireSat. SpaceQ’s tracking of federal Moon program contracts, checked against Government of Canada open data, puts the funding committed to Gateway and Canadarm3 at $1.68 billion since 2019.
In March, the CSA ended its Lunar Rover Mission, a small rover Canadensys Aerospace was building to fly on a Firefly lander in 2029, after its preliminary design was finished. The report says the robotic mobility know-how could be used on other missions and for commercialization. The agency’s larger Lunar Utility Vehicle, meant to haul cargo and help astronauts on the surface, moved ahead with $14.6 million in contracts to three Canadian companies in July 2025.
WildFireSat reset and a new RADARSAT satellite
The CSA terminated its WildFireSat contract with the supplier in April 2026, just after the year closed, following what the report calls a comprehensive review of the project and its fit with the government’s needs. The supplier was Spire Global Canada, whose contract was worth about $72 million. The report says the government is working with industry and stakeholders to keep developing the wildfire-monitoring mission.
The RADARSAT Constellation Mission, Canada’s three radar satellites, handled more than 500,000 imagery requests from federal users for maritime surveillance, disaster response and climate research. The government announced $47 million to build, test and launch an additional satellite for the constellation, most of it for parts to speed up delivery.
The CSA also extended operations of SCISAT, Canada’s longest-running satellite, which tracks the chemistry that controls ozone, to 2028-29. It archived and validated 25 years of data from MOPITT, a Canadian instrument on NASA’s Terra satellite that was switched off in April 2025 when the spacecraft ran short of power.
Fewer services built on space data than targeted
The CSA counted 91 services to Canadians that depend on space data, short of its target of 111 and the lowest figure in the three years the report covers.
The space sector itself employed 14,622 people in 2024 and added $3.8 billion to gross domestic product, both above the CSA’s targets.
An internal self-assessment of how well the CSA follows legislation and Treasury Board policy found potential compliance concerns in procurement and real property, including long-term contract planning and tracking of reinvestment in its buildings. The agency says it developed an action plan to be in place by September 2026; the report, released in November, gives no update on whether it is.
The agency ended its own operations at the David Florida Laboratory, Canada’s spacecraft test centre in Ottawa, and licensed it to MDA Space, which began offering testing services in fall 2025. The report calls the licence an interim measure while a longer-term strategy is worked out.
Planned spending falls by nearly half by 2028-29
The CSA plans to spend $913.9 million in 2026-27, falling to $475.9 million by 2028-29, as funding for Canadarm3 winds down and cuts from the government’s Comprehensive Expenditure Review take hold. Planned spending figures tend to change as new money is approved or programs change: the agency’s plan for 2025-26 called for $834 million, and it spent $1.16 billion. The report says it expects more money for Canadarm3 and WildFireSat in future years.
The CSA carried $243 million of unspent authority into future years, nearly all of it capital project money, which it describes as an inherent part of managing the space program. Its unspent capital was more than twice the year before.
Because the report covers the year to March 31, it still describes two astronaut flights as coming. Jeremy Hansen flew around the Moon on Artemis II in April, and Joshua Kutryk launched to the International Space Station on Crew-13 on Oct. 1.
Alex MacDonald, appointed CSA president on Nov. 4, takes over from acting president Jean-Claude Piedboeuf, who signed the year’s financial statements in August. MacDonald told an industry conference in May that the agency must “rapidly pivot away from our gateway activities” and focus on lunar surface robotics, close to the direction the report sets out for Canadarm3.

Заголовок: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
Полный текст:
In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park's elephant population.

Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.

Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.

Accidental savanna

Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).

Заголовок: 'Arrival' at 10: Denis Villeneuve's alien visitation classic that reminded us it's good to talk
Полный текст:
How the 'Dune' director turned a little-known short story into one of the best sci-fi movies of the 21st century

In many of the biggest science fiction franchises, conversing with alien races is an absolute doddle. In " Star Trek ", universal translators come as standard, while C-3PO has spent the last 49 years reminding everyone in "Star Wars" that he's fluent in over six million forms of communication.

But in "Arrival" — which was released 10 years ago in November 2016 — making first contact proves to be rather more challenging than maintaining your Duolingo streak. In fact, working out how to establish a dialogue with extraterrestrial visitors becomes the whole point of this powerful and heartbreaking story, as the fate of planet Earth hinges on the interpretation of a single noun.

The film's journey to the big screen began when a screenwriter best known for his work on horror franchises such as "Final Destination", "A Nightmare on Elm Street" and "The Thing" read a short story in an online magazine. Eric Heisserer was so impressed by Ted Chiang's "Understand" that he bought himself a collection of the author's short stories. One in particular, the Nebula Award-winning "Story of Your Life", piqued his interest.

"It had a very profound emotional effect on me," he reminisced to Deadline . "I was in tears, and I was both heartbroken and uplifted. My head was just full of big ideas. I had to walk around the block a couple of times afterward and just hug my friends. The next day, I was like, 'Oh god, I want to give this to other people.'"

So when 21 Laps (the production company that later went on to make " Stranger Things ") invited Heisserer to discuss possible future projects, the writer mentioned "Story of Your Life". The producers were also smitten.

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

"I was so excited, but I had that dread that a lot of producers get, which is, 'Are the rights available?'" 21 Laps' Dan Levine told the Hollywood Gold podcast. "You read something that blows you away, and then you find there aren't the rights, and there's no chance, you have to move on. So we were trying to track down this Ted Chiang, and he had no agent. He had a day job. He was impossible to find, so we started the hunt for Ted Chiang."

An up-and-coming Canadian director named Denis Villeneuve had also found his way on to 21 Laps' radar after his 2010 French-language drama "Incendies" earned rave reviews and an Academy Award nomination. He told the producers that he'd always wanted to direct a science fiction film — a hint of things to come? — and they showed him "Story of Your Life".

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

He was also drawn to the story, while the now-located Chiang was suitably impressed by the director's work on "Incendies" to make a deal for the rights. And with Amy Adams also interested in playing the lead role of linguist Dr Louise Banks, the film that would eventually become "Arrival" was ready to proceed — or, at least, it would be once Villeneuve had completed his first three Hollywood movies, "Prisoners" (2013), "Enemy" (2013) and "Sicario" (2015).

With 12 alien spaceships arriving simultaneously around the globe, "Arrival"'s poster-friendly elevator pitch could almost have been borrowed from " Independence Day ". Indeed, the question of whether these whisper-quiet, chocolate button-shaped craft belong to the " Day the Earth Stood Still " / "Close Encounters" friendly extraterrestrial camp, or have the invasion of planet Earth on their minds is a mystery the world's governments are desperate to solve.

"Denis didn't really see this as an alien invasion movie — more an alien arrival movie," producer Aaron Ryder told SFX magazine. "What would be the protocols that were in place? How would they be implemented? How would people react? What would the government be doing? What would the news organisations be saying? That was the tone and the texture, which is established right up front."

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

These Hollywood blockbuster components were not part of "Story of Your Life". But even though Heisserer's script was not a direct translation of Chiang's tale, he retained the most important bits — namely Dr Banks' efforts to establish a means of communication with seven-legged extraterrestrial heptapods, and the profound effect their language has on her perception of time.

Designed by Carlos Huante, the heptapods themselves are like giant elongated hands, alien visitors light years away from the "Star Trek" tradition of actors with a few ridges glued to their foreheads. Like the evil 456 in " Torchwood: Children of Earth ", they're enclosed in gaseous chambers and make sounds imperceptible to the human ear.

This, however, is where "Arrival" gets really interesting. Working alongside physicist colleague Dr Ian Donnelly (Jeremy Renner), Banks gradually exchanges foundational vocabulary with two heptapods they name Abbott and Costello. They discover that the alien visitors use a sophisticated written language of circular "logograms", squirted into their atmosphere as if it were sentient squid ink.

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

"The idea in the short story is of circular language that has no beginning and no end," Villeneuve explained in an interview with IndieWire . "We were looking for no relation to any human language. I had to figure out how to produce logograms from my aliens while avoiding being long and boring. The sounds were an expression of their emotions, with more intellect coming from the signs. This beautiful species uses written language as their first means of expression instead of movement or gesture. They produce words out of their bodies."

But Banks and Donnelly's research project has a purpose. With the world's military on high alert — and, ironically, struggling to communicate — they need to work out how to ask the aliens a fundamental question: Why are you here?

The heptapods' answer — "offer weapon" — is tantalizingly ambiguous. Are they planning to attack? Or is, as Banks suggests, 'weapon' simply being used as a synonym for 'tool'?

SPOILERS AHEAD

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

Aside from a bomb planted on the heptapod ship by a rogue US soldier, "Arrival" is mostly free from the big-budget explosions that are part-and-parcel of most alien visitation movies. Instead, the film's denouement delivers a twist — the crux of Chiang's story — that rivals "The Sixth Sense", "Fight Club" and "The Prestige" in its audacious sleight of hand.

It turns out the "weapon" in question is actually the heptapod language, which, thanks to their non-linear perception of time, gives speakers a unique perspective on the past, present, and future. Therefore, those scenes we assumed to be flash backs to the life and tragic death of Louise's daughter, Hannah, are actually flash forwards , as her increased understanding of heptapod-speak gives her memories of a life she hasn't yet lived.

Villeneuve put on multiple test screenings to ensure the big reveals hit properly.

"I wanted to screen it with people who knew nothing about the project," he said. "What we discovered is when someone in the audience felt too lost — if intellectually they were not engaged — the ending was less powerful from an emotional point of view. So we tried to give as few clues as possible, but enough clues to be able to stay engaged and follow the story."

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

Those subtle hints become obvious on second and third viewings, whether it's a lingering shot of a wedding ring absent in the movie's "present" or a conversation about the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (the notion that the structure of a language can influence the way its speakers think). The absence of young Hannah's father also takes on tragic new meaning when we realize it's Ian, who'll leave after Louise tells him about their daughter's sad fate.

"We were walking on this tightrope of trying to play things so it could play both ways, because of the reveal at the end," Adams recalled in a Vanity Fair conversation with Villeneuve. "I had to do so much work to understand how I play a character so that the first time you watch it you think that it's one thing, and the second time you watch it you can see it from a totally different perspective."

While Adams didn't get the Oscar nomination her performance deserved, everything else paid off, with the film making over $200 million worldwide from its reported $47 million budget. (The film did win an Academy Award for sound editing, while receiving further nods for best picture, director, and adapted screenplay.)

(Image credit: Paramount Pictures)

Villeneuve has famously gone on to become Hollywood's go-to guy for intelligent sci-fi, thanks to " Blade Runner 2049 " and the smash-hit " Dune " saga, and will next be given the opportunity to resurrect James Bond.

Normally we'd take this opportunity to say no one could have foreseen Villeneuve's subsequent ascendancy but — in a story involving heptapods and some clever people at 21 Laps — who can be so sure?

Заголовок: Intellian CEO Unpacks Terminal Strategy for Aero and Military as Ground Tech Player Diversifies
Полный текст:
Intellian Technologies has expanded its presence in the ground tech market from a maritime specialist into a diversified player, with a new upcoming launch for the aviation market and new offerings for government/military customers. CEO Eric Sung recently spoke with Via Satellite about the growth drivers as Intellian expects to climb from around $300 million in revenue to $500 million within a few years. In this interview, Sung details the new in-flight connectivity terminal Low-Earth Orbit (LEO), surging military and sovereign-network demand, new U.S. manufacturing, and insight into the company’s future roadmap.

Intellian’s revenue base by market has diversified in recent years as the company has expanded beyond maritime into new markets. In 2019, when the company won the first Via Satellite’s inaugural Satellite Technology of the Year award , its revenue mostly came from maritime. But now the company covers military defense and aviation, as well as enterprise and mobility, and infrastructure like gateway antennas.

“We have diversified our business to cover different product lines and markets. There is a lot of opportunity to grow business purely from the terminal perspective, but at the same time, there is a lot of demand from the military government area for secure communications. There are new sovereign constellations and D2D [direct-to-device]. Everybody needs a ground gateway infrastructure solution. I expect growth is going to come from multiple market sectors,” Sung said.

Sung told Via Satellite that the company did around $230 million in revenues last year, and is on track to reach around $300 million this year. He expects the company to reach $500 million per year in the next two to four years.

“For the next few years, the goal is to hit the $500 million mark, specializing in the satellite communication business. This year we are expecting 25% year-on-year growth,” said Sung.

The percentage of Intellian’s military government business is increasing. In 2026, the company projects that government/military business will make up around 20% of its entire business. Yet, the company’s commercial sector and gateway infrastructure offering is also growing fast.

A New Offering for the Aero Market

The company has made some significant recent moves into the aviation market. During SATShow 2026, Intellian unveiled the OW11FA Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) user terminal for OneWeb, developed in a strategic partnership with Panasonic Avionics for in-flight connectivity (IFC). Sung said the company had “all the building blocks” for aero with its flat panel technology, but had not focused on it before.

“The market was really keen on having an alternative IFC terminal based on LEO. So Starlink is doing great. Everybody is excited about it,” Sung said. “This was one of the basic drivers of why we started to develop this terminal. It has a very sleek form factor, relatively low cost, and can deliver different levels of throughput.”

Sung said that Intellian will begin to roll out the terminal in 2027 through a new service working with Panasonic and Eutelsat. In the next two years, he expects to see a new customer base using the Eutelsat OneWeb network for IFC with Panasonic.

While aviation is still a strong market for the satellite industry, Starlink has won some of the largest IFC deals in recent years. Sung says Starlink has completely changed the whole industry, but he believes there is a positive side, which is a dramatic increase in the total addressable market for satellite connectivity.

“The satellite industry is becoming mainstream. Before it was a niche player, niche market, and mobile was everything. But now satellite is leading the innovation. It already created a new market segment. Because of this new disruptive service and approach, many of the industry was struggling to maintain the business as they did before,” Sung said. “The bright side is that a company like us and also the many of the operators work together and develop a new solution as an alternative service, alternative product.”

The goal will be for Intellian to help through partners deliver smaller form factor, more efficient and more capable antennas for use in aero in both Ku- and Ka-band, and Sung believes that this will enable service providers to offer competitive services at price points, with hardware that is comparable to what Starlink is doing, and with similar features.

Government and Sovereign Demand

Intellian is also seeing growing demand for building sovereign networks in different regions around the world. Sung said this can be seen in Europe, but he also highlighted South Korea, which is building the ‘K-LEO’ sovereign LEO constellation, as well as China and India’s progress to build expansive sovereign LEO programs. He sees Intellian contributing in this area with gateways and user terminals.

“Everybody needs a gateway solution, and then also many of them need flat panel technology, phased array technology, and the user terminal to serve the network,” Sung said. “For D2D [direct-to-device] people may think that the terminal is just a cell phone, which is mainly true. However, the D2D network may need a special application [such as an] enterprise application that uses different techniques. This is where we can help with sovereign networks.”

In the United States, the company recently debuted a next-generation tactical Wideband Global Satcom (WGS) flyaway terminal for communications-on-the-pause (COTP). Intellian has been working with the U.S. government for the past 10 years and provides an X/Ka maritime tactical terminal that works with the WGS constellation.

“We developed those technologies, from which we created this land flyaway terminal. I see the size of opportunities [in the U.S.] as really high. With this type of capability and terminal, it can provide high throughput leveraging LEO and MEO, and then also it can provide resilient and secure communication for the U.S. military and also other militaries that have a demand to use a WGS, and even a non-WGS satellite. Any customer that wants to use a military grade secure communication, this is the right solution to use,” he says.

He expects to see strong demand for this solution, not only from the U.S. but also from European customers.

Intellian has added its first international manufacturing product line in the U.S. and is working to set up a U.S. based factory that manufactures ground antenna systems. It is now manufacturing out of its California factory.

“This factory will be able to produce all of our military government terminals for [the] U.S. government. This means that we can replicate this kind of factory in other areas like Europe to serve IRIS² [and] serve government customers there,” Sung said.

Future Technology Roadmap

The company is continually investing in new tech and looking at future solutions that support Q-band, V-band, and E-band. It is also looking at providing high-end amplifier as a part of the gateway solution, and building its own gateway orchestration software solution.

“This is on the roadmap that we are driving right now internally,” Sung said. “We will use AI to create orchestration of this global infrastructure of the gateway solution.”

He added that Intellian is building a Ku- and Ka-band flat panel terminal for LEO and MEO, and a solution that can cover military Ka-band for the government satcom and secure connectivity, saying “We need to have a different variety of terminals from the low cost, that can compete with Starlink, for example.”

NASA’s Mars Exploration Program will start another Mars Sample Return study, this time a yearlong one set to begin in January to find new ways to return the samples the Perseverance rover is collecting on Mars. The agency ended the earlier MSR mission last year because of cost concerns.
George Tahu, program executive for Mars Exploration, described the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture (PSRA) strategy team at a virtual NASA Town Hall for the planetary science community, SpacePolicyOnline reported. He said the team will review lessons learned and past recommendations, assess current agency and industry capabilities, and consider whether some constraints can be removed and new acquisition approaches used. “The goal is to develop a high-level architecture approach and recommendations by the end of next year,” Tahu said.
A NASA spokesperson said in a statement to SpacePolicyOnline that the team will be small and drawn from inside the agency:
The strategy team will comprise of three, year-long detail opportunities for engineers and scientists currently serving as NASA civil servants.
NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA) developed the MSR together. The mission’s estimated cost climbed to $11 billion. In January 2025, outgoing NASA Administrator Bill Nelson left the decision on how to proceed to the incoming Trump administration (NASA Watch on the cancellation). That administration’s fiscal 2026 budget request called for canceling the mission. Congress provided $110 million for Mars Future Missions, but not specifically for MSR.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has said several times that returning the samples would be one of the most important scientific achievements in history.
NASA Watch commentary: The study gives the Perseverance samples a way forward after a year in which the Planetary Science Caucus and four senators pushed Congress to keep the capabilities built for Mars Sample Return alive. A small in-house team is being asked to question old constraints and look at new ways of buying the mission, and it could well find something far cheaper than the $11 billion design. What it will deliver, though, is a high-level architecture at the end of 2027. It will still have to be funded, built and launched. Not doing a mission is a non-starter, and Isaacman has said as much. China is planning to launch Tianwen-3 in 2028 and return samples in 2031, so NASA has little time to spare once the team reports.

Заголовок: California's brand-new Air & Space Center, home of the space shuttle Endeavour, opens today
Полный текст:
The California Science Center's brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center —the home of NASA's space shuttle Endeavour —officially opened to the public today (Nov. 13).

LOS ANGELES — The California Science Center officially opened its brand-new Samuel Oschin Air & Space Center to the public today (Nov. 13).

After more than three decades in development, folks can finally visit the Los Angeles science museum's massive new wing. For most of us, the biggest draw is its centerpiece: the retired space shuttle Endeavour , sitting upright in launch position, towering at nearly 200 feet (61 meters) tall.

"It just takes your breath away when you see that reveal and the doors open and you get to look at it for the first time. It's just — it's overwhelming," former NASA astronaut Garrett Reisman told Space.com during a visit to the museum. Reisman flew on two space shuttle missions during his astronaut career, the first of which was on Endeavour.

The space shuttle Endeavour. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future)

"There are people that come from all over the world, and when they come to Los Angeles, they're going to have the opportunity to see it, too," Reisman added. "The exposure it's going to have is just a force multiplier. There are so many people that can have that opportunity to bring their kids here and show them [the shuttle] and have that experience."

Entering into this exhibit is an experience in and of itself, as I can personally attest; I was among of group of reporters who got a sneak peek at the new wing on Oct. 28. A video presentation ends in a dramatic reveal: Visitors walk into a space where the enormous shuttle, which flew 25 missions to Earth orbit from 1992 to 2011, feels truly larger than life.

The new Endeavour exhibit features a replica launch tower, from which you can look down at the shuttle. (Image credit: Future)

There are a number of interactive exhibits around the base of Endeavour, which you can slide down to (though, of course, you can also take the elevator or stairs). From a shuttle landing simulator to a replica of a shuttle cockpit that you can sit in, to shuttle tires and space tech from across decades of spaceflight history, there's an incredible variety of space artifacts to both observe and interact with.

As for Endeavour itself: It is open, so you can peer inside to see the robotic arm tucked away among a myriad of handles, straps and electronic gear inside. And you can see the shuttle from underneath all the way to the top.

A replica of the space shuttle Endeavour's flight deck. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future)

You can lie on the floor underneath the shuttle's engines, for example, and then take an elevator up the launch tower to come face-to-face with Endeavour's nose. There's even a transparent floor at the top that allows you to stand above the shuttle (though if you have a fear of heights, this might not be for you).

This is the abbreviated description, but know that if you are visiting the California Science Center, you will want to budget a serious amount of time to explore all that this new center has to offer.

External view of the replica Endeavour flight deck at the new California Science Center exhibit. (Image credit: Olivia Hemaratanatorn/Future)

The new air and space center is designed for all ages, and for civilians and astronauts alike. For instance, looking at Endeavour spurred some memories for Reisman: He reflected on his time aboard the shuttle and his time as an astronaut and pinpointed specific places on the shuttle that played important roles in his mission.

"I'm looking at handrails that I held onto during a spacewalk ," he said. "They're the same handrails. My hand was in the glove, but it was wrapped around those handrails. And I practiced for a long time exactly how I was going to do that, how I was going to root my tether, and all that kind of stuff. And I get to stand [here] now. When you go up the elevator there, you can actually have a direct view of those handrails, and every time I see that, I'm thinking about that spacewalk."

But you don't need to have completed a spacewalk to get that view. And, as of today, the general public is welcome to visit the museum, which is free to the public — as is the new aerospace center with its Endeavour exhibit.

However, due to the excitement over this new center opening, you will need to make a reservation online to attend. And, while the museum is free to the public, there is a cost associated with reserving slots during these busy first few days.

The third-quarter financial disclosure landed one day after York announced its acquisition of Outlook Industries on Nov. 12, positioning the company’s corporate expansion alongside a multi-year wait for renewed SDA contracting momentum.

Заголовок: Starship returns to Starbase and a successful tower catch
Полный текст:
Starship descends into the waiting arms of the launch pad tower at Starbase. Image: Adam Bernstein/Spaceflight Now.

SpaceX flew it’s most ambitious Starship flight to date, hoping to demonstrate its revolutionary rocket is fully reusable by recovering both its first and second stages, but although the Ship upper stage reached orbit, deployed 26 Starlink satellites and successfully returned to Starbase, the booster diverted to a fiery splashdown off shore in the Gulf.

The catch occurred at 3:20 p.m. CST (2120 UTC) after Ship 42 reentered the atmosphere over the Pacific Ocean and made a supersonic flight across Mexico and the South West United States before turning out over the ocean and lining itself up for a catch at Staircase’s pad 2.

It was the first time the upper stage of an orbital launch vehicle has returned to Earth and a crucial step to making Starship a fully reusable rocket.

“The epic day has arrived, thanks to the incredibly talented team at SpaceX,” said company founder Elon Musk in a social media post.

The integrated Starship vehicle had lifted off from Starbase in Texas at 4:47 p.m. CST (5:47 p.m. EST / 2247 UTC) on Friday, Nov. 13.

The flight plan called for Super Heavy Booster 22 to return to pad 2 at Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launching from there but it diverted to a splashdown offshore.

Starship lifts off on its 15th flight from Starbase, Texas at 4:48 p.m. CST on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. Image: Adam Bernstein/Spaceflight Now.

“GNC [Guidance, Navigation and Control] triggered that abort. It was doing what it was supposed to do, basically detected that the booster was not in the place that it was supposed to be to proceed with the catch, did an automated abort, and then headed out to that offshore splashdown location,” SpaceX commentator Dan Huot said in an update about 16.5 hours into the mission. He clarified an earlier update he gave on the SpaceX webcast: “I did a disservice to our booster GNC guys last night. It was not a GNC issue that caused us not to come back.”

The vehicle exploded and disappeared from view before appearing to rise back out of the sea as remaining propellants burned off. Three previous boosters were caught by the launch pad tower but Version 3 of the Super Heavy is yet to make a successful return.

Super Heavy Booster B22 explodes before hitting the water off shore after diverting from a potential catch by the launch pad tower’s chopsticks. Image: Adam Bernstein/Spaceflight Now.

Following the successful deployment of 26 Version 3 Starlink satellites, Ship 42 entered a long coast phase of 14 orbits of the planet.

SpaceX had options to end the mission early with splashdowns off Hawaii and Chile but everything went smoothly and the Ship was cleared to land at Starbase.

[Дополнительно: The Guardian – Space]
Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight. The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times. Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights. The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship. Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.

Заголовок: Think you have good eyesight? Try counting the stars in the Pleiades tonight
Полный текст:
Every November, I give myself a completely unscientific eyesight test using one of my favorite sights in the night sky — the Pleiades. How many stars can you see?

Every autumn, I conduct an eyesight test that no reputable optometrist would understand.

I go outside, find the Pleiades and count how many stars I can see. Usually I start confidently. One, two, three, four, five. Then things become contentious. Is that another star? Did I actually see it, or did I decide I ought to see it because I know it's there? I look away, look back and begin again.

This is not, I should emphasize, a meaningful test of eye health. What it tests, rather, is how badly I've prepared for looking at the night sky.

The Pleiades sit roughly 444 light-years away in Taurus and are right now becoming extremely convenient in the evening sky. You don't need a telescope to find them. You don't even need binoculars. In fact, you're likely to catch their collective brightness in your peripheral vision every time you go outside and look up.

But every November the Pleiades remind me that naked-eye observing isn't as simple as opening the back door and looking up. How many Pleiades I can see can change depending on what I do during the next 10 minutes.

What's happening and when to look

You can easily see the Pleiades as a bright misty patch in your peripheral vision during winter. (Image credit: Haitong Yu via Getty Images)

The Pleiades, also known as Messier 45 (M45) or the "Seven Sisters," are an open star cluster in Taurus. They're one of the closest clusters to the solar system and some of the youngest stars you can see with the naked eye — just 100 million years old. They're basically newborns.

In mid-November, they rise in the east in the early evening and climb higher as the night progresses, making this an excellent time to get acquainted with them. Look east after dark for a tiny, compact group of stars. If you know Orion, which rises later, the Pleiades are above and to the right of it from mid-northern latitudes. Nearby you'll also find orange Aldebaran and the much broader V-shaped Hyades cluster. The Hyades are closer to the sun , but their stars are about 625 million years old.

The name "Seven Sisters" creates an immediate observational trap: people assume they're supposed to see seven stars. That's not necessarily true. In fact, six is a common naked-eye result under decently dark conditions (note that the shape of the six brightest is like a mini Big Dipper /Plough), while people with sharp eyesight under darker skies may see more. The cluster itself contains about 1,000 stars. The number you personally distinguish depends on eyesight, sky brightness, atmospheric conditions and how well your eyes have adapted to darkness.

That makes M45 much more interesting to me than a simple tick-box target. So tonight, don't just find the Pleiades — count them.

How and when I'm watching it

Counting the stars you can see in the Pleiades is a fun way to test your naked-eye observing skills. (Image credit: Siesei / 500px via Getty Images)

I'm going to run my Pleiades eye test in stages. First, I'll step outside and look almost immediately. I'll count the individual stars I can distinguish without spending ages convincing myself about marginal ones. Then I'll wait. After about 10 minutes (without looking at my phone or bright outdoor lights, of course), I'll count again. Full dark adaptation takes considerably longer, but even 10 minutes can make an obvious difference when you've just come from a brightly lit house.

I'll then try my trusty 10x50 binoculars. This is where the experiment stops being subtle. The little naked-eye knot of brightness suddenly becomes a field filled with stars. The Pleiades don't just become brighter through binoculars. Their whole character changes because stars that were below my naked-eye threshold appear. I'll also use the averted vision technique, looking slightly to one side rather than directly at M45. It's one of the best demonstrations of the technique, with its fainter stars seemingly popping into view as your more light-sensitive peripheral vision takes over.

Stargazer's corner: November 13-19, 2026

It's a good week to see "Earthshine" on the crescent moon. (Image credit: Jeff Schneiderman via Getty Images)

The moon is returning to the evening sky this week, waxing from a thin crescent toward first quarter. It reaches first quarter around Nov. 17, so moonlight becomes progressively more noticeable during the first half of the night. Look southwest during twilight, and you'll see the beautiful sight of a crescent moon sporting Earthshine, sunlight reflected from Earth onto the moon's night side.

Overnight, Nov. 15-16, don't miss Mars and Jupiter in conjunction. The two planets will appear just over a degree apart, rising in the east during the evening before climbing high into the southern sky in the hours before sunrise.

The following night, Nov. 17-18, the Leonid meteor shower peaks. This is one shower where staying up later actually matters. Leo, the constellation containing the shower's radiant, doesn't rise until late, so the better opportunity comes after midnight and toward the predawn hours.

Asterism of the week: The Kids

Auriga is one of the easiest constellations to find in the Northern Hemisphere's winter night sky. (Image credit: Starry Night)

Auriga, "the Charioteer," is easy to see in the northeastern and eastern sky during November evenings, but have you spied the asterism close to its brightest star, Capella? It's known as the "Goat Star," though its Latin name is the diminutive of capra, meaning "little she-goat." The reason is esoteric — Capella represents Amalthea, the mythological goat that suckled the infant Zeus — but there is a neat asterism (shape of stars) nearby that suddenly makes sense. Close to Capella is a triangle of faint stars that are known as The Kids — Epsilon, Zeta and Eta Aurigae — traditionally imagined as the offspring of Capella. It's one of those little patterns that makes a constellation much easier to recognize.

Заголовок: 'Martian Isolation' is an upcoming sci-fi survival horror game that looks like 'The Martian' and 'Event Horizon' had a horrific child
Полный текст:
It looks like 'The Martian,' but due to international copyright laws, it's not.

"Martian Isolation" is an upcoming single-player, first-person survival horror game that's just been revealed with a suitably creepy launch trailer. And yes, it does look an awful lot like " The Martian ," doesn't it?

There's a lot of survival gameplay on display here that mirrors Mark Watney's tale of survival on the Red Planet, as your stranded protagonist is forced to explore the Martian surface to acquire resources, grow plants, and repair their base.

That comparison to Andy Weir's sci-fi masterpiece does fall away as you get further into the trailer, though, when the horror part of the game's description comes into play: Flickering lights, creepy figures stalking the halls of your Martian habitat, and blood dripping from the walls.

Oh yeah, that's some good creepy sci-fi horror right there. It's giving " Event Horizon ", and that's always getting a thumbs-up from me.

There's no release date scheduled at this time, with the 'Martian Isolation' Steam page simply listing it as "coming soon," though the YouTube trailer description does say it "will be available on Steam in 2027".

You can't pre-order yet, but if this looks like your jam, you can add it to your wishlist.

Beyond that, we know shockingly little about this title. It's the debut game from Golden Milestone Studio, but there's very little information out there beyond a name. The latest blog post on the game's Steam page says that they're a "small team," but what we've seen so far is encouraging.

There seems to be a pronounced split between the survival and horror elements of the game along the day/night cycle. Daytime sees you exploring the Martian surface, smashing rocks, cleaning solar panels, and doing sick jumps on a quad bike.

Заголовок: Dense Galaxy Clusters Foster Mechanisms That Throttle Star Formation
Полный текст:
The Cosmic Noon was when the Universe's Stelliferous Era Began, and star formation was prodigious during that epoch. But since then, star formation has slowed to a relative crawl, despite the fact that we can watch them forming in regions throughout the Milky Way. What happened to the hydrogen gas that forms stars? New research found clues in a particulary dense galaxy cluster.

Star-forming regions are plentiful in the Milky Way, and they're some of the most visually glorious sights in the galaxy. In these regions, the powerful light from massive young stars shapes and energizes gas into glowing arrangements of filaments and billowing clouds. Astronomers study these intently, and astrophotographers share their enthusiasm.
One of the most well-known star forming regions is the stunning Orion Nebula, captured in all its glory by space telescopes like the Hubble and the JWST, and by astrophotographers on the ground. Most of us have seen some of these images, even if only in passing.
Despite the presence of so many star-forming regions, the Milky Way only forms about 6 or 7 new stars every year. This pales in comparison with the cosmos' peak star formation rate about 10 billion years ago. That period of time is called the Cosmic Noon, and during that epoch, star formation was as much as 30 times greater than it is today, all across the Universe, including in the Milky Way.
But that all changed.
The star formation rate has slowed precipitously, and today it's dropped by about 97%. What caused this drop in star formation? Stars form from cold, dense gas, so something must have happened to the gas.
Astronomers know that environmental effects play a leading role in diminishing gas supplies and slowing star formation, both inside galaxies and between galaxies in galaxy groups. Stellar winds can blow gas away, and astrophysical jets from active galactic nuclei (AGN) can heat gas and disperse it. There are other types of disruptions, like gas stripping via galaxy mergers, and galaxy deformations from the same mergers. Sometimes galaxies can merge and gas can be spread out into space in tidal tails. In other cases, galactic star-forming gas is heated through interactions with the much hotter intergalactic medium, or even stripped away by these encounters.
Since most galaxies exist in galaxy groups, researchers try to understand the drop in star formation in these environments. But measurements of the gas supply in galaxy groups are rare.
New research to be published in Astronomy and Astrophysics measured how the supply of molecular gas, the raw material of star formation, is shaped by a galaxy's wider environment in dense galaxy clusters. It's titled "Probing the molecular gas content of galaxies in an over-dense group at z~0.7: A test case for environmental quenching," and the lead author is Jonathan Freundlich. Freundlich is an astrophysicist at the University of Strasbourg, Astronomical Observatory (ObAS). The work is focused on a distant galaxy group called COSMOS-Gr30.
This image shows a dense region of the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group about 6.5 billion light-years away from Earth. The observations were made using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope. The image was the ESO's Picture of the Week on the 13th of November 2017. Image Credit: ESO/T. Contini (IRAP, Toulouse), B. Epinat (LAM, Marseille)
When astronomers want to probe molecular hydrogen (H2), the raw stuff of star formation, they face an obstacle. Despite being by far the most abundant molecule in the interstellar medium and the primary ingredient in the giant molecular clouds (GMCs) where stars form, H2 is virtually undetectable in radio observations. Since star formation needs cold gas, radio is the way to observe it. Astronomers make us of the fact that carbon monoxide (CO) is the second most abundant component of GMCs, and observe it as a proxy for H2. In particular, they measure what are called CO(2-1) emissions, which appear when CO drops its energy state and releases a photon with radio levels of energy. Then they rely on a standard conversion factor between H2 and CO to turn CO observations into H2 observations.
That's what they did in this research that focuses on COSMOS-Gr30, an exceptionally dense group of galaxies.
"We investigated the impact of group environment on molecular gas reservoirs at an intermediate redshift by observing the CO(2-1) emission from the galaxy group COSMOS-Gr30 at zâ¼0.7 with the Institut de Radioastronomie Millimetrique (IRAM) NOrthern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) and 30m telescope," the authors write. This is a very dense environment where massive cosmic filaments intersect and host a large structure of ionized gas that's about 100 billion square light years in size.
This is the COSMOS-Gr30 galaxy group, located about 7 billion light years away, as seen with the JWST. The contours show the structure of diffuse ionized gas in between the group's member galaxies, as observed with the Multi-Unit Spectral Explorer instrument on the ESO's Very Large Telescope. Image Credits: Casey et al. 2023, Epinat et al. 2018, 2024, Freundlich et al. 2026.
The researchers measured the gas in the interstellar medium (ISM) inside of the galaxies as well as the gas in the intergalactic medium (IGM) between the galaxies. These simultaneous measurements generated a more comprehensive look at star-forming gas and its availability in dense galaxy cluster environments. It revealed mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in dense clusters.
"Deep MUSE (Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer) observations reveal a large, massive structure of ionized gas surrounding eight galaxies of the group, including one active galactic nucleus (AGN) host," the authors write. "This gas is not pristine and was likely expelled from the galaxies through both internal processes, such as star formation and AGN outflows, and external processes in the dense environment, such as ram pressure stripping and tidal interactions."
The results also show that less than one-third of the gas displaced from COSMOS-Gr30's member galaxies and moved into the diffuse structure is cold enough to form stars.
The researchers found that galaxies in this dense environment have only about 20% to 40% of the molecular gas found in typical main-sequence galaxies. Main-sequence galaxies are benchmark galaxies that form stars at a steady, typical rate.
Astronomers have studied molecular gas and its availability for star formation inside galaxies before, and they've done it for the intergalactic medium, too. But this work takes it a step further by characterizing gas availability in dense cluster environments. The research "... highlights the importance of simultaneously probing gas reservoirs within galaxies and the surrounding intragroup medium to capture environmental quenching in action," the authors explain.
"In the case of CGr30, the depletion of molecular gas within galaxies, combined with the presence of an extended gas structure, provides a consistent picture of environmental quenching," the researchers write.
This is the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) radio interferometer, located in the Hautes-Alpes at an altitude of 2550m. It has 12x15m radio dishes, and was used in this work to observe CO emissions in the galaxies of the COSMOS-Gr30 group. Image Credit: IRAM-gre via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).
They do state a caveat with their results, and that regards some of the uncertainties in their work, including the star-formation rate (SFR) and how accurate the CO observations are as a proxy for molecular hydrogen.
"Although the uncertainties are significant, this suggests that environmental processes efficiently deplete molecular gas reservoirs in the galaxies of this group," the authors write.
More observations of COSMOS-Gr30 will address these uncertainties, and ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, will provide important observations. It's the most powerful radio antenna array in the world, more powerful than NOEMA used in this work. It has 66 high-precision 12 meter antennas that can collectively create a baseline up to 16 km wide. It can zoom into regions like COSMOS-Gr30 to uncover unseen detail.
"Furthermore, more precise SFR measurements are necessary to decrease the uncertainties, and larger samples of target galaxies in groups will allow us to assess group-to-group variance," the authors conclude.

Заголовок: Кто в мозге отбирает наши воспоминания
Полный текст:
Кто в мозге отбирает наши воспоминания

112 человек рассматривали незнакомые картинки, а электроды в их мозге тем временем слушали отдельные нейроны. Позже в тот же день людей просили вспомнить увиденное. Так исследователи из Cedars-Sinai нашли один из «фильтров», который решает, что мы запомним. И нашёлся он там, где его не очень-то ждали, — в миндалевидном теле.

Миндалина это структура размером с грецкий орех глубоко в височной доле. Её давно знают как центр эмоций, социального поведения и страха, а её вклад в память связывали в основном с эмоционально яркими событиями. Новая работа показывает, что она участвует и в запоминании вполне будничных картинок.

Откуда у людей электроды в мозге? Все участники — пациенты с эпилепсией: электроды им вживляют, чтобы отслеживать приступы. Для науки это редкая возможность записать работу отдельных нейронов у живого человека.

В миндалине нашлись нейроны-«специалисты»: одни особенно отзывчивы на лица, другие на животных, третьи уже на пейзажи. Чем сильнее такой нейрон реагировал на картинку «своей» категории, тем выше был шанс, что человек её потом вспомнит. Результат подтвердился на двух независимых наборах данных.

Перспективы при этом заманчивые. Проблемы с памятью при болезни Альцгеймера и височной эпилепсии отчасти связаны со сбоями в миндалине. Тогда она может стать новой мишенью для нейромодуляции или клеточной терапии. Следующий вопрос — отбирает ли миндалина также звуки и запахи.

Заголовок: Shape-Shifting Robotic "Slugs" Could One Day Crawl Across Alien Worlds
Полный текст:
Robots have been a mainstay of our early space exploration efforts. But they normally have wheels. Or in some cases, rotors. While those solutions are great on flat ground, they struggle with jagged boulders or tight crevices. So engineers have been working on alternative robotic form factors, and a recent paper in Nature Machine Intelligence from researchers at Colorado State Universityâs Adaptive Robotics Lab, describes a unique morphology using a design principle typically seen in architecture rather than robotics - tensegrity.
Tensegrity was originally made popular by Buckminster Fuller in the mid-20th century. Itâs a blend of the words âtensionâ and âintegrityâ, and at its core it uses rigid rods that push outwards against elastic cables that pull inwards. So, instead of relying on heavy metal hinges, the rods âfloatâ on a web of tension.
This isnât the first time the idea has been brought to space exploration, though. NASA has been exploring its use cases for over a decade, perhaps most notably with the SUPERball - a spherical cage designed to withstand high-speed planetary landings without parachutes by absorbing the shocks of impact across its network of cables.
Fraser talks about some other robots that could end up exploring other worlds.
But this is one of the first times the idea has been applied to robotics. The CSU researchers have developed what they call the Tensegrity-based Continuum Robot (TeCoBot). Measuring in at around 587 mm (~2 ft) long and weighing around 600 grams, the cylindrical bot combined a squishy, flexible spine with adaptable dual mechanical claws, which provide the real interesting use cases of the technology.
TeCoBotâs body is made out of four stacked icosahedral tensegrity modules that create a continuous, flexible backbone. Each module is built around six lightweight rods suspended inside a 3D printed stretchy lattice. Three cables made up of 40-lb braided fishing wire run through the center of the robot, and by pulling on each of them with small motors attached to its base, the robot can bend in any direction - like an âelephantâs trunkâ as a press release puts it. It can also scrunch down to around half its original size if all three lines are pulled at the same time.
But whatâs most interesting about the technology is its modularity, which relies on the claws on either end. These claws are swappable, so if a robot needs to handle delicate cargo engineers can put a soft-padded claw on it. But, if needed, those soft pads can be swapped out for a heavier duty gripper claw that uses a worm gear to clamp and hold onto another gripper without draining any battery.
Fraser talks about the concept of "grey goo" - or self-replicating robots able to automate space exploration.
This unlocks all sorts of additional opportunities. As a stand-alone single robot, TeCoBot is already relatively capable - it can inch along like a caterpillar, roll sideways, and even climb vertically. It also exhibits what roboticists call âembodied intelligenceâ that means its body can naturally give way when bumped or when it runs into something without needing a whole control system to adjust to the changed environment.
But when they combine together, they unlock whole new operating modes. Using their claws to grab one another, three TeCoBots can self-configure into a wide variety of shapes. The paper discusses three robots wrapping themselves around a large pipe, and forming a H-shaped walker to crawl through tight spaces. But perhaps most interestingly for anyone who hates cleaning as much as this author, they are also capable of teaming up to clean off a table.
Those feats might not seem immediately applicable to space exploration, but the underlying modularity and adaptability would be extremely useful in the rough craters of the Moon or underground caverns on Mars. Weâve already reported on a snake robot designed to explore those exact locations, and this seems like a step up in functionality from that.
Video of the TeCoBot in action. Credit - Adaptive Robotics Lab YouTube Channel
That being said, it still has a long way to go before weâd see it on another heavenly body. Currently, engineers have to manually control the bots via a WiFi connection - which isnât exactly easy on deep space missions. But they do plan to make improvements on the design, upgrading the motors for faster movement and adding swarm intelligence to allow dozens of these modular robots to band together. If that development goes as planned, these elephant trunk styled robots might serve as some of our most intrepid deep space explorers.

Заголовок: Astronomers trace mystery radio signals back to cosmic odd couple of white dwarf and sun-like star
Полный текст:
"It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths, we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

Astronomers have traced a mysterious radio signal back to a cosmic odd couple comprised of a dead star, a white dwarf, and its stellar companion, a sun-like star.

The white dwarf in the newly discovered system, designated GPM J071507−114153 and located around 5,000 light-years away, spins once every eight minutes, sending out radio pulses. These radio pulses have been seen from binary systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars before, but rarely from a system like GPM J071507−114153.

GPM J071507−114153 belongs to a class of celestial objects called long-period transients (LPTs) known to produce radio signals that switch on and off over intervals of minutes or hours. Around a dozen LPTs have been detected since the team behind this research found the first in 2021. Several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and a companion star, but it has been unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. That means the discovery of GPM J071507−114153 and finding that the pulses come from close to the white dwarf could be a significant step toward understanding the nature of LPTs.

The unusual system consists of a small and highly energetic white dwarf pulsar, orbiting a much larger star similar to our sun. (Image credit: ICRAR)

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion," team leader and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKA), Sam McSweeney, said in a statement . "So we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself."

The pulses seen by the team also allowed them to detect stellar flares erupting on the sun-like star.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence,' which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface," team member Natasha Hurley-Walker of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR), Curtin University, Australia, said. "It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5,000 light-years away."

South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope. (Image credit: South African Radio Astronomy Observatory (SARAO))

Hurley-Walker and the team at ICRAR have been at the cutting edge of rare star systems like this.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia," Hurley-Walker said. "We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position."

After the radio telescopes detected this LPT, it was confirmed using the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea in Hawaii. The visible light follow-up of Keck also confirmed that the star in GPM J071507−114153 was a G-type star, just like the sun.

MeerKAT and the MWA are both precursors for the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope project. That means the future is bright for LPTs.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKA telescopes are completely built," McSweeney said.

The team's research was published on Thursday (Nov. 12) in the journal Nature Astronomy.

Заголовок: Pentagon rebrands principal AI shop as ‘Super Intelligence Office’
Полный текст:
The redesignation follows President Donald Trump’s push to replace references to artificial intelligence with “super intelligence” across the federal government.

WASHINGTON — The Defense Department announced today that it has redesignated its Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO) as the Super Intelligence Office (SIO).
The DoD said the new name does not reflect a change in mission but rather aligns the office’s designation with the Trump administration’s broader effort to replace references to artificial intelligence with “super intelligence” across the federal government. Cameron Stanley, the department’s top AI official who also helms the SIO, said in a statement that the rebrand also reflects the Pentagon’s priorities moving forward.
“We have moved beyond experimental prototypes. As the Super Intelligence Office, our mission is to harness the full power of sovereign Super Intelligence to ensure decisive military superiority across every domain,” Stanley said.
The redesignation follows President Donald Trump’s September announcement that all federal agencies should replace references to AI with the term super intelligence, or SI. At the time, he argued that the word “artificial” made the technology sound fake, despite its growing capabilities.
The terminology shift has raised questions within the tech community, where “superintelligence” has historically referred to a specific, hypothetical form of general artificial intelligence that exceeds overall human intelligence — a capability that does not currently exist.
The Pentagon has been among the federal government’s most aggressive adopters of AI technology, with the CDAO leading efforts to expand its use across military operations and department functions. Those efforts include making artificial intelligence tools more widely available to military personnel through GenAI.mil an enterprise platform providing users access to commercial generative AI models.
The office’s portfolio includes the Maven Smart System, an AI-enabled intelligence and targeting platform, and the War Data Platform, a central data hub formerly known as Advana. The CDAO has also spearheaded numerous exercises and experimentation efforts aimed at integrating artificial intelligence and other advanced capabilities across the department.
The CDAO’s transition to SIO “will roll out across digital systems, enterprise applications and component headquarters over the coming weeks,” the DoD said. “Existing operational programs, industry solicitations and defense partnerships will continue uninterrupted under the new banner.” The department has also launched SI.mil, which will serve as the renamed office’s primary digital domain.

Заголовок: Obruta Space Solutions signs testing deal with Northern Ireland’s Resonate
Полный текст:
Ottawa-based Obruta Space Solutions said it has signed an agreement with Resonate Testing, a lab in Newry, Northern Ireland, that would see its spacecraft docking hardware put through the vacuum, vibration and shock tests needed to prove it can fly.
The companies announced the Technical Collaboration and Mutual Support Agreement in a news release. The Ottawa company develops autonomous rendezvous, proximity operations and docking (RPOD) technology.
Its primary product is the RPOD Kit, a modular package aimed at satellite servicing, space debris removal and extending the life of aging satellites. The companies say the agreement is meant to move the kit up the technology readiness levels.
Resonate would run thermal vacuum (TVAC) testing, which mimics the airless heat and cold of orbit, along with vibration and mechanical shock tests. The work would be aligned with European Cooperation for Space Standardization (ECSS) requirements. The companies say that gives Obruta a path into European and European Space Agency (ESA) mission opportunities.
The testing, along with engineering and qualification planning support, would be carried out under future commercial contracts the two companies have yet to agree.
Kevin Stadnyk, Obruta’s chief executive, said the partnership “provides an established, ECSS-aligned environmental testing pathway that accelerates our RPOD Kit toward flight heritage.”
Resonate will introduce Obruta to contacts and programs in the U.K., Ireland and the European Union, and Obruta will do the same for Resonate in Canada and the wider North American commercial space sector. The two also plan to look at joint conference appearances, technical case studies and trade missions, subject to mutual approval.
Resonate is an independent, accredited lab that tests space hardware alongside battery, fire and mechanical work. It offers TVAC, vibration and shock testing in one location and says it recently passed 50 space customers. Tom Mallon, its founder and managing director, said the deal shows the role Northern Ireland can play in testing and qualifying new space technology.

Заголовок: Gemini Astronaut Photos Inspired Early Earth Observation Program
Полный текст:
NASA astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. captured this image of the area surrounding the Red Sea and Nile river valley on November 14, 1966, during their four-day mission in space. Gemini XII was the final flight of NASA’s Gemini Program.

NASA

Astronauts James A. Lovell Jr. and Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr. orbited Earth from November 11 to 15, 1966, on Gemini XII , the final mission of NASA’s Gemini program.

In addition to successfully completing rendezvous maneuvers and spacewalks, procedures vital to sending American astronauts to the Moon, the crew was also spurring the development of a different field of exploration, observing Earth from space.

The photos taken by Lovell, Aldrin, and other Gemini astronauts demonstrated the value of orbital imagery for studying Earth’s surface. Their images helped scientists make the case for a dedicated Earth observation satellite program. One of strongest advocates for accelerating the use of Earth-observing satellites was William T. Pecora, the director of the United States Geological Survey from 1965 to 1971. In a 1969 statement, Pecora noted that the Earth Resources Observation Satellite (EROS) program he championed, and which later paved the way for Landsat , was “conceived in 1966 largely as a direct result of the demonstrated utility of Mercury and Gemini orbital photography to Earth resource studies.”

For more than five decades, Landsat and other Earth-observing satellites have provided invaluable data used around the world to monitor crops, wildfires, flooding, vegetation health, land use, and countless other changes to our planet.

Заголовок: Hermeus recruits Northrop Grumman to Quarterhorse drone program
Полный текст:
The defense giant will supply mission systems for Hermeus’ Quarterhorse unmanned aircraft, adding a new partner among a team of industry heavyweights.

WASHINGTON — Northrop Grumman is partnering with Hermeus to supply mission systems for the startup’s aircraft, adding another industry player to the team as Hermeus pushes to field a high-speed drone.
In a press release published Thursday, Hermeus said Northrop will provide “integrated mission systems design, development, integration, and sustainment” for Hermeus’ aircraft. The partnership “creates a path to equip Hermeus’ aircraft with technology across sensing, communications, navigation, and command and control, allowing the aircraft to operate more intelligently and take on more complex missions,” the release adds.
“We’re building a new class of aircraft that gives the warfighter improved speed, range, and flexibility while integrating into the existing Force,” Hermeus CEO Zach Shore said in the company’s release. “Adding Northrop Grumman’s battle-tested mission systems will push what those aircraft can do in real world scenarios and help us field operational capability faster.”
Founded in 2018, Hermeus is currently developing its Quarterhorse drone with funding from the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit. Military officials have expressed strong interest in the platform, which the company is pushing to fly at speeds as fast as Mach 3 through an iterative design process. The drone achieved supersonic flight earlier this year.
Northrop is a key supplier of mission systems across the defense industrial base, including radars, electronic warfare kits and navigation equipment for US military platforms.
In a separate release, Northrop said it will integrate its mission systems onto the Quarterhorse. Northrop Program Manager Kyle Mimken told Breaking Defense in a statement that “at a high level,” the company will bring “electronic warfare, communications, sensing and navigation along with the payload-integration and systems-engineering experience needed to make those capabilities work together on an aircraft.”
Mimken declined to comment on which specific systems the company plans to integrate, but stressed that Northrop’s contributions will help make the aircraft more survivable and effective. He added that the partnership’s “immediate focus” is mission systems integration and coordinating with Hermeus to prepare for flight testing.
“We expect to begin trials of elements of our mission-system kit in our testing environments in the summer,” Mimken said.
Northrop’s addition marks another industry heavyweight on the Quarterhorse team. In September, Hermeus revealed that it will use autonomy software supplied by defense tech firm Anduril for upcoming flight tests.
The Quarterhorse is powered by Pratt & Whitney’s F100 fighter jet engine. Shortly after announcing the Anduril partnership, Hermeus executives told Breaking Defense that the company had reached an agreement with Pratt to manufacture the F100 under license — the first such deal for an American firm. Hermeus officials believe the arrangement positions the company to be virtually the only vertically integrated planemaker in the business.
Hermeus is also building its own turbine-based combined cycle (TBCC) engine based on the F100. A TBCC engine combines a jet turbine with a ramjet engine to create an integrated propulsion system capable of pushing an aircraft to hypersonic speeds exceeding Mach 5. Hermeus’ TBCC concept, dubbed Chimera, would serve as the propulsion system for the company’s envisioned hypersonic aircraft, the Darkhorse.
