Заголовок: REVIEW: Spectrum Optics SkyPilot 127
Полный текст:
The smart telescope revolution has grown rapidly over the past few years. Most of these scopes focus primarily on electronic imaging, though, and while amateur astronomers may marvel at the images, they also still enjoy the simple pleasure of looking directly through a telescope.
That’s where the SkyPilot 127 from Spectrum Optics ($999) takes a different approach. Rather than replacing direct observing with a screen-based experience, the SP127 combines a traditional 5-inch (127 millimeters) f/15 Maksutov-Cassegrain telescope with a smart guidance and imaging system.
Dual purpose
At first glance, the SP127 looks like a conventional catadioptric with a standard finder on a motorized alt-azimuth mount. But looks can be deceiving.
The secret lies in that “finder.” On closer inspection, it is not a finder at all, but a 2.1-inch (53 mm) f/4 ED refractor outfitted with a digital camera. This second optical tube is the heart of the SP127’s electronically assisted system, serving as both guide scope and imager. The guide scope determines the telescope’s position through plate solving, slews to selected targets, maintains tracking, and captures images. Spectrum Optics also includes the same intelligent camera and 53 mm refractor in its separately sold SPi53 Smart Telescope system.
The camera is built around a Sony IMX662 CMOS color sensor with 2.9-micrometer pixels and a resolution of 1920×1080 pixels. It includes 64 gigabytes of onboard storage.
The MirroSky app, available for iOS and Android, is central to the SP127’s operation. It controls target selection, image capture, live stacking, and display, while the guide scope and camera work together to find objects and produce live-stacked images.
Meanwhile, the Maksutov is dedicated primarily to visual observing. The optical tube weighs approximately 6.5 pounds (2.95 kilograms) and measures 14.6 inches (370 mm) long. A Vixen-style dovetail makes it easy to remove the optical tube from the mount. Total weight for the assembled SP127 is about 26 pounds (11.8 kg).
In addition to the guide scope/imager, the SP127 comes with a 25 mm Plössl eyepiece, a 90° 1¼” star diagonal, a screw-on visual back, an adjustable tripod with steel legs 1.5 inches (3.8 centimeters) in diameter, cables, an AC adapter, and a Bahtinov focusing mask for the guide scope. The camera’s nosepiece is also internally threaded to accept standard 1¼” filters.
In its standard configuration, the included camera photographs through the 53 mm refractor rather than the Maksutov. Although the camera is removable, Spectrum Optics recommends a separate camera for imaging through the Maksutov because its long focal length and narrow field are not well-suited to the included camera’s plate-solving system. That doesn’t mean you have to invest in more equipment, though; I took some very nice shots of the Moon simply by holding my iPhone to the Mak’s 25 mm eyepiece.
The SP127’s hybrid arrangement works well in practice. After the user selects a target in the app, the guide scope directs the mount to the correct location, then tracks the sky. The observer can view the target visually through the Maksutov while the guide scope stacks and displays images via the app. A word of caution, however: Be careful not to shake the instrument when looking through the eyepiece. Even a slight motion will blur the image being photographed.
Like most Maksutov-Cassegrain systems, the SP127 excels at medium and high magnifications. Its 1,900 mm focal length is especially well-suited for observing the Moon, planets, planetary nebulae, and double stars.

2175 S Grand Ave
Santa Ana, CA 92705
1-888-879-5143

Trial run
For this review, I arranged to receive a sample SP127 directly from Spectrum Optics. It arrived securely packed and in perfect condition.
Setup was easy, thanks to the well-illustrated paper manual that came with the scope. After I aligned the guide scope with the Maksutov during the day, as the instructions suggested, the scope was ready to go. I had everything together in under half an hour.
Control is handled entirely through the MirroSky app. To initialize the scope to the sky, the system uses onboard sensors combined with date, time, and location information supplied by the connected smart device. The camera includes dual-band Wi‑Fi capability supporting both 2.4 and 5 gigahertz connections. During use, the app’s interface was straightforward and easy to navigate. Target acquisition was quick and accurate. Chosen objects were always centered in the field of view. The app also provides guided tours and a database containing more than 100,000 stars, solar system members, and deep-sky sights.
Tracking performance was accurate for visual observations and short-exposure imaging. Since the SP127 uses an alt-azimuth mount, field rotation may become evident around the edges with longer exposures.
The SP127 can be powered by eight user-supplied AA batteries in the mount, a suitable external 12-volt power source, or the included AC adapter.
I found that the Maksutov performed very well. Lunar views were well-defined, with crater walls, rilles, and other surface features standing out crisply. I was especially impressed when, in moments of steady seeing, the SP127 detected a few of the craterlets on the floor of Plato. It passed another tough test by resolving Schröter’s Valley, a sinuous rille near craters Aristarchus and Herodotus.
Planetary performance also proved impressive. Multiple cloud bands as well as the Great Red Spot were clearly visible on Jupiter, and shadows cast by Galilean moons could also be seen on the planet’s cloud tops.
Double stars were another strong point, thanks to the long focal length. The Trapezium in the Orion Nebula, for instance, was striking. The included eyepiece did well, but the view really sparkled when I swapped in my own eyepieces with shorter focal lengths.
Throughout it all, I was very impressed with the crispness of the images, showing the high quality of the Maksutov’s optics. Like most catadioptric telescopes, the SP127 focuses by moving the primary mirror. This takes tight manufacturing tolerances to maintain a precise focus without tilting the mirror. I found that alignment stayed spot-on after swapping eyepieces and refocusing the view.
I was equally impressed with the imaging results using the 53 mm guide scope. The app allows you to customize settings, including gain, exposure length, number of frames to capture, and dark frames. After I experimented with the settings, the Orion Nebula appeared in vivid color after only two minutes of exposure, even as it was setting in my light-polluted sky. The Pleiades also recorded beautifully, although not all members squeezed into the guide scope’s approximately 1.6° by 0.9° field. The Horsehead Nebula, the Whirlpool Galaxy, the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules, and more displayed details exceeding what you might expect from such a small aperture, especially after post-processing using apps like PixInsight, GIMP, and Photoshop.
Final thoughts
The SkyPilot 127 is one of the most original entries in today’s smart telescope market. For observers who still enjoy looking through an eyepiece but appreciate the convenience of app-driven targeting and imaging, the SP127 offers something genuinely special. In a small but growing group of smart telescopes that combine traditional eyepiece observing with integrated electronic imaging, the SP127’s hybrid design makes it an appealing bridge between conventional astronomy and the smart telescope revolution.
Contributing Editor Phil Harrington received the Walter Scott Houston Award in 2018 for his lifelong work in astronomy.

Заголовок: Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded
Полный текст:
The Juno Propulsion co-founder and CEO didn’t grow up dreaming about space, but she’s now on track to make history there. Her Tukwila, Wash., startup aims to fly the first rotating detonation engine in orbit next year.

Juno Propulsion co-founder and CEO Alexis Harroun is working on rotating detonation engines at her startup. (Juno Propulsion Photo)

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners .

A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

“I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she said. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”

Harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion , a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

The technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris .

That’s a big goal for a company that, when the July 2025 NASA call came , was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

Harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she said, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”

No astronaut story

Harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun said watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen , who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun said, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant , awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

“She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and launches go off as planned.”

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and said it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

Working on a engine in the University of Washington Department of Aeronautics & Astronautics, from left: Professor Carl Knowlen, Juno intern Ben Cabot, Alexis Harroun, Ariana Martinez and A&A graduate student Ben Fetters. (UW Photo)

During college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she said.

She spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

“That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she said. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister , still advises her and the company.

“He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this company,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a new master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

“At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and said, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and said it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

After finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun said. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”

Starting a company comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

“I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she said. “So it made that calculus really easy.”

The next Rocketdyne

Alexis Harroun, second from left, with Lucas Heflin, Ari Martinez, and Jill Cornell. While her work at Juno Propulsion takes her mind to outer space, Harroun is more attracted to her home planet and pursuits in nature in her free time. (Photo courtesy of Alexis Harroun)

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she said. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”

That company built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris . Juno wants to play a similar role with a new technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

The first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun said. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”

Building a company has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she said, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun said, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”

Заголовок: Gadi Eisenkot could be Israel’s next leader. His military experience will drive his approach.
Полный текст:
Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a new government, but it won’t be easy.

JERUSALEM — In 2019, Gadi Eisenkot, then at the end of a four-year run as chief of staff of Israel’s military, gave an interview to The New York Times.
In it, he proudly talked about having driven Jerusalem to take a more direct confrontation with Iran, including claiming to strike “thousands” of Iranian targets in Syria. He also warned that Iran was seeking to “strangle Israel from Lebanon, Syria and the Gaza Strip,” a multifront conflict that Jerusalem would need to be prepared to fight and win in.
Today, Israel is engaged in exactly that kind of multifront conflict — and Eisenkot is hoping to once again lead efforts to plan for victory, only this time as the next Prime Minister of Israel.
On Nov. 7, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog announced that he had concluded discussions with the various Israeli political parties in the wake of the Oct. 27 election, and tasked Eisenkot, the leading opposition figure to sitting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, with forming a government.
It won’t be an easy task. Out of the 120 members of the incoming Knesset, parties representing 67 members recommended Eisenkot, and only 46 recommended Netanyahu. Eisenkot could have up to 42 days to try to form a government, but that is not guaranteed as a deadline; it took 80 days for Israel to form a government after elections in 2021.
To form a new government, Eisenkot will need the support of 61 Knesset members. His Yashar party has 21 seats. His preferred coalition partners include the Together party, with 12 seats; the left-leaning Democrats, with eight seats: and Yisrael Beiteinu, which has seven, for a total of 48.
Eisenkot has also been backed by the majority Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, who have 11 and 8 seats respectively — enough to get him over the line on paper. However, the leader of Yisrael Beiteinu, Avigdor Liberman, has rejected forming a government with the Arab parties.
Which is to say, there is no guarantee that Eisenkot will be able to make the complex horse-trading work to form a government. And as he tries to manage that, he is also warning Netanyahu away from any expansion of conflict in the region, writing in a Wednesday letter that the current government must “[e]xercise restraint and caution against dangerous moves that can wait until a new government that has won the Knesset’s confidence is sworn in.” He added that security forces should only be deployed due to a “direct and immediate threat.”
A day later, Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz said “we do not require approval from the opposition or any legal authority to direct the IDF to carry out targeted operations,” referencing Israel’s operations in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran. Katz also met with Israel’s chief of staff on Thursday while Eisenkot met with Netanyahu about the security situation.
If Eisenkot does manage to form a new government, there are hints as to how he could look to shape defense policy in his past experiences with the IDF and his previous statements since entering politics.
A History of War
Eisenkot was born in 1960 in the Israeli city of Tiberias, which sits on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. His family, which had emigrated from Morocco before Eisenkot was born, moved to the southern Israeli city of Eilat when he was a child. He enlisted in the IDF at age 18 and served in the Golani Brigade, one of Israel’s most famous infantry brigades. The brigade was also historically known for being a place of empowerment for soldiers from Mizrahi backgrounds, meaning Jewish immigrants from Arab and Muslim countries.
Eisenkot served in the IDF for four decades, rising to command positions, heading the Judea and Samaria Division during the Second Intifada and heading operations in Northern Command in the wake of the 2006 Lebanon War. He became deputy chief of staff in 2013 and then head of the IDF in 2015. He was in charge of Northern Command during the Israeli strike on a Syrian nuclear facility in 2007.
His IDF biography notes that “Eisenkot was the Chief of General Staff during Operation Good Neighbor — which redefined the IDF’s role in the Middle East — and Operation Northern Shield, which not only emphasized the threat of terrorist organizations but also exhibited the strength of the IDF in combating those threats.” Good Neighbor was an operation that provided aid to Syrians during the Syrian civil war, while Northern Shield was a short operation in December 2018 aimed at eliminating Hezbollah cross-border tunnels from Lebanon.
During his time as chief of staff, Israel began shifting resources to focus on Hezbollah and Iran’s role in Syria. “We are in the midst of a tense and challenging time. The Middle East is transforming into an unrecognizable reality characterized by instability and volatility. These challenges require the IDF, more than ever, to be determined, sophisticated and measured,” Eisenkot said when he took over command in 2015.
With the Syrian civil war raging, the Iranians had taken advantage of the chaos to establish bases and move weapons via Syria to Lebanon. Israel acted to stop this entrenchment through what was called the Campaign Between the Wars (CBW).
Overshadowed by the war that began with the Hamas attack and massacre on Oct. 7, 2023, the CBW involved thousands of strikes in Syria occurring over regular intervals — effectively, a nonstop use of force to ensure that an enemy cannot build up to the point of launching a true military campaign.
The former general is considered hawkish on how he would deal with Hezbollah, referencing the “Dahiya doctrine” of striking the Beirut neighborhood where Hezbollah has forces. On the Iran nuclear threat, a report at The Jerusalem Post indicated in September 2026 that Eisenkot has suggested a tactic of creating “kill zones” around various nuclear sites, though Eisenkot has not directly commented on that report.
Soon after Eisenkot left the army, there was speculation that he could enter politics, which is a traditional route for Israeli top commanders. While Israel has a three-year “cooling off” period before military officials can run for office, at least 14 of the 24 chiefs of staff since Israel’s founding in 1948 have gone on to enter politics, including Yitzhak Rabin, who became prime minister twice, and Ehud Barak, who also held the office. And both of Eisenkot’s predecessors at the helm of the IDF, Gabi Ashkenazi and Benny Gantz, went into politics.
Eisenkot ran as part of the National Unity Party slate, a coalition of several parties, in the 2022 elections. He has served in the Knesset since, where he has sat on a subcommittee examining the IDF’s actions around the Oct. 7 attacks and on a number of committees for defense issues and foreign affairs. He also served as chair of the Caucus for Advancing a Regional Security Arrangements and the Caucus for IDF Reservists.
After the Oct. 7 attack, Eisenkot and Gantz joined the Israeli war cabinet run by Netanyahu. However, Eisenkot has been critical of Israel’s objectives in Gaza, especially after his son was killed there in December 2023. He said in 2024 that Israel should not be deceived into believing Hamas could be completely defeated, a break from Netanyahu’s general statements. Eisenkot also opposed a preemptive strike on Hezbollah during an Oct. 11, 2023 cabinet meeting, over concerns it would split Israel’s military focus.
Eisenkot resigned from the cabinet in June 2024, saying “despite the efforts of many, alongside those of my colleague, the cabinet you [Netanyahu] headed was prevented for a long while from making determining decisions, which were needed to realize the war’s goals and improve Israel’s strategic position.” In June 2025 he also resigned from the Knesset and the National Unity party.
As Israel geared up for elections, he urged Gantz to resign from his party leadership role in September 2025. Days later, Eisenkot founded the Yashar party that would run in the October 2026 elections.
The former chief of staff has also staked out a position on a major domestic issue, saying Israel should draft ultra-Orthodox Jews into the army. Currently they are exempt, and around 50,000 avoid service.

Заголовок: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
Полный текст:
Heinz von Foerster thought population would grow exponentially and "squeeze" us all to death.

As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.

It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus —one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.

Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote.

NASA astronaut Suni Williams rides through New York City as the Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: Photo by Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images)

New Yorkers got a space-y surprise on Wednesday (Nov. 11): Retired NASA astronaut and U.S. Navy Captain Sunita "Suni" Williams rolled down 5th Avenue in the back of a classic convertible wrapped in patriotic decals as Grand Marshal of the Veterans Day Parade.

What is it?

On Wednesday, New York City's 107th annual Veterans Day Parade made its way through Manhattan to the cheers and respectful nods of thousands of onlookers.

The parade is an annual tradition on the holiday, which honors veterans of the U.S. armed forces. As part of the parade, veterans, active-duty soldiers, firefighters, marching bands, youth cadets and more march through the city and honor those who have served and sacrificed in the U.S. military.

This year, the parade featured Suni Williams as its grand marshal. "I’m proud to join New Yorkers and Americans from around the country in honoring the service, sacrifice, and commitment of veterans from every generation," she said during the event.

Why is it incredible?

Williams was selected for NASA's astronaut program in 1998 and retired from it in December 2025 . She spent 608 days in space during her astronaut career, the second-most by an American astronaut behind Peggy Whitson , who racked up 695.

Williams also had an extensive career in the U.S. Navy. She began as an ensign in 1987 before serving in a number of different roles. For example, she was a diving officer and a naval aviator and also provided helicopter combat support during Operation Desert Shield and Operation Provide Comfort. She further served as a squadron safety officer and finally as a captain, a rank she achieved in 2017.

During this time, Williams supported relief efforts following Hurricane Andrew, trained within the U.S. Naval Test Pilot School and gained a wealth of further experience flying as a military pilot.

Williams is part of a longstanding tradition of astronauts serving in the U.S. military. From test pilots to naval officers and more, there's a strong link between the U.S. armed forces and NASA's astronaut program.

Заголовок: I saw Saturn’s rings in seconds with the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian telescope — full review
Полный текст:
Celestron’s StarSense Explorer tech makes this 150mm Dobsonian so easy to operate — but its tabletop design makes me wonder whether beginners should go bigger.

Saturn was only a night past its annual opposition when I pointed the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian straight at it. The planet was at its biggest and brightest of the year, the seeing was good and its famous rings were visibly opening up after appearing edge-on from Earth in recent years. It was an obvious target for a new telescope.

Finding it took seconds. After selecting Saturn in Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app, I followed the on-screen arrows as I moved the telescope across the sky. As I got closer, the app zoomed in until a bullseye turned green. I looked through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, then swapped to the 10mm to see a pale yellow Saturn at 75x magnification, with its rings sharply defined and its giant moon Titan visible in orbit.

At 25 lbs (11.33 kg), the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian is a relative heavyweight. Jamie Carter

The supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces provide 30x and 75x magnification, respectively, but are obvious candidates for future upgrades. Jamie Carter

The StarSense Explorer smartphone dock uses a small mirror. Jamie Carter

It was a stunning view, and exactly the kind of experience a beginner needs from a first telescope. There was no frustration and no wondering whether I was looking in the right place. StarSense took me straight there — but, crucially, I moved the telescope myself. I’ve always liked that combination of hand-holding and DIY observing that Celestron’s StarSense tech gives you.

I’m less convinced by the tabletop telescope it’s attached to. Although this $599 RRP (£379) model is significantly smaller than the Celestron StarSense Explorer 8-inch Dobsonian telescope I’ve previously reviewed, it still weighs 25 lbs (11.33 kg). You need to place it on something sturdy before you can use it comfortably. After living with it in my backyard, I’m not convinced the tabletop format is the advantage it initially appears to be.

An iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted securely into the StarSense Explorer smartphone dock during testing. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

What StarSense Explorer does well

The Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian comes with a red dot finder for manual navigation. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

I’ve used Celestron’s StarSense Explorer system on a variety of telescopes and have always been impressed by how easy this type of smartphone navigation is to use. The technology works just as well here and, for me, it remains one of the best ways of making a traditional optical telescope accessible to a complete beginner.

This isn’t a computerized GoTo telescope. There are no motors to slew across the sky automatically and no tracking system to keep an object centered. Instead, a smartphone sits in a dock attached to the telescope, and its camera looks at the sky via a small mirror. Celestron’s StarSense Explorer app analyzes the reflections of the stars it sees, works out exactly where the telescope is pointing and tells you which direction to push it to reach the object you want to observe.

My iPhone 16 Pro Max fitted perfectly into the dock, and the initial alignment process was identical to what I’d used before. Once that was done, I used StarSense to find the Pleiades (M45), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Double Cluster in Perseus and Saturn. It worked every time, with the target appearing in the eyepiece when the app told me I had reached it.

I can find all of those objects without an app, but that’s not really the point. Beginners often struggle to translate a star chart or an astronomy app into actual telescope movements. StarSense gives you confidence that you’re heading in the right direction while still requiring you to operate it physically.

That makes it a useful way to learn the night sky. After repeatedly pushing the telescope from one familiar object to another, you begin to understand how everything fits together. That’s very different from pressing a button and watching a GoTo or smart telescope move itself, and it’s why I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, even on a relatively wide-field telescope like this one.

The 5.9-inch mirror produces lovely wide-field views

A Newtonian reflector uses curved and flat mirrors to gather and focus light into an eyepiece. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The StarSense system may be the headline feature, but the reason to buy any Dobsonian is aperture. This one uses a 150mm (5.9-inch) parabolic primary mirror with a 750mm focal length and a relatively fast f/5 focal ratio. That combination gives it fairly low-power, wide-field views that are particularly well suited to large star clusters.

The Pleiades was one of my favorite views. At 30x through the supplied 25mm eyepiece, the telescope gave me a sharp field of stars and a particularly good view of what I call “Carter’s Whip” — the curving line of stars running through the cluster. I saw little obvious softness towards the edges, and focusing was straightforward.

The 150mm f/5 optics are particularly well suited to wide-field views of objects such as the Pleiades. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) was a different proposition. From my light-polluted backyard, I could see Andromeda’s bright core, but not its outskirts or its satellite galaxies. That’s largely a consequence of observing a galaxy from a city, not a criticism of a 150mm telescope, but it’s a useful reminder of what visual astronomy is actually like. Don’t expect the colorful, detailed views of galaxies and nebulas you see in astrophotos, such as the stacked images a smart telescope can give you.

Saturn was more rewarding, but I would have liked more magnification when the seeing was this good. Add a Barlow lens if planets are a priority — it can double the magnification of any eyepiece you use it with.

Celestron StarSense Explorer Dobsonians are available with apertures up to 12 inches. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

Overall, I was impressed by the telescope’s optics. The views were sharp and contrast-y, and there’s enough aperture here to make a serious start in visual astronomy. However, the two supplied 25mm and 10mm Kellner eyepieces are decidedly entry-level — and obvious candidates for upgrading in the medium term.

The focuser is a weak point. It’s a fairly basic 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion design, but I noticed some wobble and vibration while using it. That’s a shame because the focuser is one of the parts of a telescope you constantly interact with, and something smoother and more precise would make the entire instrument feel more accomplished.

The supplied red dot finder is of fairly basic quality. Jamie Carter

A tabletop telescope needs the right table

A grab handle makes it easy to move the Celestron StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian into position. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The tabletop design isn’t necessarily as convenient as it sounds. I expected this scope to feel considerably more convenient than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Dobsonian. The base has built-in grab handles, but the assembled telescope's shape and weight make it awkward to lift onto a table — I certainly wouldn’t recommend it to anyone with a bad back. You could move the optical tube and base separately, but that starts to cancel out the convenience of owning a relatively compact tabletop telescope.

You also need to choose your table carefully. It has to be sturdy enough not to introduce vibrations, but not so large that you have to stretch across it to reach the eyepiece as the telescope points to different parts of the sky. I found myself bending and stretching into some awkward positions.

Once it’s in position, the Dobsonian mount worked well. The balance was good, and I didn't need to adjust the altitude tension, while the movements offered a useful mix of resistance and fluidity as I followed StarSense around the sky. At 75x, however, keeping Saturn centered was more difficult than I expected. It was easy to over-nudge the telescope, then correct in the opposite direction.

Celestron sells an optional tripod for the telescope, and after using the tabletop base, I can see why that might be attractive. However, I’d personally rather put the money towards a larger Dobsonian whose base is designed to sit directly on the ground.

Putting it together was harder than using it

The 1.25-inch rack-and-pinion focuser is quite basic, and produced some wobble and vibration during testing. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

This scope doesn’t arrive in one piece. Assembly took about 90 minutes, and it required all manner of screws and screwdrivers. The main problem was getting the screws into the holes in the Dobsonian base, which took so much effort that I ended up with a blister on my hand. That’s not what I expected from a telescope aimed at beginners, especially when almost everything about using it has been designed to make things easy.

Once built, things improved considerably. My review sample arrived well collimated, so I didn’t have to adjust the mirror alignment. The tube rings, phone dock and general construction were all good enough for a telescope at this price, and nothing about the telescope felt particularly fragile. Once the telescope is outside, on a suitable table and aligned, it’s an impressively straightforward instrument to use.

Why I would still choose the 8-inch version

The mount's rack is a handy place to store eyepieces. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The more I used the StarSense Explorer 150mm Dobsonian, the more I wondered who really benefits from the tabletop format. It’s certainly smaller than Celestron’s 8-inch StarSense Explorer Dobsonian, but it’s still a substantial object to store, and I didn’t feel any more inclined to grab it for a quick observing session.

Going bigger offers an optical advantage. An 8-inch/203mm aperture collects about 83% more light than a 150mm aperture, which matters when you’re observing faint deep-sky objects. The 8-inch StarSense also had a much nicer 2-inch Crayford focuser, and generally felt like a telescope with a little more room to grow into.

The supplied 25mm Kellner eyepiece gives 30x magnification. Jamie Carter

Visual astronomy matters more than ever

StarSense uses arrows and an on-screen bullseye to guide the telescope toward objects, but you still have to move the telescope yourself. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

Dobsonians are the perfect companion to smart telescopes. The latter have completely changed what beginners can photograph from their backyards, particularly under light pollution. They can reveal galaxies and nebulas that are extremely difficult or impossible to see visually. I use them all the time. But they are no substitute for navigating to and actually seeing objects in the night sky with your own eyes.

The two approaches don’t need to compete. A smart telescope has to be pointed and then left alone for an hour or four to stack images. That time could be spent pushing something like the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian around the sky, and actually looking through an eyepiece at the same objects. One shows you far more than your eyes can detect, but the other lets you see the photons yourself — and make a human connection with the night sky.

Where the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits against its rivals

The base itself moves easily, but is a pain to construct. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

At $599 RRP (£379), the StarSense Explorer 150mm sits in an interesting part of the beginner telescope market. There are smaller tabletop Dobsonians like the Celestron Moon Mission 100mm without smartphone navigation, but I think StarSense is worth paying extra for, particularly for a first-time telescope owner.

If you mainly want to observe planets and the moon, a refractor like the Celestron StarSense Explorer LT 70AZ also makes sense. However, if you want to go relatively large, I do recommend the StarSense Explorer 150mm Tabletop Dobsonian — with an important qualification. Its optics are good, StarSense is superb, and it’s an excellent way for a beginner to learn their way around the night sky, but I’m not convinced that 150mm is the sweet spot for this particular design. It’s too big to feel genuinely convenient as a tabletop telescope, yet not big enough to deliver the full advantages of a larger Dobsonian.

If space is tight, this is a very capable first telescope. If you have room for the 8-inch StarSense Explorer, I’d go bigger.

Climate action has stalled for five years as fossil fuel development keeps growing.

ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.

Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement .

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.

Заголовок: UK to buy three new mine-hunting drone motherships under Norway agreement
Полный текст:
MILAN — The UK this week formalized plans to purchase three new mine-hunting “motherships” that can deploy unmanned mine countermeasure assets, as part of a defense cooperation agreement with Norway.
Under the UK-Norway Lunna House Agreement, signed last December, the British government announced its intention to join the Norwegian P1118 Standardized Vessel Program to develop offshore support vessels as motherships for autonomous mine-hunting systems.
The decision, for which £90 million ($119.1 million) has been allocated, was formalized on Thursday by British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting and his Norwegian counterpart, Tore O. Sandvik, at the Atlantic Future Forum in Oslo.
“This deal strengthens our ability to protect freedom of navigation, which is critical to our security and our economy …[We are] using the biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the Cold War to put the latest modern technology in the hands of our sailors,” Streeting said.
The British Ministry of Defense said the vessels, built on the same family as Norway’s naval version of the P1118 design, will help keep sailors “further from danger” and, as a result, support “anti-submarine warfare capabilities on NATO’s northern flank.”
The first ship is expected to arrive in 2031, and the deal includes an option for London to order three more.
The threat posed by naval mines, especially in the Strait of Hormuz, has surged since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran launched mine-laying operations to restrict navigation of the waterway. In Thursday’s announcement, the British MoD called these operations “illegal.” It said they caused “major disruption to the global trade in energy,” adding that the new mine-hunting capabilities will help the UK stay ahead of this threat.

Заголовок: Exclusive: Sagittarius Logistics Raises $1.2M to Build Inland Launch Capabilities
Полный текст:
There’s a new launcher in town.

CO-based Sagittarius Logistics, a startup founded last year by former employees of Masten Space Systems, announced the closing of a $1.2M pre-seed round today. The money will fund early development of its reusable-launch program.

The round included funds from Nova Threshold, Felicis Scout Fund, Ingenuity VC, and Space Venture Studios.

Location, location, location: Sagittarius arose out of the ashes of Masten Space Systems, which went bankrupt in 2022 after going over budget on a lunar lander. Unfortunately, the name Phoenix was already taken.

While the IP is all new, Sagittarius was founded by Masten Space Systems’ founder David Masten, and three former Masten employees—CEO Jonathan Slavik, COO Jenna Edwards, and chief of production Daniel Sinkel. Sagittarius is built on the idea that global launch demand is going to continue outstripping supply for the foreseeable future.

The company’s solution, however, is not to simply add another rocket to the market, but to build an entirely new launch system that can fly on tight timelines, and from a wider range of launch sites across the country.

“A lot of the unique aspects of what we’re designing at Sagittarius—with our core IP—allows us to book launches faster, book launches from inland launch sites that we control, [so] we’re not competing for launch slots at the Cape,” CEO Jonathan Slavik told Payload. “That’s where a lot of the business value comes in, and we see ourselves as a much more durable launch solution.”

To open up launch possibilities at non-coastal sites, Sagittarius is building reusable launchers that can abort mid-flight without exploding over population centers. The company’s technology would allow for the first and second stages of its launch vehicles to return to land in the event of an abort, according to Slavik.

“We are able to throttle back, separate the fully reusable first and second stage, and land them either at downrange locations or back at the launch site,” Slavik said. “That capability allows us to meet much more stringent safety requirements for overflight…[and] we believe we have a unique IP-protected path to a level of safety to enable that kind of overland flight.”

Parks and rec: Sagittarius is building three rockets:

• Yellowstone: Sagittarius’ suborbital vehicle is aiming for a pathfinder flight in mid-2027 to validate much of the tech and IP for follow-on models.

• Sequoia: The company’s first orbital vehicle is targeting the ability to bring four tons of customer payload to LEO, and is expected to fly its first mission in the early 2030s.

• Denali: Sagittarius’ heavy-lift vehicle is expected to be capable of carrying 30 tons to LEO, according to Slavik.

The timeline for development is aggressive, but Slavik told Payload that the company has already made major strides. Sagittarius is acquiring a rocket engine from an undisclosed supplier, which will arrive fully tested and hotfired. Its to-do list ahead of the pathfinder mission includes completing the tanks and vehicle structure, as well as the guidance, navigation, and control systems.

While the company plans to raise successive funding rounds to finance each step of its maturation, Slavik told Payload that the three vehicles would require over $1B in capital to bring to market.

“It would be foolish to say anyone can get to space without a total capitalization over a billion dollars. We’re looking at somewhere north of that, but not astronomically beyond it,” Slavik said. “We’ve built Sagittarius in our fundraising structure, and plan to really climb the capital ladder in a way that we view as very capital-efficient—only raising enough to get to that next milestone.”

Заголовок: Nov. 13, 1971: Mariner 9 orbits Mars
Полный текст:
On May 30, 1971, Mariner 9 launched, setting off on its mission to Mars. On Nov. 13, 167 days later, it entered orbit around Mars, making it the first spacecraft to orbit another planet.
With Mariner 8, Mariner 9 was one half of the Mars 71 mission. But when Mariner 8 launched on May 9, it failed to achieve orbit and tumbled out of the sky after five minutes, crashing into the Atlantic Ocean. As a result, Mariner 9 inherited all of 8’s goals in addition to its own, giving it an extensive list of objectives: surface mapping, atmospheric monitoring and analysis, surface data collection, and returning around 3,000 photographs.
When Mariner 9 arrived at Mars, it encountered a global dust storm. Because it had been designed for longevity, the orbiter was able to wait out the storm and begin its mission afterwards. (Soviet spacecraft Mars 2 and Mars 3 did not fare as well.) Over the course of about a year, Mariner 9 returned 7,329 photos and mapped 85% of the martian surface. It also revealed a dynamic and active world – including shield volcanoes, dry river valleys, ice at the martian poles – and gave researchers close-up views of the surfaces of Phobos and Deimos.
Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

[Дополнительно: Space.com]
At the time, scientists didn't know much about the Red Planet. NASA had several Mars flybys before Mariner 9 . Those flybys showed that Mars had a cratered surface , so some scientists thought that Mars looked just like the moon. Then Mariner 9 blew blew their minds. It saw some tall structures sticking through the clouds. When the dust settled, images from Mariner 9 revealed that these structures were the tops of huge volcanoes. One volcano, Olympus Mons , is the tallest in the solar system. Mariner 9 also spotted an enormous canyon called Valles Marineris . This canyon is five times longer than the Grand Canyon in Arizona. Mariner 9 worked for one year in orbit. When it ran out of gas, NASA shut it off. But the spacecraft remains one of the most famous Mars voyagers of all time. The Mariner 9 spacecraft, seen here in a NASA model, was the first to orbit Mars in 1971. Mariner 9 cemented its place in space history when it entered into orbit around Mars, the first human-built spacecraft ever to do so. The NASA spacecraft actually beat the Soviet Union's own Mars 2 spacecraft to the Red Planet, even though Mars 2 "had an 11-day head start," NASA said in a mission description .

Заголовок: 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases
Полный текст:

The phases of the Moon
The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.
Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

Different names for different types of Full Moon
There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.
For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.
Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.
Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.
Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.
Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.
Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.
Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.
Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.
Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.
Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.
Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.
Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.
Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.
In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.
Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.
Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.
Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.
Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.
Common questions about Full Moons
What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.
How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Заголовок: Canadian Lunar Rovers Ready for Next Phase—And An Earlier Launch
Полный текст:
Three Canadian companies are racing Moon-cart concepts.

Canadensys, MDA Space, and Mission Control collectively received C$14.6M ($10.3M) in July 2025 for a Phase 0 lunar-utility-rover study supporting Artemis. And now, work is almost done.

Phase shift: This year, NASA unveiled its plan to build a Moon Base —an undertaking that will require a transportation network that includes big rovers. As a result, CSA is expected to boost funding for its rover projects, and a new RFP should drop within days that will downselect to two companies to keep building in 2027 alongside science-instrument procurements.

MDA Space is a competitor in the rover procurement, as well as the maker of Canadarm3—originally intended to be used for Gateway. A company official told Payload that lunar mobility will enhance Moon Base support alongside possibly repurposed robotics, under examination through a funded task authorization with CSA.

Moon Meccano: CSA is asking industry to design a fully robotic rover, roughly the size of two pickup trucks side by side, that must fit on a 1.5m-by-1m pallet. Mid-design phase, CSA chose to shelve designs for the four-ton rover initially envisioned for 2034—at least temporarily—and asked companies to instead target a two-ton product that could ship ~3 to ~4 years faster.

Given the Moon Base timeline, waiting until 2034 risked the tech becoming “obsolete,” Mission Control CEO and founder Ewan Reid told Payload. “As a collective industry, an ecosystem in Canada, I think we all looked at ourselves and recognized that,” added Reid, whose company has developed tech, instruments, and software for several Moon missions already.

The companies emphasized the rover tech has applications for other Moon projects, even if their concept isn’t selected.

“We’re actively part of rover programs for the US, and for the European Space Agency as well,” Canadensys President and CEO Christian Sallaberger told Payload. The company has also won dozens of CSA lunar contracts in ~15 years—suggesting sustained Canadian demand.

More Moonbits: Separately, NordSpace plans to launch its self-funded TERRY Moon rover next year. And Canada recently canceled a planned mini-rover by Canadensys, but the country is pushing forward on sovereign launch .

Заголовок: Double-catch drama: Why Starship's Flight 15 is so important to SpaceX
Полный текст:
SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented double-catch mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap .

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.

SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship 's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description .

The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6 . "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

Composite photo showing the Super Heavy booster of SpaceX's Starship megarocket coming in for a landing on the launch mount on Oct. 13, 2024. (Image credit: SpaceX via X)

The catch

Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

Why so many launches?

The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)

SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."

The gap

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling , which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is " more likely than not ." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

Полный текст:
On August 7, 2027, Earth will have a close encounter with the mountain-sized asteroid 1999 AN10 . In this chart, the red ellipse marks the orbit of 1999 AN10 in 2027. Stalks on this line are at the beginnings of months. Chart via Guy Ottewell . Used with permission.

Mountain-sized asteroid to pass close to Earth on August 7, 2027

A space rock around 800 to 1,800 meters wide (about 0.5 to 1.1 miles) is set to soar close by Earth on August 7, 2027.

The asteroid — named 1999 AN10 — has been labelled potentially hazardous by NASA, but there is no chance of it impacting Earth in 2027. It will safely pass us in August with a separation of about 389,855 kilometers (242,240 miles), or roughly the same distance away as the moon.

If the asteroid is not going to hit us, why is it labeled a potentially hazardous asteroid? A potentially hazardous asteroid is any space rock that comes as close as 0.05 astronomical units ( AU ) from Earth and that’s larger than 140 meters (460 feet) in diameter. The label reflects the potential that at some point in the future — if this large space rock gets nudged by another passing object — its orbit could be altered in a way that would cause it to hit Earth. Currently, 1999 AN10 has a zero chance of hitting Earth during its 2027 flyby.

So this isn’t something to be scared of. But it is something to get excited about! The asteroid is so big and will come so close that you’ll be able to spot it with binoculars as it glides by. 1999 AN10 will peak around magnitude 7.3 as it passes through the night sky over North and South America. Its closest approach is at 7:12:05 UTC on August 7, 2027. That would be 2:12:05 am CDT on August 7 for the Americas.

Overnight on August 7, 2027, asteroid 1999 AN10 will pass through the constellations Taurus , Aries , Pisces and Pegasus .

The potentially hazardous asteroid 1999 AN10 will pass through the constellations Taurus , Aries , Pisces and Pegasus overnight on August 7, 2027, as it whizzes by Earth. Simulation via Tony Dunn .

Will asteroid 1999 AN10 hit the moon?

If the asteroid will pass about 1 lunar distance from Earth, does that mean it could hit the moon? How close will it get to the moon?

Well, moon lovers, don’t worry. The closest the asteroid will come to the moon is 763,391 km, or 474,349 miles. That’s about twice as far as it will get from Earth! So, as you might have guessed, it means the asteroid will pass Earth on the opposite side to the moon at that time.

If asteroid 1999 AN10 is going to pass Earth at about 1 lunar distance, is there a chance it will hit the moon? No, because at the time of passage, the moon will be on the other side of Earth. Simulation via Tony Dunn .

More about potentially hazardous asteroids

Astronomers discovered 1999 AN10 on January 13, 1999, at the Lincoln Laboratory Experimental Test Site in New Mexico. It’s an Apollo-class asteroid, meaning its orbit crosses Earth’s orbit around the sun.

The asteroid travels around the sun once every 643 days, following an elongated orbit that takes it from inside Earth’s orbit to well beyond Mars’ orbit.

It’s a potentially hazardous asteroid because of its large size. NASA says any impactor larger than 1 to 2 kilometers (.6 to 1.2 miles) in size would have worldwide effects. It could blast massive amounts of dust into the atmosphere, dimming sunlight for months and threatening global civilization.

Astronomers have cataloged roughly 2,500 known potentially hazardous asteroids. But they estimate that’s only about half of the population. However, they believe they have found 90% of the biggest potentially hazardous asteroids.

This illustration shows an asteroid on one side of Earth with the moon on the other side. Image via Batman111 from Pixabay .

Other notable potentially hazardous asteroids

99942 Apophis

• Close approach: April 13, 2029

• Distance: About 32,000 km (20,000 miles) above Earth’s surface

• Size: Approximately 375 meters (1,230 feet)

Apophis will pass closer to Earth than many geostationary satellites. Scientists once worried about a possible future collision, but additional observations ruled out an impact risk for at least 100 years. NASA’s OSIRIS-APEX spacecraft will study it after the encounter.

101955 Bennu

• Potential impact date: September 24, 2182

• Size: About 500 meters (1/3 mile) wide

• Impact odds: Approximately 1 in 2,700 for that date, according to NASA’s 2021 orbital analysis.

NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission collected a sample from Bennu and returned it to Earth in 2023. Scientists are studying the sample to learn about the early solar system.

2001 WN5

• Close approach: June 26, 2028

• Distance: About 248,700 km (154,500 miles) from Earth’s center

• Size: Approximately 940 meters (0.58 mile)

This asteroid will pass inside the moon’s orbit. It will be a bit brighter than 1999 AN10, peaking at magnitude 6.7.

1997 XF11

• Closest approach: October 26, 2028

• Distance: About 929,000 km (577,000 miles) from Earth

• Size: Approximately 700 meters (0.43 mile)

This asteroid attracted considerable attention after its discovery in 1997. Early calculations suggested a possible future collision. Better observations ruled that out.

Заголовок: SpaceTY Plans to Fly Lunar Synthetic Aperture Radar Satellite
Полный текст:
A commercial satellite designed to image the Moon’s surface and collect data on underground structures is desired to launch in 2027.

A model of Tianyi-200 on display at SpaceTY’s booth during the 4th Extraterrestrial Construction Conference in November 2026. | Image: SpaceTY

Following its attendance at the 4th Extraterrestrial Construction Conference (第四届地外工程建造学术研讨会) 1 between November 6th and 8th, held at Tsinghua University (清华大学), commercial satellite maker SpaceTY (天仪研究院) announced on November 13th that it is actively working on a lunar synthetic aperture radar satellite. 2

That satellite has been dubbed Tianyi-200 (TY200卫星 3 ) and is based on a dual-band radar payload, with a design expected to weigh around 100 kilograms, be powered by deployable solar panels, and controlled autonomously by locally run artificial intelligence systems 4 . Due to its small mass, enabled by lightweight components, the company also refers to it as a lunar exploration microsatellite.

The synthetic aperture radar the satellite is designed around is planned to beam P- and Ku-band signals at the lunar surface, from a currently unspecified orbit, to capture images at a resolution as low as 0.25 meters 5 while penetrating several meters below regolith 6 . By utilizing those bands, SpaceTY hopes to collect detailed data on the Moon’s geological structures and support the study of lunar lava tubes.

In addition to that, SpaceTY said that Tianyi-200 will be aligned with China’s state-led lunar exploration programs, which will see Chang’e 7 launch next year and then humans later this decade , to assist in the consideration of potential landing sites, surveying of possible resources, and early studies of where human-made structures could be located.

To assist with the satellite’s development and use in lunar orbit, SpaceTY says they are working with Tsinghua University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (上海交通大学), China University of Geosciences, Beijing (中国地质大学(北京)), the Deep Space Exploration Laboratory (深空探测实验室), and SJTU Cangqiong Satellite Systems Shanghai Co Ltd (上交苍穹卫星系统(上海)有限公司) 7 , among unnamed others.

In their announcement, SpaceTY stated that they are looking to launch the satellite before the end of 2027 via a dedicated launch solution. A launch provider was not named, but it was said that Tianyi-200 will open a low-cost route heading directly into orbit around the Moon via China’s commercial space industry, indicating that a non-Long March rocket should launch it. The only current launch vehicle with the ability to send the satellite towards the Moon is CAS Space’s Kinetica-2, using the ‘Kinastra (力巡)’ upper-stage to perform orbit insertion as well after a multi-day coasting period.

If SpaceTY’s satellite reaches lunar space successfully next year, they would become the first non-governmental entity in China to lead a mission to the Moon.

Ahead of announcing Tianyi-200, SpaceTY has accumulated a wealth of experience flying dozens of satellites, building synthetic aperture radars, and selling space-based services to customers. Their most recent satellites were deployed in May and September . Alongside that, Shanghai Jiao Tong University has already been to the Moon through jointly working on Pakistan’s ICUBE-Q , delivered via Chang’e 6.

Back in April , SpaceTY raised 1.3 billion Yuan (194.85 million United States Dollars, as of November 13th) via the sale of company shares to upgrade and expand their satellites capabilities and applications.

Additionally, the international C3 constellation of thirty cubesats and four 200-kilogram resource surveying satellites will be sent to a 1:3 resonance orbit around 2030.

With the unveiling of Tianyi-200, China’s space sector is moving on gaining another key commercial capability for affordable robotic lunar exploration. Others are the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology’s methane-fuelled lunar lander and the ‘ Xingtu-1 Lunar Probe (星途一号月球探测器) ’, a small lunar lander with remote sensing tasks during a period prior to landing.

Полный текст:
United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.

The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today , 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."

A United Launch Alliance Vulcan Centaur launches 40 Amazon internet satellites from Florida on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: ULA)

Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024 , and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update .

That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.

The Vulcan Centaur rises into the sky on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: Vulcan Centaur)

Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.
