Заголовок: Mirach is your guide star to finding 3 galaxies
Полный текст:
Mirach in the constellation Andromeda helps stargazers locate the Andromeda Galaxy, the Triangulum Galaxy, and "Mirach's Ghost."

The post Mirach is your guide star to finding 3 galaxies first appeared on EarthSky .

Here is the Great Square of Pegasus, connected to the constellation Andromeda via the star Alpheratz . See Mirach? You can find the Andromeda galaxy ( M31 ) — the large spiral galaxy next door to our Milky Way — by star-hopping with Mirach.

The 2027 EarthSky Lunar Calendar is now available! A unique and beautiful poster-sized calendar. Keep up with all phases of the moon every night of the year. Order yours today!

Mirach, also known as Beta Andromedae, is a star in the constellation Andromeda . It’s only moderately bright. But it’s an important star to stargazers, as it can act as a signpost to three galaxies: the Andromeda galaxy ( M31 ), the Triangulum galaxy ( M33 ) and a galaxy known as Mirach’s Ghost ( NGC 404 ).

Mirach is what’s known as a red giant star , a star in the final stages of its evolution whose outer layers have expanded. It has about three to four times the sun’s mass and 100 times the sun’s diameter. It shines with about 1,900 times our sun’s total brightness . But Mirach is rather far away, at 200 light-years . That’s why it shines in our sky at only 2nd magnitude , a respectable brightness but not as bright as many other stars.

But it’s bright enough to be a useful signpost to three galaxies. Read on to find out how to spot them.

View at EarthSky Community Photos . | Jeremy Likness in Newport, Oregon, captured this telescopic view of the Andromeda galaxy on September 10, 2026. Jeremy wrote: “The numbers are mind-numbing. 2.5 million light-fyears? One trillion stars? This week we had a run of clear, dark skies. My target: M31, the Andromeda galaxy. Our nearest galactic neighbor.” Thank you, Jeremy!

Finding the Andromeda galaxy with Mirach

Draw an imaginary line from Mirach to the star Mu (µ) Andromedae (see below). Then, continue extending that line for about the same distance between those two stars to reach the Andromeda Galaxy.

Under dark, moonless skies, the Andromeda galaxy appears as a smudge in the sky to the unaided eye. Even if the moon is out or under skies with moderate light pollution (like the suburbs), you can see it through binoculars . At about 2.5 million light-years away, the Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large spiral galaxy to our Milky Way. And it’s the most distant thing you can easily see with your eye alone.

A star map of the constellation Andromeda showing the locations of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Triangulum Galaxy ( M33 ). Image via IAU .

Finding the Triangulum galaxy (M33)

The Triangulum Galaxy (M33), in the constellation Triangulum, is much fainter than the Andromeda Galaxy. Some people with excellent eyesight have been able to see it unaided by telescopes or binoculars, in extraordinarily good viewing conditions. Even so, it can still be a challenge to find M33 with binoculars and small telescopes.

To find Triangulum, you’ll use the same two stars as above, but star-hop in the opposite direction. Follow an imaginary line from the star Mu (µ) Andromedae to Mirach, then continue to draw that line past Mirach, for twice the distance between Mu Andromedae and Mirach, to reach the Triangulum Galaxy.

Here are 2 of the 3 galaxies you can find via the star Mirach in the constellation Andromeda. M31 is easy to find on a dark night, from a rural location . M33 is tougher to spot. Chart via IAU .

View at EarthSky Community Photos . | Andy Dungan imaged this galaxy on October 29. 2025, from Colorado. Andy wrote: “Triangulum is the second closest galaxy to our own and located near the 1st closest, Andromeda, in the night sky.” Thank you, Andy!

Finding Mirach’s Ghost (NGC 404)

When you look at Mirach, you’re looking almost exactly in the direction of the galaxy labeled NGC 404 but known affectionately among astronomers as Mirach’s Ghost. That’s because the remote, fuzzy galaxy lies right next to the moderately bright star, just 1/10 degree from Mirach. A full moon is 1/2 degree wide, so you can see that’s very close.

Mirach’s Ghost is faint, just magnitude 11 in brightness. Many amateur astronomers try to spot it with their small telescopes, but due to its proximity to the brighter 2nd-magnitude Mirach, seeing the galaxy is not easy.

NGC 404 is located about 10 million light-years away, just beyond our Local Group of galaxies. The Local Group is a cluster of galaxies that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda and Triangulum galaxies. NGC 404 does not appear gravitationally bound to our Local Group.

NGC 404 , also known as Mirach’s Ghost, is the bluish-white object next to orange-colored Mirach. This image was taken by Tom Wildoner using a camera attached to a 4.7 inch (120 mm) refractor telescope. Image via Tom and Jane Wildoner at The Dark Side Observatory . Used with permission.

Bottom line: Stargazers use Mirach, a moderately bright star in the constellation Andromeda, to locate three galaxies. It can help you find the Andromeda Galaxy, the Triangulum Galaxy and a galaxy known as Mirach’s Ghost (NGC 404).

Заголовок: 'Don't panic': SpaceX pens familiar message on Starship ahead of historic double-catch test flight
Полный текст:
SpaceX has inked a familiar phrase on the Starship rocket that will fly a historic mission today (Nov. 13) — "Don't panic." And the company has invoked those words before.

SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.

The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X , and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic."

Another look at Ship 42 at the pad on Nov. 12. (Image credit: SpaceX)

The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic " The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy ": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.

And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42."

SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic."

The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun , with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!"

Starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.

If all goes according to plan, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14 , which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).

The Ship 42 upper stage rolls to its launch pad at SpaceX's Starbase site on Nov. 12, 2026 ahead of Starship's Flight 15. (Image credit: SpaceX)

Ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.

That's the plan, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.

The two stages of the Starship rocket that will conduct Flight 15 at their Starbase launch pad on Nov. 12, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX)

Both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has said.

The chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.

Don’t Panic April 8, 2025

The company has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.

The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said last month , during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.

В 1961 году астроном Фрэнк Дрейк сформулировал уравнение, оценившее шансы найти внеземной разум, и на симпозиуме в Грин-Бэнке познакомился с Карлом Саганом. Их сотрудничество в Корнелле привело к идее не только слушать космос (SETI), но и послать ему понятный сигнал (METI).

Pioneer 10 стартовал 2 марта 1972, Pioneer 11 — 5 апреля 1973, неся первые «приветствия» человечества.

Успех вдохновил миссию Voyager. В 1977 стартовали два зонда с “Золотыми пластинками” — аудио‑ и фотолетописью Земли, отправленной в межзвёздное плавание на миллиарды лет.

Заголовок: ESA Confirms Latest Prometheus Tests Not Connected to Themis Hop Preparations
Полный текст:
Credit: ArianeGroup / ESA / DLR

The European Space Agency (ESA) and ArianeGroup have confirmed that Prometheus engine tests conducted in Lampoldshausen in October were carried out independently of preparations for the long-delayed inaugural flight of the Themis reusable booster demonstrator.

In a 6 November press release, ArianeGroup announced that it had completed a series of hot-fire tests of the latest iteration of the Prometheus rocket engine at DLR’s P5 test bench in Lampoldshausen on 29 October.

“The successful hot fire test conducted on [the] P5 test bench in Lampoldshausen increases engine operations maturity,” an ArianeGroup spokesperson told European Spaceflight. “The tests were conducted independently of Themis flight preparations.”

An ESA spokesperson added that the operating profile for Themis’s inaugural flight had already been tested using the same engine configuration as the one currently mounted on the demonstrator.

One of the objectives of the late-October test campaign was to validate the performance of a new combustion chamber produced using a Cold Gas Spray additive manufacturing process. The process is intended to allow the engines to be produced faster and more cheaply than with traditional manufacturing methods.

In its 6 November press release announcing the completion of the latest Prometheus hot-fire test campaign, ArianeGroup revealed that it is now preparing an improved version of the Prometheus engine, known as Mark 2, for a forthcoming test campaign.

This upgraded version of the engine will power a subsequent variant of the Themis reusable rocket demonstrator known as Themis 1E. The vehicle will feature upgraded structures and propellant tanks, allowing it to undertake longer flights at higher altitudes.

Themis remains grounded

During an ESA press conference in January 2026, Toni Tolker-Nielsen, then acting Director of Space Transportation, explained that teams were “waiting for spring” to conduct Themis’s inaugural flight test from the Esrange Space Centre in Sweden. ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher added that the agency was targeting the first quarter of 2026 for the flight.

Spring came and went, as did summer and autumn. Now, with winter returning to northern Sweden, Themis remains stuck on the launchpad as snow once again threatens to bring testing at Esrange to a halt.

Speaking at an ESA press conference on 22 October , the new Director of Space Transportation, Géraldine Naja, acknowledged uncertainty over whether the first hop could be completed before the end of 2026. She explained that ArianeGroup and SSC Space, the operator of the Esrange facility, would decide by the end of November whether to attempt an inaugural flight this year.

Заголовок: Сантиметр против ИМТ!
Полный текст:
Сантиметр против ИМТ!

Индекс массы тела считают за секунду: вес делим на квадрат роста, и если вышло 30 или больше, тогда ставим «ожирение». Удобно. Только формула понятия не имеет, из чего состоит тело: человек с солидной мускулатурой легко получит высокий ИМТ почти без лишнего жира.

Свежая работа в Nature показывает, во что обходится такая простота. Учёные проверили подход CAD-obesity — «комбинированное антропометрическое определение ожирения». Он добавляет к ИМТ мерки, связанные с избытком жира, например окружность талии. Логика понятна: жир, который откладывается на животе, связан с более серьёзными последствиями для здоровья, чем жир в других местах.

Ожирение новая система делит на два типа. Если вдобавок есть хотя бы одна из 18 конкретных проблем со здоровьем — например, сердечная недостаточность или апноэ сна. Тогда это «клиническое ожирение»: жир уже вредит органам. Если нет — «доклиническое»: жира много, но органы пока работают нормально.

Подход предложили в прошлом году, а теперь проверили на медицинских картах больше 800 тысяч человек из Китая, Испании, Великобритании и США. По трём когортам, где за срок до 15 лет умерли больше 50 тысяч человек, сравнили, что точнее предсказывает риск смерти.

Новая система нашла ожирение ещё у 5–9% людей, которых ИМТ записал бы лишь в «избыточный вес». Бывает и наоборот: 1–3% тех, кому ИМТ «поставил» ожирение, она отнесла к избыточному весу. При миллиарде людей с ожирением в мире это, по словам соавтора работы, хирурга Франческо Рубино из Королевского колледжа Лондона, миллионы неверных ярлыков. В его практике были пациенты, которым отказывали в лечении, хотя они были куда больнее других: ИМТ чуть не дотягивал до порога для операции.

С рисками картина тоже интересная. Ожирение по новой системе повышало риск смерти на 6–7% по сравнению с людьми без лишнего веса, а «клиническое» — заметно сильнее, чем «доклиническое». У тех же, кого в ожирение записал только ИМТ, дополнительного риска не нашли вовсе.

Так что, возможно, у кого-то из нас ожирения и нет. Есть только слишком самоуверенная формула 🙃

Заголовок: Gama Raises €15M Seed to Boost Europe’s Solar Array Supply Chain
Полный текст:
Europe continues to stack the building blocks for a more robust space economy.

Gama, a French startup developing ultra-light deployable solar arrays, announced a €15M seed round yesterday to boost Europe’s solar array supply chain.

The round included funds from a mix of European and US VCs, including Transition Ventures, Planet A, Draper Associates, and Manta Ray.

• The funds will be used to develop a high-volume production facility outside of Paris, France, which will be capable of producing 100 MW of solar arrays annually.

• The first units—called Wings—are expected to start rolling off the line next year.

• Gama also plans to hire ~60 employees in engineering roles across mechanical, electrical, and software.

The tech: Gama was initially founded to develop solar-sail technology—which uses the Sun’s energy to propel spacecraft into deep space—but the company quickly transitioned into developing solar arrays to solve the ever-present supply-chain headache for other satellite operators.

Nearly every spacecraft in orbit relies on solar panels to power its payloads, but solar cells are built by a small number of providers and can often come with lead times as high as a year or more, according to CEO Andrew Nutter.

Additionally, as power needs increase, the size of the solar arrays required to run each satellite grows larger, causing them to become floppy—and less effective at gathering sunlight. While traditional solutions involve adding weight to increase rigidity, Gama’s solution uses software—uploaded into customer flight computers—to help point the entire spacecraft more accurately, and to solve the floppy-array problem without additional mass.

“Our approach is to make [solar arrays] as thin and light as possible, so you can have more surface area, and you reduce the cost and the mass. Then, as you get to bigger surface areas, transfer some of that complexity—and the requirements for stability—into the software side,” Nutter said.

Gama is targeting $10 per watt on its solar arrays, and will deliver its first demonstration Wing in the middle of next year.

Shining light: Gama’s fundraise represents one of the largest seed rounds for a European space startup in recent years. It’s a signal that European VCs are growing increasingly comfortable making big bets on the future of the region’s space ecosystem. But it’s also reflective of the demand Gama has seen—and expects to continue seeing—as Europe scales its footprint in orbit.

In September, Gama signed a partnership with US satellite builder Eclipse Space to supply deployable solar arrays for Eclipse’s satellite platforms. For future customers, Gama has its eye on the growing pool of satellite-bus manufacturers across the continent.

“We needed funding because there was demand or volume, and so we needed the factory quite quickly,” Nutter said. “The vision is very simple: If we can consolidate the volume from multiple satellite-bus manufacturers, we can give the industry cheaper prices.”

Clarification: This article was updated to clarify a point about Gama’s software. It helps the entire spacecraft point more accurately .

Заголовок: Tesla and SpaceX merger talks hit a new stage, and one hurdle remains
Полный текст:
Tesla and SpaceX merger talks are reportedly advancing, and a deal could arrive by December.

Tesla and SpaceX are moving closer to a combination, with a deal announcement possible as soon as December, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. The companies have also discussed a scenario in which the announcement slips into early 2027.

Boards and advisers on both sides are now working through the terms of the deal and the governance structure of the combined company, according to the report. One open item is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. Bloomberg had previously reported that the two companies were aiming to announce a deal in the first half of next year and close it before the end of President Donald Trump’s term, so a December announcement would pull that schedule forward by months.

Tesla shares rose as much as 1.9% to $398.35 after the report, while SpaceX gained 0.6% to $140.63. SpaceX carries a market value of about $1.9 trillion following its June IPO, and Tesla is valued at about $1.55 trillion, which would make a combination the largest corporate deal on record. Neither company responded to requests for comment.

The talks became official on October 20, when Elon Musk said on SpaceX’s third quarter earnings call that both companies had formed special committees of independent directors to study a merger, as Teslarati reported . Musk said he could not take part because he is “a conflicted party” and called the process “an odd kabuki dance.” He also noted that Tesla would need approval from 50 percent of all outstanding shares, a bar the company missed in 2025 when a board declassification proposal won support from only 39.4 percent.

China remains the biggest structural problem. Bloomberg’s sources said the companies still need to work out how to isolate Tesla’s large and profitable manufacturing business in China from SpaceX’s U.S. government and defense contracts. JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta described those two factors last month as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulatory and shareholder approval. Musk has repeatedly said Tesla has no plans to separate its China business, a position he restated in August after ARK Invest predicted a merger announcement before the end of the year.

Washington adds another layer. Democrats took control of Congress in this month’s midterms and have pledged to investigate Musk’s business and political activities, which could bring added scrutiny to a deal involving one of the Pentagon’s most important launch and satellite contractors.

The report also lands three weeks before Tesla’s December 3 annual meeting at Giga Texas. That ballot has only three items, led by the re-election of Musk, board chair Robyn Denholm and JB Straubel, and includes no merger proposal. Any deal announced in December would likely require a separate special meeting for Tesla shareholders to vote on it.

The two companies already share a growing list of projects, including the Terafab semiconductor plant in Texas. Tesla’s next generation Roadster, which uses cold gas thrusters built on SpaceX hardware, turned up on display at SpaceX headquarters last month and has become one of the clearest public examples of that overlap.

Image Details

Mangroves have replaced rice fields in parts of Burma’s Myeik District. The TM (Thematic Mapper) on Landsat 5 captured the image on the left on February 14, 2010, and the OLI on Landsat 9 captured the image on the right on February 2, 2026.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison.

Scientists began using satellites to map mangrove forests in the 1970s after the launch of the first Landsat satellite. For decades, the story they told about mangroves was dominated by loss and decline. Research published in Science suggests that the tide has turned.

A global rebound began around 2010, the scientists found, led by the expansion of mangrove forests in Asia, Australia, and South America. The researchers analyzed Landsat imagery collected between 1984 and 2023, looking for signs of changes in the extent and density of mangrove canopy.

They tallied losses of nearly 3,000 square kilometers (1,200 square miles) between 1984 and 2010, followed by an unexpected increase of nearly 2,000 square kilometers (770 square miles) of mangroves after 2010. They also found that many of today’s mangrove forests have denser, more closed canopies than they did in 2010, a sign of healthier, less degraded forests, particularly in South America.

“Other research groups have mapped and analyzed long-term changes in select regions, but these are the first global mangrove maps that cover such a long period,” said Zhen Zhang, an environmental scientist at Tulane University. “About two-thirds of the expansion was due to mangroves colonizing new areas and the other third due to restoration and regrowth in degraded areas,” he added.

One of the most notable reversals occurred in Southeast Asia—especially Burma (Myanmar). The country lost mangroves rapidly in the 1980s and 1990s due to the expansion of agriculture, aquaculture, and firewood harvesting in coastal areas, but the trend reversed around 2010, when mangrove area began expanding in many places. The authors attribute the turnaround to increased awareness and restoration efforts after the devastating Indian Ocean tsunami in 2004 , strengthened legal protections for forests, and high rates of sedimentation that opened up new mudflats for colonization.

The pair of Landsat images above shows expansion of mangrove forests in Palaw Township in Burma’s Myeik District—an area that has seen both significant regeneration of degraded mangrove forests and the spread of trees into new areas since 2010. In this region, much of the regeneration appears to be occurring in abandoned rice fields (brown) south of the village of Kyauktaung. People on nearby Pyin Bukyi Island, meanwhile, have experimented with conservation projects and tree planting efforts to support mangroves. Despite the gains, deforestation remains a common challenge in Burma, which lost 28.6 percent of its mangrove area between the 1980s and 2010. Since then, the country’s mangrove area has grown about 10 percent.

Mangrove trees are relatively small—averaging about 13 meters (43 feet)—but mighty from an ecological perspective, with mangrove ecosystems storing up to four times as much carbon as taller inland tropical forests. The trees play an important role in protecting coastal communities from erosion and storm surges, and their distinctive stilt-like roots provide habitat and vital nursery grounds for fish, shrimp, crabs, and other marine life.

In several areas, such as around the mouth of the Amazon River and in northern Australia, extensive deposition of sediment has created new mudflats that mangroves have successfully colonized, contributing to steady increases in each of these regions since the 1990s. At the northern and southern edges of their range, including the southeastern U.S., warming temperatures and fewer freezes have also allowed mangroves to push into areas that were previously too cold, Zhang explained.

There are some areas, however, where losses have outweighed gains. Substantial mangrove losses in the Niger Delta, for instance, have reduced the total mangrove area in West and Central Africa since 2010. North America and southern Africa, meanwhile, have seen widespread degradation after tropical cyclones devastated broad swaths of mangroves. “The global successes we’ve seen with mangroves during the past decade should not be seen as grounds for complacency,” cautioned Zhang. “This underscores that conservation and slowing deforestation can lead to huge positive impacts when coupled with natural expansion and regeneration.”

Заголовок: Senate Appropriations CJS Subcommittee Proposes $24.9 Billion for NASA in FY2027
Полный текст:
The Senate Appropriations Committee released five more FY2027 bills this evening, including the Commerce-Justice-Science bill that funds NASA. The CJS subcommittee is proposing $24.874 billion for NASA, slightly more than the $24.438 billion approved by Congress for FY2026. By contrast, the Trump Administration requested $18.8 billion in FY2027.

NASA implemented a major reorganization earlier this year, merging and/or rearranging the mission directorates and budget structure. The subcommittee’s report explains that the changes happened too late and lacked sufficient detail for them to be incorporated in this bill, however.

The text , explanatory statement , and a summary are posted on the committee’s website. The bill also funds the Department of Commerce (including NOAA), the Department of Justice, and the National Science Foundation.

Total funding for NASA, and for NASA’s science and exploration programs, are shown below.

Source: Senate Appropriations Committee explanatory report on FY2027 CJS bill.

Source: Senate Appropriations Committee explanatory report on FY2027 CJS bill.

Source: Senate Appropriations Committee explanatory report on FY2027 CJS bill.

The committee released two other bills on Tuesday. A schedule for the full committee to meet and consider the subcommittee recommendations hasn’t been announced. None of the 12 FY2027 appropriations have cleared Congress yet. The government is operating under a Continuing Resolution that expires on December 11.

The House Appropriations Committee approved its version of the CJS bill on May 13, but it has not passed the House yet. Like the Senate, it rejected the deep cuts proposed by the Administration, recommending $24.4 billion. The bill cleared the committee on a party-line vote because Democrats objected to provisions in the Commerce and Justice sections of the bill. During subcommittee markup, Democrats also opposed the level of funding for NASA’s science programs — $6 billion. While $2 billion more than the $3.9 billion requested, it is $1.3 billion less than FY2026.

A few highlights from the Senate committee’s report ( not a comprehensive list ):

Science: $7.43 billion

The Committee rejects the mission terminations proposed in the fiscal year 2027 budget request for Earth Science, Planetary Science, Astrophysics, and Heliophysics. The Committee is concerned by the plan to end 53 missions across Science, which was again driven by budgetary pressure rather than scientific value. … Further, the Committee affirms the importance of NASA upholding its commitments to our international partners and expects future budget requests to sustain funding to fulfill these commitments, including for missions such as Laser Interferometer Space Antenna and Rosalind Franklin ExoMars Rover.

• Earth Science: $2.188 billion

• Supports selection of new Venture class missions; directs NASA to continue development of Landsat Next with launch of first satellite in 2031 ($165 million); supports reformulated Earth System Observatory ($330 million); applauds selection of two Earth System Explorers ($174 million); rejects proposed termination of Terra, Aqua and Aura; provides up to $97.5 million for Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition (CSDA); supports continued funding for GLOBE.

• Planetary Science: $2.617 billion

• Supports the Mars Sample Return mission “to the extent it serves as a critical strategic demonstration of the technologies, systems, and operational capabilities required for future human missions to Mars as well as to return samples for scientific inquiry.” Directs NASA to integrate MSR into the Moon-to-Mars program “as a proving ground for human exploration rather than as a standalone science mission.”

• Expresses concern about delays in announcements of opportunities (AOs) for New Frontiers and Discovery and associated expected reductions to scientific community and workforce due to the irregular pace. Directs NASA to immediately issue the AO for the 5th New Frontiers and next Discovery and return to previous cadence.

• Directs NASA to continue the DAVINCI and VERITAS Venus missions ($263 million and $49 million respectively); funds New Frontiers at $500 million including $430 million for Dragonfly; provides not less than $22 million for OSIRIS-APEX to study the Apophis asteroid after it flies by Earth; supports New Horizons’s extended mission ($12 million); supports sustained operations of Juno ($27 million); rejects proposed termination of Mars Odyssey Orbiter and Mars Express; provides $98.6 million for NASA’s support of ESA’s Rosalind Franklin Mars rover; provides the requested $110 million for Mars Future Missions including Skyfall; provides not less than $20 million for Uranus Orbiter and Probe.

• Astrophysics: $1.656 billion

• Not less than $98.3 million for Hubble; $208 million for JWST; not less than $63 million for Chandra; $129.9 million for LISA; not less than $288.6 million for astrophysics research; not less than $52 million for education and outreach.

• Roman Space Telescope: $166.8 million for launch and operations plus $47.8 million for Exoplanet Exploration Science program competitive grants to allow American scientists to make discoveries with Roman data; requires NASA to provide an update on implementing the Roman Standing Review Board recommendation to have a single authority for operations.

• Habitable Worlds Observatory: $300 million, with detailed instructions on many aspects of the program.

• Heliophysics: $880.3 million

• $247.8 million for Heliophysics Research; $338.1 million for Living with a Star, including not less than $25 million for the Parker Solar Probe operations and $34 million for the Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe [IMAP] operations; and $236.9 million for Heliophysics Explorer, including $60.7 million for HelioSwarm. Expects NASA to maintain the cadence for the Heliophysics Explorer program with an AO for MIDEX no later than mid-2027.

• Supports reformulated Geospace Dynamics Constellation and provides $100 million with goal of achieving a trailblazer launch in 2027.

• Provides up to the requested amount for Space Weather and recognizes its relevance to safeguarding human health on long duration deep space missions; encourages NASA to work with NSF, NOAA, DOD to help them improve their operational space weather assets.

• Biological and Physical Sciences: $88 million

• Directs NASA to continue research into understanding the effects of living and working in low- and micro-gravity environments on humans and other living organisms, including $6 million to continue the consortium created in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2024. Supports NASA taking advantage of commercial space stations as a cost effective means to further Biological and Physical Sciences.

Aeronautics: $910 million

• Directs NASA to establish a Center for Excellence for Aerospace Engineering with instructions on how to choose a location and the Center’s responsibilities ($10 million); provides not less than the FY2026 level for Assured Autonomy Research; provides not less than $35 million for HiCAM plus $15 million for partnerships with industry and academia; provides up to $25 million for Open Fan Flight Demonstrator; provides not less than $50 million for Subsonic Flight Demonstrator.

Space Technology: $825 million

• Provides up to $110 million for Nuclear Thermal Propulsion and no less than $50 million for Nuclear Electric Propulsion; recognizes the importance of reliable lunar surface power and the long-term value of nuclear surface power while noting the relative affordability, mobility and near-term readiness of solar surface power; provides $10 million for a nuclear propulsion Center of Excellence; provides $15 million for the Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability mission to inspect orbital debris; encourages NASA to continue development of ISRU within available funds; supports proposal for commercial radioisotope power systems; supports partnering with commercial industry to reboost NASA science assets whose orbits are decaying.

Exploration: $8.282 billion

The Committee provides $8,282,000,000 for Exploration, which is $499,000,000 above the fiscal year 2026 enacted level. The Committee believes the Nation deserves a safe, robust, and ambitious human spaceflight program that establishes a sustainable American presence. … The Committee encourages NASA to reduce technical and schedule risk, improve affordability, and increase mission cadence by leveraging fixed-price partnerships and commercial service approaches wherever appropriate. These efforts shall be executed within a fully integrated exploration architecture, including transportation, habitation, mobility, logistics, and communications, which strengthens the domestic industrial base, preserves critical workforce skills, and advances a sustainable pathway to Mars. … While acknowledging remaining challenges, the Committee expects NASA to maintain stable requirements, realistic schedules, and transparent cost and risk assessments.

• SLS: funded in the bill at $1.495 billion “complemented” by $1.025.0 billion in last year’s reconciliation bill. The committee encourages NASA to preserve a viable path forward for SLS flights after Artemis V.

• Orion: no less than $1.222 billion.

• Approves redirecting funding allocated for Gateway in last year’s reconciliation bill to activities that directly support continuous human presence on the Moon.

• HLS: no less than $2.277 billion to support all currently contracted missions for two independently developed lunar landers, as well as the development of heavy cargo landing services derived from these crewed systems.

• Lunar Spacesuits (xEVA): not less than $830 million.

• Commercial Lunar Transportation Services: not less than $230 million.

• Moon Base: Directs NASA to leverage existing capabilities within CLPS and LSII to rapidly advance Moon Base and where to focus initial investments.

• Fission Surface Power: up to $250 million.

• Requires a technical review of the Moon Base architecture by the National Academies.

Space Operations: $4.125 billion

• Urges NASA to prioritize full utilization of the ISS; fully funds crew and cargo missions at the FY2026 level; provides sufficient funding for the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle; provides up to $299.8 million to support development of Commercial LEO Destinations (CLDs); directs NASA to qualify commercial suborbital vehicles and procure flights for NASA suborbital crew; provides not less than the FY2026 level for modernization of NASA’s communications architecture; provides $15 million to develop returnable uncrewed vehicles with downmass capability.

Заголовок: AST SpaceMobile presses case for developing own launch vehicle
Полный текст:
WASHINGTON — AST SpaceMobile executives expressed confidence in the company’s ability to field a new reusable launch vehicle in just two years despite widespread industry skepticism and conflicting accounts of where the vehicle will launch from.
The company, which is developing a constellation of direct-to-device satellites, held an “unveiling” event in New York Nov. 12 to discuss its Blacklift launch vehicle that the company announced Nov. 6. The company said then it was developing Blacklift to provide its own way to launch its BlueBird satellites given a constrained launch market.
“We’re not doing this thing because we want to be in the launch business. We want this because we have so much demand of our satellites and, as you have seen it, we cannot get enough launches on time,” Abel Avellan, chief executive of AST SpaceMobile, said at the event.
Blacklift, with a payload capacity of 20 tons to low Earth orbit, will be able to carry up to five BlueBird satellites per launch. The vehicle will be used exclusively for AST’s satellites, with a goal of launching twice a month.
Although the company billed the event as an unveiling, the company showed no hardware beyond videos of engines from Firefly Aerospace that AST is acquiring for Blacklift and animations of the vehicle itself. Much of the event focused on the BlueBird satellites, such as a tour of the Midland, Texas, factory where the company builds those spacecraft.
The company did provide a few technical details about the rocket. Blacklift will be a three-stage rocket, using seven of Firefly’s Miranda engines in its first stage, two Firefly Vira engines in the second stage and one Vira engine in the third stage. That is a nontraditional approach in a launch market where most vehicles optimized for low Earth orbit payloads use only two stages.
Avellan said the three-stage approach is tied to plans to recover and reuse the first stage. “When you have three stages, the first stage will go up not that much and will come back down very easily, compared of going back very high and then trying to maneuver that back to Earth,” he said. However, existing reusable rockets such as Falcon 9 and New Glenn, and those in development by Relativity Space, Rocket Lab and Stoke Space, use two-stage designs.
Blacklift will also entirely use carbon composite materials, which he said comes from the company’s experience using those materials on its spacecraft as well as Firefly’s experience from its vehicles. Composites, he said, reduce the vehicle’s dry mass by 40% compared to metallic structures.
Perhaps the most notable aspect of Blacklift is the vehicle’s schedule, which calls for a first flight in late 2028. AST argues that its decision to use Firefly engines, rather than develop its own, makes that schedule feasible.
“A typical design cycle of a rocket could be over a decade. Eighty percent of that is on the engine,” he said.
“We’re starting this program on third base,” he added. “We bypass 10 years of engineering and R&D.”
In addition to buying the engines from Firefly, AST said in its presentation it was buying other components, from avionics to separation systems, from “heritage suppliers,” although Avellan said in his talk that the company would be “95% vertically integrated” on the rocket. He said the company is starting to make composite tanks at its Midland factory using existing tools, with 10 tanks completed by January for testing.
“What remains is integration, stage testing, and licensing: exactly what the plan is built around,” the company stated in a slide.
However, it is not clear how well the company’s experience with composite structures will translate to tanks. Rocket Lab, another company using carbon composites for launch vehicle structures, had a composite propellant tank built for the first stage of its Neutron rocket damaged in qualification testing in January. In October, Rocket Lab reported another issue with the tanks, causing it to delay the vehicle’s first launch to sometime in 2027.
Another issue is where Blacklift will launch from. In a Nov. 9 earnings call, Avellan indicated that the vehicle would initially launch from the same pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, built for Northrop Grumman’s Antares and being updated to support Firefly’s Alpha and the joint Firefly/Northrop Eclipse vehicles.
“Our first launches are going to be upgrades on existing launch, which Firefly already have prearranged for their Eclipse configuration,” he said. “Wallops will require an upgrade that we can fit in the timeframe that we have.”
He provided similar comments at the unveiling event. “We have a launch site, a site which is Wallops. It’s the same place where Antares used to fly, and where the Eclipse from Firefly will fly, and that were upgrading that facility.”
“Antares heritage pad at Wallops, already being upgraded for Miranda engines,” stated a slide in AST’s presentation.
However, a spokesperson for the Virginia Spaceport Authority, which operates the commercial launch pads at Wallops, told SpaceNews Nov. 12 that while it has engaged in “early, preliminary conversations” with AST about hosting Blacklift launches, those talks do not include Pad 0-A, the pad built for Antares.
The options available to AST at Wallops include renovating Pad 0-B, which is used for smaller solid-fuel rockets, or building a new pad. Either would be significantly more expensive and time-consuming than using Pad 0-A, as AST claims it can do.
The company did not disclose how much it plans to spend developing Blacklift beyond the $1.3 billion contract with Firefly that includes engines for the first three rockets, a license to allow AST to produce its own engines and engineering services.

Заголовок: OIG To NASA: Watch Your Commercial Contracts
Полный текст:
The NASA Office of Inspector General (OIG) has identified five top management and performance challenges facing the agency, which it says will underpin its oversight work in the year ahead. The OIG announced its 2026 Top Management and Performance Challenges Report on Nov. 12.
The OIG’s five challenges are:
- Establishing a human presence on the Moon
- Managing a robust U.S. presence in low Earth orbit
- Improving management of major programs and projects
- Managing cybersecurity risks and emerging technology
- Sustaining mission critical capabilities and support services
On the Moon, the OIG points to technical challenges with the Artemis human landing systems and next-generation spacesuits as NASA pursues its Ignition initiatives and a long-term lunar presence. It says NASA must also closely monitor its acquisition strategy for lunar delivery services to develop a permanent Moon base and meet “demanding mission timelines.”
For low Earth orbit, the OIG says the transition that comes with the retirement of the International Space Station “will require adequate oversight, significant financial investment, and reliable crew and cargo transport capabilities.”
On program management, the OIG writes:
To ensure the success of major programs and projects, NASA must commit to realistic schedules, adequate budget resources, and transparent reporting. The Agency’s shift toward more service-based commercial acquisitions offers potential benefits but also demands heightened oversight to control costs and mitigate risks.
On cybersecurity, the OIG points to NASA’s decentralized approach to information technology management and the need to make sure grantees and contractors meet strict security standards that protect intellectual property.
The final challenge covers modernizing aging infrastructure, keeping a highly technical workforce and overseeing the commercial partners, contractors and grantees that provide support services. NASA has been rebuilding that workforce after the 2025 cuts, converting what Administrator Jared Isaacman has called thousands of contractor positions back to civil service and recruiting technical staff through its new NASA Force program.
NASA Watch commentary: The OIG’s call for heightened oversight of commercial service contracts comes as Axiom Space is suing Vast Space, alleging that a mission plan Vast delivered to NASA under a private astronaut mission agreement was built from Axiom’s proprietary work, and that a milestone payment was tied to NASA accepting it. Vast says the suit is about competition, not fraud, and the court will sort out the facts. But protecting intellectual property and keeping close watch on commercial providers are exactly what the OIG says NASA has to get right. With final commercial space station proposals due Dec. 14 and both companies bidding, NASA will need to show it can do that.

Заголовок: DND Departmental Results Report shows space gains and a delay
Полный текст:
The Department of National Defence (DND) says in its latest results report that it spent $47.8 billion in the 2025-26 fiscal year, 34 per cent more than the roughly $35.7 billion it first planned.
The 2025-26 Departmental Results Report measures what National Defence and the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) achieved against its plan. DND says the increase reflects faster investment to re-equip the military and the Canadian Coast Guard’s move into the department in September 2025. The increase meant Canada reached NATO’s benchmark of spending 2 per cent of gross domestic product on defence.
In space, DND awarded its Surveillance of Space 2 contract, began a military satellite partnership with Telesat and MDA Space and opened a race to build a Canadian launch vehicle. Those items are spread across the report’s sections on the Arctic, procurement and innovation.
Satellite communications
Under its Arctic work, DND lists “establishing a strategic partnership with Telesat Corporation and MDA Space” to build up the CAF’s military satellite communications through the Enhanced Satellite Communications Project – Polar (ESCP-P). The contract, though, came after the fiscal year ended March 31. In August, the Defence Investment Agency awarded Telesat an initial $2.3 billion to deliver the project’s first phase, with MDA Space also sharing in the work.
Ground network infrastructure for the Tactical Narrowband SATCOM – Geosynchronous project, which covers the CAF’s narrowband military satellite communications, “was delayed due to resourcing constraints,” the report says. Full operational capability, the point at which the system is fully in service, is now forecast for March 2027.
The Aurora Incremental Modernization Project upgraded the sensors and mission systems of the CP-140 Aurora, the patrol aircraft the CAF uses for surveillance and submarine hunting, to keep the fleet flying until it retires in 2030. The project was cut back in 2024 to a secure data link on 12 aircraft, the supplementary report on major capital projects says. Self-defence systems and “wideband global satellite communications are no longer being delivered,” and two aircraft were not modified. Wideband satellite links carry large amounts of data, such as sensor feeds, from wherever an aircraft is flying. The last upgraded aircraft was delivered in May 2025, and the Auroras are to be replaced by up to 14 new aircraft under the Canadian Multi-Mission Aircraft project.
Watching orbit and the Arctic
DND awarded the Surveillance of Space 2 contract to MDA Space in February 2026. The $32 million deal, placed through the Defence Investment Agency, pays for ground-based telescopes to detect and track objects in Earth orbit.
In its research and development work, DND says prototyping and testing produced “advances across space domain awareness,” one of five areas it lists alongside semi-autonomous systems, cyber resilience, quantum technologies and sensing. Space domain awareness is the ability to know what is in orbit and what it is doing.
For the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) modernization, DND awarded a $48.4 million contract for an experimental Polar Over-the-Horizon Radar prototype in the Northwest Territories, and agreed with Australia to co-develop Arctic radar technology. DND’s plan for 2026-27 says the polar radar program has since been replaced by NORTHWATCH, which will combine ground and space-based sensors.
The same NORAD section credits the “Gateway to the Stars” challenge with advancing communications by low Earth orbit satellites. It is run by DND’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security (IDEaS) program, and Halifax’s Galaxia and Toronto’s Kepler Communications have both won contracts under it.
A Canadian rocket
Launch the North, an IDEaS challenge for “Canada’s sovereign access to space,” supported the space capabilities in the Defence Industrial Strategy launched during the year, the report says. In March, DND picked NordSpace, Canada Rocket Company and Reaction Dynamics for $8.3 million each toward a small rocket that can reach orbit by 2028. Separately, DND signed a 10-year, $200 million lease for a dedicated pad at Maritime Launch Services’ Spaceport Nova Scotia.
New IDEaS challenges opened in the year include one on “exploiting connection of Earth and space systems” to extend communications coverage, and another for tactical-grade clocks “for GPS-denied environments in the North.”
What to expect in the next report
The 2026-27 report will cover the ESCP-P contract. DND’s plan for that year also sets out a $25 million Space Rocketry Challenge and a review meant to turn the Royal Canadian Air Force into an “Air and Space Force.”

Заголовок: A Brief-ish History of METI. Part III: The Legacy of Frank Drake & Carl Sagan
Полный текст:
Carl Sagan and Frank Drake were pivotal to the development of the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) and Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI), as exemplified by the Pioneer Plaques and Voyager Golden Records.

Welcome back to our continuing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles, how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox," and the earliest experiments. In our second, we looked at the pioneering work of Cornell Professor Frank Drake, the "father of SETI," and how his efforts led to the first true experiment in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI): Project Ozma and the Arecibo Message.
We also touched on how these efforts led to his lifelong collaboration with fellow Cornell Professor and famed science communicator Carl Sagan. Today, we will see how this collaboration attracted the attention of NASA and led to the most ambitious projects to send messages to space, ones that might even be found by an extraterrestrial civilization (ETC) someday. These are none other than the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records, which are now in the outer Solar System or have entered interstellar space.
Sagan and Drake
As noted in our last installment, Carl Sagan and Frank Drake first met in 1961, a year after Project Ozma took place. To build on the momentum the experiment created, Drake organized an informal symposium at the Green Bank Observatory (where Ozma was conducted) in 1961. To prepare for the event, Drake formulated an equation that summarized the challenges SETI researchers faced. This became known as the Drake Equation, which remains foundational to the fields of SETI and METI.
The equation states that the number of extraterrestrial civilizations in our galaxy that we could communicate with (N) depends on several variables. These include the annual rate of star formation in the galaxy (R*), the fraction of those stars with planets (fp), the number of planets with conditions suitable for life (ne), the fraction of planets that will develop intelligence (fi), the fraction of planets with intelligent life that will develop transmission technologies (fc), and the average length of time a civilization will be able to produce signals (L). Mathematically, the equation is expressed as:
N = R Ã fp Ã ne Ã fl Ã fi Ã fc Ã L
As one of many prominent scientists attending the symposium, Sagan was impressed with Drake's theories and advocacy for using radio astronomy to search for possible ETCs. However, their interactions predated this meeting and included correspondence when both were young graduate astronomy students. Sagan became aware of Drake when he heard of his work measuring Venus's high temperature. After this meeting, the two became close colleagues and professors at Cornell University, where they went on to collaborate on several landmark projects.
Pioneer Plaques
In the early 1970s, the last Apollo mission successfully landed astronauts on the Moon (Eugene A. Cernan, Harrison H. Schmitt, and Ronald E. Evans). This historic accomplishment effectively ended the "Space Race," and NASA was busy contemplating its next moves. It was decided that the Pioneer program, which had sent nine probes to explore the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Mercury between 1958 and 1968, should shift focus to the outer Solar System, exploring the Main Asteroid Belt, Jupiter, Saturn, and the interstellar medium.
This made the probes especially significant, as they would be the first missions to achieve escape velocity from the Solar System. For this reason, journalist and science correspondent Eric Burgess (who was also the Pioneer program's chronicler) suggested that the probes carry a message, should an extraterrestrial species find them someday. Burgess approached Carl Sagan with the idea after hearing him lecture about communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence at a conference in Crimea.
Sagan was enthusiastic about the idea and approached Frank Drake to help design a message that could be interpreted by an ETC. NASA agreed to the plan and gave them three weeks to prepare it, and the two decided to create plaques that could be mounted on the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions. Linda Salzman Sagan, Carl Sagan's wife at the time, prepared the artwork, with additional contributions from space artist and science journalist Jon Lomberg, a long-time collaborator of Sagan's.
The result was the Pioneer Plaques, a pair of six-by-nine-inch (~23 cm by 15.25 cm) gold-anodized aluminum plates. Each contained an engraved pictorial message identifying the probes' place of origin, who sent them, and when they were sent. From top to bottom, left to right, the message included the following details:
- The hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen (the most common element in the Universe)
- The location of the Sun based on its distance from 15 nearby pulsars
- A depiction of the Solar System, showing the flight path of the probe from Earth
- A silhouette of the spacecraft
- Figures of a naked man and a woman, with the man raising his hand in greeting
A detailed view of the visual message on the Pioneer plaques, developed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake. Credit: NASA Ames
The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 probes launched on March 2nd, 1972, and April 5th, 1973 (respectively), becoming the first robotic missions to explore beyond Mars and the Main Asteroid Belt. The Pioneer Plaques have the distinction of being humanity's first interstellar message of greetings. But in a few years' time, Sagan and Drake would take things a step further, creating something that was meant to convey what life on Earth was like.
Voyager Golden Records
The success of the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions motivated NASA to contemplate an even more ambitious mission: dual probes to explore the planets of the outer Solar System. The twin Voyager 1 and 2 probes would launch in the summer of 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment of the outer planets. The mission would conduct close-up studies of Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn's rings, and larger moons. But as the mission progressed, NASA chose to use the alignment to include Uranus and Neptune - what came to be known as the "Grand Tour."
Since these missions would also achieve escape velocity from the Solar System, NASA decided to follow the precedent established with the Pioneer Plaques. This led Voyager project manager John R. Casani to suggest that the Voyager 1 and 2 probes also carry a "message in a bottle" containing information about humanity. He delegated the task to Carl Sagan, who was joined again by Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan, and the three created a metal phonograph record containing information encoded in its grooves.
A record was chosen because it would outlast magnetic tape in the outer-space environment. This time, Sagan and crew were given six weeks to create the records and a budget of $1,500, the equivalent of about 8,780 USD today, though Sagan and his colleagues contributed money of their own. The fruits of their labors were the Voyager Golden Records, a series of 12-inch (30.5 cm) gold-plated copper disks containing sounds and images that portrayed the diversity of life and culture on Earth.
The outer cases were etched with pictograms (see above) similar to the Pioneer Plaques, showing where the probes came from. They also contained instructions for playing the record. In the upper left corner of the case, there is a drawing of the phonograph record and the stylus in the correct position for playing it. Around it, conveyed in binary arithmetic, are the time it takes for the record to complete one rotation (3.6 seconds), the total duration (1 hour), and how it should be played from the outside in.
The upper-right corner contains instructions for constructing pictures from the record. From top to bottom, these include a representation of the signal that indicates the start of a picture, how the signals must be grouped as a series of 512 vertical lines per picture, and what the first image looks like (a circle) to confirm the signals are being processed correctly. The drawing in the lower left-hand corner of the cover is the pulsar map (similar to the Pioneer Plaques) and a drawing of the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen.
The Voyager Golden Record (right) and its protective casing with instructions on how to play along with information about its origin (left). Credit: NASA
The record contains 115 encoded images that show human anatomy (a silhouette of a man and a pregnant woman), the structure of DNA, demonstrations of eating and drinking, major locations on Earth, sports and leisure, our planet's geography, and mathematical/scientific concepts. It also contains sound recordings of greetings in 55 languages, whale calls, and music from various cultures and eras (including Beethoven and Chuck Berry). Said then-President Jimmy Carter of the Records:
This is a present from a small, distant world, a token of our sounds, our science, our images, our music, our thoughts and our feelings. We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.
The cover also features a "radioactive clock" in the form of an electroplated uranium-238 sample. Since this element has a half-life of 4.51 billion years, the recipients can calculate how long the probe has been in space. Unlike the Pioneer Plaques, the Voyager Golden Records had a dual purpose: as a message to any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted them, or as a time capsule for future generations of human explorers should they find them first. As Sagan noted at the time:
The spacecraft will be encountered, and the record played only if there are advanced spacefaring civilizations in interstellar space, but the launching of this 'bottle' into the cosmic 'ocean' says something very hopeful about life on this planet.
Where are they now?
Based on its current trajectory and velocity, Pioneer 10 will reach Aldebaran, a star roughly 65 light-years away in the Taurus constellation, in over two million years. Meanwhile, Pioneer 11 is headed for the Aquila constellation and will pass near one of its stars in about 4 million years. On August 25th, 2012, Voyager 1 made history by becoming the first probe to exit the heliosphere and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2 exited from a different location on November 5th, 2018, becoming the second.
They will be joined by Pioneer 10 and 11 probes around 2057, though this will be difficult to verify since both probes are unpowered and cannot send data back to Earth. These plaques and records are unique in that they remain humanity's first attempts to send physical messages into space intended for extraterrestrial recipients and/or future generations. They also established a legacy that continues to this day and is part of a larger debate surrounding the ethics of METI.
This illustration shows the positions of NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes outside the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past Pluto's orbit. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech
These missions have also inspired debate about what a modern message should be and have inspired some experiments. In a series of NASA-led studies that appeared in the AGU journal Earth and Space Science, an international team of scientists proposed what a modern Golden Record should contain. In the first study, titled "Message in a BottleâAn Update to the Golden Record: 1. Objectives and Key Content of the Message," the team summarized the importance of the "Message In A Bottle" (MIAB) and what should motivate future efforts:
These records not only offer a snapshot of Earth and human civilization but also represent our desire to establish contact with advanced alien civilizations. Our goal is to share our collective knowledge, emotions, innovations, and aspirations in a way that provides a universal, yet contextually relevant, understanding of human society, the evolution of life on Earth, and our hopes and concerns for the future. Through this time and space traveling capsule, we also strive to inspire and unify current and future generations to celebrate and safeguard our shared human experience.
Modern attempts to fashion a MIAB include the message attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to rendezvous with Jupiter and study its moon Europa. The message was unveiled in March 2024, about seven months before the mission launched, and consists of a triangular tantalum plaque - known as the Europa Clipper Vault Plate - measuring about 18 x 28 cm (about 7 x 11 inches) that features graphic elements on both sides. The inward-facing side features an engraving of U.S. Poet Laureate Ada Limón's handwritten "In Praise of Mystery: A Poem for Europa."
The outward-facing panel contains etchings of soundwaves that illustrate Earth's connection to Europa. Each etching is the word "water" spoken in one of 103 languages from around the world, which were converted into waveforms. Each waveform radiates outward from a symbol representing the sign for "water" in American Sign Language (ASL). Since the Europa Clipper is searching for possible evidence of life inside the icy moon, the Drake Equation is also etched into the plate.
Rather than being a message intended for extraterrestrials, this "Golden Record for Europa" honors the spirit of the original records, aiming to spark the imagination and offer a unifying vision. As Lori Glaze, director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA, said in a statement:
The content and design of Europa Clipper's vault plate are swimming with meaning. The plate combines the best humanity has to offer across the universe â science, technology, education, art, and math. The message of connection through water, essential for all forms of life as we know it, perfectly illustrates Earth's tie to this mysterious ocean world we are setting out to explore.
The "Message in a Bottle" plate attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to Jupiter. Credit: NASA
These messages highlight the major shift in consciousness that accompanied the Space Age. With humans now venturing out into space and exploring beyond Earth's orbit, a new awareness was taking root, one which saw humanity in cosmological terms. We were not only pondering the existence of extraterrestrial intelligence and civilizations. We were also considering how we might communicate with them and fashioning messages that might someday reach them... unless we get to them first!
These messages also raise the question of whether ETCs might be doing the same: could advanced civilizations be sending probes with their own messages, ones that share what life is like on their respective homeworlds? The fact that we have sent out four MIABs to date has motivated some scientists to consider the possibility that space is littered with derelict spacecraft, some of which could be messenger probes. Perhaps some of them are even here in our Solar System, lingering near Earth or in the far expanse of the Kuiper Belt.

Заголовок: 'Man of Tomorrow': Release date, plot, cast & everything we know about the 'Superman' sequel
Полный текст:
James Gunn's new DC universe might be done, but the follow-up to 2025's Superman is still on the way.

It feels like yesterday when we were discussing Superman , the first big-screen entry in James Gunn's rebooted DCU. Now Gunn is out , and Skydance (the company formed by the merger of Warner and Paramount) is already dismantling his grand plans for the DCU.

That means that Man of Tomorrow, which arrives next summer, will be the final entry in Gunn's ambitious, and occasionally divisive, DC experiment. The DCU's first chapter — officially titled 'Gods and Monsters' — gave us Supergirl and Clayface (as well as TV shows like Peacemaker S2 and Lanterns ) in the run-up to Clark Kent and Lex Luthor 's return.

Man of Tomorrow looks to be upping the stakes from Earthly villains to intergalactic baddies with the introduction of Brainiac, and it may well have been the herald of the first Justice League movie in the rebooted DCU.

Gunn has yet to prove audiences actually care about more than Batman and Supes, which might explain why this follow-up is also an ensemble of sorts. As the Marvel Cinematic Universe prepares to unleash Avengers: Doomsday , Secret Wars, and even a fresh X-Men reboot, their DC counterparts have always struggled to get their dream team off the ground.

We'll never know what might have been, but we can still enjoy Gunn's DC swansong when it lands in 2027. Here's everything we know about James Gunn's Man of Tomorrow.

When is Man of Tomorrow coming out?

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

Man of Tomorrow will be released theatrically in the United States on July 9, 2027. Most international territories are expected to get it around the same time.

Only a few months after Superman's release and successful box office run, DC Studios and Warner Bros. Pictures confirmed the sequel would be coming two years after Clark Kent's return to the big screen.

How to watch Man of Tomorrow

(Image credit: DC / Warner Bros)

Man of Tomorrow isn't out yet, but you can watch the rest of the DCU so far (it's pretty good for the most part) in preparation first.

When the movie hits theaters on July 9, 2027, it'll likely remain exclusive to big screens for at least two or three months, depending on how successful it is.

With that said, we know Warner Bros. (now part of Skydance) isn't the most patient when it comes to theatrical runs based on its track record, so the chances are Man of Tomorrow will hit HBO Max sooner rather than later, probably by early autumn 2027.

Watch Superman and the rest of the DCU on HBO Max:

Basic (Ads): $10.99/month or $109.99/year
Standard (No Ads): $18.49/month or $184.99/year
Premium (4K): $22.99/month or $229.99/year

Is there a Man of Tomorrow trailer?

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

No, we're still waiting for the first Man of Tomorrow trailer. Looking at the timeline of Superman's fantastic marketing campaign, however, we can guess the sequel will get a first trailer before 2026 ends, probably in time for Christmas.

Is Brainiac the main villain in Man of Tomorrow?

(Image credit: DC Comics)

Yes, James Gunn has officially confirmed Brainiac is the main threat Earth is facing in Man of Tomorrow. This explains why other heroes will be joining Superman in a fight against the alien mastermind, but the plot is looking a bit more complex.

In typical comic book fashion (and somewhat reminiscent of Thor: The Dark World ), the main hook in Man of Tomorrow appears to be a reluctant alliance between the first movie's villain, Lex Luthor, and Kal-El (aka Clark Kent). "Enemies to allies" is always a fun dynamic to have in a sequel, especially when stars David Corenswet (Superman) and Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor) delivered strong and memorable performances the first time around.

The actual plot remains under wraps, but we can guess Brainiac — one of DC's biggest and most iconic alien villains — will be a tough nut to crack, thus requiring some sort of unofficial team-up that will include returning heroes like Mister Terrific, Guy Gardner, Hawkgirl, John Stewart, Blue Beetle, and even Kara Zor-El (Supergirl). There are other names circling the project that could lead to even bigger appearances, but don't expect to learn much about them before the movie's marketing kicks off.

Why should you care about Brainiac? Well, he's a super-intelligent techno-organic alien from the planet Colu with an obsession with knowledge and self-improvement. A perfect foe for Luthor, Earth's greatest mind, but also a breath of fresh air for Superman, who's been stuck battling either Kryptonian menaces or just Luthor too long on the big screen.

Who is in the cast of Man of Tomorrow?

(Image credit: HBO Max)

As a direct continuation of Superman, Man of Tomorrow is bringing back plenty of actors in both main and supporting roles, including:

• David Corenswet (Superman / Clark Kent / Kal-El)
• Nicholas Hoult (Lex Luthor)
• Rachel Brosnahan (Lois Lane)
• Nathan Fillion (Guy Gardner / Green Lantern)
• Edi Gathegi (Michael Holt / Mister Terrific)
• Isabela Merced (Kendra Saunders / Hawkgirl)
• Skyler Gisondo (Jimmy Olsen)
• Frank Grillo (Rick Flag Sr.)
• Sara Sampaio (Eve Teschmacher)
• María Gabriela de la Faría (Angela Spica / The Engineer)
• Neva Howell (Martha Kent)
• Pruitt Taylor Vince (Pa Kent)
• Wendell Pierce (Perry White)

New cast members with publicly announced (or previously established) characters include:

• Lars Eidinger (Brainiac)
• Aaron Pierre (John Stewart / Green Lantern)
• Milly Alcock (Kara Zor-El / Supergirl)
• Xolo Maridueña (Jaime Reyes / Blue Beetle).

Last but not least, we also know Adria Arjona, Andre Royo, Matthew Lillard, and Sinqua Walls are part of the cast, but their parts remain a secret for now.

Who is Adria Arjona playing in Man of Tomorrow?

(Image credit: Disney)

Much of the current Man of Tomorrow speculation centers on Adria Arjona's role in the story. While many have theorized she could be playing Wonder Woman — something that neither Gunn nor Arjona has straight-up denied — the earlier reports and rumors suggested she could be Maxima .

Such a role would fit Gunn's penchant for throwing lesser-known comic book heroes and villains into his movies wherever possible. If you're not an avid reader or longtime DC fan, all you need to know is that Maxima is an alien conqueror from the planet Almerac obsessed with Superman as her perfect mate and king. She's also morally ambiguous, at least when she first appeared, so that makes her a particularly interesting character to bring in for a more complex and nuanced sequel.

With Brainiac spearheading the roster of new DC icons joining Man of Tomorrow, it also isn't hard to imagine another alien figure factoring into the plot, though the flick is getting extremely crowded as it is.

Is James Gunn returning to write and direct Man of Tomorrow?

(Image credit: Warner Bros. Pictures)

Yes, James Gunn is the sole writer and director of Man of Tomorrow.

Despite his previous role as co-chairman and co-CEO of DC Studios, Gunn is extremely hands-on when it comes to most DCU projects. In fact, it seems he had already begun working on his next movie after Man of Tomorrow, though his unceremonious exit will almost certainly mean the end of those plans.

He's also co-producing alongside Peter Safran, who was also ousted in November 2026's DC Studios shakeup.

The rest of the crew includes Sam McCurdy (Peacemaker, Shogun) as cinematographer, Fred Raskin (Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3, Supergirl) as editor, and David Fleming (Superman, Anaconda) as the main composer, among others.

Заголовок: York Space Entering Unmanned Systems Market With Deal For Australian UGV Developer
Полный текст:
Satellite developer and operator York Space Systems on Thursday said it has agreed to acquire Australia’s Outlook Industries in a deal that would expand it into a new market area, unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), with plans to bring production of at least one system to the U.S.

Deal terms were not disclosed but the company did say it did not have to file a a Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission because the transaction costs were immaterial in terms of cash or equity consideration. Australia’s government must approve the deal.

The first platform York is planning to introduce and build in the U.S. is Shadow, a long-endurance UGV the Denver-based company said is “Built to withstand gunfire and harsh environmental condition” that “is engineered to support survivability in active conflict zones.” Shadow has the battery power and an automatic fuel-powered generator for between 30 to more than 45 days of endurance.

York told Defense Daily that Shadow is commercialized and in production and that the company is evaluation its domestic manufacturing options, including contract manufacturing and production in its own facilities. The company described the UGV as about the “size of shopping cart with a wider, lower profile.”

“The design is mature and thus allows us to scale this manufacturing with little capital investment given current production capabilities,” the company said.

With the acquisition pending, York is standing up a new division, York Terrestrial Systems.

The company plans to connect Shadow to its multi-orbit satellite terminal technology and ground-based antenna infrastructure to create its own resilient, globally distributed “integrated ecosystem for unmanned operations” at the edge, it said. York previously acquired satellite terminal developer All.Space , which operates as a standalone subsidiary, and satellite ground communications infrastructure operator Atlas Space Operations.

The addressable market for unmanned ground systems is estimated at $3.1 billion, which York said it will now be able to address. The company also believes that its investments in software and space connectivity will open it to the larger $10.3 billion market for unmanned maritime systems.

“The opportunity extends beyond connectivity to how these platforms are tasked, controlled, and operated,” York said in an email reply to questions. “While each domain has distinct requirements, applying a common software architecture across different vehicle types creates a path for York to expand into the USV and UUV markets.

Dirk Wallinger, York’s CEO, said in a statement that “The future of national defense will be defined by the ability to deploy and coordinate large fleets of unmanned systems while keeping the people commanding them farther from danger. York has been building the architecture that makes that possible, from proven spacecraft and global ground infrastructure to mobile terminals and mission software. With Outlook, we intend to deliver the unmanned systems operating at the edge of the network as well. This is a defining step in our ability to provide the integrated systems our customers will need to fight and win.”

Outlook has less than 20 employees.

This story was first published by Defense Daily

Заголовок: Italy’s Revolv Space Closes Series A Funding Round
Полный текст:
Revolv Space, a new Italian space company, has closed its Series A Funding round worth 5 million euros ($5.6 million). Revolv Space designs and manufactures motion and power generation systems

Revolv Space , a new Italian space company, has closed its Series A Funding round worth 5 million euros ($5.6 million). Revolv Space designs and manufactures motion and power generation systems for satellites. The series A funding round was led by Deep Ocean Capital SGR , which joins Revolv’s shareholders through its Deep Blue Ventures and Deep Blue Space Ventures funds. The company announced the funding round, Nov. 11.

About two thirds of the capital raised will go toward industrializing the company’s already qualified motion products and increasing their production capacity. Revolv reports its technologies have been validated through both ground testing and in-orbit operation, and have already found commercial demand among international customers. Revolv now aims for efficient, sustainable serial production, so it can deliver at high volume and establish itself as a reliable partner for satellite constellation programs.

With this round, Revolv Space has raised a total of 8.6 million euros ($9.6 million) since its founding. The new capital will speed up the industrialization efforts of the company. The company reports eight international customers, 27 units in orbit and more than 83 units produced and delivered.
