Заголовок: Asteroid Bennu's Sample Delivers Another Surprise
Полный текст:
Researchers compared the samples from asteroid Bennu with the Murchison meteorite and measured the amino acid β-alanine in both. Using new techniques, they were able to measure not only their isotopic compositions, but isotopic differences between individual atoms in the same molecule. The results show that some of the same pre-cursors to life formed in different conditions and positions in the protoplanetary disk.

One of the most interesting discoveries in recent years is that some of the molecules necessary for life are found on asteroids and comets. Sample return missions from asteroids have shown that these rocky bodies are far more than just rock. They host some of the fundamental building blocksâamino acidsâthat are used to construct proteins.
These discoveries are a collective a-ha! moment. It's becoming clear that some of the precursors for life could be widespread in the Solar System. And if they're widespread in ours, they could be widespread in others. The idea that life could appear elsewhere in the galaxy got a boost.
NASA's OSIRIS-REx was a big part of this when it returned a sample from asteroid Bennu in 2023. Examination of those samples revealed the presence of 14 of the 20 amino acids that make up proteins in Earth life, along with four of the essential building blocks for DNA and RNA.
Now, researchers have compared one of those molecules with the same molecule from another source, the Murchison meteorite, to see how they differ. The research is published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and is titled "Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of β-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite." The lead author is Ophélie Mcintosh, a former postdoctoral researcher in Penn Stateâs Department of Geosciences.
âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule. - Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State.
"Amino acids are central to prebiotic chemistry, and their abundances and isotopic compositions provide critical constraints on the synthetic mechanisms and environments in which they formed," the authors write. "Samples delivered to Earth from the carbonaceous asteroid (101955) Bennu by NASAâs OSIRIS-REx mission offer an opportunity to investigate amino acids preserved in pristine material unaffected by terrestrial contamination."
β-alanine (beta-alanine) isn't used by Earth organisms to build proteins, but it does play other roles in terrestrial life. Finding it in extraterrestrial rocks is interesting because that can provide some insight into pre-biotic chemistry and what conditions were like in the very early Solar System.
This research is focused on the different compositions of β-alanine found in Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Since the Bennu sample was collected and preserved in a sterile capsule before being opened in laboratory conditions, it's especially valuable scientifically.
This sample of the Murchison meteorite sits in the National Museum of Natural History, Washington, D.C. Image Credit: By User:Basilicofresco - Derivative work from Image:Murchison meteorite.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4301968
âAmino acids are the building blocks of proteins and peptides, but they are also found in carbon-rich meteorites and asteroid samples, so they can provide a direct link between space chemistry and the origins of life on Earth,â lead author Mcintosh said in a press release. âMost studies focus on the distribution and quantification of amino acids, so our question about how theyâre formed is quite new. We used very unique isotope instruments, including one that exists only at Penn State, to help answer those questions.â
A mission to collect an asteroid sample and return it to Earth is an extremely complicated endeavour. Scientists were hopeful that in the time that passed between planning and launching the mission and getting their hands on the sample, new laboratory techniques would be developed to investigate the sample as deeply and thoroughly as possible. That's what has happened in this case. The researchers were able to measure and compare the different isotopic compositions of β-alanine in the Bennu sample and in the Murchison meteorite sample.
They not only compared bulk compositions. In this work, they were actually able to measure and compare isotopic carbon differences in carbon atoms in the same molecule. This level of detail is new.
A device unique to Penn State allowed the measurement of isotopic averages in extremely small samples. It's called pico-CSIA, for Picomolar-scale compound-specific isotope analyses. A second device, a modified GC-Orbitrap (Gas Chromatography-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer) measured specific compositions at specific locations in β-alanine molecules.
âIsotope ratios provide a measurable tag that can link molecules to specific reservoirs or processes,â said paper co-author Christopher House, professor of geosciences at Penn State. âFor our study, isotopes provided clues to an older history for specific atoms in a molecule.â
Looking at isotopic composition is a way to look further back in time for the β-alanine's formation history. Typically, researchers are looking at processes inside the asteroid body itself for clues to how it formed.
But examining isotopic composition from molecule to molecule is more fundamental, and carbon plays a critical role. It acts as scaffolding for organic moleculesâEarth life is carbon-based after allâand records isotopic differences between molecules and within molecules. "Intramolecular isotopic measurements, which capture the position-specific carbon isotopic distribution within a molecule, offer a particularly powerful approach as they can reveal reaction mechanisms, constrain precursor reservoirs, and reflect environmental conditions.
âThis intramolecular information provides a much more detailed isotopic fingerprint,â lead author Mcintosh said. âInstead of simply asking whether a molecule is enriched or depleted in a particular isotope, we can investigate how that isotope is distributed within the molecule and use this pattern to distinguish between possible formation pathways.â
This work takes isotopic composition to a whole other level. Especially when used on such a carefully handled sample as that from Bennu.
âBeing able to analyze the isotope values for each carbon and nitrogen within the beta-alanine molecule is a dream for geochemistry,â House said. âAnd here it is coupled to the ability to study a pristine asteroid sample returned to Earth by NASA.â
The isotope values from atom to atom within the same molecule were wildly different, which came as a surprise to the researchers. They may have formed before Earth did.
There was a lot of waiting and anticipation leading up to Bennu's successful sample collection maneuver. Once it was complete, there was more anticipation of the sample's arrival on Earth, and what we'd learn from it. That's partly what makes this research so interesting. Credit: NASA Goddard
âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule,â said project principal investigator Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State. âThe preservation of such startling differences is an indicator of the primordial nature of these molecules. We are working with molecules formed at the very dawn of the solar system, possibly even before the formation of Earth.â
The intramolecular isotope differences show that, while their formation pathways were the same, they took place in much different environments, or in different batches. It shows that the same chemical can form in different environments in the protoplanetary disk, and that the disk is spatially heterogeneous.
âOne of the main things we discovered, for both glycine and beta-alanine, is that they might have formed in different environments or places in the solar system,â Mcintosh said. âThis broadens our understanding of the type of environments where you can form those very important molecules for prebiotic chemistry.â
The figure below shows elevated 13C in the Bennu sample, and it's particularly important. "The substantially greater 13C enrichment of the carboxyl carbon in Bennu is consistent with the incorporation of carbon from isotopically distinct precursor reservoirs, potentially reflecting differences in the local chemical environments in which β-alanine or its precursors formed," the authors write.
This summary figure shows the carbon isotopic compositions across Solar System bodies, including Bennu (blue diamonds) and Murchison (grey squares). The figure presents bulk carbon values in different planetary bodies. Carbon is important because life is carbon-based, and it's like the structural scaffolding for organic molecules. Within a single molecule, carbon records isotopic differences in a way that other atoms like nitrogen and hydrogen don't. Notice the he greater 13C in carboxyl carbon (COOH) in Bennu, which is particularly important. Image Credit: Mcintosh, O.M., Baczynski, A.A., Rasmussen, C. et al. Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of β-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Commun Earth Environ (2026).
âWhen you compare the Bennu and Murchison samples, the carbon isotope average is so close that when you factor in margin of error, theyâre basically the same,â Mcintosh said. âBut when you look at intramolecular carbon, theyâre completely different.â
"The samples display similar intramolecular isotope distributions, consistent with a common synthetic route, but differ markedly in their position-specific carbon and nitrogen isotope compositions," the authors explain.
That means the source materials were distinct isotopically. So they must have came from different locations and environments in the young Solar System. The authors say that the differences are hard to reconcile with any known processes taking place inside parent bodies. Instead, they reflect different chemical pathways in different parts of the protoplanetary disk.
An illustration of a protoplanetary disk. This work shows that the same organic molecules can form in different parts of the disk, though with different isotopic compositions. This suggests that prebiotic chemistry can form in a wider variety of conditions. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle (SSC) - February, 2005
âBeta-alanine is a prominent example of the amazingly diverse collection of amino acid-like molecules found in space samples,â Freeman said. âIt can help us understand why there are so many different types of these compounds and where and how they were made. Ultimately, this helps us understand ways that space organics potentially shaped the unique chemistry in life.â
These results could also be helpful as missions to detect and study potential biosignatures elsewhere in the Solar System are launched. Missions to Jupiter's icy moons could benefit from these results, for example.
"Additionally, isotopic analyses of amino acids and other prebiotic molecules in Bennu samples and other pristine astromaterials provide a critical abiotic baseline for the search and identification of chemical biosignatures within our Solar System.

Заголовок: Delivering first Columbia-class sub in 2028 is ‘absolutely achievable’, sub czar says
Полный текст:
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the direct reporting portfolio manager for Submarines, said that delivering the first Columbia-class submarine in 2028 is still a ‘heavy lift.’

WASHINGTON — Delivering the first Columbia-class submarine by the Navy’s 2028 goal is doable — although not an “easy” task, the Pentagon’s first-ever submarine czar said today, seemingly offering a more optimistic outlook on his previously shared view of the goal.
Vice Adm. Rob Gaucher, the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DPRM) for Submarines, said in April that hitting the 2028 target would amount to a “wicked heavy lift.” Today, however, he said the goal is “absolutely achievable” amid an increase in operations in recent months.
“To be clear, delivering District of Columbia in 2028 is still not easy, so it does remain a heavy lift, and we have plenty of work to do,” Gaucher said during the Submarine League Annual Symposium today. “But it is absolutely achievable. My confidence grows each week as we review deck plate performance, align on goals, improve our production planning, and address day-to-day production bottlenecks.”
This is a more optimistic view of the goal from April when Gaucher said they still needed to work through “hiccups” since the submarine had never been operated before. He further said at the time that a 2028 delivery time would not be met if it meant long-term consequences for the program.
Although the first Columbia-class submarine, the District of Columbia, was first slated for delivery in 2027, Navy leaders said in 2025 that the delivery date could shift to 2029 amid supplier issues. Even so, Navy leaders have consistently said this year that they are aiming for a 2028 delivery date for the submarine.
That estimate comes after the Navy and its shipbuilding partners who are building the District of Columbia, General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding, established an acceleration plan in 2025 to deliver all modules for the Columbia-class submarine to the final assembly yard at General Dynamic Electric Boat in Groton, Conn., by the end of 2025.
Rear Adm. Todd Weeks, then the program executive officer for strategic submarines, said at the WEST 2026 conference in February that the acceleration plan had resulted in a construction “ramp-up” for the Columbia-class, and that full-rate construction of the vessel was slated for the early 2030s.
Weeks, who is now the portfolio acquisition executive for industrial operations, said at the time that the District of Columbia was approximately 65 percent complete, and that the second Columbia-class submarine, the future Wisconsin, was roughly 35 percent complete.
The Navy initially stated in 2024 that several shipbuilding programs were suffering from delays due to shipyard workforce and supply chain challenges, and as a result, reported that the District of Columbia was expected to face a 12 to 16-month delivery delay.

Заголовок: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
Полный текст:
A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.

A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered.

When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

"For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis," Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville said in a statement .

Several other supernova imposters have been observed over the past decade or two. Until now, no one knew what causes these stars to repeatedly cry wolf. Thanks to Chandra ’s X-ray vision, Aghakhanloo has led a team of astronomers who think they have now uncovered an explanation.

How did a cosmic vampire hide as a supernova?

The supernova imposter is named AT 2016blu, and is a type of star that we call a 'luminous blue variable,' or LBV. These are the most massive and luminous stars in the universe and their extreme characteristics result in them being highly unstable, undergoing intermittent bouts of mass loss as they eject material from their outer layers into the surrounding space.

However, faking a supernova is not part of their typical behavior, so a new way of looking at AT 2016blu was needed.

"To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized that we needed X-ray data that was timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst," team member Núria Torres-Albà, also from the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, said.

Aghakhanloo’s team were granted the opportunity to commandeer Chandra to target an outburst of AT 2016blu at the earliest opportunity. That opportunity arose in March 2026.

A comparison between Chandra images from 2001–02 and 2026 at top, and optical light images at bottom, showing the supernova imposter outbursts and associated X-rays. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/University of Virginia/M. Aghakhanloo et al; Optical: NSF/KAIT.)

Chandra had previously and coincidentally looked in the direction of NGC 4559 back in 2001 and 2002 and did not notice anything unusual back then. This time around, however, it captured a powerful blast of X-rays coinciding with yet another false supernova outburst.

The X-ray detection allowed Aghakhanloo’s team to assemble a picture of what is happening.

"Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen," he said.

Chandra’s X-ray observations indicate that AT 2016blu has an unseen companion, a compact, high-gravity object that is either a neutron star or a stellar-mass black hole on an elliptical 113-day orbit around the luminous blue variable.

Neutron stars and stellar-mass black holes are the core remnants of massive stars that have gone supernova for real, meaning that at one time AT 2016blu was a binary star system .

Blue star falls victim to a cosmic vampire

Each time the compact object reaches the point in its orbit that is closest to the luminous blue variable, its powerful gravity is able to pull material from the unstable star. This sets in motion a chain of events that results in the brilliant outbursts.

As the stolen starstuff is dragged away from the wounded star and towards the compact object, it forms an accretion disk swirling around the neutron star or black hole so fast and growing so hot that it emits X-rays. These are the X-rays that Chandra saw.

The X-rays are immense, energizing the surrounding cloud of material that had been ejected by the luminous blue variable years before. The cloud is heated and glows extremely brightly in visible light, creating the impression of a supernova.

"We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays," said team member Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. "The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical."

An illustration shows a black hole feeding on a star (Image credit: NASA/CXC/A. Hobart)

Calculations suggest that each year a 440 billion trillion pounds of material at minimum is stolen by the compact object, and possibly two orders of magnitude more than that. This is a huge amount, yet it is only 800 millionths of the mass of the sun , and AT 2016blu’s luminous blue variable is at least 33 times the mass of the sun.

Nevertheless, it is far greater than the maximum rate of material that a neutron star can safely accrete, referred to as the Eddington limit . It’s little wonder that the accretion onto the compact object unleashes such extreme energies.

AT 2016blu is also connected with another mysterious and rare astrophysical phenomenon, that of ultra-luminous X-ray (ULX) sources. The identity of whatever it is that is powering ULXs remains unclear, but the involvement of compact objects such as black holes and neutron stars is high on the list.

AT 2016blu is bright enough to be considered a ULX, so could it act as a Rosetta stone connecting supernova imposters with ULXs? It’s too early to say that; only one other supernova impostor has so far been found to have X-ray emission typical of material being stolen from one star and accreting onto a compact body, and that is SN 2010da, but in that case it is known that the companion is another massive star, a red supergiant, rather than a compact object.

The X-ray detection of AT 2016blu is described in a paper published on Monday (Nov. 9) in The Astrophysical Journal .

Заголовок: AUKUS review was ‘best thing’ for trilateral pact: Colby
Полный текст:
WASHINGTON — A 2025 review of the AUKUS agreement has given the US, Australia and the UK an opportunity to have more candid conversations about the challenges facing the trilateral agreement, according to a senior Pentagon official.
Initiated by the Trump administration last year, the AUKUS review allowed the US to communicate more openly with its two partners about the agreement’s progress, production timelines and budget realities, according to Undersecretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby. Speaking today at the Submarine League Annual Symposium, Colby called the review “the best thing” that ever happened to the trilateral pact.
“If we’re going to actually do this, here’s how it’s going to work, and we’re going to give you as much heads up as possible,” Colby said. He added that failing to address those challenges directly — and instead simply hoping the agreement would work out — would actually undermine AUKUS.
It also prompted what he described as “very productive conversations” with Australia about “reconciling and understanding” how the submarines should be employed, while acknowledging that “everybody has political constraints.”
“At some point in the 2030s, a president’s gonna make a decision to go ahead with this,” Colby said. “We want to understand and operate like in the way that we operate in NATO, which is, … all the alliance leaders have the political authority about whether they’re committed or not.”
The AUKUS agreement was first inked under the Biden administration. Under Pillar I, the US agreed to sell at least three Virginia-class submarines to Australia in the 2030s, while the trio of nations work toward developing a new class of SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered submarines for the Australian and British navies. The agreement’s subsequent Pillar II focuses on cooperation among the three nations to develop and field advanced military capabilities.
Within six months of US President Trump’s second term, his administration announced a review of the agreement to assess whether it aligned with the president’s “America First” agenda. By October 2025, Trump had reaffirmed his support for the pact.
“At the end of the day, this is a practical arrangement that involves the eventual sale of our crown jewels, our military capabilities,” Colby said.
In a separate speech at the symposium today, Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh, commander of submarine forces for US Pacific Fleet, said the three nations are on schedule with AUKUS plans — with some aspects even progressing faster than expected.
“The most consequential allied initiative is AUKUS, which is on plan and in several areas ahead of schedule,” Cavanaugh added. “I see progress in AUKUS every day.”
Diana Stancy contributed to this report.

Заголовок: Avoiding the Starlink Trap: Why the Satellite Industry Must Think Smarter, Not Bigger
Полный текст:
It’s undeniable that Elon Musk has radically shaken up the satellite industry. With thousands of satellites launched and thousands more planned, Starlink has managed to position itself as the dominant force in satellite connectivity. However, beneath the surface lies an important question for satellite network operators (SNOs), mobile network operators (MNOs), governments, and the wider space industry: Is the Starlink model truly the most efficient, cost-effective, and sustainable approach to global connectivity?

Starlink’s constellation strategy is to blanket the planet with coverage using Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites. But this brute-force approach, while impressive, comes with critical disadvantages that the industry can no longer afford to ignore. Operators should instead consider an alternative approach, focusing on smarter, regionally focused constellations that deliver targeted, fixed broadband coverage with significantly fewer satellites, substantially lower capital expenditure, and much greater sustainability.

The Fill-Rate Fallacy

A disadvantage of the Starlink approach-and other large LEO constellations is the low utilization or “fill rate” of satellites. Our analysis suggests Starlink’s global coverage model leads to a fill rate of around 8% to 10%. This is unsurprising given that about 71% of Earth’s surface is covered by water, and only 1% consists of densely populated urban areas where broadband demand is highest. More than 90% of these satellites spend most of their operational lives over oceans and remote, unpopulated areas, representing inherent inefficiency.

To put this into perspective, the next generation Starlink V3 satellite weighs about two tons and will alone provide more than 1 Tbps of throughput. Assuming a constellation of 7,500 satellites doing minimal productive work, the scale of unused capacity becomes astonishing — about 6,750,000 Gbps of throughput will be provided to marine wildlife, with the remaining 10% for the human population. In terms of mass, 13,000 tons of satellites circulating around planet Earth, virtually unused but which need to be maintained, replaced and launched again to keep the constellation alive. This inefficiency isn’t just financially troubling; it’s environmentally unsustainable and sets a troubling precedent for orbital congestion.

The satellite industry can and must embrace smarter alternatives. Smaller, regionally focused constellations operating at higher altitudes, in eccentric or novel orbits, offer an intelligent, sustainable solution. With fewer satellites, operators can provide coverage to specific high-demand regions efficiently and reliably. Rather than 4,000 satellites, a modest constellation of 12 to 24 satellites can achieve comparable, if not superior, results across an entire hemisphere. It should be noted, however, that some low altitude LEO constellations can still provide advantages for direct-to-mobile applications to unmodified handsets.

This approach, while less headline-grabbing than Musk’s “bigger is better” philosophy, is vastly more sustainable. With higher fill rates of around 60% to 70% utilization, operators achieve greater cost efficiency, even if the satellites themselves have to be more capable and therefore more expensive. Satellites in eccentric orbits have longer lifetimes, reduced overall capital expenditure, improved solar exposure, and lower ongoing operational costs, translating into lower lifetime-adjusted cost per bit delivered. A strategically targeted constellation can deliver cost per bit metrics potentially 10 to 15 times cheaper than massive LEO systems. This is a compelling financial argument for any operator, government, or investor weighing the risks and returns of satellite connectivity investments.

Why Relying on Musk Isn’t the Answer for Sovereignty

Another important advantage of opting for novel constellations is their inherent technical superiority for high-reliability communications. Satellites placed in novel orbits can enjoy significantly higher dwell times, remaining visible to user terminals for longer durations. This means fewer satellite handovers and less risk of communication interruptions — vital for delivering reliable, high-quality connectivity. With typically three satellites simultaneously visible at any given time, redundancy and resilience are significantly improved, enabling better service level agreements (SLAs) that meet stringent enterprise and governmental requirements.

Consider the analogy of the Suez Canal: relying on a single massive constellation like Starlink is akin to depending on a single maritime route. A blockage, interruption or political dispute could cripple global connectivity, much like a blockage at Suez can disrupt global shipping. By contrast, deploying multiple smaller, strategically targeted novel constellations would diversify the connectivity infrastructure, making global satellite communications far more robust and reducing reliance on one dominant player.

Beyond economics and environmental considerations, there’s a strategic imperative for governments and sovereign states to carefully consider their reliance on satellite constellations like Starlink which are outside of their control. Recent geopolitical shifts highlight the risks inherent in depending on a single foreign entity-especially one as politically and commercially influential as Musk’s SpaceX.

Worrying scenarios could occur where sovereign states lose control over their communications infrastructure and become vulnerable to geopolitical manipulation or outright service interruption. Recent events in the Ukraine demonstrated the impact on the frontline when Starlink access speeds were reduced, let alone switched off. Countries cannot afford a collapsing frontline. Given the potential land lost along the kill-zone, an investment in a small 12 to 24-satellite constellation appears cheap.

Instead, countries and regions could pursue independent satellite ecosystems, from domestic satellite manufacturing to national launch programs, ensuring long-term strategic autonomy. The smaller, targeted constellation model enables true sovereignty by lowering initial capital investments, enabling independent TT&C from a specific country and encouraging localized value-chain creation.

How Can MNOs Protect Market Share?

From a mobile network operator perspective, the advantages of smaller, smarter constellations become even clearer. With upcoming demand for direct-to-device services, mobile operators risk ceding market share to, or being locked out completely by Musk’s expansive Starlink network.

MNOs now have an opportunity to enhance their 5G networks with satellite overlay by collaborating directly with satellite network operators who deploy constellations designed explicitly for 5G integration and telco-grade resilience. Though terminals for these targeted constellations may initially involve higher antenna costs, overall cost-effectiveness remains attractive. The lower lifetime costs per bit, greater resilience from satellite redundancy, and significantly better fill rates make it economically viable, even highly profitable, for MNOs.

Smarter, Not Bigger

The message is clear: the industry must pivot away from the capital intensive Starlink model towards smarter, targeted satellite solutions. Embracing smaller constellations doesn’t just save money and protect the environment — it empowers sovereign states, fosters innovation within regional space sectors, and sustains long-term business viability.

Satellite network operators, mobile network operators, and governments must collaborate now. The time to act is before our orbits become congested with numerous inefficient satellites. It’s an opportunity to define a truly sustainable and sovereign approach to global connectivity.

It’s time the industry stopped chasing the Musk mirage of “more satellites equal better connectivity.” Less can indeed be much, much more.

Christof Kern is the business development lead for Satellite and Space with TTP and a senior satellite and space industry executive with over 25 years of international leadership experience including SES and Eutelsat. He has played a key role in shaping satellite investment programs, strategic fleet and spectrum development, corporate expansion and next-generation satellite architectures across GEO, MEO and LEO.

Заголовок: Ukraine Reports More Restrictions to Starshield Access
Полный текст:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported more restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield access, telling European leaders that the service is limited on terminals in motion to 100 miles per hour.

This slowdown impacts Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said Thursday at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland.

“Because of the speed restrictions, we simply cannot catch up with [Shahed drones] in time. Near the frontline, we cannot use our aircraft. Only drone interceptors can operate there. And without the speed we need, shooting down these ‘Shaheds’ becomes much harder,” Zelenskyy said. “This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed by Russia.”

Zelenskyy said that Ukraine is working to get information from the U.S. on the disruptions. He also stated that the Ukrainian military has investigated the circumstances and determined they are “not random errors but systematic speed restrictions.”

This comes after Ukrainian forces experienced a similar slowdown last month , putting Ukraine’s access to satellite communications at the center of international news.

Last month, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk responded by saying that any restrictions on the Starshield, the government variant of Starlink, are determined by the U.S. government and the president. However, Musk later stated that SpaceX did restrict Ukraine’s use of commercial Starlink service for violating its service terms and using it for offensive strikes.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in the U.S. have called for investigations into the decisions. Republican Congressman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, spoke out in a Thursday statement that he is “deeply concerned” by the reports and called for a full investigation into the disruptions.

In addition, a bipartisan group of nine senators called for an investigation by the Department of Defense (DoD) last month.

In the satellite industry, it has renewed calls for alternatives to Starlink and greater European sovereign control over certain communications capabilities.

Novaspace CEO and industry analyst Pacôme Révillon said these disruptions have put additional light on the issue, which has been known and ongoing for two to three years. Speaking on a Via Satellite webinar on Wednesday, Révillon noted that Starlink has been a key enabler for Ukrainian forces throughout the war, but it’s not ideal to be “fully dependent on a single source that you cannot control” for certain use cases.

“Part of the solution may come from IRIS² within a few years, part of the solution may come from additional sovereign constellation programs within several years. A piece of the answer may also be from commercial suppliers as an augmentation or diversity option,” Révillon said. “When is there going to be actual choice or diversity for certain capabilities? It’s getting closer, but it’s not there yet.”

The recent disruptions spurred at least one new partnership in Europe between Finnish company Iceye and Nokia , which recently announced a plan to develop a satcom capability for Ukraine, signing a letter of intent with the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine. Iceye CEO Rafal Modrzewski said last month that “Ukraine needs secure, sovereign and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls.”

Rafel Jorda Siquier, CEO and founder of British satellite company Open Cosmos, argued that the on-off switch for these capabilities cannot be “outside the control of those relying on it.”

“Europe needs sovereign, interoperable satellite communications and Earth observation capabilities that provide resilience, operational independence and assured access when it matters most,” Siquier said in a Thursday statement. “This is not about superseding international partners, but ensuring Europe has the capacity to act independently when required, as well as to work seamlessly with allied systems. These developments reinforce the urgency of calls across Europe and the UK to deliver highly assured satellite services under our own control.”

Via Satellite spoke with Open Cosmos exec James Cemmell and industry consultant Christian von der Ropp about the Starlink restrictions in Ukraine, and how Europe moves forward in this week’s On Orbit podcast episode. Listen to the episode here.

Полный текст:

WASHINGTON — The Space Development Agency (SDA) has awarded SpaceX a contract worth almost $10 million to study how the company’s laser communications terminals can best integrate with the agency’s missile defense related satellites.
The study will look at hardware, software and connectivity challenges with transmitting data from the agency’s Tracking Layer of missile warning, tracking and targeting satellites in low Earth orbit (LEO) with the SpaceX Plug and Play, or Plaser, optical communications terminals (OCTs), an SDA spokesperson told Breaking Defense today.
The Plasers provide the satellite-to-satellite laser links at the heart of the Space Force’s nascent Space Data Network Backbone, being built by SpaceX to provide high speed, low latency communications between Defense Department satellites ― with a near-term focus on the Trump administration’s Golden Dome missile defense initiative.
The contract, announced on Wednesday, is worth $9.9 million with options worth up to nearly $12.7 million and covers work through Oct. 7, 2027, including completion of a “risk reduction study, the delivery of representative hardware, and support to missile warning and tracking system integration.”
Issues with connectivity between the SDN Backbone, SDA’s Tracking Layer and the medium Earth orbit missile warning/tracking satellites being developed by Space Systems Command (SSC) now are a key concern for the Space Force. As first reported by Breaking Defense, the OCTs on those constellations are incompatible because they each use a difference optical waveform standard for data transmission.
One approach for integrating SDA’s Tracking Layer with the Plasers, experts previously told Breaking Defense, is to place SDA OCTs on board translator satellites, called Space Exchange Points, being developed by SSC to link its missile tracking/warning birds to the SDN Backbone. Other approaches include buying Plasers to equip future Tracking Layer birds or even developing new transmission standards.
The SDA spokesperson said the new study is a first step, and thus there are a number of potential hardware and software pathways for consideration.

Заголовок: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
Полный текст:
On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement.

The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired.

When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down.

Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.

The European Space Agency's Rosetta spacecraft captured these photos of the Philae lander descending toward, and then bouncing off, the surface of Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko during its historic touchdown on Nov. 12, 2014. (Image credit: ESA/Rosetta/MPS for OSIRIS Team MPS/UPD/LAM/IAA/SSO/INTA/UPM/DASP/IDA)

Why it mattered

The European Space Agency 's Rosetta and Philae expedition was a first-of-its-kind mission, an endeavour to not just rendezvous with a comet and watch it change over time as it approached the sun (that was Rosetta's job), but also to soft-land a probe on its icy and rocky surface to see what a comet is truly made of.

The Rosetta and Philae mission succeeded on both counts, but Philae's historic landing was marred by its turbulent touchdown. Philae actually landed three different times on Comet 67/P , all because the harpoons designed to secure it in place didn't fire as planned.

After the first landing, Philae bounced up and drifted around the comet for two hours, making another bounce before Rosetta's cameras lost track of it. Scientists figured it was stuck in a shady spot where sunlight couldn't reach its solar panels. Because it was solar-powered, Philae needed to be facing the sun properly to generate enough power for sustained operation on the comet's surface.

Still, Philae did have some power stored in batteries, which lasted for more than two days on the surface. That allowed Philae to perform some science with its 10 instruments in the time it had on Comet 67/P. Most notably, Philae found organic molecules that had never been detected on a comet before.

The Rosetta orbiter continued to orbit Comet 67P until September 2016, and it was in that month -- just weeks before Rosetta itself landed on the comet on Sept. 30, 2016 -- that the spacecraft rediscovered the Philae lander lying on its side in a rocky crevice.

Заголовок: I Am Artemis Katie Spicer
Полный текст:
4 Min Read

I Am Artemis Katie Spicer

For Katie Spicer, embracing opportunity and challenge has led to giant leaps during her time at NASA. Now as the NASA lander integration lead for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander, one of the commercially provided human landing systems for NASA’s Artemis program, Spicer will have her handprint on history.

NASA’s Katie Spicer stands in front of the crew cabin prototype for Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lunar lander. The lander is one of two commercial human landing systems that will help safely ferry astronauts from lunar orbit to the Moon’s surface and back for the agency’s crewed Artemis missions in 2028.

NASA/Bill Strafford

Spicer works in the Flight Operations Directorate at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where she evaluates and monitors design and development of Blue Origin’s lander. The design of the Blue Moon lander is rapidly evolving as Blue Origin continues to develop a streamlined lander test article for the agency’s Artemis III rendezvous and docking mission in low Earth orbit as well as a fully functional lander for a crewed lunar landing in 2028.

Spicer works closely with her NASA and Blue Origin counterparts to ensure the design of the Blue Moon lander can support the overall Artemis mission objectives.

“I look at the design of everything Artemis crews will touch, work with, or interface with to ensure systems will function the way crews will need them to,” Spicer said. “In some cases, the design might meet requirements, but I delve deeper into details. How easy will it be for crew to grab handles or handrails? Can they operate push-button displays in microgravity? Are the hygiene systems as user-friendly as possible in the limited space that’s available in the spacecraft? And, are there proper procedures and training to ensure the crew can safely and effectively use the systems? Evaluating all these operational details with crew perspective is part of my job.”

Spicer has spent her career looking at the small details in the big picture.

After earning a bachelor’s degree in microbiology from the Pennsylvania State University in State College, Spicer spent several years working as a full-time homemaker and raising three children. She got her start at NASA working part-time in the historic Life Sciences Laboratory , performing duties such as washing dishes, cleaning lab equipment, and running tests for scientists.

“I went from tidying up and keeping my home running to maintaining the historic lab where the Apollo crews were quarantined when they came back from the Moon and the Moon rock samples were stored,” Spicer said.

From there, Spicer began working with science payloads on the space station. She helped operate the Human Research Facility racks in the International Space Station National Laboratory and worked with scientists and crew to ensure in-flight processes and protocols were completed. It was there that Spicer found a love for the fast-paced dynamic of real-time space operations.

Spicer became a flight controller at NASA Johnson’s Mission Control Center in 2018. The learning curve to become a flight controller was steep, but it did not deter her. Spicer studied and trained for five years to earn the ultimate instructor and flight controller certifications.

“Unlike most people I work with, I don’t have an engineering degree,” Spicer said. “On my own, I studied engineering principles. I passed boards and certification tests. I learned to speak ‘engineer!’”

Spicer spent five years as an Operations and Support Officer in the space station’s flight control room in Mission Control, also known as the “front room” to spaceflight.

Now, when she looks at the Moon in the night sky, Spicer says she’s humbled and honored to be part of the team that’s sending astronauts back to the lunar surface.

“I’m reminded of the great responsibility that NASA has in this endeavor, of the legacy of the courageous Apollo crews who went before, and inspiring the next generation of space explorers to keep going and reaching for the stars!” she said.

As part of a Golden Age of innovation and exploration, NASA will send Artemis astronauts on increasingly difficult missions near the lunar South Pole to explore more of the Moon than ever before. In addition to providing economic benefits and advancing scientific discovery through its Moon missions, NASA will establish an enduring human presence on the lunar surface and build on the agency’s foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

Заголовок: SpaceX's Starship megarocket will launch to orbit on Nov. 13. Will you be able to spot it in the night sky?
Полный текст:
"It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size."

SpaceX's Starship megarocket is slated to launch on its ambitious 15th flight test as soon as this Friday (Nov. 13). Will you be able to spot its leviathan upper stage, known as Ship, or its Starlink satellite passengers as they circle Earth during the historic orbital jaunt?

Flight 15's 75-minute launch window opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) on Nov. 13 . Starship will fly from SpaceX 's Starbase site in South Texas, where it will be 4:45 p.m. at the opening of the window — about an hour before sunset. The launch could therefore be especially dramatic for folks in the area.

"As it launches towards the southeast, and it will be daylight, then the prospects for viewing from the U.S. are going to be in Texas and the states along the Gulf of Mexico," Robert Massey, deputy executive director at the Royal Astronomical Society, told Space.com. "They could see the exhaust plume (the ' jellyfish ') with the sky darker for observers further east."

If all goes to plan, Starship's Super Heavy booster will propel the Ship upper stage through the densest part of Earth's atmosphere before returning to Starbase for a powered landing and capture via the "chopstick" arms of the "Mechazilla" tower system . Ship, meanwhile, will go on to orbit Earth approximately 14 times over the following 22 hours, during which time it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites before returning to Starbase for its own ambitious catch attempt.

When should I look for Starship and its Starlink train?

Satellite visibility in the night sky depends on a cocktail of factors, from the size of the spacecraft to its reflectivity, orbital inclination and position relative to the Earth and sun.

Ship is big — about 171 feet (52 meters) tall — so it will be a viable target for skywatchers, experts say.

"It certainly will be visible in twilight hours. It should be very bright, considerably brighter than the Starlink satellites due to its size," professor James Osborn of Durham University told Space.com. "Where and when is a bit more tricky."

Starship Flight 14 rises away from its launch tower during the September 2026 test flight from Boca Chica, Texas. (Image credit: Photo by Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Ship and its Starlink satellites may be seen in the 90 minutes directly after sunset on Nov. 13 and before sunrise on Nov. 14, as the probes catch the sunlight on either side of Earth's colossal shadow as they drift through the twilight sky.

The spacecraft will initially appear as a string of bright, evenly spaced lights, with Ship most likely appearing significantly brighter than the Starlink satellites. However, Osborn noted that the lack of publicly available data makes it challenging to forecast exactly when the spacecraft will appear.

"During its 14 orbits over 22 hours, the spacecraft is between inclinations of 30.5 [degrees] N and S of the equator," explained Massey. "So it will be best viewed between those latitudes, and then lower in the sky up to latitudes of 40 N and 40 S. That's pretty much the whole of the contiguous U.S."

Space.com skywatching columnist and veteran meteorologist Joe Rao shared further details on what stargazers may see with the naked eye as Ship drifts silently through the autumn sky.

Starlink satellites form a trail of star-like points in the night sky soon after deployment in 2023. (Image credit: Photo by Arda Kucukkaya/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station , but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," explained Rao. "The Starlink V3 satellites are much smaller, so not as bright, perhaps ranging anywhere from 2nd to 4th magnitude, depending on the angle of illumination with reflected light from the sun ."

Magnitude is the scale used by astronomers to measure the brightness of objects in the night sky. The lower the magnitude, the brighter the object! The unaided eye can make out objects with a magnitude of around +6.5 under ideal dark sky conditions, while the planet Venus currently shines at magnitude -4.41.

The Starlink train will likely fall further behind Starship as the 22-hour mission progresses, while the train itself will become more elongated, according to Rao. "For locations where it will make a high arc across the sky, the Starship should be visible for at least a few minutes, although because it is orbiting at a lower altitude (170 miles/275 km) compared to the ISS, it probably will appear to move somewhat faster. "

How can I track Starship after launch?

There are multiple handy resources that should allow you to track Ship and the newly deployed batch of V3 Starlink satellites following their scheduled launch on Nov. 13, including the websites Heavens-Above , Star Dash , Orbital Radar and Find Starlink .

Be sure to keep an eye on our Starship Flight 15 live blog for all the latest news along with our launch timings article containing details on how to watch SpaceX's potentially historic orbital launch attempt.

Полный текст:
Built by Game Aerospace Composites, the GB1 Gamebird — designated the T-19A by the Air Force — was funded through corporate and civilian donations and will form the foundation of a new aerobatic flying team.

WASHINGTON — The US Air Force today unveiled a new aerobatic aircraft that officials say will help train future generations of pilots.
Dubbed the T-19A Kestrel, the aircraft arrived at the Air Force Academy today with a flying demonstration. Officials say the Kestrel is the academy’s first powered aerobatic platform — an aircraft designed to perform high-G maneuvers typically associated with flying displays. The platform will give cadets aviation experience earlier in their training and form the foundation of a new aerobatic flying team.
Calling the Kestrel program “historic,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach said in a press release that officials went “from an idea to four aircraft built and delivered” in just 10 months. The aircraft recently finished certification flights, according to the release.
“This aircraft will provide an opportunity to train our cadets in ways that were previously not possible,” Air Force Academy Superintendent Lt. Gen. Paul Moga said in the release. “We will strengthen their aviation skills and develop the confidence, discipline and leadership required of future Air Force officers.”
In response to questions from Breaking Defense, an Air Force spokesperson said the service accepted four two-seat, single-engine GB1 Gamebird aircraft built by Game Aerospace Composites, which were funded through corporate and civilian donations. The Air Force officially designated the aircraft as the T-19A.
“The gift is worth $3 million and the Air Force invested approximately $400,000 to supplement the gift of initial spares, and the procurement of necessary support equipment and aircrew flight equipment for the initial cadre and future cadets,” the spokesperson said. The service will also budget approximately $1 million annually to sustain the aircraft.
The Kestrel’s arrival comes as the Air Force grapples with a critical pilot shortage. Despite hitting a key recruitment benchmark in September, officials say a shortfall of 2,000 aviators will likely take years to resolve.
The T-19 is far from the Air Force’s only investment in boosting its pilot training pipeline. The service is also working to field its newest training jet, the T-7 Red Hawk, which is years behind schedule. Air Force officials say the Red Hawk will better prepare aviators for advanced aircraft compared to the aging T-38 Talon it’s replacing.

According to the release, Moga picked six active-duty pilots from the Academy’s 306th Flying Training Group to form the aerobatic team’s curriculum. The pilots will also perform at recruiting events and air shows across the United States. Officials eventually hope to establish a nationally competitive aerobatic and demonstration flying program with the Kestrel.
Additionally, the Kestrel program will establish “a cadet leadership pipeline,” through which select students will receive annual mentorship on the T-19. Over the long term, officials aim to deliver “a premier capability that evolves to include greater cadet involvement in training, demonstrations and program operations,” the release says.
Following its arrival, the aircraft has been “fully cleared” for use at the Academy, the release says. The Academy’s Davis Airfield will serve as the hub of all Kestrel operations.

Полный текст:
Память, которая дорисовывает лица

Мы привыкли считать, что глаза работают как камера: что перед нами, то и видим. Случай 28-летнего Карла, описанный в журнале Cortex, показывает, что мозг способен вклеивать в картинку детали из памяти и вполне буквально.

Карлу удалили артериовенозную мальформацию, то есть аномальный клубок сосудов, в правой задней височной области мозга. Эта зона участвует в обработке зрительной информации, речи, контекстной памяти и узнавании обстановки, так что вмешательство там чревато сюрпризами. Сюрприз и случился: после операции Карл начал видеть на лицах людей черты своей серой полосатой кошки Луны — миндалевидные глаза, огромные зрачки, полоски. Вживую и на экране.

Подмена работает в обе стороны: иногда глаза знакомого человека проступают на морде Луны. А если первым Карл увидел кого-то из людей, его черты могут «перескочить» на других или обратно на кошку. Эпизоды часто длятся часами, порой весь день. При этом чужие черты не выглядят наклейкой — они естественно вписываются в лицо и меняются вместе с ракурсом и расстоянием. Карл узнаёт, чьи это черты, а значит, мозг достаёт их из долговременной зрительной памяти.

Похоже, у Карла прозопометаморфопсия — редкое расстройство, при котором искажаются форма, положение, цвет или текстура черт лица. Его иногда называют «синдромом демонического лица».

Как изучать то, что видит только сам пациент? Команда Брэда Дюшейна из Дартмутского колледжа несколько месяцев генерировала изображения с помощью ИИ и дорабатывала их по комментариям Карла, пока он не признал их похожими. Это реконструкции того, что он запомнил.

Но ни один такой случай сам по себе не объясняет, как именно мозг совершает подмену. Пока это наблюдение за одним пациентом: ценная зацепка, до готовой теории ещё далеко.

Following third-quarter financial results that held flat compared to the prior year, Gilat Satellite Networks sharply reduced its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast from 13% to 3%.
In quarterly results reported on Nov. 10, the satellite ground segment and networking provider lowered its 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $455 million to $475 million, down from its previous projection of $500 million to $520 million.
Diverging Defense and Commercial Segment Performance
The guidance cut stems from external schedule setbacks across satellite launch manifests and commercial aviation programs. Delays in satellite launches and in-flight connectivity (IFC) equipment deliveries slowed revenue conversion across commercial business lines, weighing on overall top-line expansion despite strong military demand.
For the third quarter, Gilat recorded total revenue of $116 million, remaining flat year over year. Underlying segment performance highlighted a pronounced split between government and enterprise markets: defense revenue surged 53% to approximately $37 million, while commercial revenue declined 4% to roughly $70 million as IFC rollout schedules shifted to the right.
Full-Year Financial Trajectory
With third-quarter top-line performance constrained by launch availability and commercial aviation terminal rollouts, the updated $455 million to $475 million guidance represents a $45 million reduction at the midpoint compared to earlier full-year expectations.
While growing military communications demand continues to expand Gilat’s defense business, near-term consolidated growth remains dependent on the stabilization of satellite launch schedules and the pace of scheduled IFC deliveries across commercial airline fleets.

Заголовок: 'Warhammer Survivors' is the perfect gateway into the 40K universe
Полный текст:
This Vampire Survivors spin-off has a lot of love for the famous grimdark sci-fi universe, but without the intimidatingly dense lore and complex systems.

We've had no shortage of great Warhammer 40K games lately, but most aren't exactly aimed at the casual crowd. Warhammer Survivors changes that, finally providing curious gamers with an easy entry point into the grim darkness of the 41st millennium.

Developed by Auroch Digital (in collaboration with Vampire Survivors' Poncle), this new spin on the survivors-like roguelite subgenre mixes the sci-fi 40,000 setting with the pure fantasy Age of Sigmar universe. This means heroes and enemies from all over the Warhammer mythos meet together in a bite-sized game that anyone can figure out and enjoy in less than five minutes.

When you look at the alternatives, that's a remarkable achievement for a franchise that's notoriously hard (and often expensive) to get into .

Warhammer Survivors isn't bogged down by dense lore, involved mechanics, or massive campaign playthroughs. It's more of an "inspired by" effort that gives casuals a small taste of the series' iconic characters — including Boltgun 's Malum Caedo — and factions like the terrifying Tyranids, the raucous Orks, and the foul forces of Chaos.

All of 40K's (and Age of Sigmar's) recognizable elements are on display, but they serve more as flavoring sprinkled on top of Vampire Survivors' successful formula.

If you're new to the Survivors-like subgenre, it's a unique gaming experience. You battle an endless onslaught of enemies that slowly march towards you, with your character passively attacking automatically. You only need to move them around sprawling arenas and select level-up upgrades and items after collecting enough gems (skulls in this case).

The moment-to-moment gameplay is as simple as it can get outside of walking sims and interactive "experiences," but there's a deceiving depth to item synergies and how to correctly "build" characters to endure all the carnage.

Unlike Poncle's original game, Warhammer Survivors struggles a bit to get going. The early hours are sluggish until you unlock certain meta upgrades, but its still got that Vampire Survivors magic at its core.

As far as "podcast/gym games" go, this is a perfect fit. There's just enough going on to keep one's brain engaged, but minimal inputs and a tight overarching design lead to a rhythm that's easy to get into without using much brainpower. It's oddly satisfying to weave through enemies and level up your firepower, watching a single Astra Militarum grunt grow into a full Lasgun-spamming, chainsword-wielding wrecking ball.

Achievement and unlock hunters will find enough to bite into here, too. It's unclear if the devs will continue to add more Warhammer 40K and Age of Sigmar deep cuts to this game via DLCs and free updates, but those universes have daunting depths to explore. This really could become a gateway game for future 40K fans: by the time they realize they're hooked, they'll already have 2000 pts of space marines painted and ready to play.

(Image credit: Auroch Digital)

As massive sci-fi and fantasy properties try to aggressively expand and absorb more and more fans, it's easy to pander to already-converted diehards too much. And sure, we can't wait for strategy heavyweights like Dawn of War 4 and Total War: WH40K either, but they're hardly good recommendations for folks who don't even know what a Space Marine is or why the robotic Necrons are so grumpy.

Warhammer Survivors won't answer those questions beyond the surface-level iconography, but it's fun enough to push those curious to dig deeper and embrace the same material in more mature video game genres... and maybe even pick up a few miniatures .

Warhammer Survivors is now available on PC (Steam & GOG), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 1/2, and mobile (iOS & Android). It's also playable on Game Pass.

Заголовок: Axiom Vast Lawsuit Alleges Copied NASA Mission Plan
Полный текст:
Axiom Space has sued rival Vast Space under the False Claims Act, alleging that Vast handed NASA a mission planning document built from Axiom’s proprietary work. The complaint, filed June 19 in federal court in Houston, was unsealed by a Nov. 4 order from US District Judge Charles Eskridge, according to court filings reviewed by Ars Technica.
The document, a Mission Integration and Operations Management Plan, is one of the deliverables NASA requires under its Private Astronaut Mission (PAM) agreements for crewed visits to the International Space Station (ISS). NASA awarded Vast the sixth such mission in February, and Axiom alleges that NASA’s acceptance of the plan is a condition of a milestone payment to Vast.
According to the complaint, NASA told Axiom on June 3 that Axiom’s sensitive information had turned up in a Vast deliverable. Axiom says NASA advised that the document swapped in “the PAM Provider” for Axiom’s name in some places and left Axiom’s name and company details in others.
The Justice Department declined to intervene on Oct. 23, so Axiom is pursuing the case on its own, seeking civil penalties, treble damages, litigation costs and a whistleblower award. Vast said the suit is about competition, not fraud, that the department’s decision reflects the merits, and that its PAM work is continuing without interruption. NASA spokesman George Alderman told Ars Technica the agency “is aware of the matter but does not comment on litigation.”
By Axiom’s own account, it was NASA that spotted Axiom’s name in Vast’s paperwork and flagged it. Final proposals for NASA’s commercial space station competition are due Dec. 14, and both companies are bidding.
NASA Watch commentary: “Does not comment on litigation” is a standard line, but NASA isn’t a bystander here. By Axiom’s account, NASA found Axiom’s name in a Vast deliverable and told Axiom about it, so what NASA did next with that plan, and with the milestone payment tied to it, is part of the story either way. With final proposals for the commercial station competition due Dec. 14 and both companies bidding, the people judging those bids, and everyone who has to trust the result, should know that question has been answered.

Полный текст:
Robert H. Steinau, nominated to be NASA's inspector general, told the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday he would pursue aggressive oversight and independent reviews of agency programs as NASA works to return to the Moon.

Robert H. Steinau, nominated to be NASA’s inspector general, told the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday he would pursue aggressive oversight and independent reviews of agency programs as NASA works to return to the Moon.
Steinau made the pledge in his opening testimony for his nomination hearing before the committee. A Marine Corps veteran and former Secret Service agent, he joined NASA’s Office of Inspector General (OIG) in 2009 and later served as assistant inspector general for investigations.
Steinau was the senior official performing the duties of inspector general from December 2024 until his nomination in September. Kate Sheehey, previously the OIG’s assistant inspector general for management, has held that role since.
In his written statement, Steinau said NASA’s “extraordinary ambition demands aggressive oversight.” He named Artemis landers, next-generation spacesuits and the lunar supply chain, safe operation of the International Space Station through its retirement, and what he called “dependence on a single launch provider” among the risks the office will watch, along with cybersecurity, aging facilities and workforce retention. Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., raised that last point in his opening remarks, noting NASA lost roughly 22 percent of its workforce in 2025, including 20 percent of its PhD-level staff.
Asked by Sen. Ted Cruz how he would address cost overruns and schedule delays on NASA’s major programs, Steinau said the OIG’s annual top management challenges report this year will center on returning astronauts to the Moon, and that the office builds its audits around NASA’s major programs. He described the OIG as a “truth seeker” that publishes its findings and works with the administrator and Congress on corrective steps.

Заголовок: Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting Trash—It’s About Control and Economics
Полный текст:
If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesnât work that way, and a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who we typically cover for his work on the Solar Gravitational Lens idea, makes a good argument as to why.
Dr. Turyshev has turned his attention to orbital debris at a critical juncture. According to the filings made to the FCC, SpaceX, the company that runs the largest satellite megaconstellation, had their Starlink satellites perform 144,404 collision avoidance maneuvers in the six months from December 2024 through May 2025. Even accounting for the fact that there are more Starlink satellites in orbit now than ever, that means, on average, each one is having to dodge a potential crash every week.
Fortunately, Starlinks themselves arenât exactly in the âdanger zoneâ of orbit. They typically orbit around 500-600 kilometers, along with other megaconstellations such as Amazonâs Kuiper and Chinaâs Qianfan. In the paper, Dr. Turyshev separates this orbit from those higher up. At 500-600, there is enough atmosphere left that the area is semi self-cleaning - dead satellites and debris in these orbits will burn up in a few years.
Fraser talks about the oribtal dance that keeps satellites from crashing into one another.
Higher up, though, there are bigger problems, both literally and figuratively. At around 850 kilometers, giant rocket stages from launches past lurk with no control, and little to no atmosphere to drag them down in a reasonable time frame. They could stay in orbit for decades or centuries and donât have any means of avoiding one another. When they inevitably collide, they will spray debris both into their own orbit but also into higher and lower ones, potentially causing even greater problems for the lower orbiting communications megaconstellations.
According to European Space Agency Data cited in the paper, about 96 percent of the long-term collision risk comes from these dead objects. And Dr. Turyshev further proves that, even if we stop launching rockets tomorrow, the amount of debris already up there would collide and shatter faster than nature can clear it.
This isnât a surprise to anyone who has been paying attention to the problem of space debris for any length of time. That orbital cascade, commonly known as Kessler Syndrome, has been a long-standing problem orbital dynamicists have been grappling with for decades. According to Dr. Turyshev, controlling it comes down to three separate levers.
Fraser talks about some techniques to remove space debris from orbit.
First, regulators have to ensure that satellites are designed to intentionally deorbit quickly once their missions end. Luckily, they are already moving in that direction, with the FCC recently introducing a rule requiring satellites to clear out within five years of retirement, rather than the twenty-five years that had held sway for the last few decades. According to the paper, if the reliability of disposal rises from 90 to 99 percent and a satelliteâs allowable afterlife is cut to five years, it decreases the environmental hazard by a factor of 50.
A second lever is better vision. Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems are great at tracking large bulky objects, but terrible at smaller objects the size of a bullet. But even for larger ones, thereâs still a level of âfuzzinessâ that analysts have to deal with, which means they know a general box where an object is in space, but not its exact position. When that box is large, satellite operators waste precious fuel dodging objects that never really posed a threat in the first place.
Rather than trying to track every bolt and nut floating through space, Dr. Turyshev suggests that we need to concentrate on shrinking the uncertainty zone around potential high-risk close calls. That idea aligns directly with the real-world infrastructure upgrades that are happening through NOAAâs Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), which is expanding its pilot program to reach more commercial operators this year.
Fraser discusses whether there's a limit to how many satellites we can potentially launch.
The third lever is what to do with the semi-permanent debris thatâs already in space. Instead of launching expensive missions to deorbit and grab every single one of them, Dr. Turyshev suggests an alternative he calls Just-in-Time Collision avoidance. If two dead rocket upper stages are about to crash, operators could use ground-based lasers or small swarms of shepherd satellites to move a few meters out of the way just before impact. While not quite as much of a long-term solution (since it simply avoids the immediate problem), it does offer a much less expensive solution than attempting to deorbit everything.
Economic calculations will play a major role in any future space debris solution, and right now the market is broken, as Dr. Turyshev points out. Due to agreements in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, a private cleanup company cannot simply fly up to an abandoned Soviet rocket booster and deorbit it. Technically that rocket booster is still owned by the government that launched it (even if, in this case, that government doesnât technically exist anymore). Also, orbital space suffers from the âtragedy of the commonsâ, as one firm removing a rocket booster benefits all of the other companies with equipment in orbit, despite the cost not being spread amongst them.
Dr. Turyshevâs solution is to create contracts that would pay for verifiable reductions in long-term risk - in other words, it would incentivize companies like Astroscale, which are intending to remove space debris, to remove the most dangerous pieces first. This would be financed by governments, using money from âdisposal bondsâ that pay back if the satellite successfully orbits without active intervention from Astroscale or one of its competitors.
Ultimately, this seems like a reasonable framework to build a long-term plan for space debris mitigation. But there are still some issues - like sheer scale. Even at a 99% successful deorbit rate, with potentially millions of satellites in orbit that would still leave tens of thousands of derelict ones at any given time. And thereâs definitely no clear path forward to a successor to the Outer Space Treaty. But the longer we as a space-faring civilization ignore these issues the worse the problem is going to get. Hopefully this paper helps provide part of the impetus to push towards a formal adopted solution framework. Or at the very least start a more comprehensive conversation about it.

Заголовок: SpaceX hid behind another name in the Arizona desert, and now it’s going big
Полный текст:
SpaceX puts a $50 billion price on its Arizona supercompute campus ahead of December's hearing.

SpaceX has put a price tag on the supercomputer campus it wants to build in the southern Arizona desert. In a statement Thursday, the company said it is pursuing a roughly $50 billion supercompute campus in Cochise County, about 80 miles east of Tucson. Together with a separate facility planned at Starbase, Texas, the two projects add up to more than $74 billion in planned investment.

The Arizona figure had not been disclosed before. SpaceX’s involvement only became public on November 4, when company representatives hosted a packed town hall at Cochise Elementary School for an application filed under the name Tombstone Resources LLC. A SpaceX representative told residents the filing used another name because putting SpaceX on it “draws attention” from outside the county, local station KVOA reported.

The application describes a 747-acre site near the Willcox Playa with up to nine buildings of about 493,000 square feet each. SpaceX plans to bring the campus online in four phases of roughly 1.5 GW, reaching 6 GW at full build, backed by a 24 GWh battery system and about $3.6 billion in grid upgrades. At that size, it would draw about 2.5 times more power than every data center in Maricopa County combined, according to an Arizona Republic analysis .

SpaceX says the project will create about 5,500 construction jobs and 1,000 permanent jobs, and that it could cut electricity bills for members of the local cooperatives by up to 20 percent. The campus would use dry cooling with no industrial groundwater use. Its application estimates ongoing water needs of 7 to 10 acre-feet a year, roughly what 20 to 30 homes consume.

Power is the bigger question. The site sits next to the Apache Generating Station, a coal and natural gas plant with about 1 GW of capacity that had been slated to retire by 2028. SpaceX told residents its investment could expand the station to more than 6 GW.

Local opposition is organized. A petition asking the county to deny the permit has gathered about 2,400 signatures, and the nearby playa is a landing spot for federally protected sandhill cranes, which SpaceX says its design accounts for. The Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission will hold a public hearing on December 9 in Bisbee, with written comments due November 27. If approved, construction could start in March 2027.

The Texas project faces a vote the same day. The Starbase City Commission will consider a property tax abatement for SpaceX’s $24 billion gas plant and supercompute facility at its own December 9 hearing, as Teslarati reported . SpaceX said Thursday the Starbase site has already generated more than 3,000 construction jobs, and it committed $220 million to Brownsville’s water and wastewater systems, $40 million of which has been paid.

Both campuses would expand a footprint still centered on the Memphis area, where SpaceX’s Colossus data centers run largely on gas turbines and the company won a permit for a power plant in Southaven, Mississippi earlier this year. SpaceX ended the third quarter with 1.7 GW of nameplate compute. The Arizona campus alone, at full build, would be more than three times that size.

Заголовок: ULA’s Vulcan suffers anomaly on return to flight with first Amazon Leo payload
Полный текст:
United Launch Alliance’s current flagship launch vehicle, Vulcan, returned to flight after a grounding that began in February due to recurring nozzle issues with the GEM-63XL solid rocket boosters, but the launch was ultimately unsuccessful due to an anomaly during second stage flight.

The initial nozzle issue occurred in October 2024 during the rocket’s second flight, before a similar issue occurred on the USSF-87 mission in February of this year.

A Vulcan VC6L, the most powerful configuration of the Vulcan rocket with six solid rocket boosters, an extended payload fairing, and a low-Earth orbit-optimized Centaur V upper stage, launched the Amazon Leo LV-01 mission on Sunday, Nov. 15 at 12:40 PM EST (17:40 UTC).

The flight had been delayed twice due to a commodity flow issue and later a communications issue.

Today’s first attempt at 12:11 PM EST (17:11 UTC) then held at T-20 seconds due to a pressure-reducing valve anomaly, which was resolved in time to launch at the end of the 29-minute window.

The LV-01 vehicle assembled in VIF-A prior to rollout. (Credit: ULA)

The 65-m-tall rocket, capable of carrying up to 27,200 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO), generated 17.2 MN of thrust with six GEM-63XLs and two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, using liquid oxygen and methane as propellants.

The rocket took a northeast trajectory carrying 40 Amazon Leo satellites. This was the most satellites carried on any Amazon Leo mission to date and was the first of up to 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon with ULA for its broadband constellation, a competitor to Starlink.

Mission LV-01 was to deploy its satellites to a 450 km circular parking orbit inclined 51.9 degrees to the equator, and would have used 21 separate deployment events.

The first deployment was to occur at about T+01:17 hours after liftoff, and the overall payload deployment sequence would have lasted about 25 minutes and 40 seconds. The Centaur V was going to coast for another 219 seconds before turning to execute its deorbit burn, which would have occurred nearly two hours after liftoff.

However, ULA announced that an anomaly at T+10 minutes resulted in the Amazon Leo satellites not making orbit.

This flight was the first one for the low-Earth orbit-optimized Centaur, and the anomaly occurred during the Centaur’s first burn.

Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.

Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us…

— ULA (@ulalaunch) November 15, 2026
