Had the LV-01 satellites been deployed, the Amazon Leo constellation would have had 432 satellites in orbit. As of early November, 368 satellites were in their operational orbit, with six satellites having reentered Earth’s atmosphere to date.

Amazon Leo needs 578 satellites deployed to a circular orbit at an altitude of 630 km to start initial regional service, and the first-generation network is scheduled to use up to 3,236 satellites.

Amazon obtained an extension from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on June 5 of this year for a waiver of the requirement to fly half of its satellites by July 30, 2026. This will allow the company to complete its constellation by July 30, 2029.

If the constellation is not complete by then, the FCC could limit Amazon to using the satellites that have already launched.

Infographic showing the Vulcan flight profile for LV-01. (Credit: ULA)

The Amazon Leo service has already signed up leading customers such as Delta Air Lines, JetBlue Airways Corporation, Crane Worldwide Logistics, and Hunt Energy, and will also offer its broadband product to individual users.

Amazon Leo also has flights booked on other launch vehicles such as New Glenn and the Ariane 64, but the company’s Vulcan launches are critical for building out the constellation at scale in a timely manner.

The LV-01 flight was closely watched for any repeat of the booster nozzle issue, which would likely have delayed future flights of the rocket. Instead, the anomaly occurred on the Centaur V upper stage.

The GEM-63XL, a stretched version of the GEM-63 that has successfully been used on ULA’s Delta IV Medium and Atlas V rockets, has had a decidedly mixed flight record.

The Vulcan can use zero, two, four, or six solid rocket boosters, and the boosters worked well on the first Vulcan flight.

The nozzle anomaly on Vulcan’s second flight. (Credit: Sawyer Rosenstein for NSF)

However, the second flight, using the same VC2S two-booster configuration with a standard payload fairing as in the first flight, saw a nozzle “liberation” event 37 seconds after liftoff on one of the boosters.

The rocket was able to compensate for the resulting asymmetry and loss of thrust, successfully reaching orbit with an inert demonstration payload and experiments.

Northrop Grumman (NGC), the GEM-63XL contractor, investigated the issue and successfully tested a modified GEM-63XL at its facility in Promontory, Utah, in February 2025.

Then-ULA CEO Tory Bruno stated that the failure originated in insulators bonded to the inside of the shell that later became the nozzle.

Vulcan returned to flight in August 2025 with the USSF-106 mission, and that flight, using the VC4S four-booster configuration, was fully successful with no “observations” on the GEM-63XLs. This seemed to confirm that the nozzle burn-through and liberation issue had been solved.

Leo Vulcan 1 (LV-01) payload on the move.

LV-01 is the first of 38 Leo missions on @ulalaunch ’s heavy-lift Vulcan rocket, and last week, teams successfully transported the 40-satellite payload—encapsulated inside a 70-foot-tall fairing—to the new Amazon Vertical Integration… pic.twitter.com/5zXbiAmkdO

— Amazon Leo (@AmazonLeo) October 26, 2026

However, the USSF-87 flight, using another VC4S, on Feb. 12 of this year did not go entirely as planned.

The launch was ultimately successful, but an “observation” of one of the GEM-63XL nozzles occurred 69 seconds after liftoff. The rocket experienced a similar asymmetry and loss of thrust from the booster, but it successfully compensated for the issue.

Vulcan was effectively grounded while the issue was investigated, with the U.S. Space Force suspending launches on the rocket.

NGC, ULA, and the Space Force got to work investigating the issue, and NGC successfully test-fired a GEM-63XL with an enhanced nozzle on April 15 at Promontory as part of the company’s efforts to return the booster to flight.

The investigation identified three credible causes of the nozzle liberation issue experienced on USSF-87, and NGC applied fixes to mitigate each.

The changes to the booster included design and manufacturing fixes, and these were tested on LV-01. NGC and ULA will gather data from this flight to help improve the nozzle. There appeared to be no nozzle liberation issues during the LV-01 launch.

The Vulcan core stage for LV-01 being rolled out of VIF-A for its wet dress rehearsal. (Credit: ULA)

LV-01 is the first Vulcan mission to be processed at the new Amazon Vertical Integration Facility (VIF-A), built to process Amazon Leo missions.

Previous Vulcan flights were processed in the Vertical Integration Facility – Government (VIF-G), which will be used to integrate national security and Amazon Leo missions, allowing two rockets to be prepared simultaneously.

The core stage for LV-01, known as V-012, was rolled out to SLC-41 this summer from VIF-A for a wet dress rehearsal before being rolled back for flight preparations.

Technicians stacked the six GEM-63XLs and payload on the vehicle, which was rolled out to the pad on Nov. 12 on the new Amazon Vulcan Launch Platform, which, like VIF-A, is dedicated to Amazon Leo flights. The launch readiness review on Nov. 11 cleared LV-01 for launch.

If the LV-01 flight had gone well, ULA was prepared to ramp up its Vulcan flight cadence, with the LV-02 mission for Amazon Leo already being processed in VIF-G.

The Space Force and NASA were monitoring the flight, as national security payloads and the Boeing Starliner crewed spacecraft are planned to launch on Vulcan in the future.

After the LV-01 flight’s anomaly, there will be an investigation, and future flights will depend on any corrective measures ULA needs to take.

Заголовок: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
Полный текст:
An exoplanet seems to have stopped transiting in front of its host star.

One nice thing about discovering exoplanets is that, once you work out how long their orbits take, they continue to show up like clockwork. The timing is so regular, in fact, that we can use variations to detect the gravitational influence of additional planets in the same exosolar system. And the precise timing is useful in that we can rely on it to point telescopes at the system when we know some of the light we detect has passed through the planet's atmosphere.

Except when we can't.

On Monday, researchers reported on an exoplanet that simply stopped showing up. TOI-2535b is a hot Jupiter-sized planet we've been observing as it transits between its host star, TOI-2535, and Earth for about seven years now. But it recently stopped showing up, and researchers suspect that's due to an unseen companion orbiting in a different plane.

Заголовок: Constellation Space launches its platform for managing fleets of satellites with AI tools
Полный текст:
Seattle space startup aims to optimize operations for a growing number of satellite constellations, aided by machine learning.

Constellation Space’s software platform uses machine learning to optimize satellite data transfer. (Constellation Space Illustration)

Seattle-based Constellation Space is rolling out its flagship software platform, which uses machine learning to streamline operations for fleets of satellites and the ground networks that serve them.

“We build models in-house for things like weather, attenuation, signal jamming, demand … and synthesize all of that to help operators understand what their ground contact plan looks like in the future, and how to optimize their fleets,” CEO Kamran Majid told GeekWire.

The Constellation Platform is tailor-made for a growing number of satellite constellations in low Earth orbit. Keeping track of thousands of satellites — and the best opportunities for downlinking data from each of those satellites — is becoming an increasingly complicated task.

Constellation Space, which was founded last year , draws upon Majid’s experience as a NASA engineering intern and as a software engineer working on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network.

“At Starlink, I saw firsthand how manual mission-control processes break down as constellations scale,” he said. “I started Constellation to help smaller teams get ahead of link failures instead of spending their time rebuilding pass plans and recovering from outages.”

A video produced by Constellation Space features its operations platform for satellite fleets.

Majid’s fellow co-founders include chief technology officer Raaid Kabir , a veteran of Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture, and Omeed Tehrani and Laith Altarabishi , who were previously software engineers at Capital One. “We’re a team of six people right now,” Majid said.

One year into its existence, Constellation Space has already gained traction. Several months ago, the startup said it raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Y Combinator, Nvidia, OpenAI, Samsung Next and other investors.

Majid said an early version of the Constellation Platform has attracted more than 10 customers, including Amazon Web Services. It’s also used by more than 20 academic institutions. “Our annual contract value this year is $2.25 million,” he said.

The platform combines forecasts for factors affecting satellite transmissions — including space situational awareness, weather conditions, signal-to-noise ratios, signal jamming and bandwidth demand — to predict how many gigabytes of data can be transmitted during a given pass. Operators can then use that data to optimize transmission settings and schedules.

Its machine-learning model is pre-trained on data from a global network of sensors. Once it’s deployed, the model adapts to each fleet’s specific hardware and ground stations. Constellation Space says satellite operators can boost downlinked data per pass by as much as 36%.

Majid said the journey from SpaceX to startup has been “really interesting.”

Constellation Space CEO Kamran Majid (Constellation Space Photo)

“The mindset is very similar,” he said. “I was previously an engineer. Now I’m finding myself in more of a business role. The mindset is just ‘first-principles thinking’ about everything. Eliminate all the requirements that don’t make sense before you even start to think about solving the problem. Those core tenets have stayed as we’ve progressed as a venture, and I think that’s been really important to our success so far.”

Setting up the startup in the Seattle area, where more than half of the world’s satellites are built , has also been interesting.

“We are a Y Combinator company , so we were in San Francisco for a couple of months, and there was a lot of pressure from the community in SF to have everyone be in San Francisco. We definitely felt that a little bit,” Majid said.

“But operating in the satellite sector of the space industry, Seattle is becoming more and more of a hub for the space industry in general,” he said. “Space companies are either completely moving here, opening up headquarters here, or just branching out here. It’s that, mixed in with Seattle just being known as a tech hub — and also, we all love Seattle.”

Заголовок: Pakistani astronaut set to become 1st international visitor to China's Tiangong space station this month
Полный текст:
China will fly its first foreign astronaut on the Shenzhou 24 mission, with a Pakistani pilot set for a roughly week-long stay aboard the Tiangong space station.

An astronaut from Pakistan is set to launch on China's Shenzhou 24 mission in the coming weeks and become the first-ever international visitor to the Tiangong space station.

A pair of astronaut candidates from Pakistan have been training at the Astronaut Centre of China in Beijing, following an agreement reached between China and Pakistan in Islamabad in February 2025 and a subsequent selection process.

China's human spaceflight agency confirmed in a Nov. 7 press statement that the upcoming Shenzhou 24 mission will carry one of the astronauts. The agency also released a mission patch .

"China and Pakistan are all-weather strategic cooperative partners," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Nov. 9. "Having the Pakistani astronaut on board China's spaceships will mark the first-ever joint mission of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program."

It is not yet known which of the two candidates will fly on Shenzhou 24. They were named in Pakistani press reports as Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud, both pilots from the country's military forces. The pair were chosen from a wider pool of around 20 finalists.

The chosen candidate will fly as a payload specialist on Shenzhou 24 along with two Chinese colleagues, while the other will be on standby as a backup. While the Chinese astronauts will be starting a six-month-long stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will spend roughly a week in orbit aboard Tiangong during a standard crew rotation period. He will then return to Earth aboard the departing Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, along with two Chinese astronauts who will have completed a six-month-long stay in orbit.

The arrangement means changes to China's usual "three in, three out" Tiangong crew rotations. One of the three Shenzhou 23 astronauts, who arrived at Tiangong on May 24, will stay aboard and complete China's first-ever year-long stay in orbit, while the Pakistani astronaut will take their seat aboard Shenzhou 23 to return home.

During his stay in space, the Pakistani astronaut will be responsible for four research payloads selected from more than 300 proposals, according to Pakistan's space agency, SUPARCO.

China has not announced a timeline for the launch of the Shenzhou 24 mission, but it is expected to lift off before the end of November. The Shenzhou 23 astronauts currently aboard Tiangong are closing in on 180 days in orbit, nearing an end to their six months in space.

Shenzhou 24 will launch from Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in the Gobi Desert on a Long March 2F rocket. The identities of the crew for China's human spaceflight missions are typically closely guarded, and will only be revealed in a press conference a day ahead of launch. Shenzhou 24's Long March 2F rocket will be rolled out to the pad around a week ahead of launch.

The partnership between the two countries has already produced Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites , including a lunar cubesat , and a Pakistani-built rover due to fly on the Chang'e-8 lunar landing mission.

Заголовок: Germany, Poland tap SATIM to analyze military satellite imagery
Полный текст:
WARSAW, Poland — SATIM, a Polish maker of AI-based analysis tools for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, has obtained a contract from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence to supply software for the automated analysis of satellite imagery.

The company is building on its ongoing cooperation with Germany’s Rheinmetall to support the German SPOCK-1 satellite reconnaissance program.

The solution will support Warsaw’s MikroSAR earth-observation program, SATIM said in a Nov. 12 statement. Advanced by a consortium of Finland’s ICEYE and Wojskowe Zakłady Łączności No 1, a subsidiary of Polish state-run defense group PGZ, the national satellite reconnaissance system is the first component of the military space capabilities Poland aims to develop in the coming years.

“Access to SAR imagery is only the first step. The value comes from extracting useful intelligence quickly, consistently and at scale,” said Jacek Strzelczyk, the CEO of SATIM. “This contract allows us to support Poland’s sovereign reconnaissance capabilities and demonstrate how automated analysis helps analysts make more effective use of radar data.”

SAR satellites can acquire imagery regardless of sunlight conditions and through cloud cover. However, interpreting the collected imagery and properly identifying detected military equipment can be both a challenging and time-consuming process. These difficulties create opportunities for specialized software suppliers such as SATIM, according to company representatives.

“Interest among users increased following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine where cloud cover is frequently an issue. SAR radars can see through clouds, but their imagery is also very difficult to interpret. Our solution offers a very high level of accuracy, reaching 90–95% for most object classes,” Mateusz Raczyński, a SATIM spokesperson, told Defense News. “We can identify objects across approximately 300 classes, including vessels, aircraft, and vehicles.”

On Nov. 2, SATIM announced that it had reached another milestone with Rheinmetall in their collaboration supporting the SPOCK-1 program.

“The automated analysis pipeline supplied by SATIM to Rheinmetall has now entered operational testing phase, supporting the German Armed Forces’ analysis of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery,” the Polish business said.

Meanwhile, SATIM is working on securing further customers for its services across the world.

“Being a Polish company, we first established cooperation with the German industry that was open to validating our software and after that including it to support the SPOCK-1 program, one of the major ISR programs globally. Now we are also extending our work with Poland,” Raczyński said. “We are also active in other markets. Our solutions are used in the United States, Japan, Qatar, and the UAE. Next month, we are going to Vietnam to explore this market, as well.”

Это совместные проекты, доступ к технологиям, подготовка кадров и взаимная выгода. Работаем в многостороннем и двустороннем форматах. Заголовок: iSpace Moving on From Hyperbola-1 in Favor of Unproven Reusable Rocket
Полный текст:
An imminent retirement of the occasionally successful rocket was denied, but supposed booked future flights are yet to appear after a long gap.

The Hyperbola-1 Y10 vehicle during pre-launch processing ahead of its eighth mission in July 2025. | Image: iSpace

Fifteen months ago now, iSpace’s Hyperbola-1 launch vehicle flew for the eighth time since July 2019, completing its fourth successful mission into Earth’s orbit. Since then, it has not flown again, and the company has been reluctant to speak on its plans with the vehicle in that time.

However, on November 9th , an indirect update was shared by iSpace Chairman and General Manager Peng Xiaobo (彭小波) speaking with Wen Wei Po (文匯報) , a Hong Kong (香港) based newspaper, as part of an exclusive interview about the company’s current plans.

Within it, the Chairman confirmed that the majority of iSpace’s focus has been shifted towards the partially reusable Hyperbola-3 launch vehicle 1 , which is yet to fly, leaving Hyperbola-1 as a launch solution with a limited future and a much reduced number of staff working on it. The shift was rationalized as a response to the wants of satellite operators, specifically building constellations requiring multiple launches.

How much of a future Hyperbola-1 has was not clarified by Peng Xiaobo, other than that it is not being immediately abandoned and that contracts signed with customers will be fulfilled, without saying how many those were. It is understood that Hyperbola-1 did not sell well in comparison to its competitors 2 .

Given the time since the launch vehicle’s last flight, limited news about a next one, and the reduced focus now on it, iSpace may opt to transfer customers onto their upcoming Hyperbola-3. That would allow them to avoid paying out potential fees if Hyperbola-1 were to fail again, while freeing capital up for efforts on their reusable launch vehicle.

Considerable amounts of capital have been raised by iSpace this year in the name of progressing Hyperbola-3 towards flight in the near future. A 5 billion Yuan (749 million United States Dollars, as of November 10th) ‘Series D++’ round was completed in February , while the first billion of a 7 billion Yuan (1.04 billion United States Dollars) ‘Series E’ raise was reported to have been gathered in September.

When that flight will happen is unknown, beyond that it will make use of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site’s Commercial Launch Pad 2, for which iSpace has a purpose-built transporter-erector and local launch preparation facilities . A first-stage landing attempt should be part of that, with a dedicated drone ship undergoing operational rehearsals since June.

Hardware updates about the launch vehicle this year have been spread out and about small parts of it. These included drop tests of landing legs, static load testing of its 5.2-meter-wide fairing and 4.2-meter-diameter propellant tanks. Those follow on from separate cryogenic tests held last year.

Meanwhile, liquid methane and liquid oxygen-burning engines for the launch vehicle, which iSpace developed themselves, have so far only been fired up individually on test stands and not integrated with either stage. Firing those with a stage is an unavoidable critical test and verification of systems that the company knows they have to complete, and as such is constructing a suitable test stand over eleven kilometers away 3 from their existing facilities in Wenchang to the northeast.

At present, it appears quite unlikely that Hyperbola-3 will fly anytime soon, before year’s end or in the first months of 2027. Hopefully, iSpace is taking its time on the vehicle’s parts to ensure it is nowhere near as failure-riddled as Hyperbola-1.

Заголовок: I used the Vaonis Vespera 3 for weeks and here’s who I would recommend it to — full review
Полный текст:
I photographed nebulas and star clusters over multiple nights with the Vaonis Vespera 3. It’s one of the most capable smart telescopes I’ve used, but it won’t be for everyone.

I’ve spent a lot of time with smart telescopes , from relatively inexpensive Seestar models to the original Vaonis Vespera and the Vespera Pro . They all promise essentially the same thing — you put a telescope outside at night, choose something interesting on your smartphone and let the technology take care of the rest. The Vaonis Vespera 3 does that exceptionally well, but after spending several nights with it, I’m convinced it’s designed for a rather different kind of buyer.

The telescope’s optical arm folds into its curved body when switched off. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

At $2,490/£2,199, this is hardly an impulse purchase for the beginner who’s curious about astronomy – you could buy several perfectly capable smart telescopes for the same money. Yet I found myself increasingly impressed by what the Vespera 3 could achieve, particularly when I returned to the same object over several nights. The images were sharp, the colors were excellent and I almost never had to think about the battery.

The Vespera III weighs 13 lbs (6 kg) including the tripod. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

That doesn’t mean the experience was flawless. I sometimes spent longer than I’d have liked waiting for the telescope to get ready, but once it began photographing the sky, the Vespera 3 reminded me why I love smart telescopes so much.

Why I kept returning to the same objects over several nights

The Vespera 3 uses a Sony IMX585 sensor to produce 8.3MP images. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

One of my favorite things about smart telescopes is watching a photograph develop as more light is collected. What begins as a fairly ordinary patch of stars gradually becomes something much more interesting. First a faint cloud of gas appears, then more structure emerges, and eventually you have an image that, only a few short years ago, would have been difficult to capture without specialist equipment.

With the Vespera 3, I spent several nights photographing the Pleiades (M45), the famous star cluster in Taurus. The Pleiades make an excellent subject for testing a telescope because the stars are bright, but the surrounding nebulosity is much harder to capture convincingly. The Singularity app used to control Vespera 3 stacks each image as it goes, but keeps them in sight as an optional time-lapse, so you can see exactly why you’re spending so much time on one object.

Even better, the Vespera 3’s PerseverENS feature lets you add data to an existing observation over multiple nights (it’s actually called multi-night observation in the app). Instead of having to call it a night or start again every time the weather interrupts an imaging session, you can return to a target and continue building the image over weeks — or years. This is excellent for faint nebulas, but also for anyone who lives somewhere with unpredictable weather.

The Vespera 3 also has CovalENS, Vaonis’s mosaic imaging system, which captures adjacent sections of sky to produce a larger image. That’s helpful for objects such as the Pleiades and large nebulas, which occupy a substantial area of the sky.

Mosaics inevitably take longer than conventional images — if it images six sections of the night sky, it takes six times longer for the same image quality — but they also make the telescope more versatile than its native field of view (2.5 x 1.4 degrees) might suggest.

I was impressed by what it captured from an urban location

Various filters can be popped in and out of the lens. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

Smart telescopes are particularly useful for people living under light-polluted skies. A conventional optical telescope can show you the moon, the planets and some brighter star clusters, but faint nebulas are largely out of reach. The Vespera 3 tackles that problem by taking repeated short exposures and combining them automatically. As the exposures accumulate, faint details become clearer, and the image becomes less noisy.

I photographed the Orion Nebula (M42), one of the most rewarding deep-sky targets for almost any telescope. Its bright central region makes it a quick capture, but the surrounding clouds of gas give a camera plenty more to uncover. The color in M42 via the Vespera 3 was particularly striking: stars looked sharp, the background was pleasingly clean, but the colors had a richness you don’t always see from less expensive models.

The branded adjustable tripod provides a stable platform. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The Vespera 3 uses a 50mm refractor telescope and an 8.3-megapixel Sony IMX585 camera sensor. Those specifications are identical to the Vespera 2, but the Vespera 3 has a new optical system, which uses four lenses in three groups, including two extra-low-dispersion elements. Vaonis has also introduced internal baffling to reduce unwanted reflections from nearby artificial lights. For urban astronomers, every little helps. I wouldn’t claim that the Vespera 3 makes dark skies unnecessary. It doesn’t — and if you do take a trip to dark skies with the Vespera 3, your images will improve — but it can produce extremely satisfying images even from a city.

The main chassis of the telescope sports a large logo. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

For anyone who wants more control over their images, the Vespera 3 also saves lossless TIFF files that can be exported to a PC or Mac using a USB-C cable. That means you can take the images into your preferred editing software for further processing, rather than relying entirely on the results produced by the Singularity app.

The supplied tripod is sturdy and dependable. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

I wish choosing what to photograph was more intuitive

There’s something wonderfully simple about looking at a map of the night sky, spotting an interesting object and tapping it to point your scope in that direction. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy using Seestar smart telescopes. I did miss that experience with the Vespera 3.

Vaonis’s Singularity app has an extensive catalog of galaxies, nebulas, star clusters and other targets, but I found myself browsing lists when I’d rather have been exploring an interactive sky chart.

There is a section devoted to constellations, which initially got my hopes up. I thought it might allow me to photograph an entire constellation, capturing its familiar star pattern as a wide-field image. Sadly not — each constellation has a diagram showing where the catalog’s deep-sky objects are located. That’s useful if you already know what you’re looking for, but it isn’t the same as being able to see the sky overhead and choose a target visually.

However, the telescope can still find and photograph the objects in its catalog, and the automated tracking works well once you’ve made your choice.

It takes a while to get started

A fabric canopy between the tripod’s legs keeps accessories close at hand. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

That smart telescopes give you instant gratification is something of a selling point — but it’s also a myth. Yes, they save an enormous amount of work compared with traditional astrophotography equipment. There’s no separate tracking mount to align, no camera to attach and no laptop required to control the imaging process. However, automation doesn’t necessarily mean instant results.

For example, every time the Vespera 3 is switched on, it needs to establish its position by identifying stars overhead. Its Star Zone Search and autofocus procedure took around five minutes, with a percentage displayed in the app to show how far it had progressed. That’s not an unreasonable wait for a sophisticated astronomical instrument, but it felt a little drawn-out when I was eager to begin photographing something. If there are clouds, expect it to take much longer.

Once the Vespera 3 had aligned itself, I could choose a target and leave the telescope to work. The optical arm moved into position, the camera began collecting exposures and an image gradually appeared on my smartphone.

I was less impressed by the touch-sensitive power button. Its softly illuminated indicator didn’t always make it obvious whether the telescope was switched on. More than once, I had to check my phone’s available Wi-Fi networks to establish whether it was on or off.

Not having to worry about battery life is bliss

The Singularity app allows re-framing of objects. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

Vaonis claims the Vespera 3 can operate for up to 11 hours. I didn’t run it continuously until the battery was exhausted, but it lasted longer than every observing session I attempted. That did change how I used it, because I could concentrate on the target instead of keeping an eye on the remaining charge or wondering whether I should connect a portable battery.

The new, improved tripod also makes a difference. It’s tall, adjustable and reassuringly stable, with a useful canopy strung between its legs for holding any accessories — perhaps filters, a red torch or snacks.

I wouldn’t buy it primarily for the sun or planets

A holding page that appears while the telescope slews has a voice that talks about the object you’re about to see. (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The Vespera 3 is capable of photographing the moon and the sun, although solar photography requires a properly fitted optional solar filter. Unfortunately, that costs a further $179/ £159 , which is rather steep.

It’s also not the best choice for detailed planetary images. The 245mm focal length is ideal for framing many galaxies and nebulas, but Jupiter and Saturn remain small subjects.

Another omission is an equatorial tracking mode. Some cheaper smart telescopes — such as the Seestar S50 Pro and the DwarfLab Dwarf 3 — offer EQ mode for more advanced imaging, but the Vespera 3 relies solely on its motorized alt-azimuth mount. That doesn’t stop it from producing excellent photographs, but it does mean more experienced users have one less option to experiment with.

I’d recommend it to someone who knows they’ll use it

The biggest question surrounding the Vespera 3 isn’t whether it works — it’s whether it’s worth the money. After all, it costs far more than the Seestar S50 Pro, which also has built-in imaging filters, whereas the Vespera’s light pollution ($229/£219), dual-band ($399/£370) and solar (£179/£159) filters are optional purchases. They do, however, make a significant difference — with the dual-band filter giving nebulas more contrast, color and detail.

Overall, the Vespera 3 offers a slightly more polished imaging experience than the many entry-level smart telescopes on the market. I enjoyed its clean, colorful images and appreciated the ability to work on the same subject over several nights, while the excellent tripod and battery endurance make it particularly well suited to longer observing sessions.

I wouldn’t recommend it to everyone, but I can see why someone who already loves photographing the night sky might happily pay extra for the Vespera 3.

Заголовок: Satellite snaps rare birds-eye view of the ISS | Space photo of the day for Nov. 12, 2026
Полный текст:
A satellite looks down at the International Space Station in orbit. (Image credit: HEO)

A commercial satellite has spotted the International Space Station (ISS), giving us a unique view of the orbiting lab from above.

What is it?

Most of the time, when we see the ISS, it is from down here on Earth or from the viewpoint of the astronauts onboard, peering out the windows at the station's limbs, solar arrays and instruments.

But in this snapshot, which was posted on X on Nov. 9 by the Australian company HEO, we can see the station stretched out in all its glory.

HEO specializes in using satellites in low Earth orbit to capture images of other spacecraft, though longer-term the company aims to capture observations far out into the solar system. HEO doesn't build the satellites that take these photos; rather, the company's software tasks the spacecraft to image targets as they come into range.

This great photo of the ISS from above, for example, was taken by a satellite operated by BlackSky, a Virginia-based company that holds a non-Earth imaging agreement with HEO .

So far, HEO and its partners have captured imagery of a variety of spacecraft in orbit, including the ISS, China's Tiangong space station and the European Space Agency's ERS-2 satellite (while it was hurtling back to Earth in 2024).

Why is it incredible?

While it might seem that satellites are just hovering above Earth, the space station and other spacecraft in LEO are hurtling through space at roughly 17,500 mph (28,160 kph), hundreds of miles above our planet's surface.

A snapshot of a satellite from above is therefore far from mundane. Rather, it requires incredible coordination and technical skill; satellite operators must know precisely when their target will present itself, and their equipment must be capable of getting the shot.

Заголовок: The 'eclipse of the century' will plunge these 8 wonders of the Roman Empire into darkness on Aug. 2, 2027
Полный текст:
Ancient Roman cities, temples and amphitheaters across the Mediterranean will fall into the moon's shadow during the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027.

Ancient Egyptian temples will inevitably dominate the story of the total solar eclipse on Aug. 2, 2027 .

After all, the path of totality crosses Luxor, home to Karnak, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the ancient world's most famous monuments. But follow the moon 's shadow west and another ancient civilization comes into view. Before reaching Egypt, totality will sweep across the Mediterranean and North Africa, passing over an extraordinary collection of Roman cities, fortresses, theaters, temples and triumphal arches. Many lie within what became Rome's North African provinces, a region that produced some of the empire's wealthiest and most impressive cities.

From beachside Baelo Claudia in Spain and military Tamuda in Morocco to Timgad and Djémila in Algeria and the jaw-dropping El Jem Amphitheater in Tunisia, Roman ruins will experience between two and more than five minutes of darkness — creating extraordinary possibilities for eclipse chasers and photographers. Here are some of the best places to watch the moon's shadow cross what was once the Roman Empire. All times, totality durations and historical cloud cover data come from Time and Date .

1. Baelo Claudia, Spain

Baelo Claudia's Roman ruins overlook Bolonia beach and the Strait of Gibraltar. (Image credit: Andrea Pucci via Getty Images)

Location: near Tarifa, Andalucía, Spain

Start of totality and duration: 10:44 a.m. CEST; 4 minutes, 31 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 12%

Altitude of the sun: 37 degrees above east

Roman ruins, an Atlantic beach and the mountains of Africa could all share the frame with the eclipsed sun at Baelo Claudia. Founded in the second century B.C., this remarkably well-preserved Roman city near Bolonia beach includes a forum, basilica, theater, temples, baths and a decumanus maximus (east-west street), all set against forested hills and a vast coastal sand dune. For photographers, the possibilities are exceptional — columns and temples may provide an ancient foreground, while wider compositions could incorporate the beach and dunes. On particularly clear days, Morocco is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar — potentially putting Roman ruins, two continents and a total solar eclipse into one extraordinary scene.

2. Málaga Roman Theatre, Spain

The Roman Theatre at the foot of the Málaga Alcazaba dates back to the 1st century BC. (Image credit: Manfred Gottschalk via Getty Images)

Location: Málaga, Spain

Start of totality and duration: 10:48 a.m. CEST; 1 minute, 57 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 9%

Altitude of the sun: 39 degrees above east

Few eclipse locations can offer two civilizations in the same photograph. Málaga's Roman Theatre was built in the first century B.C., when the city was part of the Roman province of Hispania, and today sits directly beneath the Alcazaba, the imposing Muslim-era palace-fortress that dominates the hillside above. Although its totality is considerably shorter than locations farther south, the photographic possibilities are compelling. From a carefully chosen position, it may be possible to frame the darkened sun with the theater's ancient stonework and the walls of the Alcazaba rising behind it. Another major advantage for eclipse chasers is that this extraordinary historical setting sits in the heart of Málaga, making it one of the most accessible ancient sites on the path of totality.

3. Tamuda, Morocco

The ruins of Tamuda near Tétouan preserve a Roman military fortress. (Image credit: Carole Raddato via Wikipedia CC BY-SA 2.0 )

Location: Tétouan, Morocco

Start of totality and duration: 08:45 a.m. GMT; 4 minutes, 51 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 14%

Altitude of sun: 38 degrees above east-southeast

Long before the Romans arrived in northern Morocco, Tamuda was already a thriving Mauretanian settlement. Founded around the third century B.C. in the Martil Valley, near modern Tétouan, the Romans established a fortified military camp here in the first century A.D., whose massive stone walls remain the defining feature of this archaeological site. Tamuda combines long totality, promising weather and an atmospheric archaeological foreground — yet remains far less famous than the Roman sites across the Strait of Gibraltar.

4. Timgad, Algeria

The Roman Arch of Timgad, Algeria. (Image credit: Antonio Ciufo via Getty Images)

Location: near Batna, Algeria

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 5%

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Few places in the 2027 path of totality combine ancient architecture and long totality quite like Timgad. Founded around A.D. 100 as the Roman colony of Thamugadi, this remarkably well-preserved city sits on an open plateau at the foot of Algeria's Aurès Mountains. Its grid of streets, forum, theater, temples, baths and columns survives alongside its most famous monument, the three-arched gateway traditionally known as the Arch of Trajan. A relatively high sun will make close architectural compositions challenging, but Timgad's wide-open site provides plenty of possibilities for carefully planned wide-angle images.

5. Lambaesis, Algeria

Arch of Commodus at the Roman site of Lambaesis, Algeria. (Image credit: Ethel Davies / robertharding via Getty Images)

Location: near Batna, Algeria

Start of totality and duration: 10:01 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 20 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 5%

Altitude of sun: 51 degrees above east-southeast

Just 12—15 miles (20—25 km) west of Timgad lies its military counterpart. Lambaesis was the principal base of Rome's Legio III Augusta, the legion that helped secure Rome's African Empire. Rather than an entire gridded colonial city, the attraction here is monumental military architecture, most notably the imposing remains of the heart of the fortress. The eclipse circumstances are almost identical to nearby Timgad, with more than five minutes of totality and historically excellent prospects for clear skies. Scout both sites beforehand, study where the sun will stand above the ruins, and decide which offers the strongest alignment — and the easiest access — on eclipse morning.

6. Djémila, Algeria

The mountain setting of Djémila, ancient Cuicul, could provide a dramatic backdrop to just over two minutes of totality. (Image credit: Nirian via Getty Images)

Location: Djémila, Algeria

Start of totality and duration: 10:02 a.m. CET; 2 minutes, 2 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 11%

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 50 degrees above east-southeast

Djémila trades a long eclipse for one of the most spectacular settings on the path of totality. Known to the Romans as Cuicul, this exceptionally well-preserved city was built in mountainous terrain around 2,950 feet (900 meters) above sea level — an unusual setting for a Roman settlement — and its ruins include temples, forums, houses, baths, arches and a theater. The surrounding green hills and mountains give eclipse photographers a very different backdrop from the flatter, more arid landscapes farther south. The catch is totality, which is significantly shorter than at other Roman ruins.

7. Sbeitla, Tunisia

The Roman temples of ancient Sufetula at Sbeitla, Tunisia. (Image credit: Renee Vititoe via Getty Images)

Location: Kasserine, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:06 a.m. CET; 5 minutes, 19 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 4%

Altitude of sun: 54 degrees above east-southeast

Sbeitla could be one of the great archaeological settings for the 2027 eclipse. Known in Roman times as Sufetula, the city prospered under Roman rule and today contains some of Tunisia's most impressive ancient ruins. Its centerpiece is an unusual group of three remarkably well-preserved temples dedicated to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, standing above the forum and reached through the monumental Arch of Antoninus Pius. That high sun will require some careful positioning and probably a wide-angle composition, but eclipse photographers will have an extraordinary collection of arches, columns and temples to use as foregrounds.

8. El Jem Amphitheater, Tunisia

El Jem is Africa's biggest Roman amphitheater. (Image credit: Westend61 via Getty Images)

Location: El Djem, Tunisia

Start of totality and duration: 10:09 a.m. CET; 4 minutes, 23 seconds

Historical cloud cover: 2%

Altitude of eclipsed sun: 56 degrees above east-southeast

It may be the third-largest and one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters in the world, but El Jem offers another reason to consider it for totality. Unlike Rome's Colosseum — which it closely resembles — visitors can explore its multi-tiered seating, climb high into the surviving structure for panoramic views and visit the underground passages once used by gladiators and animals. Built around A.D. 238, El Jem combines one of Rome's greatest surviving monuments with some of the most promising eclipse conditions on the entire track.

Заголовок: Exclusive: Spaceium Opens License for Refueling Hardware
Полный текст:
Spaceium’s goal is to launch gas stations into orbit. The first step? Making sure spacecraft builders have access to the pump.

Today, the company is opening up access to its OpenPort refueling tech, allowing any company to build and license the hardware for $1—a low price because Spaceium plans to make its money by selling fuel to spacecraft.

“We are not a port business,” Spaceium cofounder and CEO Ashi Dissanayake told Payload. “We are not here to sell a refueling interface and make money. We want to develop this whole space economy so that any spacecraft can get filled.”

Gas up: When a satellite runs out of fuel in orbit, its useful life is over. Many compare that business model to throwing out a car every time the gas light comes on.

Companies such as Spaceium are hoping to change that calculation. Being able to refuel satellites can allow for:

• Operating as long as a satellite’s electronics and other systems still work;

• Maneuvering without worrying about conserving fuel;

• Travelling farther into deep space, without needing to carry all of its fuel at launch.

The specs: Fuel can flow both ways through the androgynous OpenPort, meaning it can act as both fuel pump and refueling port rather than having one distinct part to serve each function. This is the key to unlocking a network of refuelers, since traveling fuel depots can fuel up with Spaceium—and then refuel spacecraft themselves.

“It was a request from a customer,” Reza Fetanat, cofounder and CTO, said. “We got all of the requirements from customers, and that was something they wanted.”

The port, which is fuel-agnostic, also doesn’t add a new piece onto spacecraft—it replaces the port that’s traditionally used to fuel up the spacecraft for the first time on the ground, giving longer-term purpose to a part that typically becomes useless weight after launch.

Eyes on the competition: Orbit Fab, which is also hoping to become the gas station of choice in orbit, has its own RAFTI refueling port, which it made available to industry via an open license in October 2021.

What’s next: Spaceium already has some flight heritage, launching a mission in November aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-15 that tested the Spaceium-built robotic arm that will assist in the refueling process on the company’s future depots.

Next up—Spaceium will send OpenPort to the ISS in the first half of 2027. There, the hardware will demo xenon transfer on a spacecraft docked outside the ISS.

NASA’s Hubble Offers Cosmic Sampler of Targets for Roman

A collage of strong gravitational lenses observed by Hubble, some of which will be followed up by observations with the Roman Space Telescope, which launched in August 2026. Lenses like these will be used to investigate the evolution of galaxies and dark matter.

Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

A gallery of gravitational lenses captured by NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope showcases the diversity of this cosmic phenomenon and lays the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

Gravitational lensing, first predicted by Albert Einstein, occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object, such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies, bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. The effect is similar to that of a giant lens in space that allows astronomers to view objects much farther away than any telescope could see on its own.

The lenses in this image formed from the precise alignment of a distant background galaxy with the mass of a foreground galaxy, creating distorted and magnified images of the background galaxy that appear as arcs around the foreground galaxy.

Astronomers will use these observations of a large and varied population of gravitational lenses to construct lens models that will help determine how much mass is in the lensing system’s foreground galaxy – and potentially prove or dispel a theory about dark matter. Astronomers study the amount of distortion of the lensed background galaxies to determine the quantity and distribution of mass in the foreground galaxy, including its invisible dark matter.

Hubble views the cosmos primarily in visible and ultraviolet light with some infrared coverage, providing a comprehensive, high-resolution view of individual objects. Roman sees primarily infrared light and some visible, over a much larger field of view to create panoramas of the universe. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and UV prowess for individual objects.

With Hubble’s high-resolution imaging and precise models, researchers should also be able to detect small imperfections in these gravitationally lensed galaxy arcs that would indicate the presence of small clumps of dark matter. Researchers could use these previously undetected clumps to confirm the cold dark matter theory, which predicts the existence of many small dark matter clumps of between a million to a billion solar masses. In contrast, the dark matter halo of our Milky Way galaxy is around 1.3 trillion solar masses.

By studying Hubble lens images in detail, researchers intend to build a super-intelligence tool to efficiently search similar arcs in the upcoming Roman images. The Hubble images are expected to both yield their own results on dark matter and pave the way for analysis of Roman’s larger sample of lenses.

The unique lenses in this image display some of the different characteristics researchers will see as they collect a diverse and numerous assortment of lenses to test in their models. Panel A is an example of an arc-counterarc configuration, in which the lensed background galaxy appears as a duplicated pair of arcs. The lensed galaxy is being magnified by a pair of foreground galaxies whose combined mass bends the light of the background galaxy around them.

The diversity of lenses in this image demonstrate some of the characteristics researchers will uncover with Hubble and Roman. Each lens differs significantly from others in the panel.

Credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America)

Panel F is an Einstein Ring, in which the alignment of the background galaxy and approximately spherical mass of the foreground lens are so perfectly situated that the lensed galaxy almost fully encircles the foreground galaxy. Panel I shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, in which the background galaxy is replicated four times, appearing as smeared dots around the foreground galaxy. Panel C also shows a quadruply lensed galaxy, with double knots that are most likely strong star-forming regions in the background galaxy.

Some of the magnified and warped background galaxies appear blue and some appear red. These bluish arcs indicate young stars, while reddish arcs indicate older stars. Roman and Hubble will explore these differences to better understand how galaxies evolved earlier in the universe.

Most of the foreground lensing galaxies are elliptical galaxies, which are older, denser, and more compact. Lensed images of background galaxies only occur when the mass density of the foreground galaxy reaches a critical point.

But not all of these foreground galaxies are ellipticals, and researchers can use these differences to explore the evolutionary paths taken by these galaxies. In panel G, the foreground galaxy appears elongated, which may be true or a trick of perspective, and in panels B and F, the foreground galaxies appear to have spiral arms.

Panel D’s foreground galaxy has a visible dust lane, which is rare in a lensing galaxy and the kind of detail that Hubble’s sharp, visible-light vision excels at revealing. The lensed background galaxy could be an Einstein Ring, with the dust lane “breaking” our view of the ring. Because infrared light is less obscured by dust, future Roman infrared observations could help determine whether the arcs form a more complete Einstein ring.

These strong lenses were first detected with The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument at Kitt Peak. Hubble subsequently observed them, and Roman will take further observations. Images like these are an example of the kinds of collaborative efforts that routinely take place between NASA’s Great Observatories to build a comprehensive picture of the cosmos. As Roman joins the family of large space observatories that includes Hubble, the Chandra X-ray Observatory, and the James Webb Space Telescope, a new window opens onto the universe, revealing sights previously hidden while expanding our cosmic knowledge for all of humanity.

Through NASA’s Lens: Capturing Space Shuttle Endeavour’s Move to LA

A spectacular sight as NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour atop soars over the Golden Gate Bridge.

Credits:
NASA/Carla Thomas

As a new exhibit opens showcasing NASA’s space shuttle Endeavour, NASA photographers look back at the final mission. These photographers documented the iconic images shared around the world on Sept. 21, 2012, while millions watched space shuttle Endeavour fly on top of the agency’s 747 Shuttle Carrier Aircraft for the last time.

Endeavour’s new home at the California Science Center in Los Angeles will reopen the weekend of Nov. 13, displayed upright in launch position, ready to inspire the next generation of space explorers.

NASA/Lori Losey

“Chasing Endeavour’s final ferry flight over Southern California was, without a doubt, a leading highlight of my 37-year career at NASA,” said Lori Losey, lead videographer at NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. “I advocated for two chase aircraft to be used in the LA area so we could dedicate one aircraft to photo and one to video. It was this beautiful dance of alternating altitudes and swapping positions between landmarks to maximize both of us capturing the legendary imagery.”

Two photographers and one videographer, all based at NASA Armstrong, had a leading hand in preparing the Endeavour’s flight to Los Angeles, and in deciding where else the aircraft would fly around California on its final journey. Agency pilots planned the route to fly across some of California’s most iconic landmarks and the imagery team strategized about how to best capture the images.

Thousands of visitors to Disneyland and Disney’s California Adventure parks got a special treat when NASA’s Shuttle Carrier Aircraft with space shuttle Endeavour on top flew over at low level during its flyover of Los Angeles.

NASA/Jim Ross

“The most fun thing about this project was seeing the excitement of the people on the ground as we flew over the different landmarks,” said Jim Ross, NASA Armstrong’s lead photographer. “People in the Los Angeles area really came out and supported the Endeavour flyover. We saw so many supporters at Griffith Park and Disneyland.”

Photographer Carla Thomas said seeing the standing-room-only crowd below the California State Capitol in Sacramento filled her with pride. After joining the agency in the wake of the Challenger tragedy, she reflected on the opportunity to document NASA’s return to flight.

The space shuttle Endeavour and its 747 carrier aircraft makes a low-level flyover of the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum.

NASA/Jim Ross

Endeavour was escorted by NASA Armstrong’s F/A-18s and an F-15, which carried the photo and video teams in the back seats. Like many flight efforts, this journey took a significant amount of preplanning with the California Science Center, as well as groups like the Federal Aviation Administration, the Los Angeles International Airport, and NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

“The planning was my favorite part of this effort — it was fun and exciting to plan the shots,” Thomas said. “I flew the entire route with the LAPD (Los Angeles Police Department) in one of their helicopters. We had to make sure this was going to work and find any obstacles. Planning for the Hollywood sign was challenging, because it’s on the side of a hill with power lines and radio antennas, but we worked through these issues in the planning process.”

Space shuttle Endeavour atop its modified 747 carrier aircraft overflies the former Alameda Naval Air Station adjoining San Francisco Bay during the Tour of California.

NASA/Carla Thomas

The space shuttle’s flight path included other California landmarks: Dodger Stadium, the Getty Center, the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum, NASA’s Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley, the Golden Gate Bridge, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, and the Santa Monica Pier.

Endeavour helped begin assembly of the International Space Station by delivering its first components to orbit and went on to complete 25 missions. The space shuttle will soon be seen, along with some of the images from the final flight, in its permanent home inside the new Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

Shuttle Endeavour was ferried to Los Angeles, briefly flying over the California state capitol, Sacramento, then demated from its NASA 747 and trailered to the California Science Center.

NASA/Carla Thomas

Заголовок: Astronomers stunned after James Webb Space Telescope discovers the earliest pair of black hole-powered quasars
Полный текст:
Using the James Webb Space Telescope, astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!

Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers have discovered the oldest pair of supermassive black hole-powered quasars ever seen. There's just one problem: they shouldn't exist!

The compact quasar pair, spotted with the aid of the Gemini North telescope, has been designated J1602+4228AB and nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, which means "Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the universe." The compact quasar pair is seen as it was 900 million years after the Big Bang at a time when such supermassive black holes should not have had time to grow to such tremendous masses.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua isn't just the oldest and most distant quasar pairing ever seen. There is just 18,100 light-years, or roughly one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way, between the supermassive black holes, which have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million times that of the sun. That makes Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua the most compact quasar pair found during a period of the universe's history known as Cosmic Dawn , shortly after the birth of the first stars, galaxies, and black holes.

"There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our universe, much less two," research team leader Silvia Onorato of the NOIRLab said in a statement .

"We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the universe was only a thirteenth of its age and, astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today."

How were supermassive black holes over fed at Cosmic Dawn

Quasars occur when the supermassive black holes that sit at the heart of large galaxies are surrounded by a flattened cloud of swirling gas and dust called an "accretion disk," from which they feed or "accrete" matter. The immense gravity of the central black hole causes friction, heating the accretion disk and causing it to glow, often brighter than the combined light of every star in the surrounding galaxy. We see that glow as a quasar.

Finding such objects in the recent cosmic history of the 13.8-billion-year-old universe isn't troubling, though finding compact pairs of them is still extremely rare. Such pairs should be common because the merger of galaxies that brings together supermassive black holes is frequent. That should lead to an abundance of pairs of quasars with a separation less than the typical size of a galaxy.

There are three reasons this has proven tricky. Firstly, the "quasar phase" of a supermassive black hole is relatively short on cosmic terms. Secondly, even relatively close quasar pairs are very far away, making them faint and hard to detect with ground-based telescopes. Finally, at such great distances and with such a small separation between the two supermassive black holes, the individual members of a quasar pair are hard to individually resolve.

Yet, astronomers do find quasar pairs. Sometimes at distances and times that they would probably rather not, because it challenges everything we know about black hole growth.

An annotated illustration of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua showing its place in cosmic history. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Marenfeld/M. Zamani)

The trouble arises before the universe was 1 billion years. That is because, according to current models, black holes should need at least 1 billion years to feed and merge enough to reach masses millions or billions of times that of the sun.

Yet, since it began operations in 2022, the JWST has been routinely discovering supermassive black holes powering quasars as early as 400 million years after the Big Bang. If that wasn't confusing enough, the discovery of Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, the third quasar pair seen at Cosmic Dawn, could really break current models.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was uncovered in data from the JWST's Aether survey, which is conducting a census of objects in the early universe. Using JWST’s NIRSpec (Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit) instrument, the survey has uncovered 200 quasars, just under half of all currently known early universe quasars. It was while browsing the Aether dataset that the team discovered that quasar J1602+4228A is not alone, it had a companion now designated J1602+4228B.

Resolving these two quasars should have been nearly impossible from the ground. But this was possible for Gemini North thanks to perfect timing and perfect weather conditions over Maunakea , the dormant volcano on the island of Hawai'i where the telescope is located.

A definite scientific feat, Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua remains a mystery for now, but it could actually help scientists better understand how galaxies were coming together during Cosmic Dawn, a vital stage in the evolution of the universe.

"Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment," Onorato said. "It's a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times."

The team's results were published on Tuesday (Nov. 10) The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Заголовок: NeuralSat Raises €2.9M to Build Orbital Data Relay Network
Полный текст:
The Autobahn is coming for in-space data traffic.

German startup NeuralSat announced a €2.9M ($3.2M) pre-seed funding round today to develop a 72-sat in-space data relay and processing network, aimed at speeding up the flow of data to and from space.

Capnamic Ventures and Bayern Kapital led the round, which included additional participation from ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, KIEMIS Holding, and Mission E Capital. NeuralSat is also a member of ESA’s Business Incubation Center (ESA BIC) and the NVIDIA Inception Program.

Sharing is caring: Unlike other orbital compute startups—namely, those pitching orbital data centers (ODCs) as a replacement for terrestrial ones—NeuralSat is focusing primarily on the data being gathered and distributed in space today.

As the number of satellites in orbit increases—with ESA projecting ~100,000 by 2030, up from 10,200 in 2024—the amount of data being gathered is starting to hit bottlenecks on its path to Earth.

NeuralSat’s proposed constellation would allow satellite operators to share compute and communications resources, sending their data to NeuralSat nodes which can process and downlink it to available ground stations. The idea is to enable satellites to outsource some of their communications and computing resources—sacrificing self-sufficiency, but gaining extra space and power for their core payloads.

“We believe the next major evolution in space will…come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” CEO Mohd Bilal said in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”

How it works: NeuralSat’s constellation will feature two core capabilities:

• A data relay network using optical and high-frequency radio links, and targeting data rates up to 50 gigabits per second.

• A distributed computing network, so satellite operators can utilize shared processing power on orbit.

NeuralSat also plans to offer hosted-payload capabilities, allowing customers to integrate their own payloads into NeuralSat birds.

NeuralSat plans to use the new capital to fund an in-orbit demonstration mission in 2027 to “validate the core elements of its orbital data relay and processing architecture,” according to the announcement. Following the demo, NeuralSat expects to begin deploying its first operational sats in 2028.

Заголовок: ‘Rosetta Stone for Mars:’ Martian meteorite hints at ancient life
Полный текст:
View larger. | A slice of the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001 . A new analysis of the 4.1-billion-year-old meteorite provides new clues about Mars’ wet and habitable past, including large amounts of manganese oxide . On Earth, manganese oxide is a common byproduct of microbial life. Image via NASA / JPL-Caltech.

• Teghaza 001 is a rare Martian meteorite that is 4.1 billion years old. It was discovered in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022.

• The meteorite contains large amounts of manganese oxide, a common byproduct of microbes on Earth.

• The rare piece of Martian crust also provides more clues about water and habitable conditions on ancient Mars.

EarthSky’s famous lunar calendar is now available . Beautiful blue and silver poster shows every day’s moon phase for 2027. Get yours now!

Does this rare Martian meteorite hold clues to ancient life on Mars?

A rare 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite has given us new clues about ancient Mars. And some of this new information hints at the possibility of ancient microbial Martian life back when conditions on the red planet were very different.

The meteorite, called Teghaza 001 , was found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022. It’s one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found.

The researchers said on October 29, 2026, that when they examined the meteorite more closely in the lab, they found something interesting. It contains large amounts of manganese oxide . Why’s that interesting? Because on Earth, manganese oxide is a common byproduct of microbial life.

This isn’t proof of ancient life on Mars, but it’s certainly tantalizing. The meteorite also provides more clues about how wet and how potentially habitable Mars was billions of years ago.

Lead author Yang Liu at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California said :

It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique. One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars.

The researchers published their peer-reviewed results in Science on October 29, 2026.

The biggest pieces of the meteorite Teghaza 001. Image via University of New Mexico .

Large amounts of manganese oxide

One of the things that makes Teghaza 001 unique is the high level of manganese oxide within it. On Earth, manganese oxide is a common byproduct of microbial life.

Although this finding does not prove the existence of ancient life on Mars, it remains intriguing.

Carl Agee , director and curator at UNM’s Institute of Meteoritics, and colleague Karen Ziegler , a scientist and research professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at the University of New Mexico, examined the meteorite more closely. Agee said :

I realized that this one was a little bit like Black Beauty , not exactly, but it resembled it in the oxygen isotope values. I looked at it microscopically and found domains within it that had high levels of manganese oxide, a compound being looked for on Mars by the rovers as an indicator of environments conducive to life.

13 possible locations for the origin of meteorite Teghaza 001. Image via NASA / JPL-Caltech/ USGS.

Rare Martian meteorite is one of the oldest

Teghaza 001 is one of the oldest Martian meteorites ever found so far. The researchers discovered tiny zircon crystals in the meteorite. They allow age-dating of igneous rocks that form from the cooling of molten magma. The team used uranium-lead age analyses to date the tiny crystals, and Teghaza 001 turned out to be 4.1 billion years old. That makes it one of the oldest known Martian meteorites. Agee said:

There are a few parts to Black Beauty that are around that age, but that whole meteorite itself is a conglomeration of many different rock types. Teghaza 001 is just one unadulterated rock type, and it’s 4.1 billion years or older, so that was a big surprise. It’s the oldest Martian igneous rock ever found by a huge margin, but in addition to that, it seemed to have these clues in its composition that suggested it had been in an environment that had fluids and water coursing through it.

More evidence for ancient water

The meteorite also provided yet more evidence for liquid water billions of years ago on Mars. The clues come from unusual oxygen isotope compositions and altered minerals. Like previous studies, they point to a warmer and much wetter ancient Mars. As Agee explained:

We also had these anomalous oxygen isotopes, and these domains that had high manganese levels. All of that was consistent with it being from a time on Mars, from the very, very beginning when the Martian environment was different from the time in which most of the Martian meteorites that we see were formed and erupted a few 100 million years ago when Mars was a dry desert, just like it is now. This sample probably came from an environment on Mars that was more Earth-like.

This period of time on Mars is called the Pre-Noachian period. It’s the oldest geological epoch, approximately 4.5 to 4.1 billion years ago.

Going back in time

Being able to study this meteorite is like going back in time, Agee said:

This is just one single meteorite. It’s like going out, going back in time and chipping off a hunk of an outcrop, 4 billion years ago on Mars, and then we have this example of what was actually happening. That is why it’s such a valuable sample. We’ve never found one like this before.

The most exciting part about this find is its age, plus the alteration in the meteorite that indicates it has been in what I would call an Earth-like environment, with fluids coursing over the surface and volcanoes creating hydrothermal systems.

There are surface waters and so on. And that’s all reflected in the way that the meteorite has been sort of altered from its original state.

It’s not like this is very common so not only is it ancient and samples a different type of environment in a different time on Mars, but we don’t have any other samples like it. Chances are very slim or next to impossible, that we’ll get another one, like this anytime soon.

Yang Liu at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Labotratory is the lead author of the new study about the Martian meteorite Teghaza 001. Image via NASA/ JPL .

Life on the surface of Mars?

This is also the time when life on Mars’ surface would have been the most possible, as Agee noted:

If there was ever abundant life on Mars, on the surface, not sequestered away in some subsurface, that would be the time that you would be looking at the Pre-Noachian period. It’s the very earliest time, and that was when maybe Mars still had a magnetic field, and it was shielded from radiation, and there were surface waters.

There was a denser atmosphere. If primitive life was abundant in Mars. That is the time that is most likely for it to have down happened.

Origin of rare Martian meteorite Teghaza 001

We know that Teghaza 001 came from Mars. But where exactly on Mars? The researchers don’t know for sure yet, but they narrowed it down to 13 primary possible locations. Several are in the Southern Highlands region.

If scientists can identify the exact location, it could help them plan future rover missions and decide where to send them.

Bottom line: A rare 4.1-billion-year-old Martian meteorite, Teghaza 001, provides new clues about Mars’ ancient and more habitable past.

Заголовок: OwlO Cloud Emerges from Stealth to Build European Orbital Cloud Network
Полный текст:
Luxembourg-based OwlO Cloud emerged from stealth today with plans to build a sovereign European orbital-cloud network.

The company is aiming to help European satellite operators process more of their data in orbit. To do so, OwlO Cloud is planning to have at least 10 spacecraft—orbital cloud nodes (OCN)—operational by 2030. Each OCN will be equipped with data processing and storage hardware, as well as optical-comms tech, provided largely by European suppliers.

“There’s people in Europe doing a lot of those pieces: either the busses, the compute, optical comms…but nobody’s working on an integrated end-to-end system that they plan to finance, build, commission, and then operate as an actual infrastructure service,” CEO Jason Aspiotis told Payload. “Our goal as a company is to come in as an operator of this infrastructure that catalyzes all the pieces—[and] to move forward and deploy it by 2030.”

A parliament of owls: OwlO Cloud was founded this year by Aspiotis, former Axiom Space global director of in-space data and security; CTO Gert Villemos, the former CTO of Leanspace; and CSO Mike Delis, who the company describes as an “innovator in infrastructure financing.”

Although OwlO has barely left the nest, it’s already obtained buy-in from some major names in the European market to kickstart its build-out.

• OwlO was selected to take part in Thales Alenia Space’s Space Business Catalyst;

• OwlO also signed an MoU with Luxembourg-based Edge Aerospace to collaborate on the compute payloads operating on each of OwlO’s orbital cloud nodes.

To build the full constellation, however, OwlO is going to need a mix of venture investment and infrastructure financing.

Aspiotis declined to share how much money the company will need to deploy its first batch of 10 sats. However, he said he plans to use venture capital to fund the initial development of IP and R&D, and rely on infrastructure financing to fund the deployment of the constellation over time.

Who gives a hoot: OwlO comes online at a time of maximum hype for orbital data centers (ODC).

But while many ODC startups are pitching investors on the idea that space can one day host replacements for terrestrial data centers, OwlO’s ambitions are more focused on the immediate needs of satellites in orbit today—which are already gathering more data than they can reasonably process themselves, according to Aspiotis.

As a result, the company can be more targeted in its initial technology. To bring down the cost of the network, each OCN is expected to generate 10 kW of power—compared to the 100+ kW being pitched by competitive ODC networks.

“Most of the use cases that we focus on are about helping other satellites store and process their data much faster, much cheaper,” Aspiotis told Payload. “So, [we’re] playing into the ability to facilitate more near real-time intelligence from sensors residing on civil, military, science, and commercial satellites.”
