Заголовок: Is there a North Star for Mars?
Полный текст:
Is there a North Star for Mars ... a guide star for future explorers? Not in any satisfying way. But Martian stargazers wouldn't lack for things to see!

The post Is there a North Star for Mars? first appeared on EarthSky .

As the sun sets over the stark Martian landscape, stars come into view. Is there a North Star for Mars? Image via Spirit Mars rover on May 19, 2005/ NASA .

The 2027 EarthSky Lunar Calendar is now available! Makes a great gift. Get yours today!

North Star and South Star

The North Star for Earth is Polaris . Does our next-door neighbor planet, Mars, have the same North Star as Earth? If not, does Mars have a star located more or less above its north pole?

Let’s talk about what we mean by North Star . Every planet in our solar system spins on its axis. Earth’s spin is what defines the length of our day of approximately 24 hours. If you continue the imaginary line of a planet’s axis out into space, it might point to a star that’s visible to the eye.

We call such stars pole stars. On Earth, the northern pole star — less than a degree from the north celestial pole — is the beloved star Polaris. Scouts and hikers know you can use Polaris to find the direction north when compasses or GPS fails.

However, Earth’s Southern Hemisphere doesn’t have a comparable South Star. The nearest visible star to the south celestial pole of Earth is about 9 degrees away.

Artist’s illustration of the relative tilts of the orbits of Earth and Mars, Earth doesn’t orbit exactly upright with respect to our orbit around the sun. Instead, Earth’s tilt is about 23 1/2 degrees . Meanwhile, Mars’ tilt is about 25 degrees. What’s more, the orbits of Earth and Mars aren’t tilted in the same direction, as in this illustration. For both reasons — different amount of tilt and different direction of tilt — Mars doesn’t have the same North Star as Earth. Image via NASA .

A North Star for Mars?

So, does Mars have a North or South Star? The answer is … not in any satisfying way. There’s no bright North Star, and only a modestly-bright South Star, for Mars.

In the northern sky as seen from Mars, the best candidate for a North Star is located on Mars’ sky dome about 1/2 degree from Mars’ north celestial pole. That’s closer than Polaris is to Earth’s north celestial pole. So what’s the problem? Well, while Polaris is relatively bright (47th brightest of all stars in the night sky), the star near Mars’ north celestial pole is faint.

In fact, this star is barely within the limit of visibility to the eye alone. That makes it a poor candidate for a North Star.

Mars’ north pole points to a spot in the sky that’s about midway between Deneb , the brightest star in the constellation Cygnus the Swan, and Alderamin , the brightest star in the constellation Cepheus the King. See a chart of the position of Mars’ north celestial pole between the constellations Cygnus and Cepheus.

The southern sky view from Mars

Meanwhile, in the southern sky as seen from Mars, Kappa Velorum is only about 3 degrees from the Martian south celestial pole. That’s not as close as Polaris is to Earth’s north celestial pole, plus this star is only modestly bright, not nearly as bright as Polaris.

Future Mars colonists aren’t going to have a bright North Star — like our Polaris — to guide them.

On the other hand, if you were standing outside at night on the surface of Mars, you’d see some other cool stuff!

Earth and moon, as seen from Mars by the Curiosity rover in 2014. From Mars, you’d see both the Earth and moon with the eye alone. Image via NASA .

Can you see the moon orbiting Earth from Mars?

As seen from Mars, you could see Earth’s moon orbiting around Earth. From Earth, we can’t see any other planets’ satellites with the unaided eye, but this amazing sight on Mars would be visible to the eye alone. Both the Earth and the moon would appear starlike.

In general, the Earth as seen from Mars would somewhat mimic our view of Venus as seen from Earth. By that we mean that — like Venus in relationship to Earth — Earth in relationship to Mars is an inner planet. It orbits closer to the sun than Mars. Thus, Earth as seen from Mars would constantly shift from a morning to an evening “star” and back, just as Venus does as seen from our world.

And although both Earth and the moon would appear as stars to the unaided eye, observers on Mars with telescopes would sometimes see them as crescent worlds, just as we see Venus.

So … no North Star for Mars. But Martian stargazers wouldn’t lack for things to see!

This series of images shows the Martian moon Phobos as it crossed in front of the sun, as seen by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover on March 26, 2019 (Sol 2359). Image via NASA / JPL-Caltech/ MSSS.

Bottom line: Does planet Mars have a North Star akin to Earth’s North Star Polaris? No, there is not a Mars North Star. But Martian stargazers wouldn’t lack for things to see!

Заголовок: ESA Explains Delay in Signing MaiaSpace Launcher Challenge Contract
Полный текст:
Credit: MaiaSpace

The European Space Agency (ESA) has revealed that MaiaSpace’s decision to pursue a different funding arrangement from its competitors has complicated negotiations over its European Launcher Challenge contract.

Speaking during an ESA media briefing on 22 October, ESA Director of Space Transportation Géraldine Naja explained that MaiaSpace was the only one of the four companies to opt for support through launch service contracts.

“MaiaSpace is the only one of the challengers who has chosen to be supported in terms of launch contracts rather than in technical development,” Naja explained.

Under the European Launcher Challenge, funding was allocated through two components. Component A provides funding to subsidise launch service contracts, while Component B provides co-funding for the development and demonstration of upgraded launch vehicle capabilities.

During ESA’s 2025 Ministerial Council meeting in Bremen, member states committed €902.16 million to the European Launcher Challenge. MaiaSpace itself secured commitments totalling €183.4 million, all of which were allocated to Component A.

By contrast, the other three companies secured the majority of their funding commitments under Component B. PLD Space received commitments of €132.23 million, Isar Aerospace €173.8 million and Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) €175.21 million under the component. Each secured less than €37 million under Component A, with RFA receiving just €15.3 million.

On 27 August, ESA announced that it had signed European Launcher Challenge contracts worth a combined €543.6 million with the other three companies. Isar Aerospace secured the largest contract at €197.8 million, followed by RFA at €186.9 million and PLD Space at €158.9 million. At the time, the agency stated that “the contract award process with MaiaSpace is nearing completion and expected to resume in the coming weeks.”

During her 22 October comments, Naja explained that while MaiaSpace’s preference for launch-service contracts had made negotiations “a little bit more sophisticated”, the contract’s signing was a “question of days.” That was, however, three weeks ago, and ESA has yet to publicly announce that the contract has been signed.

Заголовок: Генная терапия на зубцах расчёски
Полный текст:
Генная терапия на зубцах расчёски

У средств от облысения есть нерешённая проблема — доставка. Лосьоны плохо проходят сквозь кожу, а таблетки разносятся по всему организму и рискуют задеть ткани, которым лечение ни к чему. Команда под руководством учёных из Бэйханского университета предложила необычного курьера — расчёску.

Мишень — андрогенетическая алопеция, постепенное облысение, которое встречается и у мужчин, и у женщин. Механизм такой: в восприимчивых фолликулах гормон дигидротестостерон (ДГТ) шаг за шагом подавляет рост, и с каждым новым циклом волос вырастает тоньше и короче предыдущего.

Устройство назвали Detangle. В его зубцах электроды чередуются с резервуарами, дозирующий механизм которых напоминает шариковую ручку. Электроды выставлены на разной высоте: кожа собирается в бороздки, и одновременно на неё подаются заряженные импульсы. Они помогают лекарству пройти глубже в ткань и внутрь клеток, а сама электростимуляция вдобавок активирует сигнальные пути, связанные с ростом волос.

Груз бьёт по проблеме с двух сторон. Первый компонент — небольшое кольцо ДНК с инструкцией для белка, стимулирующего рост кровеносных сосудов, — задел на лучшее кровоснабжение. Второй это короткий фрагмент РНК, работающий как глушилка: он мешает клетке производить фермент, участвующий в выработке ДГТ.

Проверяли так. Самцам мышей удаляли шерсть на спине и каждый день наносили тестостерон — получалась модель облысения, зависящего от андрогенов. Detangle применяли раз в три дня, другой группе ежедневно наносили миноксидил. К 28-му дню у мышей с Detangle шерсть покрыла почти весь обработанный участок, в группе с миноксидилом — около 70%. Анализ тканей показал заметный рост активности фолликулов и улучшение местного кровообращения.

Итог пока такой: принцип доставки показан и в том же эксперименте сработал лучше миноксидила, а дальше всё решат испытания на людях.

Заголовок: Nvidia’s board meets on Jensen Huang, and Elon Musk already has an answer
Полный текст:
Elon Musk says it would be an honor to hire Jensen Huang amid Nvidia turmoil.

Elon Musk says he would welcome Jensen Huang at one of his companies if Nvidia’s board decides to push out its longtime chief executive.

On Wednesday evening, the financial account ZeroHedge posted “Elon please hire Jensen” on X. Musk replied roughly two hours later: “That would be an honor.” Neither Huang nor Nvidia had responded publicly as of Wednesday night.

Musk’s reply came as Nvidia’s board met to decide Huang’s future. The Wall Street Journal reported that directors were preparing to oust him following reports of two extramarital relationships. One involves Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly believe was working for China’s Ministry of State Security. The New York Times separately reported a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care. Huang acknowledged being unfaithful in a memo to employees on Sunday but gave no details.

@zerohedge That would be an honor

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) November 12, 2026

Under Nvidia’s bylaws, a majority of its 11 directors can remove the CEO with or without cause. Bloomberg reported that the board has been working with an outside firm on possible replacements and may name an interim chief, with CFO Colette Kress seen as the likely pick. Nvidia shares fell more than 8 percent in extended trading, according to CNBC , and the company is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17.

Musk has more riding on Nvidia’s leadership than most tech executives. In August, he told investors on SpaceX’s first earnings call as a public company that it would build its AI infrastructure exclusively on Nvidia hardware, calling Vera Rubin “the best architecture.” SpaceX is also working with Nvidia on the compute payload for Starmind , its planned orbital AI constellation. In October, SpaceX said it had a binding commitment for a roughly $40 billion lease of Vera Rubin GPUs and related equipment, with the leases expected to begin in the first half of 2027.

The scale of that dependence is already enormous. On its Q3 call, SpaceX said it was bringing roughly 200,000 to 220,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs online each month and expects 2.5 to 3 GW of nameplate compute by the end of the year. That buildout is now reaching new sites like the proposed $24 billion power plant and supercomputer campus at Starbase .

The relationship between the two executives also goes back nearly a decade. Huang has often told the story of personally delivering Nvidia’s first DGX-1 AI supercomputer to Musk in 2016, when no other customer wanted one. “Nobody wanted to be part of it, except for Elon,” Huang said on the Joe Rogan Experience last December .

Musk did not say what role Huang might fill, and his reply stops short of a formal offer. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and still owns about 3.6 percent of its stock, so any move to a Musk company would depend on whether, and how, he leaves the chipmaker he has run for more than three decades.

Заголовок: SpaceX launches 2nd mystery mission for US Space Force in 6-day span (video, photos)
Полный текст:
SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California tonight (Nov. 11), the second such flight for the company in a six-day span.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:36 p.m. EST (8:36 p.m. local California time; 0136 GMT on Nov. 12), kicking off a mission called USSF-627.

Vandenberg hosted a similar liftoff less than a week ago: On Nov. 6, a Falcon 9 sent the USSF-432 mission skyward from the site, which lies on California's gorgeous but often foggy central coast.

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-627 mission for the U.S. Space Force from California on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX)

We don't know much about USSF-627 or USSF-432; both are classified. Some experts have speculated , however, that each mission launched a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military branch track potential targets around the world.

SpaceX didn't reveal details about either USSF-627 or USSF-432, and the company ended the webcast of both launches shortly after the first stages of their Falcon 9 rockets came back to Earth .

In both cases, that touchdown occurred about 8.5 minutes after liftoff on the SpaceX droneship "Of Course I Still Love You," which was stationed downrange of Vandenberg in the Pacific Ocean.

It was the seventh mission for USSF-627's Falcon 9 booster, which carries the designation 1103.

A Falcon 9 first stage rests on a SpaceX drone ship shortly after launching the USSF-627 mission on Nov. 11, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX)

Previous Booster 1103 missions

NROL-179 | SDA-T1TL-E | SDA-T1TL-A | 3 Starlink missions

USSF-627 was the 120th Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the rocket's 15th national-security flight of the year to date. Eighty-five of the 120 flights have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink broadband constellation in low Earth orbit , which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 is not on a record-breaking cadence this year. In 2025, the rocket flew a whopping 165 missions , and 122 of them were Starlink flights.

Заголовок: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
Полный текст:
NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.

A long-term goal at NASA has been the ability to robotically haul back to Earth specimens from the Red Planet.

NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for its troubled Mars Sample Return (MSR) program, called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture, or PSRA in space shorthand. The plan is to establish a fresh NASA strategy for gathering Mars samples collected by the Perseverance rover and launching them back to Earth.

The PSRA initiative was noted on Nov. 9 by Tiffany Morgan, director of the NASA Mars Exploration Program (MEP), during the virtual meeting of the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group (MEPAG).

Here's the PSRA strategy:

• Develop impartial recommendations for retrieving the Martian samples collected by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover and deliver them to Earth
• Assess proposed mission requirements
• Review prior lessons learned
• Evaluate current capabilities and acquisition options

Morgan noted that there will be a PSRA strategy team kickoff in January 2027 with a final report due in winter 2027-2028.

Pick-me-ups

The backdrop to the PSRA activity is that there's one busy rover already on the Red Planet snagging and bagging samples.

NASA's Perseverance Mars rover remains on the prowl within Jezero Crater following its touchdown in February 2021. That car-sized robot has been grabbing select specimens from across the area and gingerly dropping the sealed pick-me-ups on the surface of Mars , as well as stuffing them inside the rover itself.

Those collectibles may well hold signs of past life on the enigmatic, dusty and foreboding Red Planet.

NASA and the European Space Agency have for years been intently plotting out plans to send future spacecraft to Mars and haul those Perseverance-plucked bits, pieces, and sniffs of atmosphere to Earth for rigorous inspection here on Earth using state-of-the-art equipment.

This photomontage shows each of the sample tubes deposited by NASA's Perseverance Mars rover at the Three Forks sample depot, as viewed by the WATSON camera on the end of the rover's robotic arm. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS)

Sticker shock

However, over the years, multiple reviews of a NASA Mars Sample Return (MSR) project by independent groups have reported sticker shock findings. Indeed, one last price tag came in at about $11 billion, with samples being returned to Earth in 2040. That finding was deemed by NASA itself as too costly and not doable within an acceptable time frame.

Yet another appraisal group ended up finding it feasible to return Mars samples as early as 2035 for a less costly ship and shoot cost of some $8 billion.

How the PSRA review deals with MSR cost and a multitude of other concerns is in the to-be-determined column.

Why samples now?

In the first place, why are samples from Mars delivered by robotic means? Why not let a human expedition bring back the goods?

Also speaking at MEPAG was Bruce Jakosky of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Space Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder and Department of Earth and Space Sciences at the University of Washington.

Jakosky called for an integrated approach to planning human missions to Mars. He highlighted recommendations stemming from a workshop in which he participated, held last May and organized by Explore Mars, Inc.

That report focused on the impact of MSR on reducing risk for human missions, rather than focusing on the science, Jakosky told Space.com.

"The purpose is to understand the risk to astronauts and to hardware. The risk includes that from compounds that are present in the soil that are hazardous to astronauts if breathed in," said Jakosky. "This includes perchlorates and chloromethanes that have been identified already, and detection of other species that might be present. It also includes dust that can be breathed in by astronauts and that can affect hardware wear and tear," he said.

During the MEPAG gathering, Jakosky flagged the importance of returning samples prior to human missions to Mars, such as:

• Identify and characterize known hazardous chemicals to ensure astronaut safety (e.g., perchlorates and chloromethanes), and look for possible additional hazardous chemicals
• Characterize very fine dust particles that could cause respiratory issues in astronauts
• Characterize dust and regolith properties for spacesuit design and wear patterns
• Search in advance of the arrival of humans for evidence of extant life that could interact with terrestrial life
• Enhance astronaut effectiveness on the surface and science return from human missions by providing initial context and analysis
• Demonstrate successful round-trip to Mars
• Demonstrate successful round-trip travel, including entry, descent, landing and ascent from the surface of Mars.
• Demonstrate implementation of planetary protection protocols. While human missions would not use the same approaches, what we learn from doing these would make the approach for humans much easier to plan and implement.

China's program

Diagram of China's proposed Tianwen 3 Mars sample return mission. (Image credit: The University of Hong Kong/Zengqian Hou, et al.)

Yet one more forcing factor for NASA in yet another relook at MSR is that China is making progress on its Tianwen-3 Mars Sample Return mission.

According to the China National Space Administration, the country's Tianwen-3 probe will have a lander, an ascender, a service capsule, an orbiter, and an Earth reentry module.

Tianwen-3 appears on track getting the trek underway around 2028 on two Long March-5 heavy-lift carrier rockets from the Wenchang Space Launch Site in China's southernmost island province of Hainan.

China's Tianwen-3 mission is dedicated to bring back to Earth roughly 500 grams of Red Planet collectibles in 2031.

Заголовок: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
Полный текст:
Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

Fast radio bursts, flashes of energy from faraway galaxies, are invisible to our eyes. However, we can now hear their melody, thanks to a composer who has turned them into sound.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs , are among the most extreme events in the universe, releasing as much energy in a millisecond as the sun puts out in three days and briefly outshining entire galaxies. Since the first FRB was discovered in 2007, astronomers have detected thousands of them; however, exactly how these cosmic flares are launched remains poorly understood. Recent evidence points to at least one burst coming from the environment around a rotating neutron star.

Despite their power, FRBs last only a few thousandths of a second before vanishing into space. Catching one takes luck, as a telescope has to be pointed at the right patch of sky at the right moment. That changed with CHIME (the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) in British Columbia. With a very wide field of view and a supercomputer to process its data, CHIME more than quadrupled the number of known FRBs in its first year of operation alone. Between 2018 and 2023, CHIME recorded 4,539 bursts from 3,641 sources.

As pulses of radio waves, our eyes haven't evolved to see FRBs, nor can we hear them as they aren't sound waves. Well, not until now.

"Artist and composer Andrew Melchior turned all of the CHIME bursts into sound for "The Logos," an installation that has played daily at Oulu Cathedral in Finland since early April and is scheduled to run through the end of the year. Melchior and Kiyoshi Masui, an associate professor of physics at MIT, "sonified" the bursts, translating data into acoustics so that human ears can hear them.

The structure of each real signal is mapped to varying musical pitches and played through 12 loudspeakers spread throughout the cathedral. The result is a range of tones, with distant FRBs humming, rumbling, popping, and whistling.

The signals are old by any human measure. According to a description on Melchior's website , the youngest in the work are about 50 million years old, and the oldest are about 8 to 9 billion years old.

An animation shows the random appearance of fast radio bursts (FRBs) across the sky (Image credit: NRAO Outreach/T. Jarrett (IPAC/Caltech); B. Saxton, NRAO/AUI/NSF))

Physics also plays a role in what is heard. Each burst arrives with its high frequencies first and sweeps downward, stretched by its journey through intergalactic gas, "and you can hear that dispersion as it falls from the dome," Melchior told Space.com by email.

Since their discovery in 2007, the bursts are also still yielding discoveries. Last month, astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope pinpointed the host galaxy of the most distant FRB yet, one that went off when the universe was only about 3 billion years old.

The galaxy, a small, young, star-forming dwarf, was far smaller than expected. That makes it harder to square with the theory that FRBs come from merging neutron stars, researchers say, which would take billions of years to occur.

This fits better with a second theory, in which a young, highly magnetic neutron star called a magnetar produces the burst soon after a massive star explodes, according to NASA .

An illustration of a magnetar launching a FRB (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva))

Back on Earth, an upcoming event at Oulu Cathedral offers a more immediate encounter with the bursts. On Nov. 21, 30 singers will stand among the audience and "sing back to the sky in Finnish" while Melchior plays the bursts live from a keyboard, he told Space.com by email.

"The fast flashes will echo as snare-like beats bouncing through the cathedral," Masui said in a previous MIT statement .

"It should feel rich and layered, while also revealing something real about how these signals travel across billions of years of cosmic space before reaching Earth."

Заголовок: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
Полный текст:
On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program to land humans on the moon.

Gemini 12 was the last mission of the Gemini program. It had two astronauts on board: Jim Lovell and Buzz Aldrin . NASA wanted to send humans to the moon. But first, it needed to make sure crews had the right skills, like docking vehicles in space and taking spacewalks.

Before Gemini 12, astronauts struggled with spacewalks because there weren't enough handholds on their spacecraft. NASA made some spacewalk changes for Gemini 12. Aldrin performed three spacewalks and spent more than five hours working in space with no major problems. Gemini 12 also successfully docked to an unpiloted Agena booster that launched the same day.

The astronauts returned to Earth after four days in space. Both Aldrin and Lovell went on to join the Apollo program . Aldrin became the second person to walk on the moon during Apollo 11 , and Lovell became the commander of Apollo 13 .

The Gemini 12 astronauts James Lovell and Edwin Aldrin lifted off aboard a Titan launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center on November 11, 1966, an hour and a half after their Agena target vehicle was orbited by an Atlas rocket. (Image credit: NASA/MSFC)

Why it mattered

Gemini 12 may have closed out NASA's Gemini program of two-person space missions, but it established the mission also established the fundamentals of spacewalking that Apollo astronauts would use when they walked on the moon.

It's fitting that Aldrin was the primary spacewalker of the mission. A rookie astronaut (and the first to earn a Ph.D.), Aldrin set a precedent by training for his spacewalk in a neutral buoyancy pool in Maryland to better simulate working in weightlessness. Then he did it again as the second person to walk on the moon on Apollo 11.

"This approach became so successful, underwater training has become the primary spacewalk training method used by the United State, Russia and China," NASA officials said in a mission overview . "Today, NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in Houston is large enough to include mockups of major sections of the International Space Station . As such, it is the largest indoor body of water in the world, with 6.2 million gallons of water."

Astronaut Buzz Aldrin practices spacewalking tasks for Gemini 12 in an underwater mockup of his spacecraft in 1966. NASA

The Gemini 12 astronauts walk out to their launch pad with signs on their back denoting "THE END" of the Gemini program. NASA/MSFC

NASA

The Agena docking target for Gemini 12 launched into orbit just over 90 minutes ahead of Lovell (the mission commander) and Aldrin. Aldrin ended up using a sextant to help Lovell rendevous with the agena after they lost radar lock within 74 miles of the vehicle.

During his spacewalks, Aldrin installed handrails, used foot restraints and other tools that have since become routine on spacewalks in orbit. They also tested tools and techniques that Aldrin and other moonwalks would use on the moon .

Gemini 12 also tested a computer-controlled reentry technique when it returned to Earth on Nov. 15, landing Lovell and Aldrin just 3 miles from their target near their recovery ship the USS Wasp in the Atlantic Ocean, about 600 miles east of Cape Canaveral.

Полный текст:
SpaceX wants a Starbase tax break for a $24 billion gas plant and supercomputer campus.

SpaceX is asking its own company town for a tax break on a $24 billion natural gas power plant and supercomputing facility at Starbase, Texas, and the land it picked sits just outside the reach of a data center moratorium that took effect in neighboring Brownsville last week.

A City of Starbase public hearing notice says SpaceX “proposes to construct, own, and operate a gas-fired power plant and super-compute facility” on roughly 444 acres between Boca Chica Boulevard and the Port of Brownsville. The $24 billion figure covers only the initial phases, and the notice leaves room for future expansions. The Starbase City Commission will consider a property tax abatement and a related economic development agreement at a 7 p.m. hearing on December 9. The notice does not disclose the size or length of the abatement, or how much computing capacity the site would hold.

The location has a history. Over the summer, SpaceX asked Brownsville to remove the tract from its city limits and offered $220 million for water and wastewater projects in return. Brownsville approved the move in August, and Starbase later annexed the land. Brownsville’s own 90-day pause on data center applications took effect last week, and had the tract stayed inside the city, the project likely would have needed a different home.

The power side is already in front of state regulators. SpaceX has applied to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality for air permits covering 35 mobile gas turbines producing roughly 750 megawatts, according to Politico , which also noted that two of the three Starbase commissioners voting on the incentives are SpaceX executives.

Building its own plant lets SpaceX skip the Texas grid. Gov. Greg Abbott paused new data center grid connections in August pending an audit, but a facility that generates its own electricity does not need one. The air permit still has to clear the TCEQ, where Abbott also ordered a halt on data center permits.

The bigger test arrives in January. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated Abbott last week, has said she will block data center approvals until the legislature passes new protections, and she has already asked state officials to hold off on any sale of Boca Chica State Park to SpaceX until she is sworn in. Tesla and SpaceX shares both fell the day after the election , and Musk’s first reaction on X was “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

That line points to Starmind, SpaceX’s orbital compute constellation. Musk has said terrestrial compute will be “peanuts compared to orbital compute” and expects monthly orbital deployments to pass ground deployments around the end of 2028, as Teslarati reported . Until then, SpaceX still needs gigawatts on the ground. It ended the third quarter with 1.7 GW of nameplate compute, is targeting 2.5 to 3 GW by the end of this year and wants at least 10 GW more in 2027. Its existing Colossus sites around Memphis already run on gas turbines and face a lawsuit from residents over emissions.

Local reaction is split. The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, citing air quality, water use and energy bills, while some Brownsville residents told the Tribune they welcome the jobs. SpaceX did not respond to the Tribune’s questions about the project.

Заголовок: Andy Weir's 'Exoplanet' just landed on Audible, but what actually makes an exoplanet habitable?
Полный текст:
How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

Imagine you’ve crash-landed on an alien planet. Your ship is destroyed, your oxygen supply is dangerously low, and the landscape around you is completely unknown. Where would you begin looking for clues to your survival? Surprisingly, the best place to start could be the star overhead.

This is the predicament that three crew members of the Wild Blue Yonder face in Audible’s new sci-fi thriller, "Exoplanet." This sci-fi thriller is written by acclaimed comic writer Benjamin Percy, executive produced by Andy Weir (Project Hail Mary, The Martian), and features an all-star voice cast including Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose, and John Leguizamo .

Stranded on an unfamiliar planet, they encounter volcanic wastelands, unknown skies, and environments that seem to defy reason. But behind the extraordinary events of this audio drama is a very real scientific question: what makes a planet habitable?

Learning from the stars

An artist's concept illustrates a young, red dwarf star surrounded by three planets. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

In “Exoplanet”, the crew view skies that are not only unfamiliar but also seemingly different from one another. One character sees a sun as so dim that he can look directly at it, while another suffers under a blazing heat, surrounded by stretches of sun-scorched red rock.

For astronomers, the light emitted by a star is one of the most crucial tools for understanding planets orbiting it.

Using a technique called spectroscopy , astronomers split starlight into its constituent wavelengths, producing a spectrum much like a rainbow. By studying this spectrum, they can investigate the temperature, composition, and other physical properties of the star.

(Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech)

However, stellar temperature is only part of the picture. The amount of energy a planet receives depends on both the luminosity of the star and its orbital distance.

Astronomers use these measurements to determine whether a world lies in the habitable zone of a star, where temperatures could allow liquid water to exist on the surface given a suitable atmosphere.

A planet orbiting a cool red dwarf would need to be much closer to its star than Earth is to the Sun to be in this habitable zone. Unfortunately, being in this zone is no guarantee of a planetary paradise.

Hostile stars

Black holes are bad news for life, but living stars provide just as many problems. (Image credit: Audible)

A planet that sits comfortably in the habitable zone is ultimately still at the mercy of its star. Stars emit more than just the light we see. Ultraviolet radiation and X-rays can interact with planetary atmospheres, altering chemistry and even contributing to the loss of the atmosphere .

Violent stellar flares can produce bursts of high-energy radiation. A planet could offer a wonderfully balmy temperature, only to be bombarded with radiation from the host star.

The age of a star matters too. Young stars tend to be more active, with radiation that could erode a planet’s atmosphere over time. Meanwhile, as stars age and evolve, their changing luminosities can drastically alter the conditions a planet experiences.

For the stranded crew in “Exoplanet”, understanding the star overhead may therefore be as important as knowing the landscape beneath their feet.

Is the air breathable?

NASA illustration of Kepler-186f, the first Earth-size planet to be discovered in a habitable zone. (Image credit: NASA Ames/SETI Institute/JPL-CalTech via Wikimedia Commons)

Even if a planet has survived all the complications we’ve just thrown at it, there’s still a rather important question: could we actually breathe the air?

In "Exoplanet", one crew member discovers that the planet’s atmosphere contains enough oxygen for him to breathe without his spacesuit. On Earth, oxygen makes up around 21% of our atmosphere. However, finding a similar percentage on another planet wouldn’t automatically mean the air is safe to breathe.

Atmospheric pressure matters just as much . At high altitudes on Earth, the oxygen percentage remains the same, but the lower pressure means less oxygen is available to our lungs.

Oxygen isn’t the only concern, either. The fictional planet’s volcanic landscape releases gases such as sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, both of which are hazardous at high concentrations. Even an oxygen-rich atmosphere could still be lethal.

Searching for life

An artist illustration of exoplanet K2-18b, an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. (Image credit: Hubble, M. Kornmesser via Wikimedia commons)

But what if you don't just need to know if a planet is habitable? What if you need to know if something already lives there?

Before the Wild Blue Yonder arrived at the planet, probes detected dimethyl sulfide, a molecule we associate with biological activity on Earth . This is a beautifully timely detail, as this very molecule has been at the heart of a scientific debate about one of the most intriguing exoplanets discovered so far.

Astronomers have investigated possible signs of dimethyl sulfide in the atmosphere of K2-18 b , an exoplanet orbiting a red dwarf. However, both the detection itself and the biological interpretation remain heavily disputed .

Astronomers can study the starlight that filters through exoplanet atmospheres, searching for signatures of molecules that may be signs of life. (Image credit: NASA, ESA and A. Feild (STScI))

The challenge is that detecting a single molecule isn’t definitive evidence of life. Its presence can be influenced by factors other than biology, like atmospheric chemistry and stellar radiation.

Understanding whether such a molecule could actually indicate life means studying not just the planet’s atmosphere, but also the radiation it receives from its star.

More than Earth Mark 2

(Image credit: Audible)

Astronomers have discovered thousands of exoplanets. Understanding whether any could support life is, however, an extraordinary challenge.

The distance between the planet and the star might give us a good clue, but its atmosphere, geology, and stellar environment are all interconnected in determining whether life could survive. For the unfortunate crew of the Wild Blue Yonder, those distinctions could mean the difference between survival and utter disaster.

We might one day identify a planet with Earth-like temperatures, liquid water, and abundant oxygen. But even then, there’s still a huge gap dividing a potentially habitable planet from one where we could safely remove our helmets.

Заголовок: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
Полный текст:
For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.

The origin of life on Earth remains a mystery. New research shows that comets almost certainly did not bring the chemical building blocks of life to our planet.

Life as we know it is based around carbon chemistry, also known as organic chemistry. Complex organic molecules are the fundamental building blocks of biochemical compounds such as nucleobases, amino acids, sugars and so on that act as the machinery for biochemistry on Earth .

Two big questions are where did this complex chemistry originate? Did these complex organic molecules form on Earth, or were they delivered here from space?

New research led by planetary scientist Richard Anslow of the Institute for Astronomy at the University of Cambridge has now seemingly ruled out comets as the origin of complex organic molecules on Earth.

"Historically, scientists thought that comets were important for the origin of life on Earth, because they carried carbon and nitrogen-bearing molecules, so these giant space snowballs were almost like a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' that brought all the molecules a planet would need to seed life," said Anslow in a statement .

Stripping the romance from the Earth's turbulent past

Comet impacts on Earth were much more frequent in the first half-billion years of the solar system ’s existence, when there were still lots of debris leftover from the formation of the planets.

For over a century comet impacts had been considered a prime suspect in the search for what brought the building blocks of life to Earth. However, while comets bringing the building blocks of life to Earth is "kind of a romantic idea," according to Anslow, the University of Cambridge researcher added that the team's results suggest that is highly unlikely.

Anslow and colleagues arrived at this conclusion based upon computer modeling by using the very latest simulations depicting the origin and evolution of comets and their orbits, their interactions with Earth's atmosphere as they enter it, and of the hypervelocity comet impacts themselves.

In particular, they used the fate of hydrogen cyanide as a proxy for what happens to complex organic molecules in comet impacts. Hydrogen cyanide is frequently found in comets and was even detected in the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS .

An artist’s impression of a comet crashing into the early Earth (Image credit: Scarlett White)

The problem is that comets are generally moving at too great a velocity. For organic molecules to survive impact, the impact velocity would have to be below 33,500 miles per hour (15 kilometers per second).

Anslow and his colleagues found that, in general, comets travel too fast and enter Earth’s atmosphere at too sharp an angle for complex organic molecules to survive. Instead, they are mostly vaporized on impact. Even on the rare occasions that the complex organic molecules survived, they were usually not in great enough abundance to provide any meaningful prebiotic chemistry.

"It would really have to be a one-in-a-million occurrence, because not only would you need an impact at just the right speed and just the right angle, you would also need everything to happen after that point, in terms of the concentration and the speed at which the chemical origins of life got going," said Anslow. "We can’t rule out for certain that it happened that way, but it seems to be a really rare occurrence – at best, a one-off fluke."

Maybe life on Earth is a fluke

It is not yet known if the origin of life on Earth was a fluke, or whether life is plentiful in the universe, so a fluke occurrence could still have been a trigger for life on our planet.

However, researchers are coming around to alternatives, either that all the pre-biotic chemistry that resulted in life took place on Earth without requiring material from space, or asteroids instead brought those important molecules to Earth.

Scientists have found asteroids to be rich in those molecules – for example, the sample of material brought back by the OSIRIS-REx mission from the near-Earth asteroid Bennu contained all the building blocks of RNA.

However, other planets could have plausibly benefitted from comet impacts. The simulations showed that complex organic molecules in comets would stand a slightly better chance of surviving impacts on Mars , because of the Red Planet’s thinner atmosphere and lower gravity.

"This is not to say it definitely happened on Mars, of course, but it suggests it would be unlikely if it happened on Earth and didn’t happen on Mars," said Anslow. "Or the other, perhaps more likely, alternative is that it didn’t happen on either planet."

The 7 planets circling the star TRAPPIST-1, 3 of which might be able to keep liquid water on its surface. (Image credit: R. Hurt/T. Pyle/NASA)

More intriguing are the possibilities on exoplanets, specifically the peas-in-a-pod multi-planet systems around red dwarf stars such as TRAPPIST-1 , where all the planets are bunched up close.

In 2023 Anslow wrote a research paper describing how comets could gravitationally bounce from one planet to the next, losing velocity in the process so that when they crash into one of the planets, they impact is not so severe and complex organic molecules might have a chance to survive.

The team's research was published on 28 October in Scientific Reports .

Заголовок: The space rocket I could have been aboard explodes: Rhiannon Adam’s best photograph
Полный текст:
‘I was chosen to go around the Moon on a SpaceX starship. Preparations took over my life. Then, four minutes into watching a rocket on a test flight, it broke apart. And that was the end of my adventure’

This photograph was taken on 20 April 2023 from the VIP section of SpaceX’s launch viewing area, looking out from South Padre Island, Texas, towards Boca Chica, a nature reserve near the Mexican border which is home to SpaceX’s Starbase launchpad.

In 2021, I and seven other civilians were selected from an open call to go around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship flight funded by the Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The dearMoon Project included myself and another photographer. For me, the story also became about being plucked from obscurity and planted in this very surreal world I could never have imagined being a part of in a million years. At the time, only 24 white American men had orbited or landed on the moon. Being selected for something like that changes your life and your perception of your worth in the world. The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, completely took over my life. It took the air out of every room – I couldn’t talk about anything else. People stopped commissioning me because they assumed I was busy going to space; every conversation I had was about it. This was going to be the rest of my life.

That day in April was pivotal. We were there to watch SpaceX’s Integrated Flight Test 1. After four minutes, following a relatively successful liftoff, the vehicle experienced what they call in space terms an “RUD” – Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly – and broke apart in the air. We put on a brave face but secretly I was thinking: “Wow, the risks are no longer theoretical. I could have been on that.”

The dust cloud in the image emerged from the concrete launchpad and tower – obliterated by the power of the raptor engines. The debris ended up all over the local houses and SpaceX closed the launch facility for reconstruction for four months while they conducted a huge clean-up operation. Going to space feels futuristic and grandiose but there are still the practical problems – like people wiping dust off their windows.

Заголовок: Space Science Boosting Mission Begins via Improved Rocket [Long March 2D Y108]
Полный текст:
New science instruments are going to be operated in orbit for two years aboard a spacecraft and sub-satellites ahead of dedicated missions later this decade.

The Long March 2D Y108 vehicle launching from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on November 11th 2026. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

An improved Long March 2D lifted off from Launch Site 94 at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center at 19:41 pm China Standard Time (11:41 am Universal Coordinated Time) on November 11th, heading for sun-synchronous orbit carrying a single scientific spacecraft.

Belonging to the National Space Science Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院国家空间科学中心), the launched spacecraft is known as Tanluozhe-1 (探路者一号卫星), alternatively simply called ‘Pathfinder’. It was built by the Innovation Academy for Microsatellites, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院微小卫星创新研究院), who revealedthe spacecraft will release three sub-satellites in the future. The main satellite is to be known as Tanluozhe-1A, with the smaller ones to be designated B, C, and D. 1

Once confirmed to be healthy in a 600-kilometer dawn-dusk orbit, Tanluozhe-1A will perform verifications of its Magnetic and Helioseismic Imager 2 , designed by the Xi’an Institute of Optics and Precision Mechanics (西安光学精密机械研究所), while B, C, and D will fly in formation to prove the Very Large Area Gamma-ray Space Telescope Pathfinder 3 , made by Purple Mountain Observatory (紫金山天文台), the High-Resolution Atmospheric Boundary Layer Lidar 4 , from the University of Science and Technology of China (中国科学技术大学), as well as Langmuir Probes 5 and Space Weather Effects Monitors 6 from the National Space Science Center. The spacecraft and its sub-satellites are expected to operate for two years.

A render of Tianluozhe-1A after releasing sub-satellites B, C, and D in orbit. | Image: Chinese Academy of Sciences

Without going into specifics at the time, the Chinese Academy of Sciences stated in October 2025 that the Tanluozhe-1 mission will perform critical technology verifications for future space science missions beginning this decade and next. A report released in January would add that its technology tasks would allow China’s upcoming space science missions to ‘enter the fast lane’ regarding contributions to global science and new discoveries.

Four future missions were mentioned as being supported by Tanluozhe-1, being the sun-studying ‘Kuafu-2 (夸父二号)’ 7 , the Earth-like planet searching ‘Earth 2.0 (系外地球巡天)’, the lunar orbit-based Hongmeng Project (鸿蒙计划) for performing ultralong wavelength observations of the electromagnetic spectrum, and the telescope ‘enhanced X-ray Timing and Polarimetry (增强型X射线时变与偏振空间天文台)’ 8 . Those are expected to be launched within the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).

The China Aerospace Science and Technology Commercial Launch Vehicle Group’s patch for the Long March 2D Y108 launch mission on November 11th 2026. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

In their post-launch statements today, the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology , who produce the Long March 2D, and the China Aerospace Science and Technology Commercial Launch Vehicle Group Co Ltd (中国航天科技集团商业火箭有限公司) 9 , which sells it domestically, shared that the launch vehicle was improved for this mission. Those were shared to be the removal of four tail fins previously required to maintain aerodynamic stability, a new composite 3.35 meter diameter fairing, a new lighter second-stage design, as well as a miniaturized inertial measurement unit and flight computers, which are now using domestically made components. No increases to the Long March 2D’s lift capacity were stated, but more payload volume inside the fairing was stated to be available.

While working to fly those changes for the first time, launch teams also had to deal with Jiuquan’s winter season and the challenges related to its cold temperatures. For that, propellant loading operations were adjusted while thermal insulation material, which harmlessly falls away at lift-off, was installed on the first-stages engine section, the interstage, and increased on the payload fairing.

To ensure success with the changes and the winter challenges, it was said that all possible problem points were mapped out and resolved before moving forward. Efforts to maintain quality operations are in the interest of launch teams since a correction effort began in September.

Today’s launch was the 107th mission for the Long March 2D, the 283rd Long March vehicle from the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, and the 677th launch of the Long March launch vehicle series. This was also the 81st launch from China in 2026.

Liftoff video via 我们的太空 on WeChat.

Check out the previous Long March 2D launch

What is the Long March 2D?

This section is for those less familiar with China’s Long March series of launch vehicles.

The Long March 2D is also one of the oldest launch vehicles from China, performing missions regularly to low Earth and sun-synchronous orbits by the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, as a two-stage version of the Long March 4 vehicles. The two stages of the launch vehicle both burn Dinitrogen Tetroxide and Unsymmetrical Dimethylhydrazine.

The payload capacity of the launch vehicle is currently as follows:

•

3,500 kilograms to low Earth orbit

•

1,300 kilograms to a sun-synchronous orbit

The Long March 2D Y108 vehicle stood at Launch Site 94 ahead of its launch mission on November 11th 2026. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

The first-stage is powered by four YF-21C engines, which generate 302 tons of thrust burning Dinitrogen Tetroxide and Unsymmetrical Dimethylhydrazine. The second-stage is powered by a single YF-22C engine and four YF-23C verniers that generate 80 tons of thrust while also burning Dinitrogen Tetroxide and Unsymmetrical Dimethylhydrazine.

On the launch pad, the Long March 2D is 41.05 meters tall and weighs 232,250 kilograms when fully fuelled. The first and second stages have a diameter of 3.35 meters, with the fairing having a diameter of either 3.35, 3.8, 4, or 4.2 meters.

So far, the Long March 2D has flown from all three inland launch sites, the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, and the Xichang Satellite Launch Center.

Заголовок: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
Полный текст:
This dazzling collection of ancient stars could hold clues to the Milky Way's past.

The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange.

But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed.

M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini)

What is it?

The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus.

M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity .

Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old!

Why is it amazing

Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell.

Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history.

Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

Заголовок: Ловушка для частиц-призраков
Полный текст:
Ловушка для частиц-призраков

Почему во Вселенной вещества больше, чем антивещества? Искать ответ физики будут почти в полутора километрах под землёй: в Южной Дакоте началось строительство DUNE — крупнейшего в мире нейтринного эксперимента. Над ним работают Фермилаб, CERN и подземная лаборатория SURF, а всего в проекте больше 1500 исследователей.

Главные герои тут нейтрино. У них нет электрического заряда и почти нет массы, а с веществом они взаимодействуют так неохотно, что каждый день несметными количествами проносятся сквозь нас незамеченными. Отсюда и прозвище «частицы-призраки». Рождаются они, например, в недрах звёзд и летят на огромные расстояния, так что ловить их можно и на Земле.

Зачем столько усилий? Нейтрино умеют на лету менять «аромат» — так физики называют их тип, — и эти превращения связаны с крошечной разницей в массах частиц. Если точно измерить, как именно это происходит, можно приблизиться к разгадке того самого перекоса в пользу вещества. Заодно такие данные помогут уточнить Стандартную модель и лучше понять, что происходило вскоре после Большого взрыва.

Схема эксперимента такая. Ускоритель Фермилаба будет стрелять пучком нейтрино по детекторам DUNE с расстояния 1300 км, а ещё один детектор прямо в Фермилабе измерит частицы на старте. Сравнив «до» и «после», физики увидят, во что нейтрино превратились по дороге. Детекторы на жидком аргоне должны быть готовы к 2030 году, первый пучок к ним отправят к 2031-му.

Сердце установки — два криостата длиной 65,8 м, шириной 18,9 м и высотой 18,3 м каждый. Они рассчитаны примерно на 17 тысяч тонн жидкого аргона, охлаждённого до −184 °C. Такой размах понятен: раз нейтрино почти ни с чем не сталкиваются, ловить их приходится в огромном объёме вещества. На два криостата уйдёт 2600 стальных балок, их спускают по шахте на глубину 1478 м — этим занимается SURF. Первый криостат уже строят, сборка второго начнётся в следующем году.

Заголовок: Why I recommend the Seestar S30 Plus smart telescope for beginners — full review
Полный текст:
I photographed galaxies, nebulas and star clusters from a city with the Seestar S30 Plus. Here’s why I think it’s the best affordable smart telescope for beginners.

I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf.

The Pleiades (M45), photographed in mosaic mode with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

The Dumbbell Nebula (M27) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer.

Star trails photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus’s dedicated Star Trail mode. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing.

For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition.

I photographed nebulas despite light pollution

The S30 Plus is Seestar’s new entry-level smart telescope. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city.

Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become.

Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy.

It’s the perfect companion to my optical telescope

The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

I’ve always preferred spending my nights looking at the sky rather than fiddling with equipment, which is one reason I enjoy smart telescopes. Traditional astrophotography can involve a camera, tracking mount, adapters, cables, alignment, a laptop and considerable patience before the first useful exposure begins. The S30 Plus removes almost all of that.

The Seestar S30 Plus has two 3.7MP cameras — almost 80% more pixels than the original S30. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

I can put it outside, connect the Seestar app and choose a target from its built-in sky atlas. The telescope then moves to the correct position, identifies the star field, centers the object, focuses and begins imaging. Within minutes, a photograph starts appearing on my smartphone. That leaves me free to use an optical telescope alongside it — or stay inside and do something else.

The moon on a cloudy night, photographed with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The sun photographed with a Seestar S30 Plus fitted with its supplied magnetic solar filter. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

The Seestar S30 Plus is small enough to fit in any backpack. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

Its 3/8-inch tripod thread can be annoying if you’re used to 3/4-inch threads. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

The longer I leave it alone, the better the images get

The Seestar S30 Plus has built-in filters to reduce light pollution. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

Using the S30 Plus’s built-in UV/IR cut filter — which blocks ultraviolet and infrared light — I captured the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), a popular deep-sky object. As the hours went by, the dust lanes on its outskirts appeared in ever more detail. That’s how smart telescopes work — they collect and combine dozens or hundreds of short exposures, gradually revealing fainter structure while reducing noise.

So impressive is the image after only about five or six exposures that it’s tempting to stop after a few minutes — but patience makes an enormous difference. Fortunately, you don’t have to stand beside the S30 Plus. You can leave it collecting light — even overnight, thanks to its scheduling option (though it’s not waterproof, so check the weather forecast!).

Using the dual-band anti-light pollution filter, the Pleiades open cluster (M45) provided another interesting test. The S30 Plus has a mosaic mode that photographs overlapping sections of sky to create a larger image than its main camera can capture in a single frame. It’s ideal for expansive targets such as the Pleiades and Andromeda, although gathering enough exposures takes time. The app shows how much of the mosaic has been completed, and if needs be, you can continue collecting data on subsequent nights.

I also photographed the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884) and the Great Globular Cluster in Hercules (M13), both relatively swift targets, but as anyone who’s used a smart telescope knows, it’s the faint nebulas that are the real prize. For those, dark skies mean better data — and that’s exactly why a smart telescope needs to be portable.

It’s small enough to fit in my camera bag

There are new post-processing features in the Seestar app. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The S30 Plus weighs just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg) and measures 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm) when switched off. That’s small enough to fit into a camera bag in place of another lens or camera body, which is a major advantage because I travel to remote locations quite frequently. That fact that it sits on such a tiny tripod is also a boon.

I’ve recently used the much larger Seestar S50 Pro , which weighs 6.17 lbs (2.8 kg). It’s a more capable imaging instrument with a 50mm aperture and a larger 8.3-megapixel sensor, but its heavier, bulkier chassis is harder to get into carry-on luggage. The S30 Plus and the higher-spec S30 Pro also differ from the S50 Pro in that they come with a padded carry case. This has a useful carrying handle, although there’s no shoulder strap or dedicated storage for the tripod and magnetic solar filter.

It’s also worth taking along a portable battery and USB-C cable to recharge its built-in 6,000mAh battery during long sessions, though it lasts about six hours, which will suit most observing sessions.

It’s much more advanced than the original S30

Switch off the S30 Plus, and it locks into the closed position. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The original, now-discontinued S30 was already impressive, but the S30 Plus is a substantial upgrade. It has improved four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras, each producing 1,440x2,560-pixel images. That’s almost 80% more pixels than the original S30’s main camera.

The main camera’s field of view has increased slightly to about three degrees, while the wide-angle camera now covers 43.5 degrees of sky. The latter can be used for star trails, though I suspect it’s something most people will experiment with occasionally.

There’s also an EQ mode. This will align the telescope with Earth’s rotation to allow longer exposures and sharper edges, which I found worked really well. It requires an appropriately angled mount or wedge (such as the Seestar TH10 Fluid Tripod Head ) and a small tripod.

Mosaic mode, equatorial tracking and FITS file export are all supported. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

The Seestar S30 Plus features upgraded four-element apochromatic optics with ED glass, compared with the original S30’s three-element design. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter

I tested it at 51 degrees north, which randomly appears to be the cut-off point for ease of use because of the tilt it puts on the telescope. It’s when a tripod begins to topple with the weight, meaning you need a tripod whose legs can be set at a low angle (Seestar’s TC20 tripod would be ideal, and is very compact).

The app makes it all very easy to set up, and advanced imaging possibilities like this are welcome. So, too, is the option of outputting images as lossless FITS files for anyone wanting to process their images using specialist software.

That’s what makes the Seestar S30 Plus such a good beginner’s telescope. It’s easy to use immediately, but there’s plenty of scope to develop more sophisticated astrophotography skills without buying another instrument.

I photographed the moon and sun during the day

The Seestar S30 Plus replaces the original Seestar S30, which launched in 2025. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The S30 Plus isn’t limited to deep-sky photography. I photographed a near-full moon against a blue daytime sky, something I particularly enjoy doing with smart telescopes because they’re so quick to set up.

It also comes with a magnetic white-light solar filter, allowing safe photographs of the sun when the filter is securely fitted. This must always be installed before pointing the telescope towards the sun. I did have to manually guide the S30 Plus to the sun and moon on a few occasions, but it’s easy enough to do, and I actually like the option to manually take control — few other smart telescopes allow it. Once you’ve found the sun or moon, the scope centers it and keeps it in view (unless you’re on a moving ship, by the way, where tracking generally fails — something for eclipse chasers to think about).

Planetary photography is less impressive. The 30mm aperture and short focal length aren’t ideal for detailed views of Jupiter or Saturn, so for anyone primarily interested in observing and imaging planets, I’d recommend a conventional optical telescope instead.

I could spend years exploring the sky with this telescope

The Seestar S30 Plus measures just 8.25 x 5.5 x 3.15 inches (210 x 140 x 80 mm), making it easy to grab with one hand. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter)

The S30 Plus occupies an interesting position in ZWO’s increasingly crowded Seestar range. With dual 8.3MP cameras and wider fields of view, the S30 Pro is a worthy upgrade from the original S30. Meanwhile, the $999 S50 Pro has a larger 50mm aperture that collects almost three times as much light, although it’s also significantly bulkier and more expensive.

Alternatives exist outside ZWO’s range. DwarfLab’s Dwarf Mini is exceptionally portable, but its lower resolution and more limited capabilities make it less versatile. At the other extreme, Unistellar’s Odyssey has an 85mm aperture, an electronic eyepiece and opportunities to contribute to citizen science projects, but it sits in a different price bracket.

The S30 Plus will hit the sweet spot for many. It offers almost everything a beginner needs to explore deep-sky astrophotography, with built-in filters, mosaic mode and EQ tracking giving plenty of advanced features to grow into. Crucially, it’s small enough to travel with easily. Yes, you can spend more and get slightly better image data, but most beginners don’t need to.

The Seestar S30 Plus is one of the most affordable smart telescopes available, but it’s also one of the best-value offerings in its class.

Заголовок: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
Полный текст:
NASA's new UVEX space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility.

The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum.

UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) .

The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement .

"The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement.

UVEX will paint a picture of cosmic life, death and afterlife

UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV."

UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light.

"In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find."

UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars , however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas.

The supernova relic Pa 30, as seen by the Gemini north telescope. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA)

Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward in cosmic explosions we call supernovas.

This is a process that scientists are keen to understand, as these explosions fling the heavy elements forged during the stars' lifetimes into surrounding galaxies. This material becomes the building blocks of the next generation of stars, planets, and possibly even life.

UVEX will also investigate what happens to the end products of some supernovas, neutron stars, when they meet and merge.

An illustration shows two neutron stars colliding and merging. (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva))

Neutron stars contain between one and two times the mass of the sun crammed into a width of around 12 miles (20 kilometers). That means they are composed of matter so dense that, if a teaspoon of it were brought to Earth, it would weigh over 1 billion tons. That's equivalent to stacking around 9 million adult blue whales on a spoon.

So, when neutron stars in binary systems spiral together and merge, they create an environment so violent that it's the only place in the universe where scientists are sure that elements heavier than lead, like gold, silver, and platinum, are able to be forged.

Currently, neutron star mergers are detected via ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves . Scientists can then follow up on the aftermath of the mergers by observing them in electromagnetic light, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy radio waves. Thus, UVEX will add another aspect to the investigation of neutron star collisions and our understanding of where heavy elements originate.

The new space telescope's maneuverability will allow it to observe these explosive events very shortly after they happen, giving it an advantage over other instruments, including NASA's long-serving Hubble Space Telescope.

"With UVEX, we will now be able to follow up on gravitational-wave events in ultraviolet light," UVEX team member and Caltech scientist Mansi Kasliwal said in the same statement. "I can count on two hands how many spectra we have of transient events in their infancy phase with the Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is, of course, amazing and does have some ultraviolet capabilities, but it cannot rapidly pivot to observe real-time events."

An illustration of a stripped blue star (Image credit: Robert Lea)

UVEX will also be revolutionary in the study of blue stars that have had their outer layers of hydrogen stripped away by companion stars. These stars offer researchers a unique opportunity to study the interior of stars, which is usually obscured by their outer layers.

"We will be able to see what's inside the stars," Kareem El-Badry, an associate professor of astronomy at Caltech and a member of the UVEX team, said in the same statement. "We only know of a small number of stripped stars of this type now. UVEX will find hundreds."

All of the above elements discussed are the expected discoveries and investigations that UVEX will be involved with. Perhaps even more exciting, however, are the unexpected elements of the universe it will uncover.

"Every time you look at the skies in a new wavelength, you learn something new and unexpected," El-Badry said.

Заголовок: Starship Flight 15 to attempt first catch of both stages
Полный текст:
SpaceX plans to catch both Starship and its Super Heavy booster at the launch tower on Flight 15, which could fly as soon as this Friday, pending regulatory approval. The 75-minute launch window opens at 4:45 p.m. CT (5:45 p.m. ET).

[Дополнительно: Teslarati – SpaceX]
SpaceX will try to catch both Starship stages today, a first for any orbital rocket. SpaceX is set to launch Starship Flight 15 from Starbase on Friday afternoon, and if both stages make it back to the tower, the mission will go down as the first time an orbital rocket has ever been fully recovered. CT from Pad 2, a day after SpaceX rolled Ship 42 out to the pad and shared photos of the move on X . The first catch comes quickly. About six and a half minutes after liftoff, Booster 22 is scheduled to fly back to Starbase and settle into the launch tower’s chopstick arms, the first catch attempt for SpaceX’s V3 Super Heavy. SpaceX has caught the booster three times before most recently in March 2025. Ship 42 moves to the Starbase pad ahead of launch https://t.co/pMUFTHneJQ — SpaceX (@SpaceX) November 13, 2026 The second catch is the one that has never been done. Ship 42 will climb to an orbit about 275 kilometers up, deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites and complete about 14 orbits. Three of those satellites carry cameras to inspect the ship’s heat shield before it commits to coming home.

[Дополнительно: SpacePolicyOnline]
SpaceX launched the 15th Starship Integrated Flight Test (IFT-15) early this evening from Starbase, Texas. Plans to bring the first stage Booster back to the launch tower for a “catch” minutes after liftoff were scrubbed, but hopes remain high that there will be a catch tomorrow when the second stage, Starship, returns from orbit. SpaceX’s Starship is designed to be fully reusable, with both the first stage Super Heavy (“Booster’) and the second stage Starship (“Ship”) flying into orbit, returning to Earth, and launching again and again and again. (Starship is the name of the second stage, but is often used to refer to the entire vehicle.) IFT-14 in September was the first time Starship reached orbit. While everything didn’t go exactly as planned, it did achieve orbit and made a controlled landing in the north Pacific after 3 hours and 8 minutes instead of 10 hours. The first stage, Super Heavy or “Booster,”, looks white because it is filled with ultra-cold cryogenic fuel that makes it “frosty”. The upper stage, Starship or Ship, is black on the side toward the camera because it is covered with thermal protection tiles. Screenshot from SpaceX webcast.

[Дополнительно: Astronomy Magazine]
For the first time, the company will try to catch both stages of the rocket — the Super Heavy booster and the upper stage, which SpaceX calls “Ship” — with the arms of its launch tower. SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. CST) Friday from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas, pending regulatory approval. Starship launch dates often slip, so check the company’s Flight 15 mission page for the latest. SpaceX’s live webcast begins about 30 minutes before liftoff — around 5:15 p.m. EST if the launch holds at the start of the window. You can stream it on the Flight 15 mission page or on SpaceX’s X account.
