Заголовок: Canada’s Medium-Lift Rocket Ambitions Confirmed In Budget
Полный текст:
Canada will upgrade its rockets as part of its Launch the North initiative, which is aiming to support sovereign rockets flying from at least two new spaceports.

Canada is ready to give its young launch industry a boost.

The country will upgrade its rockets to medium lift as part of its Launch the North initiative, which is aiming to support sovereign rockets flying from at least two nascent spaceports on Canada’s east coast. The timeline for the upgrade is not clear, however; the smaller rockets are expected to get off the ground in 2028.

Canada’s C$142B ($100B) federal budget five-year-spending projection, released late Thursday, officially put money behind the previously announced rocket spending plans. The budget also promised new rockets, a sovereign “rocket-propulsion ecosystem,” and defense-department backed launch and testing.

The Eh-ther : Canada used to fly government-supported sounding rockets many decades ago. But the country’s launch industry largely went into hibernation, instead pouring its space dollars into robotics and medicine —to great success. But lower launch costs and rising national support—and a launch vacuum looming in Canada’s neighbor to the south—is presenting an opportunity.

• Earlier this year, the defense department awarded over 10 years C$200M ($141M) to Maritime Launch Services’ Spaceport Nova Scotia , as well as C$20M ($14M), exclusive of individual launch-contract costs, to NordSpace’s Atlantic Spaceport Complex .

• Launch the North also started up in 2026, with an initial bout of ~C$25M ($17.6M) spread between small rockets developed by Canada Rocket Company, NordSpace, and Reaction Dynamics.

• Last month, Minister of National Defence David McGuinty promised to go bigger: Small rockets are “where we start; they’re not where we stop,” he said of rocket size at Canada’s major industry conference, Space Canada’s SpaceBound.

Mapleverse: Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy , minted nearly a year ago, lists launch as one of the country’s top seven priorities—along with tech like quantum computing that also has space applications.

And Canadian companies are responding , because they are aware SpaceX’s coming retirement of the Falcon 9 will present a market gap in medium-lift rockets. Canada Rocket Company, NordSpace, and Reaction Dynamics have all discussed or unveiled prototypes of that size.

Canada’s defense-heavy budget only made a few other mentions of space, but those mentions show the country is watching global trends: for example, a mention of “weapons in orbit” is said to be a factor in drone dollars, while “space surveillance” is being promised to British Columbia on the opposite coast from Canada’s spaceports.

Топ-5 стран по числу запущенных спутников: США — 207 (62,5%), Китай — 36 (10,9%), Южная Корея — 16 (4,8%), Италия — 13 (3,9%), Испания — 9 (2,7%). Доля этих стран составила 84,9% от общего числа запущенных спутников.

Спутники связи запускали: США — 134, Китай — 20, Испания — 8, Греция — 4, Германия и Тайвань — по 2.

Больше всего спутников ДЗЗ запустили США — 36. Далее следуют: Италия и Южная Корея — по 8, Уругвай (Satellogic) — 4 и Нидерланды — 3. На долю остальных стран приходится 14 спутников.

Заголовок: SpaceX’s Anthropic deal has a catch, and Elon Musk just addressed it
Полный текст:
Elon Musk says SpaceX's Anthropic compute deal cuts both ways after Chamath floats higher prices.

Elon Musk pushed back on Sunday against the idea that SpaceX’s compute contract with Anthropic is a one way bet, after venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya argued the company could use a termination clause to charge the AI lab far more.

“It works both ways, of course. If compute becomes plentiful and cheap, SpaceX revenue will drop. No crying in the casino for either party,” Musk wrote on X Sunday evening, replying to a clip of Palihapitiya’s comments shared by AI commentator Rohan Paul.

On the All-In podcast released Sunday, Palihapitiya said either side can walk away from the agreement on 90 days’ notice. If data center supply tightens, he argued, SpaceX could exercise that option and bring the contract back at two to three times the current price, and Anthropic would have little choice but to accept. He called it “the kingmaking move,” according to BigGo Finance .

The clause itself is not new. SpaceX disclosed in its IPO filings in May that Anthropic would pay $1.25 billion per month for dedicated capacity at its Colossus clusters through May 2029, nearly $45 billion in total, with both companies able to terminate on 90 days’ notice, as Teslarati reported at the time . SpaceX’s later compute deals with Google and Reflection AI carry similar exit terms .

What has changed is the political backdrop. Palihapitiya’s thesis rests on incoming Democratic governors pulling tax incentives for data centers and slowing new construction. In Texas, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a moratorium on new data center approvals, and Deutsche Bank analysts warned last week that SpaceX’s Texas compute capacity could face delays. SpaceX and Tesla shares both fell after the midterm results .

A slowdown would favor companies that already own capacity. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and has been renting data centers to outside AI labs before the space is needed for Grok. At the Baron Investment Conference on Friday, Musk said SpaceX was “getting 50 billion a year for 35 billion dollar investments” and that it can bring a data center online in eight or nine months, compared to two and a half years for competitors. He also said SpaceX is tracking toward an annualized revenue rate above $100 billion in December, with a “best guess” of $500 billion by December 2027.

Musk’s reply points to the other side of the clause. Anthropic has signed large compute agreements with Amazon, Google and Microsoft, and if that capacity comes online faster than new construction slows, the AI lab would have its own leverage to renegotiate or leave. Musk has called Anthropic “obviously currently the leader in AI,” and it remains one of SpaceX’s largest compute customers.

SpaceX shares rose more than 2 percent in overnight trading late Sunday after closing Friday at $134.27, according to Stocktwits .

Заголовок: RFA Confirms Inaugural RFA ONE Launch Has Slipped to 2027
Полный текст:
Credit: RFA

German launch company Rocket Factory Augsburg (RFA) has confirmed that it is now targeting 2027 for the inaugural flight of its RFA ONE rocket from a Scottish launch facility.

The revised target for the rocket’s inaugural flight was announced in a post published on the company’s LinkedIn page on 3 November. The post detailed a visit from Walther Pelzer, Director General of the German Space Agency at DLR.

“We discussed what it takes to turn RFA into a global launch service provider,” the 3 November post explained. “In doing so, we received invaluable input, along with a clear expectation for 2027, one we fully share: the successful first flight of RFA ONE, the objective we’re now rallying behind on our #RoadtoLaunch.”

The statement marks the first time RFA has publicly acknowledged a 2027 launch target since the rocket planned for the flight was destacked for an investigation. The company has not yet provided a more specific launch window.

RFA announced in March that it had delivered the first and second stages of RFA ONE to SaxaVord in Scotland, with an inaugural flight planned for the summer. The vehicle was subsequently fully integrated and stacked on the launch pad in July ahead of a planned first-stage static fire test.

On 28 July, RFA announced that it had encountered an issue during testing that required the vehicle to be de-stacked for further investigation and potential corrective action. The company did not disclose the nature of the issue at the time. The setback did, however, result in the cancellation of a five-week launch window scheduled to open on 10 August.

During an earnings call on 6 August, Marco Fuchs, CEO of RFA’s majority shareholder OHB, which holds a 65.1% stake in the launch company, stated that “the first test flight is still planned for later this year.”

Fuchs explained that the rocket had been returned to the integration hall to allow engineers to re-examine its tanks, adding that it would be re-erected on the launch pad soon. He did, however, acknowledge the possibility that additional delays could arise.

“It will be re-erected soon, but as you know, launching rockets sometimes takes a few detours,” he said.

Заголовок: ESA’s Hera Captures First Close-Up Image of Didymos Binary Asteroid System
Полный текст:
The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos binary asteroid system, providing a new view of the larger asteroid that NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test mission targeted for its 2022 planetary defense experiment.

[Дополнительно: Astronomy Now]
The European Space Agency (ESA)’s Hera spacecraft has returned its first close-up view of the Didymos asteroid system, setting the stage for a major reveal on 25 November, when detailed images of both asteroids are set to be released. The observations mark the beginning of an ‘asteroid autopsy’ to examine what NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) impact really did to the asteroid moon Dimorphos in 2022. Much of Dimorphos is in shadow, while Didymos is clearly visible. The newly released image, taken by Hera’s monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera from 60 km away, shows the 780 metre-wide parent asteroid Didymos clearly, while much of the 151 metre-wide Dimorphos is concealed in shadow. The image does, however, reveal a previously unseen hemisphere of Didymos, with boulders, craters and what may be grooves or ridges across its surface. “The first thing we said was wow!” said Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel of CNRS and the Observatoire de la Côte d’Azur, in a press statement from ESA . “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.”

Заголовок: Бионическое зрение учится подстраиваться под мозг
Полный текст:
Бионическое зрение учится подстраиваться под мозг

Визуальные протезы задуманы так, чтобы обойти повреждённые глаза и зрительный нерв. Электроды стимулируют напрямую зрительную кору, и человек видит фосфены — вспышки и пятна света. Из таких вспышек в перспективе и хотят складывать изображение для людей, потерявших зрение из-за травм, неврологических или наследственных болезней.

Загвоздка в том, что мозг устроен сложнее экрана. Как объясняет один из авторов новой работы, инженерам естественно считать фосфены пикселями: чем больше электродов, тем полнее картинка. На деле электроды влияют друг на друга, ответы нейронов колеблются, и то, что подают в мозг, вовсе не обязательно совпадает с тем, что человек видит.

Проверить, сможет ли ИИ разобраться в этой путанице, взялась команда учёных. Участник был один — 27-летний мужчина, потерявший зрение после черепно-мозговой травмы. В больнице в Испании ему временно установили в зрительную кору имплант с 96 электродами. Имплант умел и стимулировать нейроны, и записывать их ответ, а сам участник описывал каждую вспышку: яркость, размер, форму и цвет.

На этих данных обучили глубокую нейросеть предсказывать, как мозг отреагирует на разные узоры стимуляции. Модель учитывала и фоновую активность мозга перед каждой пробой: состояние нейронов постоянно меняется, и это влияет на результат.

Узоры, подобранные ИИ, вызывали нужный ответ нейронов точнее, чем другие подходы, и требовали меньше тока. Ещё одна находка: записанная активность мозга предсказывала, что увидит человек, лучше, чем сами параметры электрической стимуляции. Получается, главным ориентиром для настройки должна служить реакция мозга.

Из этого авторы делают главный вывод. Фиксированный рецепт стимуляции не годится: протез должен изучать конкретный мозг и постоянно подстраиваться под его реакции.

Переоценивать результат при этом не стоит. Это ранняя проверка концепции на одном человеке и с временным имплантом. До клинических устройств подходу предстоит ещё много проверок.

Заголовок: Tenth Long March 12 Adds to GuoWang Constellation [Long March 12 Y11]
Полный текст:
Another nine connectivity satellites are in Earth orbit after launching from Wenchang.

The Long March 12 Y11 vehicle departing from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site on November 8th/9th 2026. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

Out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Sites’ Commercial Launch Pad 2, a Long March 12 lifted off at 04:24 am on November 9th (20:24 pm Universal Coordinated Time on November 8th) heading for low Earth orbit to deliver more connectivity satellites.

The connectivity satellites being launched belonged to GuoWang, being its twenty-ninth group , and were nine in number. Those were produced by the China Academy of Space Technology . After their deployment, 240 of them are in space, functioning in and heading up to operational orbits.

GuoWang satellites launched atop of the Long March 12 and the Long March 8A use the mega-constellations’ small satellite platform , weighing about 695 kilograms each. A large satellite platform, around thirty percent bigger and weighing up to 1,000 kilograms, is deployed via the Long March 5B and Long March 6A. Both platforms utilize electric propulsion systems to maneuver in orbit, powered by two solar panels.

The GuoWang (国网) constellation is operated by China Satellite Network Group (中国卫星网络集团有限公司), a state-owned enterprise and wholly backed by the Chinese government . China Satellite Network Group plans to provide worldwide internet connectivity services through the constellation. At present, domestic usage trials and agreements are taking place ahead of a general rollout starting in China.

The China Aerospace Science and Technology Commercial Launch Vehicle Group’s patch for the Long March 12 Y11 launch mission on November 8th/9th 2026. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

With its mission today, the Long March 12 has completed its tenth so far, coming almost two years after its debut flight in November 2024. Additionally, the vehicle has flown for the fourth time in four months, following prior deployments for GuoWang in August , September , and October . Another launch may follow before this month concludes, depending on hardware and payload readiness.

Domestic state-owned launch sales firm the China Aerospace Science and Technology Commercial Launch Vehicle Group Co Ltd (中国航天科技集团商业火箭有限公司) 1 stated after the mission that the Long March 12 has been flying at a ‘high density’ rate since August and will continue to do so. One of the vehicle’s last missions this year could happen around mid-December before efforts shift towards 2027.

In its post-launch statement, the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology , who manufactur and prepare the Long March 12 for flight, and the Commercial Launch Vehicle Group shared that their teams have continued to optimize pre-flight processing and preparation efforts. That enables the launch vehicle to fly within three days of being brought to the pad, and has shortened its launch day processes to nine hours. Efforts to ensure quality were also noted as being strictly adhered to.

This mission was the 10th launch of a Long March 12 vehicle, the 12th launch of the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology-supported Long March 12 series, the 282nd Long March vehicle from the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology, and the 676th launch of the Long March launch vehicle series. This was also the 80th launch from China in 2026.

Liftoff video via 解放军报 on Weibo, 海南商发 on WeChat.

Launch livestreams via ThatSpaceDogeGuy and International Rocket Launches on YouTube.

Check out the previous Long March 12 launch

What is the Long March 12?

This section is for those less familiar with China’s Long March series of launch vehicles.

The Long March 12 is a two-stage launch vehicle from the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology. The first-stage of the launch vehicle burns rocket-grade kerosene and liquid oxygen, while the second-stage uses a mixture called ‘GN-1 (高能-1)’ to boost engine performance.

The payload capacity of the launch vehicle is currently as follows:

•

12,000 kilograms to a low Earth orbit

•

6,000 kilograms to a 700-kilometer sun-synchronous orbit

The Long March 12 Y11 vehicle stood at Commercial Launch Pad 2 on the afternoon ahead of its mission. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

Four YF-100K engines power the first stage, generating a combined thrust of 510 tons while burning liquid oxygen and rocket-grade kerosene. Two YF-115 engines power the second stage, generating 36 tons of thrust while also burning liquid oxygen and rocket-grade kerosene.

On the launchpad, the rocket stands at 62.6 meters in height, while having a first and second stage diameter of 3.8 meters. Fully fuelled the Long March 12 is believed to weigh 433,000 kilograms. The fairing of the Long March 12 is also believed to have options for either a 3.8, 4.2, or 5.2-meter diameter, depending on the needs of the mission.

Currently, the Long March 12 has only flown from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, on the east coast of Hainan province.

Заголовок: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
Полный текст:
Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.

Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

The missing electrons

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

Speaking of that work, detailed again via ‘Tiangong TV’ , the three taikonauts participated in brain function research on how their minds adapt after prolonged periods in microgravity, supported the continued operation of physics experiments, and kept the orbiting laboratory in top shape. They also took care of their own physical and mental health, as that will determine who is selected for the yearlong stay in the coming days.

Attached below is a translated transcript of the newest episode:

Experiments continue to be conducted aboard the country’s space laboratory. The Shenzhou-23 crew is hard at work on their orbital duties.

Research-related experiments involving in-orbit electroencephalography testing are proceeding smoothly. Using electroencephalography data-acquisition equipment, the three taikonauts carried out a series of experimental tests, including brain-network-atlas monitoring, visual-motor processing, and behavioral responses to lighting. Ground-based researchers will conduct follow-up studies based on the downlink data.

Additionally, the crew employed near-infrared functional brain imaging equipment to perform experiments focused on identifying characteristics of brain activity in space. The data collected will help researchers conduct in-depth studies on topics such as the impact of long-term spaceflight environments on taikonauts’ brain functional networks.

The three taikonauts conducted in-orbit experiments focused on tactile perception, specifically testing mass perception and arm vibration. This project aims to investigate how taikonauts' tactile sensory capabilities evolve during spaceflight. In addition, the crew used specialized equipment and experimental software to conduct force-control tests. The data collected will be used to study the patterns of change in taikonauts’ fine motor control and the mechanisms of adaptive learning during long-duration spaceflight.

In accordance with the experiment schedule for the field of microgravity physics, the crew completed tasks such as cleaning samples from the container-free experiment chamber, replacing experimental samples, performing maintenance on the electrodes of the gimbal mechanism, and cleaning the window cover lenses. They also inspected and maintained two system experiment cabinets.

Last week, the Shenzhou-23 crew completed scheduled inspections and tests of their intravehicular pressure suits 5 and conducted in-orbit emergency survival training. The crew diligently attended to the maintenance of the space station complex, carrying out tasks such as measuring cabin temperature and air flow, and performing thorough cleaning to ensure a tidy and habitable in-orbit environment.

In-orbit health monitoring continues. Over the past week, the three taikonauts underwent comprehensive visual function assessments, intraocular pressure measurements, and eye examinations. They also performed ultrasound examinations of the neck and arm vessels and measured their body mass using a microgravity scale, all to track physiological changes in a microgravity environment. Furthermore, the crew has been actively engaged in in-orbit exercise, maintaining a sound physical and mental state to ensure the efficient progress of their mission.

Заголовок: NASA’s Moon Base plan gains a PROMISE
Полный текст:
As part of a wide-ranging update, NASA has booked PROMISE a ride to the lunar south pole. Alongside the nuclear-powered rover, miniCAST will test the utilities needed to keep Moon Base assets working.

The update at Kennedy Space Center’s MAX POWER aerospace expo also introduced six launch and orbital transportation task orders and eight providers eligible for the next generation of Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) deliveries.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman joined Moon Base Program Manager Carlos García-Galán, science chief Nicky Fox, and Dayna Ise, acting director of the program’s Utility and Infrastructure Office, to outline the next steps toward a sustained lunar outpost.

Building on the robotic campaign outlined earlier this year , NASA is moving from individual missions toward an interconnected network of transportation, prospecting, power, and communications capabilities.

Isaacman said NASA is “putting our engineers and technicians alongside theirs, whether they like it or not” to get industry hardware ready for flight. The agency is deploying its workforce across the campaign rather than waiting for commercial partners to deliver finished systems.

PROMISE gets its ride

PROMISE, the Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration, will fly on Blue Origin’s Blue Moon Mark 1 serial number five. The mission is targeting late 2028, with an 18-month prime mission near the lunar south pole.

PROMISE rover configuration shown during NASA’s Moon Base update. Credit: NASA

The starting point is Curiosity’s Earth-bound vehicle system test bed. JPL calls that rover MAGGIE , short for Mars Automated Giant Gizmo for Integrated Engineering, which has supported terrain-driving and drilling tests before commands were sent to Mars.

However, this is not simply MAGGIE with a new destination. NASA’s mission description identifies its electronics, body structure, and mobility system as the foundation, supplemented by flight spares and test-bed components from both Curiosity and Perseverance.

Curiosity’s selfie on Mars during the 2018 dust storm. PROMISE builds on the rover’s Earth-bound twin. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS

Fox said a review concluded Curiosity could continue with low risk. Other ground hardware remains available, including the lightweight Scarecrow mobility test bed, while the team is considering mounting Curiosity’s test-bed arm on a hexapod.

A flight-spare multi-mission radioisotope thermoelectric generator will provide power and heat, allowing PROMISE to survive darkness and investigate permanently shadowed terrain without relying on sunlight.

Panelists described using existing fuel processed for Cassini, with its reduced heat output still suitable for PROMISE.

“And that allows us to survive the night and to probe permanently shadowed regions near the South Pole using technologies that we’ve literally learned with our Mars rovers,” Fox said.

The payload includes copies of VIPER’s TRIDENT drill, MSOLO mass spectrometer, Near-Infrared Volatiles Spectrometer System, and Neutron Spectrometer System. The drill will sample down to one meter, supporting comparisons between different south polar locations explored by the two rovers.

Engineers work on lunar rover drill hardware in a NASA clean room. Credit: NASA

Other instruments include the LAFORGE infrared radiometer, Radiation Assessment Detector, laser retroreflector, and Lunar Dashcam. Computing and autonomy demonstrations will test onboard terrain mapping and navigation in darkness, while wheel interactions will reveal the regolith’s mechanical properties.

VIPER itself remains part of that campaign. NASA canceled the project in July 2024 , citing cost and schedule growth, but selected Blue Origin in September 2025 for a potential delivery on the second Mark 1, targeting late 2027. The delivery option was conditional on earlier work and the first Mark 1 flight.

“This was a project enabled by the fact that we saw the hardware in the garage,” García-Galán said. He estimated PROMISE would cost below $400 million, including surface delivery. NASA separately announced a $94 million base award to Blue Origin, with a further $140 million performance-based option.

The delivery sequence still depends on Mark 1 proving itself. Following Endurance’s environmental testing , NASA’s August update reported the first lander fully assembled, with communications checkouts completed and cryogenic propellant-loading tests ahead.

miniCAST starts connecting the surface

The Mini-Communications and Solar Tower, or miniCAST, combines services that isolated lunar payloads cannot provide for one another: power generation, storage, wireless charging, and communications. Marshall Space Flight Center will integrate and test the industry-supplied components.

Illustration of a lunar solar tower network shown during NASA’s Moon Base update. Credit: NASA

NASA selected Honeybee Robotics for energy storage, Redwire for power generation, and Yank Technologies for wireless power transfer . Ise described rovers using tower communications to navigate toward a power source and recharge through an induction plate on the surface.

Honeybee’s background includes LUNARSABER , a separate deployable-tower concept combining solar power, storage, communications, and navigation. Its proposed mast exceeds 100 meters, but that is not a stated miniCAST specification.

Redwire has developed Roll-Out Solar Arrays for lunar vertical-array applications , building on flight heritage from the International Space Station and DART. Yank’s recent NASA-funded wireless-power work targets kilowatt-class transfer without exposed electrical contacts vulnerable to regolith contamination.

A rover approaches surface power infrastructure in a miniCAST concept. Credit: NASA

Those projects establish relevant experience, not confirmation of miniCAST’s final hardware configuration. NASA says the initial awards cover components, with a separate solicitation for fully integrated power systems anticipated in early 2027.

“We have to do all that with almost no human interaction, right?” Ise said of recreating terrestrial infrastructure on the Moon, highlighting the dependence on automation and robotics.

Other things announced

The six Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) task orders total approximately $1.3 billion.

Заголовок: China's Mega-Constellations Mega-Article
Полный текст:
Tracking China's six mega-constellation efforts in low Earth orbit.

What is believed to be the first satellite of the Shanghai-backed Qianfan constellation in December 2023 . | Image: Genesat

This page will be continuously updated as China launches satellites for the Qianfan, GuoWang, Honghu-3, Geely Future Mobility, Tianqi, and Three-Body Computing constellations . These six constellations are expected to have a combined satellite count of 50,730 once fully deployed.

I will share when this page is updated on my Twitter (officially “X”) and Bluesky account, where you can also pester me to update it. You can jump to each constellation with the following hyperlinks:

Qianfan

The Qianfan (千帆) mega-constellation, formerly called G60 Starlink, is operated by Shanghai Spacesail Technologies Co Ltd (上海垣信卫星科技有限公司), which is partly backed by the municipal government of Shanghai. Qianfan literally means ‘Thousand Sails’ in English, which is why some media refer to it as such.

This constellation may have up to 15,000 satellites in orbit by 2030 . As of December 2025 , the deployment aims of the constellation should have 324 satellites launched in 2026, 324 in 2027, and 4,000 in 2028 and 2029, followed by 5,000 in 2030.

Each first-generation Qianfan satellite weighs 267 kilograms and can utilize 100 gigabits of intersatellite throughput to provide 20 megabits in download speed and 5 megabits of upload speed for a cell phone. For maneuvering in orbit , each satellite has an electric hall-effect thruster burning krypton to generate 20 millinewtons of thrust, with a specific impulse of 1,385 seconds.

Future second-generation satellites will weigh between 400 and 500 kilograms, while third-generation satellites will be around 1,500 kilograms. Second-generation satellites will provide maritime services along with the constellations’ terrestrial services, and third-generation satellites will improve overall services.

So far, 274 satellites have been launched for this constellation. A visualization of active satellites in orbit is available here .

2024

August 6th - 1st Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

On August 6th the first batch of satellites for Qianfan was sent into a polar orbit atop of a Long March 6A. This launch occurred from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

After launch 18 satellites were deployed from the Long March 6A Y21 ’s second-stage, at an altitude of approximately 800 kilometers .

October 15th - 2nd Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

A little over two months later , the second batch of Qianfan satellites were sent into polar orbit atop of a Long March 6A, also from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

Following launch 18 satellites were deployed from the Long March 6A Y20’s second-stage, likely at a similar altitude to the first batch.

December 5th - 3rd Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Following another two-month gap, the third batch of Qianfan satellites were delivered to polar orbit atop of a Long March 6A, once again flying from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

After launch 18 satellites were deployed from the Long March 6A Y22’s second-stage.

2025

January 23rd - 4th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Qianfan began deployment in 2025 with its fourth batch , officially group six, being sent to polar orbit by a Long March 6A, flying from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

After launch 18 satellites were released from the Long March 6A Y6’s second-stage.

March 11th - 5th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

For its first mission atop of the Long March 8 , Qianfan’s second launch of 2025 saw the deployment of group five, for the fifth batch of satellites. With the mission flying from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

After launch 18 satellites were released from the Long March 8' Y6’s second-stage.

October 17th - 6th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Following a seven-month pause, Qianfan’s Polar Group 18 was launched atop a Long March 6A from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, placing eighteen satellites into orbit. This was the constellation’s sixth launch.

2026

April 7th - 7th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Off of Commercial Launch Pad 1 at the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, Qianfan’s seventh overall group of satellites was deployed into a near-polar orbit by a Long March 8, with eighteen satellites onboard.

May 12th - 8th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

From the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, a Long March 6A delivered Qianfan’s Polar Group 09 into a near-polar orbit, with eighteen satellites released. This was the constellation’s eighth group overall.

May 17th - 9th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

A Long March 8 departed from Commercial Launch Pad 1 at the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site to deliver Qianfan’s ninth overall group into sun-synchronous orbit, with eighteen satellites being released.

June 1st - 10th Qianfan Group (2 satellites)

The first Long March 12B carried the tenth overall group of Qianfan satellites, deploying two, for the constellation’s first launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center into a polar orbit.

June 4th - 11th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Eighteen more Qianfan satellites were added to polar orbit, with the launch of its eleventh overall group via a Long March 6A from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

June 5th - 12th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Another Long March 8 flew from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site to bring eighteen Qianfan satellites into polar orbit, for its twelfth overall group. Some maritime support services were said to have been enabled after deployment.

July 4th - 13th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

Out of the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, a Long March 6A added eighteen more Qianfan satellites into a near-polar orbit, for its thirteenth launch to date.

July 5th - 14th Qianfan Group (20 satellites)

A much upgraded Long March 8A flew from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site to bring twenty more Qianfan satellites, for the fourteenth group to date, into a polar orbit.

September 15th - 15th Qianfan Group (10 satellites)

LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E, flying out of the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, became the first commercially developed launch vehicle to launch a group of Qianfan satellites, ten of them, into polar orbit, for the constellation’s fifteenth deployment.

September 15th - 16th Qianfan Group (8 satellites)

For the first sea-launch of Qianfan satellites, Orienspace’s Gravity-1 deployed eight operational satellites into a polar orbit from the East China Sea, for the sixteenth deployment overall.

November 3rd - 17th Qianfan Group (18 satellites)

CAS Space’s Kinetica-2 delivered eighteen Qianfan satellites into a polar orbit, from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, for its seventeenth deployment, becoming the largest group delivered by a commercial sector launch vehicle.

Qianfan Test Satellites

Prior to the beginning of deployments in 2024, Shanghai Spacesail Technologies Co Ltd had a few test satellites launched through its backing of German enterprise KLEO connect. Others have been launched after the start of main deployments.

So far, 6 test satellites have been launched.

2019

November 17th - KL-Alpha Duo

Via ExPace’s Kuaizhou-1A out of the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, two test satellites dubbed KL-Alpha-A and KL-Alpha-B were placed into low Earth orbit for testing Ka-band coordination. The duo had their manufacturing contracted to the Innovation Academy for Microsatellites, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院微小卫星创新研究院).

2021

August 4th - KL-Beta Duo

Two more test satellites , called KL-Beta-A and KL-Beta-B, were delivered to low Earth orbit by a Long March 6 from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center for testing laser-interconnect coordination as well as electric propulsion. Their manufacturing was also contracted to the Innovation Academy for Microsatellites, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院微小卫星创新研究院).

2026

June 9th - Qianfan Direct-To-Cell-01 Satellite

LandSpace’s Zhuque-2E carried the Innovation Academy for Microsatellites, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院微小卫星创新研究院) made ‘ Qianfan Direct-To-Cell-01 Satellite (千帆DTC01星) ’ into low Earth orbit from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The satellite will demonstrate systems and services needed for providing connectivity to handheld mobile devices.

September 15th - Enhanced Ultra High Throughput test satellite

Orienspace’s Gravity-1 carried the ‘ Enhanced Ultra High Throughput test satellite (增强型超高传输技术试验星) ’ into a polar orbit to demonstrate new systems, likely for the second-generation of the constellation. It was made by the Innovation Academy for Microsatellites, Chinese Academy of Sciences (中国科学院微小卫星创新研究院).

GuoWang

The GuoWang (国网) 1 mega-constellation, commonly called Weixing Hulianwang Digui (卫星互联网低轨) 2 by Chinese-language media and sometimes known as Xingwang (星网) 3 , is operated by China Satellite Network Group (中国卫星网络集团有限公司), and is backed by the Chinese government .

This constellation may have up to 13,000 satellites in orbit once fully deployed. As of December 2025 , the deployment aims of the constellation should have 310 satellites launched in 2026, 900 in 2027, and 3,600 in 2028, 2029, and 2030.

So far, 240 satellites have been launched for this constellation. A visualization of active satellites in orbit is available here .

2024

December 16th - GuoWang Group 01 (10 satellites)

The first group of GuoWang satellites entered a polar orbit on December 16th after being launched on a Long March 5B, with a Yuanzheng-2 upper-stage , from the Wenchang Space Launch Site.

After maneuvers with the Yuangzheng-2 upper-stage, the 10 satellites were tracked in a roughly 1,090-kilometer by 1,110-kilometer orbit .

2025

February 11th - GuoWang Group 02 (9 satellites)

A second group of GuoWang satellites was delivered into low Earth orbit by the first Long March 8A, from the Wenchang Space Launch Site. This launch had nine satellites were onboard, which were deployed into a roughly 871 by 860 kilometer orbit.

April 29th - GuoWang Group 03 (10 satellites)

The third group of satellites for GuoWang were delivered to a polar orbit on April 29th via a Long March 5B with a Yuanzheng-2 upper-stage. This launch had ten satellites deployed once in orbit.

June 6th - GuoWang Group 04 (5 satellites)

A Long March 6A launched the fourth group of GuoWang satellites to polar orbit from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, becoming the first time GuoWang satellites were delivered to orbit from the site. Five satellites are believed to have been onboard.

July 27th - GuoWang Group 05 (5 satellites)

The fifth batch of GuoWang satellites were sent to polar orbit atop of a Long March 6A, flying from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center. Five satellites are believed to have been onboard.

July 30th - GuoWang Group 06 (9 satellites)

A Long March 8A delivered the sixth group of GuoWang satellites to low Earth orbit, flying out of the Wenchang Space Launch Site. Nine satellites were believed to have been onboard.

August 4th - GuoWang Group 07 (9 satellites)

The seventh batch of GuoWang satellites headed to low Earth orbit atop of a Long March 12. Another nine satellites were believed to have been onboard.

August 13th - GuoWang Group 08 (10 satellites)

Ten more GuoWang satellites, for the constellation’s eighth batch, headed to a polar orbit atop of a Long March 5B flying out of the Wenchang Space Launch Site, with a Yuanzheng-2 upper-stage bringing the satellites toward their intended orbit.

August 17th - GuoWang Group 09 (5 satellites)

Via a Long March 6A from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, five satellites were sent into orbit for GuoWang’s ninth group.

August 25th - GuoWang Group 10 (9 satellites)

GuoWang’s tenth batch of satellites, likely with nine onboard, was delivered to low Earth orbit by a Long March 8A flying out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

September 27th - GuoWang Group 11 (5 satellites)

Through another Long March 6A launch from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, five more satellites for the GuoWang constellation were delivered to low Earth orbit.

October 16th - GuoWang Group 12 (9 satellites)

A Long March 8A delivered nine satellites for the GuoWang constellation into low Earth orbit from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site for the twelfth group overall.

November 10th - GuoWang Group 13 (9 satellites)

Via a Long March 12 flying out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, nine satellites for GuoWang were sent into low Earth orbit for the thirteenth group overall.

December 6th - GuoWang Group 14 (9 satellites)

A Long March 8A carried nine satellites for GuoWang into low Earth orbit from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site for the fourteenth group overall.

December 8th - GuoWang Group 15 (5 satellites)

Five GuoWang spacecraft were added to the mega-constellation via a Long March 6A mission to polar orbit from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center.

December 12th - GuoWang Group 16 (9 satellites)

GuoWang’s sixteenth group of satellites, nine onboard, was delivered to low Earth orbit by a Long March 12 launching from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

December 26th - GuoWang Group 17 (9 satellites)

For GuoWang’s last launch of 2025, the seventeenth group of satellites were launched atop of a Long March 8A from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

2026

January 13th - GuoWang Group 18 (9 satellites)

Starting GuoWang deployments in 2026, a Long March 8A flew from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site while carrying nine satellites for the constellation’s eighteenth group.

January 19th - GuoWang Group 19 (9 satellites)

A Long March 12 supported the deployment of GuoWang’s nineteenth group, with nine satellites being placed into low Earth orbit following a mission from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

March 12th - GuoWang Group 20 (9 satellites)

Out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, a Long March 8A carried nine GuoWang satellites into low Earth orbit as part of the mega-constellation’s twentieth group.

April 9th - GuoWang Group 21 (5 satellites)

From the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center, another five GuoWang spacecraft were placed into orbit by a Long March 6A for the twenty-first deployment of the mega-constellation.

June 17th - GuoWang Group 22 (9 satellites)

The Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site saw another nine GuoWang satellites added to low Earth orbit for its twenty-second deployment , via a Long March 12.

August 4th - GuoWang Group 23 (9 satellites)

A Long March 8A brought the twenty-third set of GuoWang satellites into low Earth orbit from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, delivering nine satellites.

August 16th - GuoWang Group 24 (9 satellites)

A Long March 12 flew into low Earth orbit to bring the twenty-fourth group of GuoWang satellites to space, out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

September 17th - GuoWang Group 25 (9 satellites)

Nine GuoWang satellites were added to low Earth orbit, for the twenty-fifth group, by a Long March 12 flying from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

September 23rd - GuoWang Group 26 (9 satellites)

Another Long March 8A flying from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site delivered nine GuoWang satellites into low Earth orbit, for its twenty-sixth group deployed.

October 10th - GuoWang Group 27 (9 satellites)

From the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site, a Long March 12 launched into low Earth orbit to deploy nine GuoWang satellites , for the twenty-seventh group.

October 25th - GuoWang Group 28 (9 satellites)

A Long March 8A brought nine GuoWang satellites into low Earth orbit after flying from the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site for the constellation’s twenty-eighth group.

November 9th - GuoWang Group 29 (9 satellites)

For its tenth flight, the Long March 12 deployed GuoWang’s twenty-ninth group with nine satellites into low Earth orbit out of the Wenchang Commercial Space Launch Site.

GuoWang GEO Segment

While not explicitly part of the low Earth orbit constellation (and not counted in the total count), GuoWang is believed to be receiving support from a few satellites, dubbed WHG or Weixing Hulianwang Gaogui (卫星互联网高轨), also known as internet high-orbit satellite in English, in geostationary space to bridge gaps in coverage or provide low-bandwidth coverage in select areas. Based on the satellite platform, likely the China Academy of Space Technology’s Dongfanghong-4 , up to 200 Gigabits per second of throughput could be available.

Currently, 3 satellites make up the geostationary support segment, being placed at: 33.6 degrees East over central Africa, 77.2 degrees West over northern South America, and 153.2 degrees East just above Papua New Guinea.

2024

February 29th - WHG-01 (33.6 degrees East)

The first WHG satellite was delivered to a geostationary transfer orbit from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center by a Long March 3B/E on February 29th.

August 1st - WHG-02 (77.2 degrees West)

A second WHG satellite was launched into a geostationary transfer orbit by a Long March 3B/E rocket a few months later, on August 1st from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center.

October 10th - WHG-03 (153.2 degrees East)

The third WHG-designated satellite blasted off from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center on October 10th atop of a Long March 3B/E heading for a geostationary transfer orbit.

GuoWang Test Satellites

While yet to be officially stated as test satellites for the GuoWang constellation (also not counted in the total count), over a dozen have been launched under a similar designation and with the same spacecraft developers as GuoWang. Test satellite designations have been designated Digui Tongxin Weixing (低轨通信卫星), Low-orbit Communication Satellites in English, and Weixing Hulianwang Jishu Shiyan (卫星互联网技术试验卫星), literally Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellite.

So far, 33 test satellites appear to have been launched.

2021

2022

Another three Low-orbit Communication Satellites were launched by a Long March 2C with a Yuanzheng-1S upper-stage on May 20th from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center to further constellation technology and service trials.

2023

July 9th - Two Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites

A Long March 2C with a Yuanzheng-1S upper-stage flew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center carrying two Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites into low Earth orbit on July 9th.

November 23rd - Three Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites

Three Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites were launched on November 23rd from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center via a Long March 2D with a Yaunzheng-3 upper-stage heading into low Earth orbit.

A single Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellite was sent into polar orbit by a Jielong-3 off of a floating platform near Yangjiang (阳江市), Guangdong Province (广东), on December 5th.

December 30th - Three Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites

2024

2025

September 16th - Four Satellite Internet Technology Experimental Satellites

2026

Honghu-3

The Honghu-3 (鸿鹄-3) mega-constellation is a joint venture between LandSpace , a launch company, and Hongqing Technology, a satellite manufacturer. LandSpace holds a 48% stake in Hongqing Technology. This constellation may have up to 10,000 satellites in orbit once fully deployed.

Pending first launch.

Geely Future Mobility Constellation

The Geely Future Mobility Constellation is backed by Chinese automaker Geely, doing business as Zhejiang Geely Holding Group (浙江吉利控股集团有限公司), with its wholly-owned subsidiary Geespace developing spacecraft and managing the constellation. This constellation will provide communication, connectivity, and positioning services. Once phases two and three of satellite deployment is completed, services will be expanded to include connectivity to mobile phones and satellite internet.

Nine satellites for the Geely Future Mobility Constellation.

Geespace plans to deploy the mega-constellation in three phases . Phase one (2022-2025) will have 72 satellites sent into orbit, phase two will add an additional 264 satellites, and phase three will add another 5,676 satellites. In total, 6,012 satellites are planned to be deployed.

So far, 64 satellites have been launched for this constellation.

Tianqi

Four Tianqi satellites being prepared for launch inside Ceres-1S Y4’s fairing.

Guodian Gaoke started deploying the constellation with many 50-kilogram satellites via many smaller launch vehicles. Over the coming years, 1,132 satellites of roughly 360 kilograms will be launched to provide mobile direct-to-device services.

So far, 41 satellites have been launched for this constellation.

Three-Body Computing Constellation

The Three-Body Computing Constellation is a computing constellation that aims to integrate space and ground computing into a single AI-enabled infrastructure, allowing for the processing of satellite data in space. ADA Space, also known as Chengdu Guoxing Aerospace Technology Co Ltd (成都国星航天科技有限公司) and shortened to Guoxing Aerospace, and Zhejiang Lab (之江实验室) are developing the constellation.

Up to 2,800 satellites are planned to be part of the constellation. To launch that many satellites, the constellation’s developers are utilizing two different designs. One satellite design, called ‘type one’, is stackable, allowing numerous spacecraft of the same design to be placed on top of each other. The other design, dubbed ‘type two’, is a more conventional CubeSat, allowing it to be a secondary payload for other missions with extra payload capacity left.

So far, 20 satellites have been launched for this constellation.

Three-Body Test Satellites

For improvements to the constellation and its systems, ADA Space and Zhejiang Lab have launched testing satellites to prove new hardware ahead of their incorporation on the main constellation. Those tests can involve one or both of the enterprises behind the constellation.

So far, 1 test satellites appear to have been launched.

2026

Zhejiang Lab launched a technology testing satellite, designated Jitian-A-04 (吉天星A-04星), via Kinetica-1 from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center to prove new GPUs from MetaX Integrated Circuits Shanghai Co Ltd (沐曦集成电路(上海)有限公司) ahead of their operational use on-orbit.

What is a mega-constellation?

A mega-constellation of satellites has no firm definition but is normally comprised of thousands of satellites when referred to in media. No solid number is stated for the beginning of mega-constellations. For the purposes of this article, I believe a mega-constellation is any satellite network boasting over 1,000 spacecraft.

Satellite constellations are typically defined as:

“A satellite constellation is a group of artificial satellites working together as a system. Unlike a single satellite, a constellation can provide permanent global or near-global coverage, such that at any time everywhere on Earth at least one satellite is visible. Satellites are typically placed in sets of complementary orbital planes and connect to globally distributed ground stations. They may also use inter-satellite communication.”
- Wikipedia’s Satellite constellation page on September 27th 2024.

Заголовок: NASA announces search for new astronauts
Полный текст:
For the first time in two years, NASA is opening applications for its next astronaut class. Announcing the call at the Max Power event at the Kennedy Space Center (KSC), NASA said this will be one of its most important classes yet, with the new astronauts training for low Earth orbit (LEO), lunar surface operations and future Artemis missions.

According to NASA’s website, only 370 people have been selected as NASA astronaut candidates (ASCANs) since the original Mercury 7 were announced in 1959.

This will be the 25th astronaut class selected in that time. Applications are open until 3 December 2026, with the selection expected in late 2027.

The most recent class, NASA’s 24th, was announced in 2025 and consisted of ten new ASCANs. It also marked the first time that women outnumbered men in a NASA astronaut class.

Each new astronaut group is given a nickname by the previous class. Astronaut Class 23 named the 2025 group the “Platypi”. It is not yet known what nickname the incoming class will receive.

Members of the 24th astronaut class talk with NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during a training session. (Credit: NASA/Joel Kowsky)

One of the Platypi is Dr Anna Menon, who became the first NASA astronaut candidate to have already flown to space on a commercial mission, Polaris Dawn .

“I pinched myself when I found out that I got to join this class and get to return to the team here at NASA,” Menon said in a January 2026 interview with NSF following her selection.

According to NASA, applicants must be US citizens and hold a master’s degree in a STEM field.

They also need at least three years of related professional experience gained after completing that degree. Pilots can instead qualify with at least 1,000 hours of pilot-in-command time, with at least 850 of those hours in high-performance jet aircraft.

All applicants must also be able to pass the NASA long-duration spaceflight astronaut physical.

The master’s degree requirement can be met instead by two years of work towards a STEM doctorate, a completed medical degree, or completion of an accredited test pilot school programme.

Applications must be submitted through the listing on USAJobs.gov.

The ten new ASCANs at their public announcement. (Credit: NASA/Helen Arase Vargas)

The call for applications follows comments from Isaacman on NSF’s The Flame Trench that he is considering extending the life of the ISS beyond 2030 if a commercial replacement is not ready.

NASA will continue to send astronauts to the ISS and to future commercial stations, all of which will need crews.

NASA is also planning a base on the lunar surface, and says the new astronauts will be prepared to fly on lunar missions.

Asked what advice she would give others, especially those thinking of applying to become astronauts, Menon said it is all about following your passion.

“And I think that would be my piece of advice…pay attention to what you love and what you are good at and pursue that with a vengeance because what I have found is that when you do that, things tend to fall into place,” Menon said. “You tend to be most productive and fulfilled and able to contribute to the world around you in wherever life leads you.”

Lead image: The ten astronauts selected as part of NASA’s 24th astronaut class. (Credit: NASA/Josh Valcarcel)

Заголовок: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
Полный текст:
Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.

It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

Заголовок: Ceres-2 Returns to Launch Customer Satellites on Second Outing [Ceres-2 Y3]
Полный текст:
The larger member of Galactic Energy’s solid-propellant Ceres series has nailed its second flight into sun-synchronous orbit.

Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 Y3 vehicle soaring from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on November 6th/7th 2026. | Image: Galactic Energy

Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 blasted off from Launch Area 95 at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center for the second time ever at 07:37 am China Standard Time on November 7th (23:37 pm Universal Coordinated Time on November 6th), flying towards a sun-synchronous orbit with four customer payloads , leaving a ‘jellyfish’ effect behind itself 1 .

One of the customers was North University of China (中北大学) 2 with the creatively named North University of China Satellite-1 (中北大学一号卫星). Its satellite is planned to monitor natural mineral resources while providing early alerts for geological disasters, with additional functions making it usable as a teaching tool. Development was led by the university with support from launch firm Orienspace 3 and Beijing Maiya Technology Co Ltd (北京劢亚科技有限公司). This satellite is also a replacement for one lost in November 2025 .

For a first satellite being flown is Zhongke Xingtu Measurement and Control Technology Co Ltd (中科星图测控技术股份有限公司) with their Xingyan-01 (星眼01星), manufactured by Beijing Juntian Aerospace Technology Co Ltd (北京钧天航宇技术有限公司), who gave it the additional designation Juntian-1-06A (钧天一号06A卫星). It is a commercial space situational awareness satellite planned to track, catalogue, and monitor the activities of other spacecraft and orbital debris after its systems are verified. Part of those are powered by artificial intelligence, as is a growing trend .

Led by Laoshan Laboratory (崂山实验室) was the ‘Guanlan Experimental Satellite (观澜试验星)’, tasked with proving out new systems for all-weather, high-precision altimetry readings of global ocean surfaces using a dual-frequency, Ka and Ku bands, co-aperture antenna configuration. That antenna was worked on by the Beijing Institute of Radio Measurement (北京无线电测量研究所), with satellite systems tasked to the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology .

Alongside them was Yunyao-1-28 (云遥一号28星) from Yunyao Aerospace (云遥宇航) is a commercial meteorology satellite joining an existing constellation. That satellite is the company’s first to be deployed this year, coming after new funding in April to improve capabilities. Last year, they trusted Galactic Energy’s smaller rocket to launch seventeen satellites between January , March , and September through dedicated and shared missions.

Xingyan-01/Juntian-1-06A (top) and Yunyao-1-28 (bottom) during production in the second half of 2026 at their respective company facilities. | Image: Beijing Juntian Aerospace Technology Co Ltd / Yunyao Aerospace

In a post-launch statement , Galactic Energy shared that in the ten months since Ceres-2’s failed first flight in January, they have thoroughly investigated all launch vehicle systems to resolve the faulty nozzle issue that occurred. In addition to that, other parts of Ceres-2 were optimized and changed to prevent future failures. What parts those are was not specified.

In the leadup to today’s flight, Galactic Energy revealed that this launch would be designated the serial number ‘Y3’. A ‘Y2’ vehicle was in production around the time of the first launch, as part of an initial batch. That vehicle was skipped over in favor of ‘Y3’ after the issue from the debut launch was well understood and after the changes were made.

The state-owned Academy of Aerospace Solid Propulsion Technology (航天动力技术研究院) 4 also spoke of the launch after its success , mentioning that they produced the three solid rocket motors powering the first three stages of Ceres-2. Alongside that, it was mentioned that they would support Galactic Energy’s efforts to fly the launch vehicle regularly into the future.

Galactic Energy’s patch for the Ceres-2 Y3 mission (left) on November 6th/7th 2026 and the Shanghai Academy of Spaceflight Technology’s patch for ‘Guanlan Experimental Satellite’ (right). | Image: Galactic Energy / China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

Elsewhere this year, Galactic Energy has had a handful of other successes. Flights of the smaller Ceres-1 in January and October have seen five customer satellites brought into orbit, while the to-be-reusable Pallas-1 had an incredible debut test flight .

Today’s mission was the 2nd for the Ceres-2 launch vehicle, the 26th flight of the Ceres family of launch vehicles (Ceres-1 and Ceres-2), and Galactic Energy’s 27th orbital launch attempt. This was also the 79th launch from China in 2026.

What is Ceres-2?

This section is for those less familiar with China’s commercial launch vehicles.

Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 is a four-stage launch vehicle that burns solid fuel in the first three stages, all powered by motors from the Academy of Aerospace Solid Propulsion Technology (航天动力技术研究院), and a storable propellant in the fourth-stage. The vehicle is based upon experiences and technologies from the smaller Ceres-1.

The payload capacity of the launch vehicle is currently as follows:

•

1,600 kilograms to low Earth orbit

Заголовок: AST SpaceMobile unveils $1.3 billion engine deal with Firefly Aerospace to power new heavy-lift rocket
Полный текст:
The company behind the Bluebird direct-to-cell satellite constellation said the addition of its own heavy-lift rocket is the final piece of its plans for vertical integration.

An artist’s rendering of AST SpaceMobile’s proposed new rocket, Blacklift. Graphic: AST SpaceMobile

Texas-based companies AST SpaceMobile and Firefly Aerospace announced a $1.3 billion agreement to license a rocket engine that will power a new, heavy-lift rocket starting in 2028, if all goes to plan.

The proposed launcher is called Blacklift and AST SpaceMobile classifies it as a 20-ton rocket, which would put it in the same category of SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan.

Following the trend of SpaceX using its Falcon 9 rockets principally to launch its Starlink satellites, AST SpaceMobile will focus its launch capacity to fly its BlueBird satellites to orbit. The company said the rocket will be capable of launching five of its BlueBird satellites at a time.

“The Blacklift rocket is the springboard to significantly expand our total addressable market, providing AST SpaceMobile with regular unconstrained access to orbit and providing for most favorable owners’ economics in the industry,” said Abel Avellan, Founder, Chairman, and CEO of AST SpaceMobile. “This will accelerate our mission to build a new layer of global connectivity, extending connectivity beyond terrestrial networks and helping to bring AI-enabled services wherever people live, work and travel.”

Few details about the rocket itself were released alongside the announcement on Friday. Left unknown are things like hight, propellant tank sizes, and proposed launch site.

AST SpaceMobile also hasn’t described its plan for going from rendering to launch in the span of about two years. An analysis from Payload Space found that it historically takes about six years to go from the start of development to a successful first launch.

The company said it will host an “unveiling event” in New York City on Thursday, Nov. 12, which may fill in some of the blanks. The company also has a third quarter earnings call scheduled for Monday, Nov. 9, at 5 p.m. EST (2200 UTC) and may offer some details at that time as well.

Miranda engine firing at full power at Firefly’s Rocket Ranch in Briggs, Texas. Image: Firefly Aerospace

In it’s announcement of the deal with AST SpaceMobile, Firefly said it would be delivering 27 Miranda engines and nine vacuum-variant Vira engines “for AST SpaceMobile’s first three rockets.” That suggests that the Blacklift first stage boosters will have nine Miranda engines each and three Vira engines on the upper stage.

For comparison, the medium-lift Eclipse rocket that Firefly is developing in partnership with Northrop Grumman features seven Miranda engines and one Vira engine. Under this new agreement, Firefly is providing a license for AST SpaceMobile to manufacture engines in the future.

The $1.3 billion agreement involves $800 million upfront from AST SpaceMobile, half of which comes in cash and the other half in Class A Common Stock. It will also pay Firefly $250 million for the 36 engines and another $250 million over the course of three years for engineering services.

“This is a bold transformational deal for Firefly, for AST SpaceMobile, and for the space industry,” said Jason Kim, CEO of Firefly Aerospace. “When a company sets out to build its own rocket, the engine is the hardest, highest-stakes decision they make, and AST SpaceMobile chose to partner with Firefly for its most powerful rocket engines.

“It’s a true win-win for both companies: AST SpaceMobile gets control of its own launch schedule, and Firefly gets added funds to rapidly expand our rocket production and reinforce the supply of launch vehicles to address record demand from the industry.”

An artist’s interpretation of the launch of an Eclipse rocket, a launch vehicle being manufactured in partnership between Firefly Aerospace and Northrop Grumman. Graphic: Firefly Aerospace

Firefly said it has performed more than 175 hot fire tests of its Miranda engines, lasting more than 4,200 seconds. The Vira engine is still in development, but takes heritage from the Lightning engine, which powers the upper stages of Firefly’s Alpha rockets.

Neither engine has made its debut on an orbital flight. Firefly’s current public estimate of an inaugural launch with its Eclipse rocket is 2027.

Firefly plans to speak more about the deal with AST SpaceMobile during its third quarter earnings call, which is scheduled for Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 5 p.m. EST (2200 UTC).

Полный текст:
A Falcon 9 rocket lifts off from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Nov. 6, 2026 on the USSF-432 mission. Image: SpaceX.

SpaceX launched another batch of satellites for a clandestine U.S. Space Force program on a Falcon 9 rocket from California Friday afternoon.

Liftoff from pad 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base occurred at 4:48 p.m. PST (7:48 p.m. EST / 0048 UTC). The rocket took a south-easterly trajectory on departure from the central California coast. The flight was originally scheduled for Nov. 1 but was delayed repeatedly, first due to delays of the Starlink 15-18 launch, and then for reasons that were not disclosed.

The mission is designated USSF-432 but is also identified as R-4 in public documents. This series of ‘R’ missions began Aug. 16 with USSF-366. More launches in the sequence followed with USSF-153 (R-2) on Sept. 10 and USSF-385 (R3) on Sept. 26.

Each R launch has placed 23 satellites in orbit, according to orbital catalog entries. They are thought to be based on SpaceX’s Starshield platform, the government version of the Starlink satellite.

According to Jonathan McDowell, the respected tracker of space launches, the R satellites are part of the U.S. Space Force’s Space Based Sensing and Targeting program.

Officially, the Space Force has declined to provide any information about the missions. Neither SpaceX or the Space Force have confirmed a successful satellite deployment on the previous flights.

The Falcon 9 first stage booster, B1095, is making its eighth flight and landed on the drone ship ‘Of Course I Still Love You,’ stationed in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Baja California, Mexico. The booster’s previous flights all took place from the East Coast at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station and Kennedy Space Center. It made a cross country transfer after launching the GPS 3-8 mission in April. The bulk of recent Falcon 9 launches have taken place from Vandenberg as SpaceX focuses its attention on launching the first Starship from Florida.

Заголовок: Stoke Space evaluating expansion of Cape site for second Nova pad
Полный текст:
Stoke Space has been granted Right of Entry by Space Launch Delta 45 to property north of its existing Space Launch Complex 14 (SLC-14) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station.

The authorisation allows engineering studies, environmental assessments and site surveys needed to develop a second launch site for its Nova rocket, and is intended to support high-cadence launch and re-entry operations as Stoke works toward the larger Nova Block 2 vehicle.

Stoke’s rebuilt SLC-14 was designed for fast-turn launch and recovery operations, and the company says the northern property, in the location of LC-15, will extend that capability as both vehicles come online.

Zoomed-in view of the northern location Stoke requested for access via Max Evans/NSF

“Every launch provider strengthens the nation’s access to space,” said Col. Brian Chatman, commander of Space Launch Delta 45 and director of the Eastern Range.

“Our team here at the Eastern Range is proud to support partners bringing more launch capability to the United States, and we look forward to enabling more launches from the Space Coast.”

Brian Wemple, Stoke’s Vice President of Launch, said the milestone reflects Space Launch Delta 45’s commitment to developing Eastern Range infrastructure for fully and rapidly reusable launch.

“It’s an honor to build the future of launch on the historic ground of SLC-14, and we are excited to carry that momentum forward with this expansion.”

From Mercury pad to Nova

SLC-14 holds a prominent place in American space history.

It was the site of John Glenn’s Friendship 7 mission on 20 February 1962, the first orbital flight by a US astronaut, and later supported the crewed Mercury-Atlas launches of Scott Carpenter, Wally Schirra and Gordon Cooper before being deactivated in February 1967.

The Missile Row of old, via NASA

The pad remained largely dormant for decades and forms part of the Cape Canaveral Air Force Station National Historic Landmark district, designated in 1984.

Stoke was allocated the complex in 2023 following a competitive process , and received the property licence in 2024.

Stoke says it restored and reactivated the site in just over a year after completing environmental assessments.

The early days of Stoke’s pad work via Joe B for NSF.

Work included a Horizontal Integration Facility, launch mount, umbilical support structure, flame trench and diverter, and propellant systems.

NSF flyovers through 2025 and 2026 showed the pad progressing to a largely complete state , with the site appearing ready to receive hardware once it arrives from Stoke’s facilities in Washington state.

The company has described the rebuilt complex as purpose-built for rapid reuse, with infrastructure sized for repeated launch and recovery cycles.

Concrete from the original Mercury-era pad was crushed and reused in some areas during reconstruction, and the prominent launch tower is painted red in tribute to the early Space Coast launch towers.

See NSF’s Stoke Nova update and later Cape progress coverage for more on the rebuilt pad.

Nova Pathfinder’s path to the Cape

Nova Pathfinder is Stoke’s first orbital configuration and is currently targeted for launch around mid-2027.

The vehicle is powered by seven Zenith full-flow staged-combustion engines on the first stage and a single Andromeda hydrolox engine on the upper stage, which incorporates an actively cooled metallic heat shield.

Pathfinder is designed to demonstrate full and rapid reuse technologies while carrying customer payloads.

Nova flight hardware is produced and tested at Stoke’s Washington facilities.

Nova Pathfinder first stage on the stand at Stoke’s Moses Lake Test Site during proto-qualification testing. (Credit: Stoke Space)

Eric Berger reported that Stoke shipped its first flight booster from Washington on 4 November, bound for Cape Canaveral.

Stoke Space shipped its flight one first stage from Washington last night, and it is bound for the launch pad in Cape Canaveral. Big step toward a launch in early to mid-2027.

— Eric Berger (@SciGuySpace) November 5, 2026

Once stages arrive at SLC-14, final mating in the Horizontal Integration Facility occurs before rollout to the pad. Ahead of this first flight, a large amount of testing is expected for both the rocket and the pad systems.

The company has said Pathfinder flights in 2027 and 2028 will generate operational experience while Nova Block 2 development continues in parallel.

Block 2 and the second pad

Nova Block 2, unveiled in September 2026 , is a larger configuration targeting 15 tonnes to low Earth orbit in a fully reusable mode.

It will use 14 Zenith engines on the first stage and an upper stage powered by the more powerful Andromeda Block 2 propulsion system.

With our Nova Pathfinder launch vehicle well under way, it’s time to share more about Nova Block 2, the larger configuration our team has been developing in parallel. Get the details in our blog post, “Scaling Nova”: https://t.co/Ok2ZptMUy4

— Stoke Space (@stoke_space) September 10, 2026

The first flight of this variant is currently planned for 2029. The proposed second pad is intended to support high-cadence operations for both vehicles once Block 2 enters service.

The announcement follows Stoke’s recent $1 billion Series E funding round , also announced in September 2026.

The company has positioned Block 2 to meet projected demand for constellation deployment and replenishment as Pathfinder establishes initial flight experience from the historic complex.

The Right of Entry is the first formal step toward opening additional Eastern Range property for fully and rapidly reusable operations.

The announcement did not give a construction timetable.

For now, Stoke’s near-term focus remains completing Nova Pathfinder and preparing SLC-14 to receive the inbound flight hardware.

Заголовок: Long March 9 Approved for Development, Sets 2030 as Debut Target
Полный текст:
China’s long-pursued giant launch vehicle can now proceed towards its first launch.

A model of the Long March 9 launch vehicle (center, grey and white) on display during China’s 2024 Space Day exhibition. | Image: China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation

For the better part of a decade, experts at the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology have been studying and trialing various designs for the gigantic Long March 9 launch vehicle. In recent years, they have settled on a single core design with a handful of variants.

Earlier this month, staff involved in developing the project gave a presentation at Northwestern Polytechnical University (西北工业大学) 1 where they provided the usual hardware trial status update on the vehicle. However, they also revealed that the Long March 9 received official approval from the Central Government sometime in October, something rumored in the past few weeks, to pursue proper development.

Specifically, just two variants have been approved and received a designation. The ‘Long March 9’ will be a three-stage launch vehicle with first-stage reusability able to send 50,000 kilograms on a translunar trajectory, while being focused beyond low Earth orbit. Meanwhile, the two-stage ‘Long March 9B’ will be fully reusable to primarily serve low Earth orbit, able to bring no more than 150,000 kilograms of cargo into space. 2

The presentation provided targeted debut years as well, with the ‘Long March 9’ aiming for 2030 and the ‘Long March 9B’ looking towards 2032. The latter’s target has moved several years closer to the present compared to official slides shown internationally in 2024.

Both variants of the launch vehicle’s reusable first-stages will be powered by thirty YF-215 liquid methane and liquid oxygen-burning full-flow staged-combustion engines, generating 200 tons of thrust each to produce 6,000 tons of thrust cumulatively. The expendable second-stage is to be propelled by another five YF-215’s to have 1,000 tons of thrust, while the third-stage will be fuelled with liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen with four YF-79 engines producing 100 tons of thrust. Details on what engines will power the reusable second-stage were not mentioned.

Its propellant tanks are set to be made of stainless steel and 10.6 meters in diameter, while the first-stage engine section protrudes to 12 meters wide, with the ‘Long March 9’ standing over 110 meters tall. About 40 meters of that height may come from its fairing, which could be as wide as 15 meters. Dimensions for the ‘Long March 9B’s reusable second-stage are yet to be provided.

Since trade shows in 2024 , it is known that the reusable first-stages not have landing legs and will be caught by moving rails, in a manner similar to the Long March 10B , positioned on dedicated drone ships at sea. The ‘Long March 9B’s second-stage is expected to have legs that unfurl from its engine sections to enable soft touchdowns on dedicated landing pads.

Once flying, both of the launch vehicle variants are expected to build space-based solar power stations , gigawatt-scale orbital computing facilities , launch large lunar landers , support a crewed Moon research station, and enable eventual crewed missions to Mars through the 2030s and 2040s.

Of course, before those efforts can be supported, the launch vehicle has to complete development. Hardware production trials and testing have been quietly taking place this decade, mostly behind closed doors. The engines powering it have been going through the same process, with the YF-215 continuing to work towards flight-like tests .

The most visible progress towards a first launch has been taking place just outside of the Wenchang launch sites, with ‘Phase One’ of the Long March 9 ‘Joint Workshop Rocket Base Project’ under construction. Groundbreaking began in April after a massive amount of land clearing , allowing it to start to rise into the skyline in recent weeks . That site is set to be completed in May 2028 to produce the launch vehicle.

Заголовок: Earth's churning mantle may have created the Great Unconformity
Полный текст:
Explaining the Great Unconformity, where Cambrian deposits sit on top of older rocks.

In the Grand Canyon, there is a line in the rock where time seems to have gone missing. Ancient crystalline rocks mark its bottom, while sandstones laid down as life started to diversify during the Cambrian explosion mark the top. “It’s called the Great Unconformity, and it’s a gap in the geologic record,” says Nicolas Flament, a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, Australia. "This gap can be anywhere between 200 million years, which is not that impressive, to more than a billion years.”

In a recent Nature study, Flament and his colleague Santosh Dhungana argue that this gap was carved with help from deep within the planet. According to their models, slow currents of hot rock in Earth's mantle pushed entire continents up for hundreds of millions of years, letting glaciers grind them down and then let them sink, allowing fresh sediments to bury the scar. The largest hole in the rock record might be a fingerprint of processes happening deep in the planet's interior.

Ice and sea

The oldest sediments resting on the Great Unconformity in North America are between 635 and 482 million years old. Geologists have traced it across most of North America and parts of northern Europe and northern China. “Something seems to have happened, in particular in North America,” Flament says.
